WHAT THIS BOOK IS

This is a plain-language guide to how a mind is grown.

Its subject is the neuroscience of developmental psychology, which the field itself calls developmental cognitive neuroscience: the study of how the brain is built, from the embryo onward, and of how perception, attention, memory, language, emotion, and the social self come online as it is built.

The book is written for two readers at once, and it will be published for both.

The layperson, learner, student, and beginner is the first reader: the book assumes no prior knowledge, explains every idea from the ground up, spells out every abbreviation the first time it appears, and defines every technical term in everyday words before using it.

The scientist is the second reader: the book names its studies with their researchers and years, states real timings wherever the literature supports them, and treats every live dispute as a dispute rather than pretending to a settled answer.

The organising principle is the one its outline states: the mind is not installed but grown, and the growing is lawful.


HOW THE BOOK IS BUILT

The book has fifteen parts, numbered in words from ONE to FIFTEEN.

Inside the parts are sixty-eight chapters, numbered straight through from 1 to 68, each carrying the tag its outline gave it: CORE for the capacities, timetables, and mechanisms; APPARATUS for the methods and frameworks; CONTEXT for the history, the clinic, and the applications.

Inside the chapters are sections, such as 12.3, and inside the sections are sub-sections, such as 12.3.4, which is where the detailed explaining happens.

The first half of the book is the machinery of development: what builds the brain, how the building is measured, what makes the built circuits plastic, and how genes, the womb, and early experience shape the outcome.

The second half is the catalogue of what develops: the senses, movement, language, the thinking faculties, the social and emotional mind, adolescence, the ways development goes differently, the classic theories weighed against the neural evidence, the whole arc of the lifespan, and the uses and ethics of the knowledge.

A gathered calendar near the end, Chapter 63, lays the whole developmental timetable out in one place, and closes by naming the timings the book refuses to state, because in this corpus a refusal is information and an invented number is the named worst failure.


A NOTE ON HOW IT IS WRITTEN

The book follows a house style meant to make reading easy.

Every sentence sits on its own line, with a blank line after it, so the eye can rest between thoughts.

There are no special typesetting symbols, only plain words.

Every abbreviation is spelled out in full the first time it appears, with the short form in parentheses right after it.

Every technical term is explained in everyday language the first time it is used.


A NOTE ON HONESTY, WHICH THIS SUBJECT DEMANDS TWICE OVER

Developmental science is famous for findings that entered the culture before they were checked, and this book carries the corrections on its face.

The brain does not finish maturing at twenty-five; that number is an artefact of studies that stopped scanning in the mid-twenties.

The claim that attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is a simple delay in cortical maturation is taught here as contested, with the 2007 finding and the 2026 reanalysis side by side.

The rodent science of reopening critical periods is robust, and its human translation record is close to zero, and the book says so.

The famous infant findings that failed large replications, from neonatal imitation to implicit false belief to the helper-hinderer preference, are taught with their replication records attached.

And because this subject touches children who are harmed, deprived, disabled, or ill, the book keeps a plain and respectful register throughout: its findings are about populations, never forecasts about any individual child, and it is a science book, not a clinical manual.


WHAT THIS BOOK HANDS THE CORPUS

This manuscript is the sibling, for the growing mind, of the corpus's treatment of the adult steady state, and it is written to mesh with the documents this directory already holds.

THE_ONTOGENETIC_AXIS keeps the framework decision about where development lives in the fifteen-layer architecture; this book informs that decision and does not take it.

The LAYER_06_09_DEVELOPMENT_AND_DISEASE_COMPANION keeps the per-cell and per-region developmental entries; this book is the narrative those entries plug into.

And for the konnectome build itself, the closing chapter states what a long, protected, staged childhood buys a mind, and what a builder should take from that.


HOW TO READ IT

You may read straight through, or open any chapter on its own.

Take your time.

Nothing here needs to be rushed, and the ideas reward slow reading.

The journey runs from a single fertilised cell to a person who remembers, speaks, plans, and cares, and every step of it is meant to be walkable by a beginner.

================================================================================

PART ONE. FOUNDATIONS: THE FIELD, ITS HISTORY, AND ITS FRAMEWORKS

================================================================================

CHAPTER 1. THE OBJECT OF STUDY: WHAT DEVELOPS, AND WHAT WOULD COUNT AS AN EXPLANATION (CORE)

This first chapter asks the simplest and hardest question in the whole book: what exactly are we trying to explain when we study the developing mind?

A newborn baby cannot speak, cannot reach for a toy, and cannot remember your name, yet three years later that same child does all of these things easily.

Something changed, and the change happened in the brain as well as in behaviour.

This chapter lays out what the field takes as its target, the three classic questions it inherited from psychology, and the standards a finished science of brain development would have to meet.

If you understand this chapter, every later chapter will read as an attempt to fill in one piece of the picture drawn here.


1.1 The explanatory target

This section defines the job of the field: connecting the growing brain to the growing mind, without cheating in either direction.

A story about the brain that never touches behaviour explains nothing about children, and a story about behaviour that never touches the brain leaves out the machinery.


1.1.1 Relating change in neural substrate to change in mind and behaviour, from the embryo through adolescence and beyond

The central task of developmental cognitive neuroscience is to line up two moving targets: the physical brain, which is being built and rebuilt, and the mind, which is gaining abilities.

The word substrate here just means the physical stuff that does the work, in this case neurons, which are the brain's signalling cells, and the connections between them.

A worked example makes the task concrete.

Between roughly seven and twelve months of age, babies stop making a famous mistake called the A-not-B error, in which a baby who has watched a toy being hidden at a new location still reaches to the old hiding place.

Adele Diamond and Patricia Goldman-Rakic showed in 1989 that monkeys with damage to a front region of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex made exactly the same error at the same short delays as human infants of seven and a half to nine months, while intact monkeys and twelve month old infants succeeded.

The prefrontal cortex is the front portion of the brain's outer sheet, heavily involved in holding goals in mind and resisting habits.

That study is a model of the whole enterprise, because a change in behaviour with age was tied to the ripening of a named brain circuit, and the link was tested rather than assumed.

The target runs from the embryo, where the brain is first assembled, through infancy, childhood, and adolescence, and onward, because brain change does not stop at any birthday.

One correction is worth stating at the outset: the popular claim that the brain finishes maturing at age twenty-five is not a finding but an artefact, produced because many studies simply stopped recruiting participants in their mid twenties, so their curves could not show change beyond the oldest people scanned.

Measures such as myelination, which is the wrapping of nerve fibres in a fatty insulating sheath that speeds signalling, continue changing into the third decade and beyond, with no single cliff edge at twenty-five.


1.1.2 Development as construction, not unfolding: why the blueprint metaphor fails

It is tempting to imagine that the genes contain a blueprint of the finished brain, and that development is just the printing out of that plan.

The metaphor fails on simple arithmetic and on simple biology.

The human genome contains roughly twenty thousand protein-coding genes, while the adult brain contains on the order of eighty-six billion neurons and something like a hundred trillion connections, so the genome cannot possibly specify each connection the way a blueprint specifies each beam.

Instead, the genes specify processes: rules for cell division, chemical gradients that cells read like signposts, and learning rules that let activity itself select which connections survive.

Development is therefore better described as construction, in which each stage builds on the products of the last, and in which the environment is a construction material rather than an outside disturbance.

A cake is a better metaphor than a blueprint: the recipe constrains the outcome, but you cannot point to the part of the recipe that corresponds to a particular crumb.

This constructionist view was argued at book length in Rethinking Innateness, by Jeffrey Elman, Elizabeth Bates, Mark Johnson, Annette Karmiloff-Smith, Domenico Parisi, and Kim Plunkett in 1996, and it frames everything in this outline.


1.1.3 Typical and atypical development as mutually informative, and the warning that atypical is not merely delayed

The field studies both typical development, meaning the common course, and atypical development, meaning courses that differ, as in autism, developmental language disorders, or genetic syndromes.

Each illuminates the other: knowing the typical timetable tells you when an atypical path diverged, and studying atypical paths reveals which parts of the system can compensate and which cannot.

But there is a standing warning, pressed hardest by Annette Karmiloff-Smith in the 1990s: an atypically developing brain is not a typical brain running late, and it is not a typical brain with one part removed.

Because every part of a developing system interacts with every other part over years, an early difference in one process can ripple into a differently organised whole.

So the field resists describing conditions as pure delays, and resists mapping childhood conditions onto the pattern of deficits seen when an adult brain loses a region to injury.

This warning returns in force in the discussion of neuroconstructivism in Chapter 3.


1.1.4 The levels the field must cross: gene, cell, circuit, system, behaviour, environment

An explanation in this field must travel across at least six levels of description.

At the level of the gene, sequences of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecule that carries inherited instructions, are switched on and off at particular times and places.

At the level of the cell, neurons are born, migrate to their positions, and grow their input branches, called dendrites, and their output cables, called axons.

At the level of the circuit, small groups of connected neurons begin to compute, joined at junctions called synapses, which are the tiny gaps where one neuron passes chemical signals to the next.

At the level of the system, whole networks of brain regions coordinate, as when visual areas and memory areas cooperate in recognising a face.

At the level of behaviour, the child does something measurable, such as looking longer at a surprising event.

And at the level of the environment, caregivers, language, nutrition, and culture feed back into all the levels below.

No single method sees all six levels, which is why this outline devotes an entire part to the toolkit, and why claims that skip levels, for example jumping straight from a gene to a school grade, deserve suspicion.


1.2 The three classic questions

Developmental psychology arrived at the neuroscience era carrying three old questions, and this section restates each of them in the form the brain sciences can actually address.


1.2.1 Nature and nurture, restated as the interaction question

The oldest question in the field asks whether abilities come from nature, meaning inheritance, or nurture, meaning experience.

Stated that way, the question is unanswerable and, most working scientists now agree, badly posed.

Every trait of every child requires both genes and environment, in the same way that the area of a rectangle requires both length and width, so asking which one matters more is asking the wrong thing.

The productive restatement asks how they interact: which genetic differences change how a child responds to a given environment, and which environments change how genes are expressed.

Gene expression means the process by which a gene's instructions are actually read out and used, and it is regulated moment to moment by the cell's circumstances, including circumstances shaped by experience.

The developmental psychobiologist Gilbert Gottlieb gave this interactive picture its clearest formulation, called probabilistic epigenesis, which Chapter 3 treats in full.

The famous rearing experiments of the 1960s and 1970s, in which Torsten Wiesel and David Hubel showed that closing one eye of a kitten during a specific early window permanently rewired its visual cortex, proved that experience does not merely fill a finished brain but participates in building it.


1.2.2 Continuity and discontinuity: stages against gradual change

The second classic question asks whether development proceeds smoothly, like a tree growing taller, or in qualitative jumps, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

Jean Piaget, the Swiss psychologist whose work dominated the twentieth century, described development as a staircase of four broad stages, each a qualitatively different way of thinking.

Later research complicated the staircase: abilities that Piaget placed late, such as some understanding of objects and number, show early precursors when tested with sensitive infant methods, and abilities within a supposed stage often develop at different speeds.

The neuroscience translation of the question asks whether brain development itself shows discontinuities, such as the rapid overproduction and later pruning of synapses, or growth spurts in particular measures, and whether such brain discontinuities line up with behavioural ones.

The honest current answer is mixed: most measured brain trajectories are curves rather than steps, but some transitions in behaviour, such as the emergence of explicit false-belief understanding near age four, remain strikingly step-like on standard tests.

Dynamic systems theorists such as Esther Thelen and Linda Smith argued in 1994 that apparent stages can emerge from continuous underlying change, the way water changes continuously in temperature and then suddenly boils.


1.2.3 Universality and variability across children and cultures

The third classic question asks which features of development are universal, appearing in every child in every culture, and which vary.

Some timetables look strongly universal: babbling, first words near the first birthday, and walking near it too, appear across cultures within broad windows.

Yet even motor milestones vary with caregiving practice, as shown by studies of cultures that deliberately exercise infants' stepping, where independent walking arrives earlier by weeks to months.

The neuroscience version of the question has a sharp methodological edge: the overwhelming majority of brain imaging studies of children have been conducted in a narrow set of wealthy countries, so the field's picture of the universal child is drawn from an unrepresentative sample.

Large recent efforts, including birth cohorts on several continents, are beginning to test which brain growth curves generalise, and the lifespan brain charts assembled by Richard Bethlehem, Jakob Seidlitz, and colleagues in Nature in 2022, from more than one hundred thousand scans, are an explicit attempt to build reference curves the way paediatricians use height and weight charts.

Until coverage improves, claims of universality should be read as claims about the populations actually studied.


1.3 What a completed developmental neuroscience would deliver

This section states three criteria by which the field can measure its own maturity, so that the reader can judge, chapter by chapter, how far the science has come.


1.3.1 The timetable criterion: every capacity assigned an onset, a trajectory, and a mechanism

The first criterion says the field is finished with a capacity only when it can state when the capacity begins, how it changes over time, and what brain mechanism carries it.

For a few capacities the field is close.

Face perception, for example, has a described onset in newborn orienting preferences, a described trajectory through a narrowing of expertise between six and twelve months, and candidate mechanisms in specific cortical regions.

For many capacities, the field has a behavioural timetable but only a sketch of mechanism, and for some it has neither.

A timetable without a mechanism is a description, and a mechanism without a timetable is not yet developmental science.


1.3.2 The perturbation criterion: outcomes predicted from early measures and altered by timed intervention

The second criterion is practical: a mature science should predict later outcomes from early measurements, and should be able to change outcomes by intervening at the right time.

Prediction is advancing slowly, because early brain measures typically explain only small fractions of the variation in later abilities, a sobering point driven home by Scott Marek, Brenden Tervo-Clemmens, and colleagues in Nature in 2022, who showed that studies linking brain measures to behavioural differences across individuals often need thousands of participants to give reliable answers.

Timed intervention has one landmark demonstration: the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, led by Charles Nelson, Nathan Fox, and Charles Zeanah, randomly assigned institutionalised Romanian children to high quality foster care and found that children placed earlier, particularly before about age two, showed better recovery on several cognitive and brain measures than children placed later.

That study, reported at length in the 2014 book Romania's Abandoned Children, is the field's clearest proof that timing itself can be causal.

But single demonstrations are not a technology, and the criterion remains mostly unmet.


1.3.3 The individual criterion: development explained for a child, not only for the average

The third criterion is the hardest.

Nearly all developmental neuroscience describes the average child, meaning the curve drawn through many children's data, yet no actual child is the average.

Two children can reach the same milestone by different routes, and the same early measurement can mean different things in different children.

A completed science would explain and predict the development of an individual child, with stated uncertainty, the way a good weather model forecasts a particular city rather than the average of all cities.

The growth chart approach of Bethlehem and Seidlitz in 2022 is a first step, because reference curves at least let an individual be located against the population.

The reader should carry this criterion through the whole book as a standing test: whenever a finding is reported for children on average, ask how much it says about any one child, and notice how rarely the answer is known.


CHAPTER 2. A HISTORY OF THE SCIENCE OF THE DEVELOPING MIND (CONTEXT)

This chapter tells the story of how a science of the developing brain and mind came to exist.

Knowing the history matters because the field's present habits, both its strengths and its blind spots, were formed by particular people solving particular problems.

The story runs from nineteenth century baby diaries and embryology, through the founding experiments of the 1980s and 1990s, to today's era of giant collaborative studies and hard questions about reproducibility.


2.1 The precursors

Before there was a named field, there were three traditions that would eventually feed it: biologists watching embryos behave, physicians timetabling infant movement, and a Swiss psychologist building a theory of knowledge out of children's answers.


2.1.1 Embryology and developmental psychobiology: Preyer, Coghill, Kuo, Schneirla, Gottlieb

The physiologist Wilhelm Preyer published The Mind of the Child in 1882, a diary-based study of his own son that is often counted as the founding document of scientific child psychology, and he also studied movement in bird embryos, uniting mind and embryo in one career.

George Coghill, working in the 1920s and publishing Anatomy and the Problem of Behaviour in 1929, traced how the salamander embryo's first movements emerge from the growth of specific nerve connections, an early proof that behaviour could be read off developing anatomy.

Zing-Yang Kuo watched chick embryos through windows cut in the eggshell in the 1930s and argued that supposedly instinctive behaviours, such as pecking, were shaped by the embryo's own prenatal experience, including the passive head movements produced by its beating heart.

Theodore Schneirla, studying army ants and mammals at mid century, insisted that development must be explained without appeals to instinct as an unexplained cause, and trained a generation in that discipline.

His student Gilbert Gottlieb showed experimentally that ducklings' famous attraction to their mother's call depends on the embryo hearing its own vocalisations before hatching, and from such results he built the framework of probabilistic epigenesis that Chapter 3 describes.

This lineage, called developmental psychobiology, supplied the field's core conviction: that nothing in behaviour is pre-formed, and that even the most instinctive-looking ability has a developmental construction story.


2.1.2 The maturationists: Gesell and McGraw and the motor milestone tables

Arnold Gesell, at Yale from the 1910s to the 1940s, filmed and catalogued thousands of infants to produce the first detailed normative timetables of development, the ancestors of the milestone checklists still used in paediatric clinics.

Gesell held that development unfolds primarily by maturation, meaning an internally timed ripening of the nervous system, with experience playing a supporting role.

His co-twin control studies, in which one identical twin was trained on a skill such as stair climbing while the other was not, found that the untrained twin caught up quickly, which he read as evidence that maturation, not practice, sets the pace.

Myrtle McGraw ran the era's most famous case study in the 1930s, training one twin, Johnny, intensively in motor skills while his brother Jimmy received ordinary care, and her results were more nuanced than Gesell's: some skills resisted training, but others, such as swimming movements and roller skating, were dramatically advanced by it.

McGraw herself came to reject the simple maturation story and to describe development as an interweaving of nervous system growth and experience.

The maturationists bequeathed to the field its calendars and its norms, and also its longest-running temptation: the habit of explaining a new ability by saying a brain area matured, without independent evidence of that maturation.


2.1.3 Piaget's genetic epistemology as a behavioural science awaiting a brain

Jean Piaget, working in Geneva from the 1920s until his death in 1980, called his project genetic epistemology, meaning the study of how knowledge itself grows, and he pursued it by setting children ingenious problems and taking their errors seriously.

He described infants building knowledge through action in a sensorimotor period from birth to about age two, then passing through preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational stages across childhood and adolescence.

His observations, such as the A-not-B error described in Chapter 1 and young children's failures on conservation tasks, in which a child denies that pouring water into a taller glass leaves the amount unchanged, are among the most replicated in psychology.

Piaget wrote almost nothing about the brain, but his theory was mechanistic in spirit, describing knowledge structures that assimilate new experience and accommodate to it.

For that reason he is best described as a behavioural science awaiting a brain: he supplied precise, testable descriptions of what changes, and left to later generations the question of what neural machinery does the changing.

The founding studies of the new field, described next, took Piagetian tasks as their starting material.


2.2 The founding of the field

In the space of about a decade, from the mid 1980s to the late 1990s, three developments turned scattered precursors into a named discipline: a brain explanation of a Piagetian error, a brain-based theory of the newborn's interest in faces, and a textbook that gave the enterprise its name.


2.2.1 Diamond and Goldman-Rakic linking the infant A-not-B error to prefrontal cortex

Adele Diamond, trained as a developmental psychologist, joined forces with Patricia Goldman-Rakic, the neuroscientist who had mapped the monkey prefrontal cortex, to ask whether Piaget's A-not-B error had a locatable brain cause.

Their 1989 study compared human infants, infant monkeys, and adult monkeys with surgical removal of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on the same hiding task.

Lesioned monkeys reproduced the infant error in detail, failing at delays of just two to five seconds, while intact adult monkeys and human infants of about twelve months succeeded.

Diamond's parallel work showed human infants improving on the task week by week between seven and a half and twelve months, exactly as prefrontal circuits are known to be maturing.

The result has been called one of the strongest brain-behaviour links in cognitive neuroscience, and it served as the field's proof of concept: a classic behavioural milestone had been explained, at least in part, by the state of a named circuit.


2.2.2 Johnson and Morton on newborn face preferences and the two-process account

At roughly the same time in London, Mark Johnson and John Morton tackled a puzzle at the other end of infancy: newborns less than an hour old will turn their eyes and head further to follow a moving face-like pattern than a scrambled one.

In their 1991 book and a paper in Psychological Review the same year, they proposed a two-process theory.

The first process, which they named CONSPEC, is a crude orienting bias, likely carried by evolutionarily old structures beneath the cortex, that draws the newborn's gaze toward anything with the rough arrangement of two eyes above a mouth.

The second process, named CONLERN, is a cortical learning system that, beginning to dominate around two months of age, gradually becomes expert in the particular faces the baby actually sees.

The elegance of the account is that a tiny inherited bias guarantees the developing cortex a rich diet of face experience, so that face expertise is neither fully innate nor left to chance.

The theory drew explicitly on parallel two-process findings in newly hatched chicks, honouring the field's psychobiological ancestry, and it remains the standard worked example of how minimal innate equipment can seed later specialisation.


2.2.3 Johnson's textbook of 1997 naming developmental cognitive neuroscience, and the Birkbeck Centre for Brain and Cognitive Development

A field becomes real when it gets a name, a textbook, and an address.

Mark Johnson supplied all three: his textbook Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience appeared in 1997, giving the discipline its name, and it has run through four editions, with Michelle de Haan joining as co-author.

In 1998 Johnson co-founded the Centre for Brain and Cognitive Development at Birkbeck, University of London, which became known informally as the Babylab, and which pioneered the routine use of infant-friendly brain measures.

Chief among these were electroencephalography (EEG), which records the brain's electrical rhythms from sensors resting on the scalp, and later near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), which uses harmless light shone through the skull to track blood oxygen changes in the cortex of an awake baby.

The Centre trained a large fraction of the field's current leaders, and its model, a dedicated laboratory where parents bring infants for short, game-like brain studies, has been copied worldwide.


2.3 Institutionalisation and expansion

Once founded, the field acquired the ordinary machinery of a science, journals, a society, and funding streams, and then expanded its age range upward into adolescence and its sample sizes upward into the tens of thousands.


2.3.1 The journals and the society: Developmental Science, Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience, the Flux Society

The journal Developmental Science was launched in 1998, with an explicit openness to brain-based studies of children that older child psychology journals lacked.

The field gained a journal bearing its own name in 2011, when Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience began publication as an open access journal.

In 2013 researchers founded the Flux Society, formally the Flux Society for Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience, which holds an annual congress and functions as the field's professional home.

These institutions matter for more than bookkeeping: shared venues let methods be standardised, let critiques circulate quickly, and let students identify themselves as members of a field rather than as odd hybrids of two others.


2.3.2 The adolescent turn: Casey, Giedd, Steinberg and Blakemore

Through the 1990s the field was mostly about infants, but a second wave turned its instruments on teenagers.

Jay Giedd and colleagues at the United States National Institute of Mental Health published landmark longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies, notably in 1999, showing that the brain's grey matter, the tissue rich in neuron cell bodies, rises to a peak around puberty and then thins across adolescence, while white matter, the tissue of insulated connecting fibres, keeps increasing.

MRI is a scanning technique that uses strong magnets and radio waves to photograph the living brain in detail without any radiation.

BJ Casey developed the influential account that adolescent risk taking reflects a timing gap, with emotional and reward circuitry maturing earlier than the prefrontal control circuitry that regulates it.

Laurence Steinberg formalised a similar dual-systems model from the psychological side in 2008, and Sarah-Jayne Blakemore established the social brain in adolescence as a research programme, showing that regions used in thinking about other people are still changing structurally and functionally through the teenage years.

This adolescent turn changed public policy conversations about juvenile justice and education, and its central framework is examined critically in Part Twelve.


2.3.3 The big-cohort era and the reproducibility reckoning

The field's third era is defined by scale.

The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study enrolled nearly twelve thousand nine and ten year olds across the United States beginning in 2015, scanning and testing them repeatedly for a decade.

The Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) in the United Kingdom scanned fetuses and newborns, the Baby Connectome Project covered the first five years, the HEALthy Brain and Child Development (HBCD) Study began following thousands of families from pregnancy, and the Generation R Study in Rotterdam has followed a birth cohort since 2002.

The reckoning arrived with the scale.

In 2022 Scott Marek, Brenden Tervo-Clemmens, and colleagues showed in Nature that typical brain-wide association studies, which look for correlations between brain measures and behavioural differences across individuals, had been run for years at sample sizes far too small to be reliable, and that thousands of participants are needed for stable results of that kind.

The same year, Bethlehem, Seidlitz, and colleagues assembled more than one hundred thousand MRI scans spanning the human lifespan into reference growth charts for the brain, published in Nature in 2022.

The lesson of this era is double: some questions the field asked for decades can only be answered at consortium scale, and some celebrated small-sample findings, in this field as across psychology and neuroimaging, are now being re-examined, a theme this outline returns to wherever a specific finding has been contested.


CHAPTER 3. THE THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS (APPARATUS)

This chapter lays out the big ideas the field thinks with.

A framework is not a finding but a way of organising findings, a set of expectations about what kind of explanation to look for.

The frameworks presented here disagree with one another in instructive ways, and most working scientists borrow from several at once.

Reading this chapter equips you to notice, in every later chapter, which framework a given study quietly assumes.


3.1 Johnson's three viewpoints on functional brain development

Mark Johnson, in an influential 2001 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience and in later work, distinguished three viewpoints on how brain development relates to the emergence of abilities.

They are best understood as three answers to one question: when a child becomes able to do something new, what changed in the brain?


3.1.1 The maturational viewpoint: abilities come on line as circuits ripen

The maturational viewpoint answers that a specific brain region ripened, on an internal timetable, and the ability it supports switched on.

On this view the mapping between regions and functions is fixed in advance, and development is the sequential activation of a pre-specified layout.

The Diamond and Goldman-Rakic story of Chapter 2 is naturally told in this idiom: the prefrontal cortex matures, and the infant stops making the A-not-B error.

The viewpoint has genuine successes, because some abilities really do track the anatomical readiness of particular circuits.

Its weakness is that it explains the timetable by pointing at another timetable, leaving unexplained why the region matured when it did, and it struggles with evidence that regions can take on unexpected functions after early injury, which a fixed layout should not allow.


3.1.2 Interactive specialization: regions become specialised through activity-dependent competition, and localisation is an outcome rather than a starting point

Interactive specialization, the framework Johnson himself championed, answers instead that abilities emerge as regions specialise through use.

On this view, cortical regions begin with broad, overlapping response properties, and through activity-dependent competition, meaning a process in which the connections that are used most successfully are strengthened while others are edged out, each region narrows to the functions it serves in the adult.

The crucial reversal is that localisation of function, the fact that particular abilities live in particular places in the adult brain, is treated as an outcome of development rather than its starting point.

The framework predicts that during development, a given task should activate more widespread and less specialised brain territory than in adults, and that specialisation of any one region depends on its interactions with the rest of the network.

Infant brain imaging has repeatedly found the predicted pattern of broad early activation that narrows and sharpens with age, for example in responses to faces and to speech.

The framework also predicts, correctly, that early brain injury often produces reorganisation rather than the fixed deficits an adult lesion would cause.


3.1.3 The skill-learning viewpoint: the infant brain recruited as the adult expert's brain is

The third viewpoint answers that nothing specifically developmental changed at all: the infant is simply a novice, and acquiring any ability recruits the same brain machinery that adults use when they acquire an expert skill.

The analogy is to adults learning to recognise birds or chess positions, where practice shifts processing into regions specialised for expert perception.

On this view, some brain changes seen across childhood are not maturation but the ordinary signature of practice, compressed into the period of life when everything is being practised at once.

The viewpoint usefully warns against attributing to age what belongs to experience, and it draws support from findings that adult brains learning new skills show region changes resembling those seen in children.

Its limit is that infants are not merely inexperienced adults, because their brains differ in connectivity, chemistry, and plasticity, so the equation of infant learning with adult expertise can only be partial.


3.2 Probabilistic epigenesis

This section presents the framework the field inherited from developmental psychobiology, which replaces one-way genetic causation with two-way traffic among all the levels of a developing system.


3.2.1 Bidirectional traffic among genes, neural activity, behaviour, and environment

Gilbert Gottlieb named his framework probabilistic epigenesis, and drew it as a now famous diagram of four horizontal levels, genetic activity, neural activity, behaviour, and environment, with arrows running both upward and downward between every pair of neighbours.

Epigenesis is the old embryological word for development as the progressive emergence of form, and probabilistic signals that outcomes are made likely, not guaranteed, by the interactions.

The upward arrows are familiar: genes influence brains, brains influence behaviour, behaviour operates on the environment.

The downward arrows are the framework's point: environments alter behaviour, behaviour alters neural activity, and neural activity alters which genes are expressed.

Gottlieb's own duckling experiments supplied the proof, since the embryo's own calls, an activity of the organism, were shown to shape the later functioning of its auditory preferences, a fact no one-way genetic story could accommodate.

Modern molecular biology has filled in the downward arrows in detail, showing, for example, that neural activity triggers immediate expression of specific genes within minutes, and the framework is now close to the field's default common sense.


3.2.2 Experience-expectant against experience-dependent plasticity

Plasticity means the brain's capacity to be changed by activity and experience.

William Greenough, James Black, and Christopher Wallace drew a distinction in a classic 1987 paper between two kinds.

Experience-expectant plasticity handles information that the species has always been able to count on, such as patterned light, the sounds of speech, and gravity.

For these, the brain overproduces synapses in advance and then lets the expected experience select which ones survive, a strategy that works because the experience is guaranteed for every member of the species.

Experience-expectant processes are tied to sensitive periods, meaning limited windows during which the relevant circuits are especially open to being shaped, which is why a cataract that blurs a human infant's vision in the first months can leave lasting deficits that the same cataract in an adult would not.

Experience-dependent plasticity handles information unique to the individual, such as the layout of your home, the words of your language's vocabulary, or how to ride a bicycle.

For these, the brain generates new synapses in response to the experience itself, a capacity that remains available across the whole of life, though its ease varies with age.

The distinction organises much of Parts Four and Five of this outline, and it explains in one stroke why some experiences must arrive on time while others can arrive whenever they arrive.


3.2.3 Canalisation and the epigenetic landscape

The geneticist Conrad Waddington, writing in the 1940s and 1950s, offered the field its most durable image: the epigenetic landscape.

Picture a ball rolling down a hillside grooved with branching valleys, where the ball is the developing organism and the valleys are the developmental paths available to it.

Canalisation names the depth of the valleys: a deeply canalised trait, such as having two eyes, is buffered against perturbation, because the ball would need an enormous shove to leave its valley, while a weakly canalised trait, such as adult body weight, is easily deflected by circumstance.

The image captures several truths at once: development is constrained but not determined, early in development small pushes can switch the ball between valleys while the same push later does nothing, and returning to a former path gets harder as the valleys deepen.

Waddington's term epigenetics has since been adopted by molecular biology for the chemical marks on DNA that regulate gene expression without changing the sequence, a related but narrower meaning that later chapters will keep distinct.

For developmental psychology, canalisation explains why most children reach the major milestones despite enormously varied environments, and why some early perturbations nonetheless leave lasting marks.


3.3 Neuroconstructivism

This section presents the framework, associated above all with Annette Karmiloff-Smith, that takes the construction metaphor of Chapter 1 to its logical conclusion for both typical and atypical development.


3.3.1 Modules as products of development rather than its starting equipment

Adult cognition looks modular, in the sense that particular abilities, such as recognising faces or parsing grammar, seem to run in dedicated, semi-independent brain systems, which cognitive scientists call modules.

Nativist theories took this adult modularity as the starting state, proposing that infants come equipped with the modules and merely fill them with content.

Karmiloff-Smith, in her 1992 book Beyond Modularity, argued the reverse: the infant starts with, at most, small biases of attention and processing, and modularity is the end product of development, arrived at through a gradual process she called modularization.

The argument dovetails exactly with interactive specialization, described above, which supplies the neural mechanism, activity-dependent competition, by which an initially general-purpose cortex could partition itself into specialists.

On this view, asking whether a module is innate is a category error, like asking whether a groove worn into a path by years of walking was there before the walking.


3.3.2 The critique of residual normality and of adult-lesion thinking about children

Neuroconstructivism's sharpest edge is methodological.

Adult neuropsychology learned about the mind from patients with strokes, reasoning that if a lesion removes ability X and spares ability Y, then X and Y run on separate machinery, with the spared ability assumed to be otherwise normal.

Karmiloff-Smith, most pointedly in a 1998 paper, argued that transferring this logic to developmental disorders is invalid, and she named the hidden assumption residual normality: the idea that in a child with a disorder, the unaffected abilities are just as they would be in a typical child.

Because a developing brain builds every ability in interaction with every other over years, an early low-level difference can subtly reshape even the abilities that test as normal, so the apparently intact parts of an atypical mind cannot be treated as controls.

The practical consequence is a demand for trajectories rather than snapshots: developmental disorders must be studied across age, tracing how a profile emerges, not photographed once in adulthood and read like a lesion chart.


3.3.3 Williams syndrome as the worked example

Williams syndrome is a rare genetic condition, occurring in roughly one in seven thousand five hundred to one in ten thousand births, caused by the deletion of a stretch of about twenty-five to twenty-seven genes on one copy of chromosome seven.

People with Williams syndrome typically show strong sociability and relatively fluent language alongside marked difficulty with spatial tasks such as drawing and assembling.

Early reports celebrated the syndrome as proof of innate modularity, reading it as language spared, space impaired, exactly as if separate modules had been separately hit.

Karmiloff-Smith's group showed the reading was wrong on both sides: the language of people with Williams syndrome, examined closely, develops along an atypical route with unusual reliance on auditory memory, and infants with the syndrome show differences in very general processes, such as how they scan faces and disengage attention, long before any module could exist.

The syndrome thus became the worked example of the whole framework: a genetic difference alters low-level biases, development compounds the alteration for years, and the adult profile of peaks and valleys is the outcome of that cascade, not a printout of which modules the genes built.

The condition is treated in its own right in the part of this outline on developmental differences, with the respect due to the people who live it rather than as a mere argument piece.


3.4 Nativism at the neural level

This section gives the opposing tradition its strongest form, because the field's live debates are not between caricatures but between sophisticated versions of built-in and constructed.


3.4.1 Core knowledge and what innate can mean neurally: architectural, chronotopic, and representational constraints

The core knowledge programme, led by Elizabeth Spelke and Renée Baillargeon among others, holds that infants possess early-emerging systems of expectation about a few domains, including objects and their persistence, approximate number, agents and their goals, and space.

The supporting evidence comes from looking-time experiments, which exploit the fact that infants look longer at events that violate their expectations, and some signatures, such as sensitivity to approximate number, appear within days of birth.

The question this poses for neuroscience is what the word innate could mean in brain terms, and the authors of Rethinking Innateness in 1996 offered a three-way answer that has become standard vocabulary.

Representational constraints would be actual knowledge wired in advance, specific connection patterns encoding specific content, which the authors argued is the strongest and least supported reading.

Architectural constraints are built-in properties of the processing machinery, such as the layered structure of cortex or the density of connections in a region, which bias what a region can easily learn without encoding any particular fact.

Chronotopic constraints are built-in properties of timing, meaning which circuits become plastic or mature in which order, so that what a region learns is biased by when it comes on line.

Restated in this vocabulary, the live question is not whether anything is innate, since architecture and timing clearly are, but whether any actual representational content is, and that question remains genuinely open, with looking-time findings themselves under replication scrutiny in some domains.


3.4.2 The two-process reconciliation in face processing

Face processing shows how the debate can end in synthesis rather than victory.

The nativist reading of newborn face preferences claimed an innate face module, while a strict constructivist reading struggled to explain why hour-old infants track faces at all.

The Johnson and Morton two-process theory of 1991, described in Chapter 2, reconciles the positions: the inherited part, the CONSPEC orienting bias, is minimal and probably subcortical, carrying no knowledge of faces beyond a crude preference for a top-heavy arrangement of blobs, while the knowledge is built by the cortical learning process, CONLERN, out of the experience the bias guarantees.

In the vocabulary just introduced, CONSPEC is an architectural and chronotopic constraint that makes face experience nearly inevitable, and the representational content is constructed.

Later evidence enriched the picture, showing that the newborn bias may reflect even more general preferences, for example for stimuli with more elements in the upper visual field, and that specialisation for faces sharpens across the first year as predicted by interactive specialization.

The reconciliation is the field's template for dissolving nature against nurture standoffs: locate the smallest bias that must be inherited, and show how development amplifies it into expertise.


3.5 The organising gradients

This closing section collects three large-scale ordering principles, each a gradient rather than a mechanism, that later chapters will use as maps.


3.5.1 The sensorimotor-to-association axis of cortical maturation

The cortex does not mature everywhere at once.

Regions serving basic sensation and movement, called sensorimotor cortex, mature earliest, while the association cortex, meaning the regions that integrate across senses and serve memory, language, and planning, matures latest, with prefrontal territories at the far end.

Nitin Gogtay, Jay Giedd, and colleagues visualised this in a well-known 2004 longitudinal mapping study, watching cortical grey matter mature in a wave from the back and centre of the brain toward the front across ages four to twenty-one.

Valerie Sydnor, Theodore Satterthwaite, and colleagues generalised the principle in 2021, arguing that a single sensorimotor-to-association axis organises not only maturation timing but also the spatial patterning of gene expression, connectivity, and plasticity across the cortex.

The gradient gives the field a one-line summary of two decades of imaging: development sweeps from the concrete to the abstract, and the regions most distinctive of human cognition are the last to settle.

It also carries the earlier warning about age twenty-five: the far end of the gradient matures late and gradually, with no sharp finish line.


3.5.2 Protomap against protocortex in cortical arealisation

Arealisation means the process by which the initially continuous cortical sheet becomes divided into distinct areas, such as visual, auditory, and motor cortex.

Two hypotheses framed the question for decades.

The protomap hypothesis, proposed by Pasko Rakic in 1988, holds that the map of future areas is specified early and intrinsically, in the layer of dividing progenitor cells, so that each newborn neuron inherits an areal address as it is generated.

The protocortex hypothesis, articulated by Dennis O'Leary in 1989, holds instead that the young cortical sheet is essentially uniform, a protocortex, and that areas are imposed from outside, chiefly by the incoming axons that relay each sense from a deep brain structure called the thalamus, the brain's central switching station for sensory information.

Decisive experiments around 2000 and 2001 showed that gradients of regulatory genes pattern the cortical sheet before any thalamic input arrives, and that shifting those gradients shifts the areal map, which established a strong protomap component.

Yet transplant and rewiring experiments had already shown that young cortex is remarkably re-specifiable by its inputs, so the settled view is a compromise: an intrinsic protomap drafts the areas, and thalamic input and activity refine, sharpen, and maintain them.

The draft-then-refine logic recurs at every scale of brain development, and Chapter 4 introduces the cellular machinery, the radial units, on which the protomap is written.


3.5.3 The dual-systems framing of adolescence, held for Part Twelve

The third organising gradient is temporal: different brain systems mature at different rates, and the dual-systems framework of Steinberg and the related imbalance model of Casey propose that adolescence is defined by the gap between an early-maturing set of reward and emotion circuits, deep in the brain, and the late-maturing prefrontal control systems at the end of the sensorimotor-to-association axis.

The framework predicts a mid-adolescent peak in sensation seeking and risk taking, and it has been enormously influential in science and in law.

It has also drawn serious criticism, on the grounds that real-world adolescent risk taking depends heavily on context and opportunity, that laboratory measures of the two systems do not always show the predicted imbalance within individuals, and that the framing can slide into treating teenagers as defective adults rather than as well adapted to their developmental stage.

This outline therefore only names the framework here, as one gradient among the organising ideas, and holds the full statement, the evidence, and the critique for Part Twelve, where adolescence is treated at length.



================================================================================

PART TWO. THE BIOLOGICAL TIMETABLE: BUILDING THE BRAIN

================================================================================

CHAPTER 4. THE EMBRYONIC BRAIN: INDUCTION, NEURULATION, AND PATTERNING (CORE)

This chapter goes back to the very beginning, to the first weeks after conception, when there is no brain at all and then, astonishingly quickly, the start of one.

The events described here happen so early that many are complete before a pregnancy is confirmed, which gives them practical as well as scientific importance.

The chapter follows three steps: how a sheet of ordinary embryonic cells is instructed to become nervous system, how that sheet rolls into a tube, and how the tube is given its addresses, front and back, top and bottom, so that every later structure forms in the right place.


4.1 From three layers to a nervous system

This section covers the founding events: the reorganisation of the embryo into three layers, the chemical conversation that designates one strip of the top layer as future brain and spinal cord, the rolling and sealing of the neural tube, and the remarkable population of wandering cells set free at its crest.


4.1.1 Gastrulation and neural induction in gestational week three

In the third week after conception the embryo, until then a simple disc of cells, performs gastrulation, a coordinated migration in which cells stream through a midline groove called the primitive streak and organise themselves into three layers.

The inner layer, the endoderm, will build the gut and lungs; the middle layer, the mesoderm, will build muscle, bone, and blood; and the outer layer, the ectoderm, will build the skin and the entire nervous system.

Which part of the ectoderm becomes nervous system is decided by a chemical conversation called neural induction.

The classic experiment was performed by Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold in 1924, who transplanted a small region of a newt embryo, now called the organizer, into another embryo and watched it summon a second complete nervous system from tissue that would otherwise have become skin.

The molecular explanation, worked out in the 1990s, is often called the default model: ectoderm cells will become neural tissue by default, but a family of proteins called bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), spread through the ectoderm, actively pushes them toward becoming skin.

The organizer works by secreting BMP-blocking proteins, with the memorable names noggin, chordin, and follistatin, and the shielded strip of ectoderm, freed from the skin signal, follows its default and becomes the neural plate, the founding tissue of the brain and spinal cord.

The default model is best established in frogs and fish, and work in chick and mammal embryos shows that additional signals, including fibroblast growth factors, cooperate in the decision, so the induction story in humans is understood as a combination rather than a single switch.


4.1.2 Primary neurulation: fusion beginning near day twenty-two, anterior closure near day twenty-five, posterior near day twenty-seven

Primary neurulation is the process by which the flat neural plate folds into a closed cylinder, the neural tube, whose walls will become the brain and spinal cord and whose hollow centre will become the fluid-filled ventricles.

During the fourth week the edges of the plate rise as neural folds, curl toward each other, and begin to fuse, with the first fusion occurring near the boundary of the future hindbrain and neck at about day twenty-two after conception.

Closure then proceeds like a zipper running in both directions, and evidence from human embryos suggests that fusion actually initiates at more than one site rather than from a single point.

The open end at the head, called the anterior or rostral neuropore, seals at about day twenty-four to twenty-five.

The open end at the tail, the posterior or caudal neuropore, seals at about day twenty-six to twenty-eight, and this outline states the range because published human timetables differ by a day or two.

The whole of primary neurulation is thus complete before the end of the fourth week after conception, which in the obstetric convention of counting from the last menstrual period is about the sixth week of pregnancy, a time when many people do not yet know they are pregnant.

The lowest end of the spinal cord forms afterwards by a separate process, secondary neurulation, in which a solid rod of cells hollows itself into a tube.


4.1.3 Neural tube defects and the folate story

When the neural tube fails to close, the result is a neural tube defect, and the location of the failure determines the condition.

Failure at the head end produces anencephaly, in which the major part of the brain and skull does not form and which is not survivable, while failure along the spine produces spina bifida, in which the spinal cord is exposed or malformed and which causes lifelong impairment whose severity depends on the level of the lesion.

Together these are among the most common serious birth malformations, affecting on the order of one pregnancy in a thousand in many populations, with wide variation across regions and diets.

The prevention story is one of the great triumphs of public health science.

Observational studies had long hinted that maternal nutrition mattered, and in 1991 the British Medical Research Council (MRC) Vitamin Study, a randomised double-blind trial in one thousand eight hundred and seventeen women who had previously had an affected pregnancy, showed that folic acid supplements before conception and in early pregnancy reduced the recurrence of neural tube defects by seventy-two percent.

Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate, a B vitamin required for the rapid DNA copying that closing a neural tube demands.

Because closure is finished by about day twenty-eight, supplements begun after pregnancy is recognised are usually too late, and this fact drove the decision by the United States in 1998, followed by more than ninety countries, to fortify staple grain foods with folic acid, a policy followed by measurable falls in the affected birth rate.

The residual defects that occur despite adequate folate are an active research area, involving genes of folate metabolism and of the cellular machinery of folding itself.


4.1.4 The neural crest and its migratory derivatives

As the neural folds fuse, a special population of cells detaches from their crest line, and these neural crest cells are one of the most remarkable inventions of vertebrate development.

Rather than staying in the tube, they transform into wanderers, migrating in streams throughout the embryo along stereotyped routes, and their descendants are astonishingly diverse.

They become the neurons and support cells of the peripheral nervous system, meaning the nerves and relay clusters outside the brain and spinal cord, including the sensory neurons of touch and pain and the autonomic neurons that regulate the heart, gut, and glands.

They become the enteric nervous system, the mesh of neurons in the gut wall sometimes called the second brain, as well as the pigment cells of the skin, the adrenaline-producing core of the adrenal gland, and, from the head streams, much of the skull, face, and jaw skeleton.

The lineage was mapped in exquisite detail by Nicole Le Douarin from the 1970s onward, using a natural cell-marking trick in which quail cells transplanted into chick embryos remain identifiable for life.

Because the crest touches so many organs, disturbances of its migration produce recognisable clusters of problems, called neurocristopathies, of which Hirschsprung disease, where crest cells fail to colonise the far end of the gut and the bowel cannot move its contents, is a classic example.

For developmental psychology the crest matters twice over: it builds the body's entire outreach nervous system, and its involvement in face and heart formation explains why some genetic syndromes pair facial features with neural and cardiac differences.


4.2 Patterning the axes

A closed tube is still only a tube.

This section describes how the tube acquires a plan, swelling into named compartments along its length and acquiring distinct fates around its circumference, all under the control of a small and deeply ancient set of signalling molecules.


4.2.1 The three primary vesicles of week four and the five secondary vesicles of week five

Almost as soon as the front of the tube seals, it begins to balloon.

By the end of week four the head end shows three swellings, the primary brain vesicles: the prosencephalon or forebrain, the mesencephalon or midbrain, and the rhombencephalon or hindbrain, with the rest of the tube continuing as spinal cord.

During week five, two of the three subdivide, yielding five secondary vesicles.

The forebrain splits into the telencephalon, which will become the cerebral hemispheres, including the cortex, the hippocampus, which is the seahorse-shaped structure essential for forming new memories, and the amygdala, an almond-shaped structure central to emotional learning, and the diencephalon, which will become the thalamus and the hypothalamus, the small structure that regulates hunger, temperature, and hormones.

The midbrain remains undivided and keeps the name mesencephalon.

The hindbrain splits into the metencephalon, which produces the pons and the cerebellum, the large movement-coordinating structure at the back of the head, and the myelencephalon, which becomes the medulla, the life-support region controlling breathing and heart rhythm.

This five-part plan, established in an embryo about the size of a grain of rice, is the permanent table of contents of the human brain: every adult structure is an elaboration of one of these vesicles, and the hollow of the tube persists as the connected ventricles inside them.


4.2.2 The anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral signals: sonic hedgehog, the Wnt and fibroblast growth factor families, the Hox genes

The vesicles and the fates within them are assigned by chemical coordinates, gradients of signalling proteins that cells read like a map reference.

Along the anterior-posterior axis, meaning head to tail, the early neural tissue defaults to a forebrain-like character, and signals including the Wnt family, retinoic acid, which is a derivative of vitamin A, and fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) act as posteriorising agents, pushing tissue toward midbrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord identities in proportion to exposure.

This is one reason vitamin A derivatives taken as medicines in pregnancy, such as isotretinoin, are potent causes of brain malformation, since they flood a system that uses the same molecule as a positional signal.

In the hindbrain, position along the axis is locked in by the Hox genes, an ancient set of genes arranged along the chromosome in the same order as the body regions they specify, which subdivide the hindbrain into segments called rhombomeres and which humans share, in recognisable form, with flies and worms.

Along the dorsal-ventral axis, meaning back to belly, the key ventral signal is a protein with the whimsical name sonic hedgehog (Shh), secreted first by the notochord, a stiffening rod beneath the tube, and then by the tube's own floor plate.

Cells translate the local concentration of sonic hedgehog into identity, so that in the spinal cord the most ventral cells, bathed in the most signal, become motor neurons, the cells that drive muscles, while successively more dorsal cells, receiving less, take on successive interneuron fates.

From the opposite side, the roof plate secretes BMP and Wnt proteins, creating a counter-gradient that specifies the dorsal fates, including the neurons that will receive sensory input.

The general lesson is that the embryo builds a brain the way surveyors lay out a city, by establishing coordinate grids of signal before any construction begins, and later chapters will show cortical areas, described in Chapter 3 as the protomap, being drafted by exactly this kind of gradient logic using FGF8 from the front of the head.


4.3 The cellular ground plan

The final section of this chapter descends from geography to workforce, introducing the cells that will actually manufacture the brain's neurons and the hypothesis that links their organisation to the shape and size of the human cortex.


4.3.1 Ventricular and subventricular zones and radial glia as the stem cells

The wall of the early neural tube is a single sheet of dividing cells surrounding the fluid-filled centre, and the layer touching the fluid is called the ventricular zone, the brain's original nursery.

Its cells are neuroepithelial cells, which soon transform into radial glia, cells with a compact body in the ventricular zone and a single enormously long fibre reaching all the way to the outer surface of the developing brain.

For a century radial glia were thought to be mere scaffolding, guide wires along which newborn neurons climb outward, a guidance role described classically by Pasko Rakic in the early 1970s.

The transforming discovery, made around 2000 and 2001 by the groups of Arnold Kriegstein, with Stephen Noctor's imaging of individual dividing cells, and of Magdalena Götz, was that the radial glia are themselves the neural stem cells: the same cell that guides migration is the mother cell that generates the neurons.

A radial glial cell can divide to copy itself, or divide to produce a neuron, or produce an intermediate progenitor cell, a transit-amplifying cell that moves slightly outward and divides again to yield pairs of neurons.

These intermediate progenitors accumulate in a second proliferative layer just outside the first, called the subventricular zone, which serves as an amplifier of neuron production.

Radial glia are thus triple-duty cells, stem cell, scaffold, and, at the end of development, the source of many of the brain's astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells, and this economy of roles is the foundation of everything in the next chapter on neurogenesis.


4.3.2 The radial unit hypothesis and the expansion of the primate subventricular zone

Pasko Rakic's radial unit hypothesis, stated in Science in 1988, ties the cellular workforce to the architecture of the finished cortex.

The hypothesis holds that each small founding group of ventricular zone progenitors, together with the radial glial fibres it sends up, defines a radial unit, and that the neurons born in one unit migrate along its fibres to stack up as one fine vertical column of cortex.

The cortex is therefore built as an array of such columns, and the hypothesis makes a clean prediction about evolution: divisions of the founder cells before neuron production begins add more units, expanding the cortical sheet in area, while divisions afterwards only deepen each column, which explains why the human cortex is a vastly wider sheet than a mouse's but only modestly thicker.

The protomap of Chapter 3 rides on this machinery, since positional identities imprinted on the founder cells are delivered by radial transport to the correct cortical addresses.

The specifically primate and human elaboration is the outer subventricular zone, a massively expanded second nursery lying outside the classical subventricular zone, first clearly described in monkeys and shown to be dominant in humans.

In 2010 David Hansen and colleagues in Kriegstein's laboratory demonstrated in Nature that this zone is populated by a special class of progenitors, now called outer radial glia, which keep an outward-reaching fibre but detach from the inner surface, and which perform a curious lunging movement of the cell body just before each division.

Outer radial glia can self-renew and generate neurons far from the ventricle, in effect multiplying the number of radial production lines, and their abundance in humans, alongside their scarcity in mice, is currently the leading cellular explanation for the evolutionary expansion and folding of the human cortex.

Genes that regulate these progenitors, including several found only in humans, are under intense study, because they sit at the join between our species' evolution and each child's development, and because their disturbance produces microcephaly, the condition of being born with a much smaller brain, showing that the ground plan described in this chapter is not an abstraction but a load-bearing wall.

CHAPTER 5. NEUROGENESIS AND MIGRATION (CORE)

This chapter tells the story of where the brain's nerve cells come from and how they get to their places.

A nerve cell, or neuron, is a cell specialised to carry electrical signals, and the human brain will eventually hold tens of billions of them.

Nearly all of those neurons are born before the baby is, in a burst of cell production during the middle of pregnancy, and each one must then travel from its birthplace to its final address.

The chapter matters because the journey is where things can go wrong: several serious brain malformations are, at bottom, failures of cells to travel correctly.

It also matters because the travel rules explain the brain's architecture: the layered structure of the cortex, the brain's folded outer sheet of grey matter, is a direct record of who travelled when.


5.1 Making the neurons

This section covers the production line itself: when neurons are made, which cells make them, and whether the making ever truly stops.


5.1.1 Peak cortical neurogenesis across roughly gestational weeks five to twenty-five

Neurogenesis simply means the birth of new neurons, and in the cerebral cortex it is concentrated in a surprisingly narrow window of prenatal life.

Gestational weeks are counted from the start of the mother's last menstrual period, so a full-term pregnancy runs about forty weeks.

Cortical neurogenesis begins around gestational week five, ramps up steeply, and is largely finished by around week twenty-five, with the middle of that window as its peak.

During the most intense stretch of this period, neurons are generated at an astonishing rate, often quoted in the older literature as hundreds of thousands of new neurons per minute averaged across the window.

The production happens not in the cortex itself but in germinal zones lining the fluid-filled cavities at the centre of the brain, called the ventricles.

The zone directly against the ventricle is called the ventricular zone, and above it sits a second proliferative layer called the subventricular zone.

Different classes of cortical neuron are born at different times within the window: the large excitatory neurons that will occupy the deep layers of the cortex are born early, and those destined for the upper layers are born later.

This tight calendar is one reason timing matters so much in prenatal harm: an insult in week ten meets a brain doing something very different from the same insult in week thirty, a principle that Chapter 22 develops under the name teratology.

The classic timetable was worked out by labelling dividing cells in monkeys, notably by Pasko Rakic in landmark work of the 1970s, and has been confirmed and refined in human tissue since.


5.1.2 Symmetric and asymmetric division and the outer radial glia

The stem cells of the cortex are called radial glia, cells with a small body near the ventricle and a single long fibre stretching all the way to the brain's outer surface.

A stem cell is a cell that can both copy itself and give rise to more specialised cell types.

Early in development, radial glia divide symmetrically, meaning one stem cell becomes two stem cells, which multiplies the founding population and, on the radial unit account of Chapter 4, sets the eventual surface area of the cortex.

Later they switch to asymmetric division, in which one division yields one stem cell and one neuron, or one stem cell and an intermediate progenitor cell that divides again to make neurons.

Symmetric division grows the factory, and asymmetric division runs it.

Primates, and humans most of all, have an additional trick: a second population of stem cells called outer radial glia, or basal radial glia, that sit in a greatly expanded outer part of the subventricular zone.

These cells were characterised in human tissue in 2010 by David Hansen, Arnold Kriegstein and colleagues, and later work by Pollen and colleagues in 2015 mapped their distinctive molecular identity, including marker proteins such as HOPX.

Outer radial glia keep a fibre reaching to the brain surface but have lost the attachment to the ventricle, and they can themselves divide repeatedly, acting as a secondary amplifier of neuron production.

Because they are scarce in the smooth-brained mouse and abundant in humans, outer radial glia are one of the leading candidate explanations for why the human cortex grew so large and so folded, a thread this chapter picks up again at gyrification in Chapter 6.


5.1.3 The near-complete neuronal complement by mid-gestation, and the narrow adult exception still in dispute

A striking fact follows from the production calendar: by roughly the middle of gestation, a fetus has close to its lifetime supply of cortical neurons.

The brain you are reading with is built, in the main, from cells older than you are, counting from birth.

Almost everything that happens after mid-gestation is therefore not the making of new neurons but the wiring, insulating, and pruning of neurons already present.

There is one narrow and famous candidate exception: the claim that the adult hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe that is central to forming new memories, continues to add new neurons throughout life in a region called the dentate gyrus.

Adult neurogenesis in this region is solidly established in rodents, and a 1998 study by Peter Eriksson and Fred Gage reported it in adult humans using a labelling chemical given to cancer patients.

But in 2018 the field split: Shawn Sorrells, Mercedes Paredes, Arturo Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues reported in Nature that markers of young neurons in the human dentate gyrus drop to undetectable levels by adolescence, while in the same year Maura Boldrini and colleagues reported in Cell Stem Cell that new neurons persist into the ninth decade.

Later work has kept both camps supplied: single-cell molecular studies have variously failed to find, and claimed to find, immature neurons in adult human hippocampus, and a 2025 study by Jonas Frisen's group reported evidence of dividing neural progenitors in adult human tissue.

The honest summary is that human adult hippocampal neurogenesis is contested, that if it exists at all it is modest in scale compared with the rodent, and that the developmental headline stands either way: the overwhelming majority of your neurons were made before you were born.

This corpus's rule applies here: where a number is unsettled, say so, and the number of new adult human neurons is unsettled.


5.2 Radial migration and the inside-out cortex

This section follows the excitatory neurons, the cortex's main signal-sending cells, on their outward journey, and explains the odd rule by which the cortex is stacked.


5.2.1 Migration along radial glia and the deep-layers-first rule

A newborn neuron in the ventricular zone is far from its destination, which may be a centimetre or more away at the building cortex near the brain's surface.

Most excitatory neurons solve the problem by climbing: they wrap around the long fibre of a radial glial cell and crawl along it, like a climber going up a fixed rope.

This is called radial migration, because the glial fibres run like spokes, or radii, from the ventricle out to the surface.

Rakic described this glial-guided climb in the early 1970s using electron microscopy of monkey cortex, and it became one of the founding images of developmental neuroscience.

The cortex is built as a stack of six layers, numbered one at the surface to six at the bottom, and the stack is assembled in a counterintuitive order.

The earliest-born neurons settle in the deepest layers, and each later wave of neurons migrates past its older siblings to settle above them.

This is the famous inside-out rule: layer six is oldest, and layers three and two are youngest.

The consequence is that a neuron's birthday largely predicts its layer, so the cortex is a kind of geological record laid down upside down, with the newest stratum on top.

Because the journey lengthens as the brain grows, the last-born upper-layer neurons have the longest climbs, and later-generated cells in the expanding primate brain can take weeks to complete the trip.


5.2.2 Reelin, the preplate, and the Cajal-Retzius cells

How do climbing neurons know where to stop, and how does the inside-out order get enforced?

A large part of the answer is a signalling protein called reelin, discovered through a mouse mutant named reeler, so called in the 1950s because the mutant mice walk with a reeling, unsteady gait.

In 1995, Tom Curran's group identified the gene disrupted in reeler mice, and its protein product was named reelin.

Reelin is secreted at the top of the developing cortex by a remarkable population of early neurons called Cajal-Retzius cells, first described in the 1890s by Santiago Ramon y Cajal and Gustaf Retzius.

Before the cortical plate exists, the first neurons to arrive form a primitive sheet called the preplate.

The first true cortical-plate neurons then migrate into the middle of the preplate and split it in two, leaving a thin marginal zone above, which contains the Cajal-Retzius cells and becomes layer one, and the subplate below, whose story Chapter 6 tells.

In reeler mice this splitting fails, the cortical plate forms beneath the preplate rather than within it, and the layers stack in roughly outside-in order, approximately inverted.

Reelin is therefore read as a positional signal that tells arriving neurons, in effect, that they have reached the top and should detach from their glial rope and settle, though the precise logic of the signal is still being worked out and reelin also acts on the final straightening and maturation of the climbing cells.
