Humans carrying two broken copies of the reelin gene have a severe malformation combining a simplified, thickened cortex with a small cerebellum, which confirmed that the mouse lesson transfers.


5.3 Tangential migration

This section follows the other great population of cortical neurons, the inhibitory interneurons, which take an entirely different route, travelling sideways rather than outward.


5.3.1 The interneurons' journey from the ganglionic eminences

Cortical neurons come in two broad families: excitatory neurons, which urge the next cell to fire, and inhibitory interneurons, which quiet it, mostly using a chemical messenger called gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

Roughly one cortical neuron in five is an inhibitory interneuron, and without them the cortex would be an uncontrolled amplifier, which is why failures of inhibition figure in epilepsy.

Astonishingly, these interneurons are not born in the cortex's own germinal zones at all.

They are born in transient bulges on the floor of the embryonic forebrain called the ganglionic eminences, principally the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences, structures that later contribute to deep-brain regions and then disappear as separate entities.

From these distant nurseries the young interneurons migrate tangentially, meaning sideways, parallel to the brain surface, travelling long distances without glial ropes, steering by chemical attractants and repellents, before finally turning to slot into the cortical layers.

This two-origins picture was established in the 1990s and 2000s by work from Stewart Anderson and John Rubenstein and others in the mouse, showing that deleting the master genes of the eminences, such as DLX1 and DLX2, empties the cortex of most of its interneurons.

Human work has confirmed that the same eminences supply the human cortex, with some continuing debate about whether primates add a modest cortical-born contribution.

The excitatory and inhibitory populations thus have separate birthplaces, separate routes, and separate genetic programmes, and must nonetheless arrive in matched proportions and wire together, a coordination problem whose failure is one candidate account of the excitation-inhibition imbalances discussed for autism in Chapter 49.


5.3.2 Protracted postnatal interneuron migration into the frontal lobe

The textbook picture long held that neuronal migration is essentially finished by birth.

In 2016, Mercedes Paredes, Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues reported in Science that this is not quite true for humans.

Studying post-mortem infant brains, they found a broad, arching stream of still-migrating young inhibitory neurons, which they named the Arc, curving along the walls of the lateral ventricles into the frontal lobe.

These late travellers are interneurons originating from the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences, and they continue arriving and settling in the anterior cingulate and frontal cortex for months after birth, with the stream dwindling across the first year.

The finding matters for developmental psychology because the frontal lobe is the seat of the slowest-maturing capacities, the executive functions of Chapter 35, and here is a mechanism by which its inhibitory circuitry is literally still being delivered while the infant is already learning.

Later work, including a 2025 study, has shown that gyrencephalic brains, meaning folded brains like ours, maintain an expanded subventricular zone that supports this postnatal interneuron traffic, and related work has traced persistent postnatal migration into the entorhinal cortex, a memory-related region.

It also offers a candidate point of vulnerability: a process still running after birth is a process the postnatal environment can disturb, though direct human evidence tying disturbed Arc migration to disorder is not yet established, and this corpus records that link as hypothesis rather than finding.


5.4 When migration fails

This section turns to the malformations of cortical development, the conditions in which the journey itself miscarries, and to what each taught about the machinery.


5.4.1 Lissencephaly, heterotopia, and polymicrogyria

Lissencephaly means smooth brain, from the Greek for smooth, and names a rare condition in which the cortical folds largely fail to form because migrating neurons stop short.

The cortex in classical lissencephaly is abnormally thick and often four-layered instead of six-layered, and affected children typically have severe developmental delay, epilepsy that is hard to control, and shortened lives.

Heterotopia means, roughly, wrong place, and names conditions in which clumps or bands of neurons halt partway and mature where they stopped.

In periventricular nodular heterotopia, nests of neurons remain stranded at the ventricular wall where they were born, never beginning the climb.

In subcortical band heterotopia, sometimes called double cortex, a whole second band of grey matter lies marooned in the white matter beneath a relatively normal cortex, recording a migration that started but stalled.

Polymicrogyria means many small folds, and describes a cortex that finished migration but organised its final layers and folding abnormally, producing a surface of excessive, shallow, fused little gyri; it is classed as a malformation of post-migrational organisation and has many causes, including prenatal cytomegalovirus infection and certain gene variants.

Clinically these conditions present along a spectrum from profound disability to, in small heterotopias, epilepsy in a person of typical intelligence, and they are among the clearest demonstrations in all of neurology that the mind's development depends on cells having reached their proper places.

They are described here plainly as biology, not as destiny: what a given child can do depends on far more than the anatomy, and the range of outcomes within each diagnosis is wide.


5.4.2 The migration genes and what each taught

The malformations became teachers when their genes were found, because each gene named a part of the machine.

LIS1, identified in 1993 as the gene deleted or mutated in many classical lissencephalies, encodes a regulator of dynein, a molecular motor that hauls the cell's nucleus along its internal skeleton of microtubules; the lesson is that migration is nucleus-hauling, a physical transport problem inside the moving cell.

DCX, identified in 1998, encodes doublecortin, a protein that stabilises microtubules; it sits on the X chromosome, of which males have one copy and females two, so males with a broken copy get lissencephaly while females, whose cells randomly use one X or the other, get double cortex, a mosaic of cells that migrated and cells that did not; the lesson is that the same gene, differently dosed, draws different anatomies.

TUBA1A and its relatives encode tubulin, the very building block of microtubules, and their mutations cause a family of tubulinopathies spanning lissencephaly and polymicrogyria-like patterns; the lesson is that the cytoskeleton, the cell's internal scaffolding, is the common final path of the climb.

FLNA encodes filamin A, which cross-links the cell's actin skeleton, and its mutations cause periventricular nodular heterotopia in which neurons never leave the ventricular wall; the lesson is that starting the journey is a separate, gene-dependent step from continuing it.

ARX, a control gene important in the ganglionic eminences, causes in its severe forms a lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia and a shortage of interneurons, and it taught that tangential migration has its own genetics, separable from the radial system.

RELN, the human reelin gene, causes lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia, closing the loop with the mouse work of section 5.2.2.

Together the migration genes converted a set of tragic anatomies into a parts list for a shared mechanism, and they stand as an early, clean success of the strategy this outline returns to throughout: let the rare, severe, single-gene cases illuminate the machinery that common development uses quietly.


CHAPTER 6. LAMINATION, THE SUBPLATE, AND THE FETAL CORTEX (CORE)

This chapter is about the fetal cortex as a structure unlike anything in the adult brain, with temporary compartments that exist only to be dismantled.

The most important of these, the subplate, is a waiting room in which the brain's incoming sensory wiring pauses for weeks before entering the cortex proper.

The chapter also covers how axons, the long output cables of neurons, find their way; when the senses first reach the cortex; how the brain gets its folds; how the cortical map is divided into areas; and why about half of all neurons made are deliberately destroyed.

It matters because the third trimester, when much of this is happening, is exactly the period a preterm baby spends outside the womb, and the transient structures of this chapter are exactly what preterm injury strikes.


6.1 The transient compartments

This section describes the scaffolding layers of the fetal cortex, which are essential for months and then largely vanish.


6.1.1 The preplate and its split

As Chapter 5 introduced, the first neurons to arrive above the germinal zones form the preplate, a thin primordial sheet present from roughly gestational weeks five to seven.

The preplate is a staging structure: it contains the pioneer neurons that will lay the first axonal paths and the Cajal-Retzius cells that will direct later arrivals.

Around gestational weeks seven to eight in humans, the first cortical-plate neurons migrate up into the preplate and split it, as section 5.2.2 described from the mouse side.

The split leaves the marginal zone at the surface, which becomes the sparse layer one of the adult cortex, and the subplate below the cortical plate.

From that moment the fetal cortex has a layered anatomy all its own, catalogued in detail by Ivica Kostovic and colleagues from the Zagreb Neuroembryological Collection, one of the world's great archives of human fetal brain tissue.

The failure of the split, as in reelin deficiency, scrambles everything built afterwards, which is why this brief embryonic event earns its own heading.


6.1.2 The subplate as the waiting room for thalamocortical axons, largest in humans, and its vulnerability in preterm injury

The subplate is the largest transient structure the human brain ever builds, and most readers have never heard of it.

It is a deep, cell-sparse but synapse-rich zone beneath the cortical plate, populated by some of the brain's earliest-born and most mature fetal neurons.

Work by Kostovic and Rakic, in a classic 1990 anatomical study, established its central function: axons growing up from the thalamus, the brain's central relay station for the senses, do not plug straight into the cortex, but instead halt in the subplate and wait there, for weeks in humans, forming temporary working synapses with subplate neurons.

A synapse is the contact point where one neuron passes signals to another.

During the waiting period the subplate is not idle storage; it is the hub of a genuine, functioning fetal circuit, the first place in the cortex where organised synaptic traffic occurs.

At its peak around gestational weeks twenty-eight to thirty-four, the human subplate is roughly four times thicker than the cortical plate itself and by some estimates occupies close to half the volume of the fetal telencephalon, the front-most division of the brain, and it is proportionally far larger in humans than in monkeys or cats.

Its enormity in our species is read as the price of our enormous association cortex: the more cortex there is to wire, and the longer the wiring takes, the bigger the waiting room must be.

After the thalamic axons move up into the cortical plate, the subplate slowly dissolves across late gestation and infancy, its neurons largely dying or dispersing, with a remnant persisting as scattered interstitial neurons in the adult white matter.

The clinical significance is stark: a baby born very preterm, say at twenty-six weeks, is living through the subplate's peak with an immature brain exposed to low oxygen, inflammation, and unstable blood flow, and subplate neurons are selectively vulnerable to exactly those insults.

Work by Kostovic, by Heiko Luhmann's group, and by Patrick McQuillen and colleagues has linked subplate damage to the injury patterns of prematurity, including impaired thalamocortical development, and Chapter 25 returns to this as the encephalopathy of prematurity.

Damage to a temporary structure can thus cast a permanent shadow, because the structure existed to guide a wiring step that only happens once.


6.2 Wiring the cortex

This section explains how growing axons navigate, and dates the moment the senses first speak to the cortex.


6.2.1 Axon guidance: netrins, semaphorins, ephrins

An axon grows from its tip, a crawling, hand-like structure called the growth cone, described by Ramon y Cajal in the 1890s as a living battering ram, soft yet able to push.

The growth cone steers by reading chemical signposts: molecules fixed on cell surfaces or diffusing through tissue, some attractive, some repulsive.

Netrins, identified in 1994 by Marc Tessier-Lavigne and colleagues, and named from the Sanskrit netr, meaning one who guides, are secreted cues that attract some axons toward the midline of the nervous system and repel others.

Semaphorins, named after the flag-signalling system, are a large family of mostly repulsive cues that fence axons out of wrong territories and collapse growth cones that stray.

Ephrins and their Eph receptors work by direct cell-to-cell touch and are laid out in graded amounts across target structures, so that an axon can read its position from the strength of the signal, a mechanism worked out in the map between eye and midbrain and confirmed in the thalamocortical system.

Slits and their Robo receptors, to complete the standard quartet, control midline crossing, deciding which axons may cross to the other side of the brain and ensuring they cross only once.

The general lesson is that wiring is not learned at this stage: the first draft of connectivity is drawn by molecular signposts, with activity refining it later, the division of labour that Chapter 16 formalises as the two-step wiring rule.

For the thalamocortical pathway specifically, axons from the thalamus navigate through an intermediate structure, pause in the subplate as section 6.1.2 described, and are guided by combinations of these same cue families along the way.


6.2.2 Thalamocortical innervation near weeks twenty-four to twenty-eight and the onset of cortical sensory response

The date on which thalamic axons leave the subplate and grow into the cortical plate is one of the most consequential in this whole outline: in humans it falls at roughly gestational weeks twenty-four to twenty-eight.

Kostovic and Judas's histological work dates the ingrowth into the cortical plate to about weeks twenty-four to twenty-six, with sensory-driven cortical circuitry consolidating over the following weeks.

Before this ingrowth, the cortex simply has no direct line to the sense organs, and after it, touch, sound, and pain can, in principle, evoke cortical responses.

Electrophysiological evidence agrees with the anatomy: from around weeks twenty-five to twenty-nine, preterm infants show cortical responses to touch and sound, and the earliest brain-wave recordings show the characteristic intermittent bursts of the very young cortex, including the spontaneous events called delta brushes that Chapter 16 discusses.

This anatomical date anchors the scientific debate about fetal pain: most reviews, including a widely cited 2005 review by Susan Lee and colleagues in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), have argued that cortical pain processing is unlikely before thalamocortical connections exist, while a 2020 reappraisal by Stuart Derbyshire and John Bockmann argued that subcortical and subplate processing leaves the question less settled.

This corpus reports that debate rather than resolving it, noting only that the anatomy sets a hard lower bound: whatever cortical experience requires, it cannot precede cortical input.

For developmental psychology the week twenty-four to twenty-eight ingrowth marks the opening of the era in which experience, in the ordinary sense of patterned sensory traffic, can begin to shape cortex, which is why fetal hearing and learning, covered in Chapter 26, date from the final trimester.


6.3 Folding and area-making

This section covers how the smooth fetal brain becomes the folded adult one, and how one sheet of cortex becomes a mosaic of specialised areas.


6.3.1 Gyrification in the third trimester and the mechanical accounts

Gyrification is the making of gyri and sulci, the ridges and grooves of the brain's folded surface.

The human cortical sheet, unfolded, is roughly the area of a large dinner napkin, and folding is how it fits in a skull that must still pass through the birth canal.

The timetable is remarkably late and fast: the fetal brain is essentially smooth until about gestational week twenty-four, the primary folds such as the central sulcus appear across weeks twenty to twenty-eight, secondary folds follow in the early third trimester, and tertiary folds continue forming through term and into the first postnatal months.

A baby born at term already has essentially the full adult folding plan, individual as a fingerprint yet following a species-typical layout.

Why the sheet folds is a genuinely mechanical question, and two accounts have competed.

David Van Essen proposed in 1997 that tension along axons pulls strongly interconnected regions toward each other, creasing the sheet between them; the idea is elegant, but direct measurements of tissue tension, notably by Xu and colleagues in 2010, found axonal tension not oriented the way the theory needs, running parallel to sulcal walls rather than across gyri.

The currently favoured account is differential tangential expansion: the outer cortical layers expand in surface area faster than the deeper tissue they are attached to, and a fast-growing skin bonded to a slow-growing core must buckle, as physical gel models by Tuomas Tallinen, L. Mahadevan and colleagues showed in 2016, reproducing strikingly brain-like folds from that principle alone.

On this view the regional pattern of folds reflects regional differences in growth rate, themselves downstream of the progenitor amplification of section 5.1.2, which ties the outer radial glia to the folded surface: more amplification, more expansion, more buckling.

Genes that derail these steps derail folding, which is how lissencephaly, polymicrogyria, and the folding differences seen in some neurodevelopmental conditions connect back to this mechanics.


6.3.2 Arealisation: the protomap-protocortex synthesis

Arealisation is the process by which the single cortical sheet becomes a map of distinct areas, such as primary visual cortex, primary motor cortex, and the language-related regions.

Two classic positions framed the question, as Chapter 3 previewed.

The protomap hypothesis, proposed by Rakic in 1988, holds that the germinal zones already carry a rough map: progenitor cells are regionally specified by graded signalling molecules before any experience, and they hand their area identity to their neuronal offspring.

The protocortex hypothesis, associated with Dennis O'Leary's 1989 formulation, holds that the young cortex starts as a roughly uniform sheet, a blank protocortex, and that identity is imposed from outside, chiefly by which thalamic inputs arrive.

The evidence forced a synthesis, and both of the original proponents' laboratories supplied parts of it.

Supporting the protomap side, gradients of transcription factors, meaning proteins that switch other genes on and off, are expressed across the germinal zone before thalamic input arrives, and mouse experiments deleting or overexpressing them, notably work on the genes EMX2 and PAX6 by Antonello Mallamaci, and on FGF8 signalling by Fukuchi-Shimogori and Elizabeth Grove in 2001, shift and resize areas: more FGF8 at the front pushes the whole map backwards.

Supporting the protocortex side, rewiring experiments by Mriganka Sur and colleagues from 1988 onward routed visual input into the auditory pathway of ferrets, and the auditory cortex receiving it developed visual maps and supported visually guided behaviour, showing that input can repurpose cortex.

Transplant experiments similarly showed early cortical tissue adopting host-region properties, and the barrel field of the mouse's whisker cortex fails to form its whisker-matched modules without its sensory input.

The synthesis, now standard, is that genes draw the protomap coarsely and early, fixing the layout and approximate proportions, while thalamic input and activity sharpen boundaries, set final sizes, and build the fine internal architecture.

Chapter 3 called this the first worked example of the outline's general theme: intrinsic constraint and experience are not rivals but successive drafts of the same document.


6.4 Sculpting by death

This section explains the strangest number in brain construction: the brain deliberately kills a large fraction of the neurons it makes.


6.4.1 Programmed cell death of roughly half the neurons produced

Programmed cell death, called apoptosis when it proceeds by the cell's own tidy self-destruct programme, is a normal, genetically controlled part of building a body, the same process that separates fingers by deleting the tissue between them.

In the nervous system its scale is startling: across many neuron populations, on the order of half of all neurons produced die during development, with figures between forty and sixty percent typical in well-counted systems, mostly in the peripheral nervous system and spinal cord where the counts are cleanest.

The phenomenon was discovered in the 1930s and 1940s by Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini studying chick embryos, who noticed that motor neurons and sensory ganglia first overproduce cells and then lose them on a fixed schedule, and that the losses grow if the limb the neurons serve is removed and shrink if an extra limb is grafted on.

In the human cortex the picture has a wrinkle: much of the death falls not only on projection neurons but heavily on the transient populations, the subplate and Cajal-Retzius cells of this chapter, and on a substantial fraction of interneurons, with mouse work showing roughly thirty to forty percent of cortical interneurons eliminated in a wave shortly after birth.

Death at this scale is not failure but specification: it matches neuron numbers to target sizes, deletes the scaffolding populations once their work is done, and removes cells that wired incorrectly.

Chapter 7's synaptic pruning is the same logic applied one level down, to connections rather than whole cells, and Chapter 17 gives the modern molecular machinery of elimination.


6.4.2 The neurotrophic hypothesis

The limb experiments demanded an explanation, and the one that triumphed is the neurotrophic hypothesis.

The idea: target tissues secrete survival factors, called neurotrophins, in limited supply; developing neurons compete for them; neurons that capture enough factor live, and the rest execute their death programme.

Neuron numbers are thus set by demand, measured at the destination, rather than dictated at the source.

The founding molecule is nerve growth factor (NGF), discovered by Levi-Montalcini with Stanley Cohen in the 1950s through a legendary series of experiments involving mouse tumours grafted onto chick embryos and, famously, snake venom as an unexpected rich source; the discovery earned the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Antibody experiments sealed the causal case: neutralising NGF in young rodents destroys the sympathetic nervous system, and supplying extra NGF rescues neurons that would have died.

NGF proved to be the first of a family: brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), purified in 1982 by Yves-Alain Barde and colleagues, plus neurotrophin-3 and neurotrophin-4, each serving different neuron populations through different receptors.

BDNF will reappear throughout this outline, because it graduated from a survival factor to a general currency of activity-dependent plasticity, figuring in the critical-period machinery of Chapter 15 and the exercise and enrichment literatures.

The neurotrophic hypothesis fits the central nervous system less cleanly than the periphery, where cell death is regulated by activity and connectivity as well as by target-derived factors, and the field's honest summary is that competition for trophic support is one major mechanism among several.

For developmental psychology the hypothesis matters as a principle: from the very beginning, the brain is sculpted by a marketplace in which use and usefulness, signalled chemically, decide what survives, a principle that experience will later exploit at the level of synapses.


CHAPTER 7. THE POSTNATAL BLOOM AND PRUNE: SYNAPSES, GLIA, AND MYELIN (CORE)

This chapter covers the brain's strategy for childhood: build far too much, then cut back what experience does not confirm.

After birth, the brain stops adding neurons in bulk and instead adds connections, support cells, and insulation at an extraordinary rate.

Synapses are massively overproduced in infancy and then pruned for a decade or more; glia, the brain's non-neuronal cells, are generated in waves; and myelin, the fatty insulation on axons, is laid down in an orderly sequence stretching into the fourth decade.

The chapter matters because this bloom-and-prune arc is the physical substrate of the sensitive periods, the learning capacities, and the long adolescence that occupy the rest of this outline.


7.1 Synaptic overproduction

This section presents the counts that revealed the bloom, and the argument about their shape.


7.1.1 Huttenlocher's counts: visual cortex peaking at four to twelve months, prefrontal cortex in the second and third years

Peter Huttenlocher, a paediatric neurologist at the University of Chicago, spent two decades counting synapses in post-mortem human brains under the electron microscope, tissue by painstaking tissue, in studies published between 1979 and 1997.

His central finding reshaped the field: synaptic density does not climb smoothly to adult levels but overshoots massively and then falls.

In primary visual cortex, at the back of the brain, synaptic density roughly doubles from birth to a peak at about four to twelve months of age, reaching some fifty percent above the adult value, then declines across childhood to adult levels by roughly age eleven.

In prefrontal cortex, the front-most region serving planning and self-control, the climb is slower, the peak arrives later, in the second and into the third year by the 1997 counts of Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, and the decline stretches through adolescence.

At the peak, a young child's cortex holds on the order of one and a half to two times as many synapses as an adult's, a fact worth sitting with: the developmental direction of travel for connections is downward.

Rakic and colleagues' 1986 monkey counts and later work by Zdravko Petanjek and colleagues in 2011, whose human prefrontal data extend the decline into the third decade, corroborated the arc, and modern in-vivo evidence from positron emission tomography imaging of a synaptic marker protein is broadly consistent.

The numbers come with honest caveats: post-mortem human material is scarce, the counts are densities rather than absolute numbers and so are entangled with tissue growth, and individual brains vary, so the peak ages are best read as windows rather than birthdays.


7.1.2 The concurrent-against-heterochronous debate

The counts raised a structural question: does the whole cortex bloom and prune on one schedule, or does each region run its own?

The concurrent view came from Rakic's group, whose 1986 monkey study, with Jean-Pierre Bourgeois and Patricia Goldman-Rakic, found synaptogenesis proceeding nearly in lockstep across visual, somatosensory, motor, and prefrontal cortex, suggesting a single brain-wide signal.

The heterochronous view, meaning different-timed, came from Huttenlocher's human data, in which visual cortex clearly peaked and pruned years before prefrontal cortex.

The debate mattered because the two views imply different mechanisms, a global hormonal or genetic clock against locally regulated, experience-keyed schedules, and different expectations about when each mental capacity's substrate is most plastic.

The field's resolution leans heterochronous for humans: the human data, the myelination gradients of section 7.4, the cortical thinning wave of Chapter 8, and gene-expression trajectories all describe a sensorimotor-to-association gradient in which the simplest areas mature first and the integrative areas last, the organising axis Chapter 3 introduced.

The reconciliation usually offered is that the onset of synaptogenesis is roughly concurrent everywhere, while the peak and the pruning phase are staggered by region, so both camps described real features of a more layered truth.

Species differences are also real: the compressed timetable of the monkey may genuinely be more synchronous than the stretched human one, and stretching a schedule exposes its staggering.


7.1.3 Overproduction as the substrate of experience-expectant plasticity

Why build twice what you keep?

The influential answer was given by William Greenough, James Black and Christopher Wallace in a 1987 paper that distinguished two kinds of plasticity, a distinction Chapter 3 flagged and this outline uses constantly.

Experience-expectant plasticity handles information that evolution can bet on: every infant with typical senses will encounter edges, faces, voices, and language.

For such universal input, the efficient design is to overproduce synapses on a genetic schedule and let the expected experience select among them, keeping the connections that carry traffic and discarding the rest.

The overshoot is thus not waste but a wager: a scaffold of candidate connections erected in confidence that the world will show up to choose among them.

Experience-dependent plasticity, by contrast, handles information unique to one life, a particular face, a particular vocabulary, and works by generating new synapses locally, on demand, throughout life.

The experience-expectant reading explains why the bloom is timed as it is: the visual peak at four to twelve months sits exactly under the period when binocular vision is calibrating, and the prefrontal bloom sits under the years when language and social norms flood in.

It also explains the cost structure of deprivation, which Chapters 13, 14, and 39 document: if the expected experience does not arrive during the window, the scaffold is pruned unselected or wrongly selected, and later experience meets a structure that has already been finalised.

The bloom, in short, is the physical form of the brain's openness, and the prune is the physical form of its commitment.


7.2 Pruning

This section covers the cutback itself, region by region, and points to where its machinery is treated.


7.2.1 Regional asynchrony: sensory cortices finish in childhood, prefrontal spines are eliminated into the third decade

Pruning is the elimination of synapses, and in the cortex much of it is the elimination of dendritic spines, the tiny thorn-like protrusions on a neuron's input branches on which most excitatory synapses land.

The regional schedule mirrors the bloom in reverse order of finishing: primary sensory cortices largely complete their pruning during childhood, with visual cortex near adult density around age eleven in Huttenlocher's data, while association cortices continue far longer.

The defining dataset for the long tail is Petanjek and colleagues' 2011 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which counted dendritic spines on prefrontal pyramidal neurons in human brains aged from birth to ninety-one years.

They found spine density in childhood roughly two to three times the adult value, and, remarkably, elimination continuing not just through adolescence but past age twenty and toward age thirty before flattening, a protraction the authors called extraordinary neoteny, neoteny meaning the retention of juvenile traits.

A cortex still shedding excess connections at twenty-five is a cortex still specifiable, still being finished by experience, and this is one of the structural facts behind the adolescent plasticity, and adolescent vulnerability, of Part Eleven.

The same fact powers a clinical hypothesis: the typical onset of schizophrenia in late adolescence coincides with the prefrontal pruning wave, and Feinberg proposed in 1982 that over-aggressive pruning might be part of its mechanism, a proposal whose modern genetic support is held for Chapter 52.

The regional asynchrony also restates this outline's refrain from Chapter 8 in synaptic terms: there is no single age at which the brain is done, because done happens region by region, and the regions that make us most distinctively human are done last.


7.2.2 The mechanisms held for Chapter 17: microglia, complement, astrocytes

Which synapses go, and what does the cutting?

The selection rule, in one line, is that activity protects: synapses that carry correlated, useful traffic are strengthened and retained, while weak and idle synapses are tagged and removed, use it or lose it made literal.

The removal work is done substantially by glia: microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, physically engulf synaptic material, guided in part by complement proteins, immune-system tags that mark weak synapses as if they were debris to be cleared, and astrocytes, the brain's star-shaped support cells, run a parallel engulfment pathway.

Those mechanisms, their discovery in the visual system by Beth Stevens, Ben Barres and colleagues, and their clinical shadows are the whole subject of Chapter 17, and this section only posts the signpost.

The point to carry forward here is architectural: pruning is not passive decay but an active, molecularly addressed demolition programme, which means it has genes, and genes mean both individual variation and disease risk.


7.3 Gliogenesis

This section covers the birth of the brain's other half, the glial cells, which outnumber or roughly equal neurons and do far more than glue.


7.3.1 Astrocytes then oligodendrocytes, and the transformation of the radial glia

Glia, from the Greek for glue, is the collective name for the brain's non-neuronal cells: astrocytes, which feed and regulate neurons and their synapses; oligodendrocytes, which make myelin; and microglia, immune cells that immigrate into the brain from outside during early embryonic life.

The production line that made neurons does not shut down when neurogenesis ends; it retools.

In a conserved sequence, the germinal zones switch from making neurons to making astrocytes, beginning in humans in late gestation, and then to making oligodendrocyte precursor cells, with human work tracing the major cortical wave of astrocyte and oligodendrocyte generation from the late second trimester through the early postnatal years.

The switch is a genuine change of identity in the progenitors, driven by an internal timer and external signals, and it explains a clinical asymmetry: an insult at twenty weeks harms neuron production, while the same insult at thirty-two weeks harms glial production and myelination instead, part of why preterm injury, as Chapter 25 details, is above all a white-matter disease.

Gliogenesis is also vastly more protracted than neurogenesis: astrocytes continue to be added and to mature across early childhood, and oligodendrocyte precursors persist as a dividing population for life.

When their work as scaffolds ends, the radial glia themselves are not discarded: most transform into astrocytes, and a specialised subset persists as the neural stem cells of the few adult germinal niches, so the cell that built the cortex retires into its support staff.

The transformation closes the loop on Chapter 4's claim that radial glia are the stem cells of the brain: they are, in sequence, the factory, the scaffolding, and finally part of the furniture.


7.4 Myelination

This section covers the brain's longest construction project: wrapping its wiring in insulation, a process that begins before birth and is still finishing in mid-adulthood.


7.4.1 The Flechsig and Yakovlev-Lecours ordering rules: sensory before motor before association

Myelin is a fatty sheath, wrapped around axons by oligodendrocytes in the brain, that speeds electrical conduction enormously, up to fifty-fold or more, by letting the signal jump between gaps in the insulation.

It is what makes white matter white.

The map of when each pathway gets its myelin was drawn first by the German anatomist Paul Flechsig around the turn of the twentieth century, who noticed in infant post-mortem material that myelination sweeps through the brain in an orderly succession of waves, and who numbered cortical regions by their myelination onset.

Flechsig's rule: pathways serving basic sensation and movement myelinate first, and the association cortices, the regions that integrate across senses and serve thought, myelinate last, with the tracts of the frontal and temporal association cortex at the very end of the queue.

Paul Yakovlev and Andre-Roch Lecours confirmed and extended the map in a landmark 1967 study of hundreds of human brains, producing the myelogenetic cycles still reproduced in textbooks: motor and sensory roots essentially complete in infancy, the great sensory relay pathways early, the corpus callosum, the bridge between hemispheres, across childhood, and the association and frontal fibres continuing, in their famous phrase, into the third decade and beyond.

The order recapitulates function: what an infant needs first is insulated first, and the sequence sensory before motor before association is the same sensorimotor-to-association gradient met in synaptogenesis, in cortical thinning, and in gene expression, one axis drawn four ways.

Myelination is thus a readout of the brain's priorities, and because myelin is measurable by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a technique that images soft tissue using magnetic fields and radio waves, it became one of the first developmental processes trackable in living children.


7.4.2 Rapid in the first two years, protracted into the third and fourth decades for association tracts

The tempo of myelination is front-loaded and long-tailed.

At birth the cerebral hemispheres are barely myelinated, which is one reason newborn movements are slow and imprecise; the first two years then see explosive myelination, and by around age two the infant brain's white matter looks, on a conventional MRI scan, grossly similar to an adult's.

Grossly similar is not finished: quantitative diffusion MRI, which measures the movement of water molecules along fibre tracts, shows white-matter microstructure continuing to mature for decades, and the lifespan white-matter studies, such as Lebel and Beaulieu's longitudinal work of 2011 and large cross-sectional studies, show different tracts peaking at different ages.

Early-myelinating projection pathways plateau in childhood or adolescence, while association tracts, above all the superior longitudinal fasciculus, the cingulum, and the frontotemporal connections, keep maturing into the late twenties and thirties, with some measures peaking around age forty before the slow decline of aging begins.

Post-mortem confirmation came from Benes and colleagues' 1994 demonstration that myelination in hippocampal-region pathways continues increasing into the fourth and even sixth decades.

The overall white-matter volume curve from the 2022 brain charts, previewed in Chapter 8, peaks just before age twenty-nine, later than any grey-matter measure.

For developmental psychology the long tail carries two lessons.

First, the physical substrate of fast, reliable long-range communication between frontal control regions and the rest of the brain is genuinely incomplete through adolescence, part of the mechanistic case in Part Eleven's account of adolescent behaviour, though this outline resists any leap from unfinished insulation to incapable person.

Second, the protraction is an opportunity as much as a limitation, because a process still running is a process experience can still direct, which is the subject of the next sub-section.


7.4.3 Activity-dependent adaptive myelination

Myelination was long taught as a fixed maturational programme, insulation laid by timetable.

That view fell in the 2010s to the discovery of adaptive myelination: oligodendrocytes and their precursors listen to neuronal activity, and active circuits get preferentially myelinated.

The pivotal experiment was published in Science in 2014 by Erin Gibson, Michelle Monje and colleagues, who used optogenetics, a technique for switching neurons on with light via an introduced light-sensitive protein, to stimulate the motor cortex of awake mice; the stimulation triggered proliferation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells and new myelination specifically along the activated circuit, and improved the corresponding limb's motor function.

Complementary work showed the loop matters for learning: McKenzie and colleagues reported in 2014 that mice genetically blocked from making new oligodendrocytes fail to properly learn a new motor skill, running on a wheel with irregular rungs, and later studies extended the requirement to spatial and fear memory consolidation.

Human correlates exist and predate the mechanism: Bengtsson and colleagues reported in 2005 that pianists' white-matter microstructure relates to how many hours they practised in childhood, with region-by-age effects suggesting the tracts still maturing at the time of practice were the ones most shaped by it, and juggling-training studies found white-matter change in adults within weeks.

The proposed logic is timing: adding or thickening myelin tunes conduction delays, and tuned delays let distant regions deliver their signals in the tight synchrony that neural computation and plasticity require.

Adaptive myelination thus adds a fourth plastic material to the brain's kit, alongside synaptic strength, synapse number, and intrinsic excitability, and it means the long myelination tail of the previous sub-section is not just a schedule but a decades-long window in which experience is still setting the brain's internal clock speeds.

A sobering coda belongs to the same laboratory: Monje's group has shown that some childhood brain tumours exploit the activity-to-myelin signalling pathway to grow, a reminder that every plasticity mechanism is also a vulnerability.


CHAPTER 8. THE MEASURED TRAJECTORIES: FROM GROWTH CURVES TO BRAIN CHARTS (CORE)

This chapter steps back from mechanism to measurement: what the living, scanned human brain actually does, size and shape and wiring, from fetus to old age.

For thirty years, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has let researchers measure children's brains safely and repeatedly, and the accumulated curves now form a quantitative portrait of growing up.

The chapter runs from the classic growth findings, through the finer distinctions the field learned to draw, to the 2022 lifespan brain charts that put the whole trajectory on one axis, and it ends by dismantling a popular myth about the age twenty-five.

It matters because these curves are the reference frame for everything else in this outline: every claim about early adversity, adolescent change, or disorder is ultimately a claim about a deviation from these trajectories.


8.1 The macrostructural course

This section gives the big-ticket numbers: whole-brain size, and the opposite fates of grey and white matter.


8.1.1 Total volume near ninety to ninety-five percent of adult by age six

The human brain roughly triples in size in its first year, and the whole-brain growth curve is astonishingly front-loaded.

At birth the brain averages about one third of adult volume; by age one it has reached roughly seventy percent; and by around age six it stands near ninety to ninety-five percent of adult volume, a figure established across the paediatric imaging literature and consistent with the 2022 brain charts.

Total brain volume then peaks in early adolescence, at about twelve to thirteen years in the brain charts data, before beginning a very slow, lifelong decline.

The early plateau hides the real story: a six-year-old's brain is adult-sized but profoundly un-adult, because size is the crudest possible measure, and the action after age six is internal, in the composition, connectivity, and insulation of tissue rather than its bulk.

The head grows with the brain, which is why head circumference is a standard paediatric measurement in infancy, tracking brain growth cheaply, and why departures from the expected head-growth curve, in either direction, prompt clinical attention.

The energy budget follows the construction schedule: positron emission tomography and metabolic studies show the child brain's glucose consumption rising to roughly double the adult rate in mid-childhood before declining through adolescence, with the peak of this expensive period coinciding, in work by Kuzawa and colleagues in 2014, with the years when body growth slows, as if the child's calories were being diverted from height to wiring.


8.1.2 The inverted-U of cortical grey matter and the steady climb of white matter

Split the brain into its two tissue classes and the single growth curve becomes two curves with opposite shapes.

Grey matter is tissue dominated by neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses, the computing elements; white matter is the myelinated wiring between them.

Cortical grey-matter volume follows an inverted U: it rises steeply through infancy and childhood, peaks, and then declines steadily across adolescence and adulthood.

The landmark longitudinal studies of Jay Giedd and colleagues at the National Institute of Mental Health, beginning with a 1999 paper in Nature Neuroscience, first drew the adolescent downslope and placed the peak around late childhood to early adolescence; the 2022 brain charts, with vastly more data, put the peak of total cortical grey-matter volume earlier, just before age six, with subcortical grey matter peaking much later, near fourteen and a half years.

The discrepancy between older and newer peak estimates is a lesson in method rather than a scandal: peak ages depend on the age range sampled, the scanners, and the statistical model, and the charts' fetal-to-centenarian coverage gives the currently best-anchored values.

White matter, by contrast, climbs steadily and long, growing through childhood and adolescence and peaking just before age twenty-nine in the brain charts, the latest peak of any major tissue class.

The adolescent grey-matter decline is not degeneration: it reflects some combination of the synaptic pruning of Chapter 7, and, importantly, the continued myelination of the lower reaches of the cortex, which makes formerly grey tissue register as white on a scan, so part of the apparent loss is reclassification, a caution argued forcefully in work by Natu and colleagues in 2019 finding little actual tissue loss where thinning is measured.

The two curves crossing, computing tissue consolidating while wiring expands, is the imaging-scale signature of the same bloom-prune-and-insulate strategy Chapter 7 described cell by cell.


8.1.3 The thinning wave: sensorimotor first, dorsolateral prefrontal and superior temporal last

Map the grey-matter decline across the cortical surface over time and it moves like weather: a wave of maturation sweeping across the brain in a fixed order.

The iconic dataset is Nitin Gogtay, Paul Thompson and colleagues' 2004 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which followed thirteen children with repeated scans from age four to twenty-one and rendered the change as a time-lapse film of the cortical surface, one of the most reproduced visualisations in neuroscience.

The wave begins in primary sensorimotor cortex, which matures earliest, spreads forward across the frontal lobe and backward through parietal cortex, and finishes last in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the lateral frontal territory serving working memory and cognitive control, and the superior temporal cortex, a hub for language and social perception.

Higher-order association areas mature only after the lower-order areas they integrate, and the order visibly parallels the sequence in which cognitive capacities consolidate, sensation before coordination before deliberation.

The wave also retraces evolution in a loose sense noted by the authors: the regions oldest in evolutionary terms mature first, and the most recently expanded association territories mature last.

Chapter 3 introduced this as the sensorimotor-to-association axis, and this is its most famous empirical portrait; the same axis has since been quantified as a principal gradient of brain organisation in adulthood by Margulies and colleagues in 2016, and shown by Sydnor, Satterthwaite and colleagues in 2021 to organise many developmental measures at once.

Two cautions attach to the classic image: the original sample was small by modern standards, and thinning is an ambiguous quantity, as the previous sub-section noted, but the ordering itself, sensorimotor early and association late, has replicated across cohorts and measures and stands among the most secure facts in developmental neuroimaging.


8.2 The finer grain

This section records the distinctions the field learned to draw once the headline curves were established: thickness against area, cortex against the structures beneath it, and structure against function.


8.2.1 Thickness and surface area as distinct developmental quantities

Cortical volume is the product of two quantities with different biology, different genetics, and different developmental clocks, and the field now insists on separating them.

Cortical thickness is the depth of the grey-matter sheet, averaging around two and a half millimetres; surface area is the extent of the sheet, folds included.

The radial unit hypothesis of Chapter 4 predicts the split: surface area reflects how many cortical columns were founded, set by the symmetric divisions of the early progenitor pool, while thickness reflects how many cells and connections each column stacked up, set by later asymmetric divisions and postnatal synaptic and myelin change.

Twin studies, notably Panizzon and colleagues in 2009, confirmed that thickness and area are essentially uncorrelated genetically, influenced by largely distinct gene sets, a conclusion genome-wide association studies of tens of thousands of brains, such as Grasby and colleagues in 2020, have upheld.

Their trajectories differ accordingly: surface area expands dramatically in infancy, roughly doubling in the first two years in work by Lyu, Li and colleagues on the Baby Connectome data, peaks around late childhood, and then contracts modestly, while thickness peaks very early, in the charts' estimate around one and a half to two years of age, and then declines nearly monotonically for the rest of life.

The practical import is that any study reporting only volume is mixing two signals that may move oppositely, and that different influences strike the two quantities differently: the poverty and income associations of Chapter 40, for instance, load principally on surface area, while many aging and psychiatric effects load on thickness.

The two-quantity lesson is a small methodological story with a large moral, repeated throughout this outline: developmental findings sharpen or dissolve depending on whether the measure carves the biology at its joints.


8.2.2 Subcortical and cerebellar trajectories

Beneath the cortex, each structure keeps its own calendar.

The subcortical structures are the deep grey-matter nuclei: among them the thalamus, the sensory relay of Chapter 6; the striatum, comprising the caudate and putamen, central to reward and habit; the amygdala, an almond-shaped structure central to threat and emotional learning; and the hippocampus, the memory structure met in Chapter 5.

In aggregate, subcortical grey-matter volume peaks in adolescence, near fourteen and a half years in the 2022 brain charts, later than cortical grey matter, but the aggregate hides diverging members: longitudinal studies through adolescence, including work from the Wierenga and Tamnes groups, find striatal volumes declining across the teen years while amygdala and hippocampal volumes are still inching upward into early adulthood.

The amygdala-and-hippocampus-late, striatum-earlier pattern is one anatomical ingredient in Part Eleven's account of adolescence, in which reward circuitry runs ahead of regulatory circuitry.

The cerebellum, the little brain tucked beneath the back of the cerebrum, long typecast as purely motor and now firmly implicated in cognition, has a trajectory all its own: it is disproportionately immature at birth, undergoes explosive growth in the last trimester and first postnatal year, which makes it acutely vulnerable to preterm birth as Chapter 25 notes, and its total volume peaks in mid-to-late adolescence, with the classic Tiemeier and Giedd longitudinal work placing the peak in the mid-teens.

Chapter 29 returns to the cerebellum's long build as a substrate of skill and coordination into adolescence.

The general rule of this sub-section is the chapter's rule in miniature: there is no single brain curve, only a family of curves, and the family's staggered peaks are themselves the finding.


8.2.3 Functional network reorganisation and the motion-artefact corrections to its first story

Alongside structure, MRI can measure function: functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) tracks blood-oxygen changes that follow neural activity, and resting-state fMRI measures which regions' activity rises and falls together while a person simply lies still, revealing the brain's functional networks.

The first developmental story, told in influential papers around 2007 to 2010 by the Washington University group of Fair, Dosenbach, Schlaggar and Petersen, was tidy and appealing: children's networks were said to be organised by anatomical neighbourhood, adults' by function, so development consisted of connectivity shifting from local to distributed, short connections weakening and long ones strengthening.

Then came the correction that renamed an era: in 2012, Jonathan Power and colleagues showed that tiny head movements, fractions of a millimetre, systematically inflate apparent short-range connectivity and deflate apparent long-range connectivity, and children move more than adults.

Much of the local-to-distributed story was therefore the artefact wearing the costume of a finding, and the field rebuilt its methods around motion scrubbing, meaning the identification and removal of movement-contaminated moments of data, and around motion-matched samples.

What survives the correction is real but more modest: the large-scale network layout is present remarkably early, visible in rudimentary form in term newborns in work by Doria and colleagues in 2010 and in the developing Human Connectome Project data, and development refines rather than installs it, with association networks, notably the default and frontoparietal control networks, segregating from one another and integrating internally across childhood and adolescence.

Network segregation measures continue changing into the twenties and relate to executive performance, a thread Chapter 35 picks up.

This sub-section doubles as this outline's first full telling of a pattern that recurs, in Chapter 11 on methods and Chapter 12 on the reproducibility reckoning: developmental differences are exactly the size and kind of signal that artefacts mimic, because whatever varies with age, movement, sleepiness, compliance, also varies with age.


8.3 The lifespan reference

This section presents the project that turned three decades of scattered curves into a single reference frame.


8.3.1 The brain charts of 2022: normative growth curves from the fetus to age one hundred

Paediatricians have plotted children's height and weight on standardised growth charts for over a century, reading each child as a percentile against a reference population.

In April 2022, the brain got its equivalent: Richard Bethlehem, Jakob Seidlitz, Simon White and colleagues published Brain charts for the human lifespan in Nature, aggregating one hundred and twenty-three thousand nine hundred and eighty-four MRI scans from one hundred and one thousand four hundred and fifty-seven people, drawn from over one hundred studies, spanning from one hundred and fifteen days after conception to one hundred years of age.

Using generalised additive models for location, scale and shape, the statistical framework behind the World Health Organization's growth charts, the team fitted continuous normative trajectories, with centile lines, for the major tissue classes and structures.

The charts delivered the milestone ages this chapter has been citing: total grey-matter volume peaking just before age six, subcortical grey matter near fourteen and a half, white matter just before twenty-nine, total brain volume peaking in early adolescence, and cortical thickness peaking before age two.

Ventricular volume, the fluid spaces, rises across life and accelerates in aging, and mean cortical thickness declines from its toddler peak onward.

The achievement was as much social as scientific: harmonising scans across scanners, protocols, countries, and decades required new statistical machinery and unprecedented data sharing, and the team published the model as an open tool at brainchart.io so that any new dataset can be placed on the reference.

The authors themselves flagged the chart's honest limits: the reference population over-represents wealthy, European-ancestry cohorts, coverage of the fetal and perinatal ranges is thinnest, and centiles from cross-sectional aggregation are not yet the longitudinal, individual-tracking instrument the clinic would ultimately want.

The charts are best read the way this outline reads them: not as the end of measurement but as the coordinate system in which every developmental claim can now be located.


8.3.2 What a normative model buys the clinic and the science

A normative model changes the question a measurement can answer: instead of asking whether a group of patients differs on average from a group of controls, one asks where this individual sits against the expected distribution for their age and sex, exactly as a paediatrician reads a weight percentile.

For the clinic, the promise runs through several doors.

A brain-volume centile gives a principled way to flag atypical growth, and the brain-charts team showed that clinical groups, from Alzheimer's disease to schizophrenia, shift systematically on specific centiles, with Alzheimer's showing the greatest deviations in grey-matter measures.

Centile scores travel across scanners better than raw volumes, which matters for any real-world use, and longitudinal centile crossing, a child dropping across centile lines, is a more sensitive alarm than any single measurement, just as it is for weight.

For the science, normative modelling dissolves a false binary: rather than sorting children into typical and atypical piles, it measures each child's deviation continuously, which suits the dimensional view of neurodevelopmental conditions that Chapter 48 develops, and work by Marquand, Beckmann and colleagues has built a parallel methodological tradition showing that patients with the same diagnosis often deviate in different places, so the average patient map describes almost no actual patient.

The honest counterweight belongs in the same breath: no brain centile is at present a diagnostic test for any psychiatric or developmental condition, effect sizes at the individual level remain modest, and the reference-population biases of the previous sub-section would, if unaddressed, hard-code inequity into any clinical tool built on the charts.

The right analogy is early days of the growth chart itself: a reference is not a diagnosis, but medicine without references is guesswork, and developmental neuroscience has finally acquired its reference.


8.4 The maturity question

This section takes on the most widely repeated claim in popular developmental neuroscience and explains why this corpus records it as false.


8.4.1 Why there is no biological endpoint at twenty-five

The claim that the brain finishes maturing at age twenty-five has escaped the laboratory and now lives in journalism, policy argument, car-rental pricing, and everyday conversation.

This corpus records it as an artefact, and the reasoning deserves to be spelled out.

First, the number is not a measurement result: no study identified a maturational event at twenty-five.

The landmark longitudinal studies that popular accounts lean on, including the National Institute of Mental Health cohorts and many diffusion studies, enrolled participants only up to their mid-twenties or so, and a curve that is still changing at the edge of the sampled age range will appear to level off there, because there is no data beyond the edge; the apparent endpoint is the cohort's age limit wearing the costume of a biological fact.

Second, studies that sample beyond the twenties keep finding change: the 2022 brain charts show white matter peaking just before twenty-nine, cortical measures still moving through the thirties, Petanjek's spine counts running toward thirty, and Benes's myelination data into the fourth decade and beyond, while Somerville's 2016 essay in Neuron, Searching for signatures of brain maturity, laid out the case that maturity itself has no agreed criterion.

Third, the underlying idea of a single finishing date misreads what development is: the brain does not cross a line from unfinished to finished but shifts gradually from faster change to slower change, and change never stops, since the same tissue that is maturing at twenty is aging at sixty and plastic throughout.

None of this means age boundaries in law are silly, since lines must be drawn somewhere for driving, drinking, sentencing, and insurance, but it means those lines are policy choices balancing many considerations, and they cannot be read off a brain scan; neuroscience can inform them but does not dictate twenty-five or any other number.

The disciplined statement is this: specific measures have specific, staggered trajectories, several of which are still changing well past twenty-five, and the popular sentence the brain matures at twenty-five is not a summary of them but a distortion of them.


8.4.2 Different measures mature at different times, and regional asynchrony is the finding

Strip away the myth and what remains is the actual discovery of thirty years of developmental neuroimaging, which is better than the myth.

Line up the peaks this chapter has assembled: cortical thickness before age two, total grey matter before six, total brain volume around twelve to thirteen, subcortical grey matter near fourteen and a half, cerebellar volume in the mid-teens, network segregation into the twenties, white matter near twenty-nine, association-tract microstructure and prefrontal spine elimination toward thirty and beyond.

There is no moment when these curves agree, and their disagreement is not noise but structure: the staggering follows the sensorimotor-to-association axis within the cortex, and a deep-to-surface, evolution-echoing order across structures.

Asynchrony is what a constructed system should show: you cannot tune the integrator before the things it integrates are stable, so the association cortices and their long tracts, the integrators, must finish last, and the bloom-prune-insulate machinery of Chapter 7 executes exactly that dependency order.

Asynchrony is also functional: at every age, the brain is a mixture of consolidated and still-plastic systems, which means every age has a characteristic profile of stabilities and opennesses, and the windows of Part Four are the local, system-by-system expression of the same staggering.

The practical habit this sub-section commends is to replace the question when does the brain mature with the questions this outline actually answers: which measure, of which system, on which trajectory, and with what functional consequence.

Asked that way, the question stops having a single number for an answer, and starts having a science.


================================================================================

PART THREE. THE METHODS: HOW A DEVELOPING BRAIN IS STUDIED

================================================================================

CHAPTER 9. THE BEHAVIOURAL TOOLKIT (APPARATUS)

A baby cannot tell you what it knows, and that simple fact shaped a century of scientific ingenuity.

This chapter tours the behavioural methods that let infants testify without words - through where they look, how they suck, what they reach for, and what they imitate.

It also introduces the marker-task logic, the clever move of tying a specific infant behaviour to a specific brain circuit whose biology is already known.

These tools matter because everything the rest of this book claims about the infant mind was, at some point, extracted through one of them, and each tool has both a strength and a trap.


9.1 Looking as the infant's testimony

The single most productive discovery in infancy research is that babies vote with their eyes.

Infants look longer at some things than at others, and by measuring those looking times carefully, researchers turned the gaze into an instrument.

This section explains the three main looking methods and the modern debate about how much they really tell us.


9.1.1 Habituation and preferential looking

Preferential looking is the simplest method of all: show an infant two pictures side by side and time how long the eyes rest on each one.

If the infant reliably looks longer at one picture, the infant must be able to tell the two apart, because you cannot prefer what you cannot distinguish.

Robert Fantz introduced this logic in studies published around 1961, showing that even newborns look longer at patterned displays, such as faces and bullseyes, than at plain ones.

Habituation adds a second idea: boredom.

Show an infant the same stimulus over and over, and looking time drops as the infant habituates, which is the technical word for getting used to something and losing interest.

Then switch to a new stimulus.

If looking time recovers, the infant noticed the change, and the size of the recovery hints at how different the two stimuli seem to the infant.

Habituation and its cousin, familiarisation, became the workhorse of infant psychology from the 1960s onward, because they need no language, no training, and no motor skill beyond moving the eyes.

The trap is interpretation.

A longer look can mean novelty preference, but under other conditions infants look longer at familiar things instead, and the balance between familiarity and novelty preferences shifts with age, stimulus complexity, and how much exposure the infant has had.

That interpretive looseness is a running theme in the modern reassessment of the whole looking-time enterprise.


9.1.2 Violation of expectation and its replication debates

The violation-of-expectation method takes habituation one step further and turns it into a probe of what infants believe about the world.

The logic runs: if an infant expects objects to behave a certain way, then an event that violates that expectation should be surprising, and surprise should show up as longer looking.

The most famous early example is the drawbridge study by Renee Baillargeon and colleagues in 1985, in which infants of about 5 months looked longer when a rotating screen appeared to pass through the space where a hidden box stood, as if solid objects could melt through each other.

Results like this were taken as evidence that young infants possess core knowledge of physics - that objects are solid, continuous, and persist when hidden - long before they can search for hidden objects with their hands.

A conceptual overview by Francesco Margoni, Luca Surian, and Renee Baillargeon in 2024 defends the paradigm and organises decades of findings.

But the method is now at the centre of an honest and unresolved replication debate.

Critics point out that longer looking at the impossible event can sometimes be explained by low-level perceptual differences between the displays rather than by violated physics.

Several individual violation-of-expectation findings have proved fragile when other laboratories tried them with larger samples and preregistered methods, meaning the analysis plan was publicly locked in before the data were collected.

The debate is sharpest for the social versions of the paradigm, in which infants were claimed to attribute false beliefs to other people.

Those infant false-belief findings, first reported by Kristine Onishi and Renee Baillargeon in 2005, have suffered repeated replication failures in the 2010s and 2020s, and this corpus treats infant implicit false-belief understanding as a genuinely open question rather than an established fact.

The ManyBabies consortium, a large international collaboration in which dozens of laboratories run the same study with the same protocol, was created in the late 2010s partly to settle such questions, and its projects on infant theory of mind are the field's best hope for a clean answer.

The fair summary for a beginner is this: infants clearly notice and track objects far earlier than Jean Piaget thought, but exactly how rich their early physical and social knowledge is remains contested, and looking time alone may never settle it.


9.1.3 Anticipatory looking and eye-tracking

Modern eye-trackers are cameras with infrared light, which is light just beyond the red end of what humans can see, that bounce that light off the cornea and pupil to compute where the eyes are pointing many times per second.

This turns the coarse measure of total looking time into a fine-grained record of exactly where an infant looks and when.

Anticipatory looking exploits the timing: if an infant looks toward a location before something happens there, the infant must have predicted the event.

A celebrated study by Victoria Southgate, Atsushi Senju, and Gergely Csibra in 2007 used anticipatory looking to argue that 2-year-olds predict the actions of a person holding a false belief.

That specific result has since failed several direct replication attempts, and anticipatory-looking measures of false belief are now widely regarded as unreliable, which is part of the broader infant false-belief replication crisis mentioned above.

Eye-tracking itself, as a measurement technology, remains extremely valuable: it delivers precise measures of attention, pupil size, and gaze-following, and it works from early infancy.

Pupillometry, the measurement of pupil dilation as an index of surprise or effort, is an increasingly popular companion measure, though a large study of 9-to-10-month-olds published in 2025 found no clear domain-general pupil response to expectation violations, another caution against overinterpreting any single measure.

The lesson of this whole section is not that looking methods are worthless - they built the field - but that the field is currently rebuilding them on larger samples, preregistration, and converging measures.


9.2 Acting as the infant's testimony

Looking is not the only thing a baby can do.

Infants can also suck, kick, turn their heads, and copy actions, and each of these behaviours has been harnessed as a channel of testimony.

This section covers the action-based methods, which have the advantage of demanding something more active from the infant than a glance.


9.2.1 High-amplitude sucking and conditioned procedures

High-amplitude sucking gives even a newborn a lever to pull, and the lever is a dummy.

The infant sucks on a non-nutritive teat, meaning a pacifier that delivers no milk, connected to a pressure sensor.

After a baseline period, the apparatus is set so that strong sucks trigger a sound, and infants quickly learn the contingency and suck hard to hear it.

As the same sound repeats, interest fades and sucking declines, and if a new sound then restores vigorous sucking, the infant discriminated the two.

Peter Eimas, Einar Siqueland, Peter Jusczyk, and James Vigorito used exactly this method in a landmark 1971 paper in Science, showing that infants of 1 and 4 months discriminate the syllables ba and pa categorically, with sharper discrimination across the adult phoneme boundary than within a category.

A phoneme is a speech sound that changes the meaning of a word, and this study founded the modern science of infant speech perception.

The conditioned head-turn procedure serves older infants of roughly 5 to 12 months: the infant is trained to turn the head toward a loudspeaker whenever a repeating background sound changes, and a correct turn is rewarded with an animated toy.

Janet Werker and Richard Tees used this procedure in 1984 to show that infants discriminate foreign speech contrasts at 6 to 8 months but largely lose that ability for non-native contrasts by 10 to 12 months, one of the most replicated findings in developmental science.

Conditioning also serves memory research.

In Carolyn Rovee-Collier's mobile conjugate reinforcement task, developed from the late 1960s onward, a ribbon connects a young infant's ankle to an overhead mobile so that kicking makes the mobile move, and the rate of kicking days or weeks later measures how long the learned contingency is remembered.

With this task, 2-month-olds remember for about 1 to 3 days and 6-month-olds for about 2 weeks, with reminders able to reinstate memories that seemed lost.


9.2.2 Deferred imitation and elicited imitation

Deferred imitation asks whether an infant can watch an action now and reproduce it later, from memory, without ever having practised it.

Because reproducing a never-practised action after a delay seems to require a stored representation rather than a motor habit, deferred imitation is widely treated as a nonverbal test of declarative memory, the kind of memory for facts and events that in adults depends on the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe that binds experiences into memories.

Andrew Meltzoff showed in studies through the 1980s, including a well-known 1988 report, that 9-month-olds can reproduce simple actions on novel objects after a 24-hour delay, and 14-month-olds after a week.

Elicited imitation, developed extensively by Patricia Bauer from the late 1980s onward, extends the method to multi-step event sequences, such as making a rattle in two steps, and measures whether children reproduce the steps in the correct order after delays of weeks or months.

Bauer's work showed that long-term ordered recall strengthens sharply across the second year of life, tracking the protracted maturation of the hippocampal system.

One famous neighbouring claim has fallen.

The report by Meltzoff and Keith Moore in 1977 that newborn babies imitate facial gestures such as tongue protrusion was a textbook staple for decades.

A large longitudinal study led by Janine Oostenbroek in 2016, testing 106 newborns repeatedly across the first 9 weeks with multiple gestures and proper controls, found no evidence of neonatal imitation, and the claim is now best taught as a probable artefact of arousal, since newborns stick out their tongues at many interesting things.

Deferred and elicited imitation at 6 months and beyond, by contrast, have held up well and remain central tools.


9.3 The marker-task logic

A behavioural task on its own tells you what an infant can do, but not which brain circuit does it.

The marker-task strategy closes that gap by borrowing a task whose neural basis has already been worked out in animals or in brain-damaged adults, and then giving the same task to infants.

If infants start passing the task at a particular age, the maturation of the known circuit becomes the leading explanation, and the task becomes a behavioural marker of that circuit.


9.3.1 Linking an infant behaviour to a known circuit: the A-not-B example

The A-not-B task is the classic demonstration, and it began with Jean Piaget's observations published in 1954.

An experimenter hides a toy at location A, the infant retrieves it, this repeats, and then, in full view of the infant, the toy is hidden at location B.

Infants of about 7 to 9 months reach back to A anyway - the A-not-B error - despite having just watched the toy go to B.

Adele Diamond and Patricia Goldman-Rakic turned this curiosity into a circuit story in a landmark 1989 paper in Experimental Brain Research.

They showed that the task is essentially the delayed-response task long used with monkeys, and that adult monkeys with lesions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex - the upper side part of the frontal lobe that holds information in mind and inhibits habitual responses - make the same error human infants make.

The developmental timing was equally telling: in longitudinal testing, the delay needed to provoke the error grows from about 2 to 5 seconds at 7.5 to 9 months to more than 10 seconds by 12 months, as if the infant's prefrontal circuit were gaining strength week by week.

Monkeys with dorsolateral prefrontal lesions performed like 7.5-to-9-month-old infants, while intact monkeys and monkeys with parietal lesions performed like 12-month-olds, tying the behaviour to that specific region rather than to brain damage in general.

The A-not-B and delayed-response pairing is often described as one of the strongest brain-behaviour links in cognitive neuroscience, and it made the task a marker of prefrontal working memory and inhibition in infancy.

Success on the task requires two abilities at once: holding the hiding place in mind across the delay, and inhibiting the previously rewarded reach to A.


9.3.2 The strengths and the traps of marker tasks

The strength of a marker task is inferential leverage: it imports an entire animal literature - anatomy, physiology, lesion data, pharmacology - into the study of human infants at almost no cost.

Marker tasks also allow honest cross-species comparison, because the same task can be run in infant monkeys, adult monkeys, human infants, and human patients.

The traps deserve equal billing.

First, tasks are rarely pure: A-not-B performance is influenced by reaching habits, posture, and even whether the infant's stance changes between trials, as Linda Smith and Esther Thelen showed in dynamic-systems studies in the 1990s, so passing or failing reflects more than one circuit.

Second, a task solved by one circuit in adults may be solved by a different circuit in infants, because the developing brain can reach the same behaviour by another route, so the inference from behaviour to circuit does not automatically transfer across age.

Third, the logic can slide into reverse inference, the error of assuming that because a region supports a task, any change in the task must reflect that region.
