The current understanding, developed by Hensch and many others, is that maturing basket-cell inhibition performs two jobs that jointly enable plasticity: it suppresses the brain's internally generated spontaneous chatter so that genuine sensory signals stand out, and it sharpens the timing of excitatory firing so that the correlation-detecting rules of plasticity, described in Chapter 16, receive clean data.

In this view the basket cell is the timer of the window: the critical period opens when these cells mature, and, as Section 15.2 explains, it closes as structures accumulate around these same cells.

The maturation of basket cells is itself experience-dependent, which elegantly explains an old observation: animals reared in darkness show a delayed critical period, because without visual input the inhibitory timer matures late.

15.1.2 The experiments that moved the window: GAD65, benzodiazepines, BDNF, Otx2

The claim that inhibition times the window rests on experiments that moved the window at will, and four are canonical.

The first used mice lacking glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65), one of the two enzymes that synthesise GABA, specifically the form that loads GABA into synaptic terminals for release.

Hensch and colleagues reported in 1998 that these mice, with weakened inhibitory transmission, showed no ocular dominance plasticity at the usual age: monocular deprivation simply failed to shift their cortex, as if the window never opened.

The second experiment rescued the first: infusing diazepam, a benzodiazepine drug that enhances the effect of GABA at its receptors, restored plasticity in the GAD65-deficient mice, and, more strikingly, giving diazepam to normal young mice before the usual window opened the critical period prematurely.

Together these showed that inhibition is not merely necessary but sufficient to set the opening time: too little GABA and the window never opens, boosted GABA and it opens early.

A one-way property emerged from this work that has become a general principle: the window opens once, and its machinery behaves like a switch, not a dial that can be flicked back and forth.

The third experiment used brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a growth-promoting protein that supports the maturation of inhibitory neurons.

Mice genetically engineered to overexpress BDNF in the cortex, reported by Z. Josh Huang, Susumu Tonegawa, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues in 1999, showed accelerated maturation of their GABA system, and their critical period both opened and closed early, compressing the whole visual developmental schedule.

The fourth experiment identified a messenger that tells basket cells when to mature: the protein Otx2, a transcription factor, meaning a protein that switches genes on and off.

Work by Sugiyama, Hensch, Prochiantz, and colleagues in 2008 showed that Otx2 is not made by the basket cells themselves but is produced elsewhere, travels into the visual cortex in an experience-dependent way, is captured preferentially by parvalbumin cells, and drives their maturation; blocking its transfer delayed the critical period, and infusing it opened the window early.

Otx2 thus acts as a molecular messenger of experience, physically carrying the message the eyes are open and working into the cortex and handing it to the cells that start the clock.

The combined lesson of the four experiments is that the timing of a critical period is not a fixed genetic clock but an adjustable, experience-sensitive circuit property, which immediately raises the question the rest of this chapter pursues: if biology can move the window, can medicine?

15.2 The brakes

A window that opens must also close, and the second discovery of the molecular era was that closure is not a fading away but an active application of brakes.

The adult cortex is not plastic-by-default with the plasticity worn out; it is plastic-at-heart with the plasticity actively locked, and this section describes the locks.

15.2.1 Perineuronal nets and their enzymatic removal

The most striking brake is a physical structure: the perineuronal net, a lattice of sugar-and-protein molecules, chiefly chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, that condenses around the cell bodies of neurons as the critical period ends.

Perineuronal nets form preferentially around exactly the cells Section 15.1.1 crowned as the timer: the parvalbumin basket cells.

Once a net has condensed around a basket cell, it stabilises that cell's connections, limits the formation of new contacts, and captures molecules such as Otx2 that maintain the cell's mature state, effectively freezing the inhibitory scaffolding of the circuit.

The demonstration that nets are a true brake, and not just a bystander, came from Tommaso Pizzorusso, Lamberto Maffei, James Fawcett, and colleagues in 2002.

They infused the adult rat visual cortex with chondroitinase ABC, a bacterial enzyme that digests the sugar chains of the nets, and found that adult monocular deprivation, normally powerless, once again shifted ocular dominance: the critical period had been chemically reopened.

In a 2006 follow-up, the same group showed the reverse rescue: adult rats made amblyopic by early deprivation recovered visual acuity and normal connection density when net digestion was combined with reopening the deprived eye.

Supporting evidence closed the loop on timing: the condensation of the nets coincides with the natural end of the critical period, and rearing animals in darkness, which delays the critical period, also delays net formation.

Perineuronal nets have since been found to gate plasticity far beyond vision; a widely cited example from Nadine Gogolla, Cyril Herry, and colleagues in 2009 showed that digesting nets in the amygdala, the brain's threat-learning hub, made adult fear memories erasable by training in the way that only young animals' fear memories normally are.

The net is thus the clearest physical embodiment of a closed window: the memory of the critical period, locked in sugar and protein around the timer cells.

15.2.2 The myelin-associated inhibitors and the Lynx1 cholinergic brake

The nets are not the only brake; at least two other braking systems close over the same period.

The first involves myelin, the fatty insulation that wraps nerve fibres to speed their signals, and which increases in the cortex as the critical period ends.

Myelin and its associated proteins, including one called Nogo, do more than insulate: they carry signals that actively discourage nearby fibres from sprouting and rewiring.

Aaron McGee, Stephen Strittmatter, and colleagues showed in 2005 that mice lacking the Nogo receptor, the molecular antenna through which these myelin signals act, kept their ocular dominance plasticity long after the normal critical period had closed, into adulthood.

A related receptor called paired immunoglobulin-like receptor B (PirB), studied by Josh Syken, Carla Shatz, and colleagues in 2006, produced a similar picture: remove the receptor, and the plasticity outlasts its normal window.

The second brake works on the brain's arousal chemistry.

Acetylcholine is a chemical messenger that, among other jobs, signals attention and alertness and promotes plasticity; its cortical effects are strong in youth.

Hirofumi Morishita, Julie Miwa, Nathaniel Heintz, and Takao Hensch reported in Science in 2010 that a small protein called Lynx1, whose levels rise in the cortex as the critical period ends, binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and damps their response, acting as a volume knob turned down on the plasticity-promoting effects of acetylcholine.

Mice lacking Lynx1 retained ocular dominance plasticity into adulthood, and, remarkably, adult Lynx1-deficient mice spontaneously recovered from amblyopia when the deprived eye was simply reopened, without any drug or training.

Lynx1 is structurally similar to the active component of snake venom toxins that block the same receptors, which has earned it the memorable description of the brain's own venom-like brake.

The larger picture from nets, myelin signals, and Lynx1 together is one of redundancy: adulthood is defended by multiple independent brakes, which is presumably why no single intervention fully rejuvenates the adult cortex, and why the stability of the adult brain, which these brakes exist to protect, is so robust.

15.3 Reopening, and the honest record

If windows are held shut by removable brakes, the therapeutic dream writes itself: release the brakes in an adult brain, retrain the circuit, and cure amblyopia, or deafness-related deficits, or perhaps disorders of social development.

This section presents the animal evidence, which is strong, then the human evidence, which is thin, and then explains why this book insists on the word thin.

15.3.1 The animal proofs: dark exposure, enrichment, fluoxetine, interneuron transplantation

In animals, critical-period reopening is not a fringe claim; it has been demonstrated repeatedly, by independent laboratories, using at least four distinct methods.

The first method is dark exposure: housing an adult animal in complete darkness for a period of days.

Work by Hai-Yan He, Quentin Fischer, Max Bear-lab and Quinlan-lab collaborations, notably He, Ray, Dennis, and Quinlan in 2007, showed that about ten days of darkness resets the composition of the adult rat's NMDA receptors toward a juvenile state, and that adult rats deprived from birth recovered vision in the deprived eye when dark exposure was followed by reopening of that eye.

The second method is environmental enrichment: housing animals in large cages with running wheels, toys, and social companions instead of standard bare cages.

Alessandro Sale, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues showed in 2007 that enriched adult amblyopic rats recovered acuity and ocular dominance, and that the effect worked through reduced cortical inhibition; later work in 2012 by Baroncelli and colleagues confirmed and extended the finding.

The third method is pharmacological: the antidepressant fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), meaning a drug that increases the availability of the chemical messenger serotonin.

Jose Fernando Maya Vetencourt, Eero Castren, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues reported in Science in 2008 that chronic fluoxetine restored juvenile-like ocular dominance plasticity in the adult rat visual cortex and enabled recovery from amblyopia, again with reduced inhibition and increased BDNF as the apparent route.

The fourth and most conceptually elegant method is interneuron transplantation: taking immature inhibitory neurons from the embryonic brain region called the medial ganglionic eminence and grafting them into an older cortex.

Derek Southwell, Michael Stryker, Arturo Alvarez-Buylla, and colleagues showed in 2010 that the transplanted young cells wired themselves in and opened a second window of ocular dominance plasticity in the host, timed not to the host's age but to the transplanted cells' own developmental age.

That experiment is the cleanest proof of the whole framework: the window travels with the inhibitory cells, exactly as the timer hypothesis of Section 15.1.1 predicts.

To these four, the recent literature adds a fifth animal thread: work from Gul Dolen's laboratory, discussed in Section 15.3.2, reporting that psychedelic drugs reopen a critical period for social reward learning in mice.

The animal record, in short, is robust, replicated, and mechanistically coherent, and nothing in the sceptical sections that follow disputes it.

15.3.2 The thin human translation record: the valproate absolute-pitch study, the failed fluoxetine amblyopia trials, the preclinical psychedelic work

The human record is a different story, and this book tells it at full length precisely because the animal story is so persuasive.

Exhibit one is the valproate study.

Valproate is an epilepsy and mood-stabilising drug that, among other actions, inhibits histone deacetylase (HDAC), an enzyme that helps keep genes packed away and silent; inhibiting it loosens gene regulation in ways proposed to favour plasticity.

Judit Gervain, Takao Hensch, Allan Young, and colleagues published a study in 2013 in which young adult men took valproate or placebo for two weeks while training on pitch-naming, testing whether the drug could reopen the childhood window for absolute pitch, the rare ability to name a musical note without a reference.

The valproate group scored significantly better than the placebo group on the pitch test.

The study's own authors called it a proof-of-concept, and the limitations are substantial: 24 participants, a modest behavioural effect far short of genuine absolute pitch, no direct measure of brain plasticity, and, more than a decade later, no published large replication.

This corpus therefore records the valproate finding as small and unreplicated: a genuinely interesting first result, not an established fact.

Exhibit two is fluoxetine, the strongest animal result put to the fairest human test.

Two randomised controlled trials asked whether fluoxetine could boost recovery in adult amblyopia.

A Finnish multicentre trial reported by Huttunen and colleagues in 2018 gave 42 adults with amblyopia ten weeks of fluoxetine or placebo alongside daily computerised perceptual training and patching; both groups improved from the training, and fluoxetine added nothing statistically distinguishable from placebo.

A separate randomised trial reported by Sharif and colleagues in 2019 in the journal Eye treated amblyopic patients aged 10 to 40 with fluoxetine or placebo alongside occlusion, and reported some greater improvement with the drug, but the study had methodological limitations and the field has not treated it as a rescue of the hypothesis.

A further placebo-controlled study posted by Lagas and colleagues similarly found no fluoxetine advantage on visual function.

So the headline animal result, juvenile plasticity restored by an ordinary antidepressant, failed the best-controlled human test so far, and this corpus records that failure plainly.

Exhibit three is the psychedelic work, which must be described with its species attached.

In 2019 Romain Nardou, Gul Dolen, and colleagues reported in Nature that a single dose of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) reopened a critical period for social reward learning in adult mice, acting through the hormone oxytocin in a reward region called the nucleus accumbens.

In 2023 the same group reported in Nature that a whole family of psychedelic and related drugs, including psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), ketamine, and ibogaine, reopened the same mouse window for durations ranging from about two days to about four weeks, with evidence pointing to reorganisation of the extracellular matrix, the same class of structure as the perineuronal nets of Section 15.2.1.

These are elegant, influential experiments, and they are experiments in mice.

Human trials of psychedelics for psychiatric conditions exist, but no human study has yet demonstrated that these drugs reopen a developmental critical period in people; the critical-period framing of psychedelic therapy is, as of this writing, a preclinical hypothesis.

15.3.3 Why this corpus reports that record as thin rather than promising

A reader may wonder why this book chooses the word thin when so many popular accounts choose the word promising, and the choice deserves a stated justification.

First, count the completed successes: the number of adequately powered, replicated human trials demonstrating reopening of a developmental critical period is, at present, zero.

The valproate study is small and unreplicated; the best fluoxetine trial was negative; the psychedelic work has not yet been tested against a critical-period endpoint in humans.

Second, the base rates are unforgiving: most interventions that work in rodents fail in human trials, across all of medicine, and plasticity drugs have no exemption from that record; fluoxetine is the cautionary example inside this very field.

Third, the brakes exist for reasons.

The stability of the adult brain is not a design flaw; it protects identity, memory, and hard-won skill, and an intervention strong enough to reopen deep windows is strong enough to destabilise things worth keeping, a risk that rodent acuity measures barely probe.

Fourth, the history of this exact topic argues for caution in language: the strict claims of Lorenz softened under testing, the age 25 brain-maturation claim in another part of this corpus dissolved into a study-design artefact, and the 17.4-year language cutoff of Chapter 13 is contested by reanalysis; fields that inherit dramatic claims do well to under-promise.

None of this is pessimism about the science.

The animal work is among the most beautiful in modern neuroscience, the mechanisms are real, and it is entirely possible that a validated human reopening therapy will exist within the working lives of this book's younger readers.

But a record is what has happened, not what may happen, and the record in humans is thin.

When it thickens, a future edition of this corpus should say so with the same bluntness.


CHAPTER 16. SPONTANEOUS ACTIVITY AND ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT REFINEMENT (CORE)

The previous chapters described windows during which experience tunes the brain, which raises a puzzle: much of the brain's precise wiring is laid down before there is any experience at all.

The eyes are wired to the brain in an orderly map before they open; the ear drives its brain targets before it can hear.

This chapter explains the resolution: before the senses work, the developing nervous system generates its own internal test patterns, waves of spontaneous activity, and uses them to rehearse and refine its wiring.

The story matters because it dissolves the crude nature-versus-nurture split: genes build a rough draft, self-generated activity edits it, and experience performs the final polish, all using the same underlying plasticity rules.

16.1 Activity before experience

The discovery that the silent, unopened sensory organs of the fetus are in fact electrically active was one of the great surprises of late twentieth century neuroscience.

This section describes the two best-understood cases, the retina and the cochlea, and the traces this activity leaves in the brain recordings of premature infants.

16.1.1 Retinal waves and their stages

The retina is the sheet of light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye, and its output cells, the retinal ganglion cells, send the eye's only messages to the brain.

In 1991 Carla Shatz, Rachel Wong, Markus Meister, and Denis Baylor, recording from developing retinas with arrays of electrodes, confirmed a remarkable prediction: long before vision begins, retinal ganglion cells fire in coordinated bursts that sweep across the retina like slow ripples on a pond, at intervals of roughly one to two minutes.

These retinal waves occur in the womb in humans and before eye-opening in mice, whose eyes open around postnatal day 13 or 14.

The waves come in three stages, driven by different machinery as the retina matures.

Stage one waves, in the mouse occurring before birth, are carried by direct electrical connections between cells called gap junctions.

Stage two waves, from around birth to about postnatal day 10 in the mouse, are the classic waves: they are driven by a transient network of cells called starburst amacrine cells releasing acetylcholine, the same messenger molecule that appeared as a plasticity signal in Chapter 15, and they propagate as well-defined travelling fronts.

Stage three waves, from about postnatal day 10 until the eyes open, are driven by glutamate, the brain's main excitatory messenger, released by the retina's bipolar cells, and they carry additional structure, including a bias to travel in the direction that, after eye opening, will correspond to the visual motion produced by moving forward.

The waves have exactly the statistical properties a self-organising wiring system needs: neighbouring cells fire together within a wave, so correlation encodes neighbourhood, and the two eyes wave independently, so correlation also encodes eye identity.

In other words, the fetal retina broadcasts a structured test pattern that tells the brain, without any light, which fibres come from neighbouring points in space and which fibres come from which eye.

16.1.2 The causal tests: wave-deficient mice and degraded maps

Correlation is not causation, and the field spent the 1990s and 2000s testing whether the waves actually instruct wiring.

The workhorse was the beta2 knockout mouse, an animal genetically lacking the beta2 subunit of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the receptor through which stage two waves propagate.

In these mice, normal stage two waves are absent or severely abnormal, while the retina and eyes are otherwise largely intact.

The consequences are exactly what the test-pattern theory predicts.

First, eye-specific segregation fails: in normal animals, the inputs from the two eyes sort into separate territories in the lateral geniculate nucleus, the visual relay station in the thalamus, the brain's central switchboard; in beta2-deficient mice, studied by Marla Feller, Michael Crair, and colleagues in the 2000s, the two eyes' inputs remain intermingled.

Second, the retinotopic map degrades: retinotopy is the orderly arrangement by which neighbouring points on the retina connect to neighbouring points in the brain, and in wave-deficient mice the terminal branches of retinal axons remain too large and too scattered, producing a blurred map in the superior colliculus, a midbrain visual centre, and in the cortex.

Third, timed pharmacological experiments, blocking or altering waves with drugs during defined windows in ferrets and mice, showed that the refinement depends on activity during a specific early period, a critical period that runs entirely before vision.

Important controls sharpened the interpretation: manipulations that silence retinal activity entirely, and clever experiments that preserved the amount of activity while scrambling its spatial pattern, indicated that it is the structure of the waves, their correlations, and not mere activity as a growth nutrient, that carries the wiring information.

Debate along the way, notably a 2003 to 2005 exchange over whether beta2 mice truly lacked waves or had altered ones, ended with the field's current consensus: patterned spontaneous retinal activity is causally required for eye-specific segregation and for the fine refinement of retinotopic maps.

The general conclusion reaches far beyond vision: the developing brain does not wait passively for the world; it simulates input in order to wire itself.

16.1.3 Cochlear spontaneous activity and the preterm delta brushes

The auditory system runs the same strategy with different hardware.

The cochlea is the spiral, fluid-filled hearing organ of the inner ear, and its inner hair cells are the sensors that convert sound vibrations into neural signals.

In 2007 Nicolas Tritsch, Dwight Bergles, and colleagues at Johns Hopkins reported in Nature the origin of spontaneous auditory activity: before hearing onset, which in rodents is around postnatal day 12, the immature cochlea contains a temporary structure called Kolliker's organ, whose supporting cells periodically release the chemical messenger adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

Each ATP release depolarises nearby inner hair cells, which fire bursts of signals into the auditory nerve, so the silent ear sends rhythmic volleys into the brain, organised along the cochlea's frequency axis.

This activity supports the survival of auditory neurons and the refinement and maintenance of tonotopic maps, the auditory equivalent of retinotopy, in which neighbouring frequencies connect to neighbouring brain locations.

Humans give us a window onto this hidden stage through premature infants.

Electroencephalography (EEG), the recording of the brain's electrical rhythms through the scalp, shows that preterm infants display a signature pattern called the delta brush: a slow wave, at roughly 0.3 to 1.5 cycles per second, with a rapid oscillation of roughly 8 to 25 cycles per second riding on top.

Delta brushes appear from around 28 to 30 weeks of postmenstrual age, peak in abundance around 32 to 35 weeks, and disappear around term, at 38 to 42 weeks.

Work by Rustem Khazipov, Milh, and colleagues showed that delta brushes can be triggered by spontaneous fetal movements and by touch, and human recordings by Chipaux, Kaminska, and colleagues showed that in the preterm infant they can be evoked in the corresponding sensory cortex by stimulation, marking them as the human face of activity-dependent map formation.

The delta brush is thought to reflect activity involving the subplate, a temporary layer of early-born neurons beneath the developing cortex that serves as a waiting room and teaching scaffold for incoming connections before dissolving as maturation completes.

The practical resonance is real, though it must be stated carefully: neonatal intensive care units monitor these rhythms because their presence and symmetry index the health of a developing brain, and research continues into how the sensory environment of preterm care interacts with this normally womb-enclosed stage of development.

16.2 The two-step wiring rule

How does an axon growing from the eye find its correct millimetre of target tissue among millions of wrong ones?

The modern answer is a two-step rule, division of labour between chemistry and activity, and this section presents each step in turn.

16.2.1 Molecular gradients rough in the map

The first step is chemical, and its intellectual father is Roger Sperry.

Working with frogs and fish in the 1940s and 1950s, Sperry cut the optic nerve, sometimes rotating the eye, and found that the regrowing fibres returned to their original brain targets, producing, after eye rotation, a world seen upside down that the animal never corrected.

From this he proposed the chemoaffinity hypothesis in its mature 1963 form: growing axons and their targets carry matching chemical labels, arranged in gradients, so that each axon can read its address from the concentration of label it encounters.

The labels were found three decades later: the Eph receptors, a family of proteins on cell surfaces, and their partners the ephrins, discovered in the retinotectal system by Friedrich Bonhoeffer's and John Flanagan's laboratories in the mid 1990s.

In the visual system the arrangement is a textbook countergradient: retinal ganglion cells express EphA receptors in a gradient across the retina, their target expresses ephrin-A ligands in a gradient across its surface, and because ephrin-A binding repels EphA-bearing growth cones, each axon settles at the position where the repulsion balances, which lays neighbouring retinal cells into neighbouring target positions.

A second, independent gradient system organises the perpendicular axis, so the target receives a two-dimensional address grid from two overlaid chemistries.

Elegant genetic experiments by Greg Lemke, David Feldheim, and colleagues, adding or removing EphA receptors in subsets of cells, showed that axons read relative rather than absolute signal levels, competing with their neighbours for position rather than obeying fixed coordinates.

The crucial limitation is precision: gradients are analogue and noisy, and in mutant and computational analyses the chemical step by itself produces only a coarse map, with each axon's terminal branches spread over a region much larger than its final territory.

Chemistry gets every axon to roughly the right neighbourhood; it cannot, alone, put it in the right house.

16.2.2 Correlated activity sharpens it

The second step uses the spontaneous activity of Section 16.1 to finish the job.

Once axons have arrived in their approximately correct neighbourhoods, their terminals and their target neurons begin adjusting connection strengths according to correlation: inputs that fire together onto a target are kept and strengthened, and inputs whose firing does not match their neighbours are weakened and withdrawn.

Retinal waves supply exactly the needed information, because within a wave, neighbouring retinal cells fire within moments of each other, so an axon terminal sitting among true neighbours experiences agreement, and a terminal that has strayed too far experiences constant disagreement.

Over days of waves, this pruning-by-correlation shrinks each axon's terminal territory to a fraction of its initial spread, converting the coarse chemical map into a sharp one.

The same rule, applied to the independence of the two eyes' waves, drives eye-specific segregation: terminals from the same eye agree with each other and disagree with the other eye's terminals, so intermingled territory becomes sorted territory.

The evidence that this step is genuinely activity-dependent is the wave-deficient phenotype of Section 16.1.2, and the evidence that it is correlation, not activity volume, that matters comes from the pattern-scrambling experiments noted there.

The two steps are not fully separable in time, and the modern view, supported by computational models from groups including Geoffrey Goodhill's, is of a collaboration in which gradients, activity, and axon-to-axon competition operate together, with activity dominating the final refinement.

The two-step rule generalises across the brain: rough in the connections by molecular address, then refine by correlated use, appears in the auditory system, the touch map, and, with experience replacing spontaneous activity, in the later tuning of every sensory cortex.

It is worth pausing on the economy of the design: a genome of some twenty thousand genes cannot specify the brain's roughly one hundred trillion connections individually, but it does not need to, because it only has to build gradient makers and correlation detectors, and let the wiring finish itself.

16.3 Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity in development

The refinement just described needs machinery: molecular devices that detect correlation and translate it into stronger or weaker connections, plus stabilising systems that keep the whole network from running away.

This section introduces the coincidence detector, the timing rules, and the stability problem, in their developmental setting.

16.3.1 The coincidence detector and the developmental receptor subunit switch

The central device is the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, a protein channel found at excitatory synapses, named after the laboratory chemical used to identify it.

The NMDA receptor has a famous quirk: at the neuron's resting voltage its channel is plugged by a magnesium ion, and the plug pops out only when the receiving cell is already electrically active, so the channel passes current only when the sending side releases its messenger and the receiving side is depolarised at the same time.

That conjunction makes it a coincidence detector, a molecular and gate that reports exactly the events Hebbian plasticity cares about: this input was active while this neuron was active.

When the coincidence occurs, calcium flows through the receptor into the synapse, and calcium is the trigger for the biochemical cascades that strengthen or weaken the connection.

Development retunes this detector as circuits mature, through the receptor subunit switch.

NMDA receptors are assembled from parts, and early in development most cortical receptors contain the subunit called GluN2B, historically named NR2B, which closes slowly and therefore holds a generous, wide window of time over which two events still count as coincident.

As circuits mature, and driven by activity and sensory experience, receptors containing GluN2A, historically NR2A, progressively take over; these close faster and enforce a stricter definition of coincidence.

The switch was characterised in developing cortex and thalamus through the 1990s and 2000s, including work by Carew, Crair, Malinow-adjacent groups and, in the visual cortex specifically, by studies showing that the GluN2A to GluN2B ratio tracks visual experience, rising with normal rearing, and reversing toward the juvenile state after dark exposure, which is one reason dark exposure reopens plasticity in the experiments of Chapter 15.

The developmental logic is intuitive: a young network learning its first structure from slow, sweeping spontaneous waves benefits from a forgiving coincidence window, while a mature network parsing fast real-world signals needs precise timing, so the brain literally swaps the parts in its coincidence detectors as its data changes.

The switch is also a hinge in disease discussions: because the NMDA receptor is where wiring rules meet molecular biology, mutations affecting its subunits appear repeatedly in studies of intellectual disability and epilepsy, a theme other chapters of this corpus take up.

16.3.2 Spike timing in developing circuits

A spike is the brief electrical impulse a neuron fires, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity is the refinement rule stated at millisecond resolution.

The canonical experiments, by Henry Markram and Bert Sakmann in 1997 in cortical slices and by Guo-qiang Bi and Mu-ming Poo in 1998 in cultured neurons, showed that the direction of change at a synapse depends on the order of firing: if the input spikes shortly before the receiving neuron, within roughly 20 milliseconds, the connection strengthens, and if the input spikes just after, the connection weakens.

Before means predictive and after means redundant, so the rule automatically favours inputs that predict their target's firing, refining Hebb's fire together, wire together into fire just before, wire stronger.

Development is where this rule was first shown to sculpt a living, intact system.

In 2002 Yang Dan and colleagues demonstrated it in the developing frog visual system, and in a memorable companion experiment showed that repeatedly moving a bar across the young frog's vision in one direction shifted the tuning of its brain cells within minutes, a real-world training effect obeying the timing rule.

In the developing retinotectal and retinogeniculate pathways, modelling and experiment together indicate that spike-timing rules can read the temporal structure of retinal waves, using the wave's slow sweep to translate arrival-time differences into strengthen-or-weaken decisions, which is one proposed mechanism for the direction-selective wiring seeded by stage three waves.

The timing rule is not universal or fixed: its window and even its sign vary across synapse types, and it changes over development, with some cortical synapses showing wide, forgiving windows early, consistent with the GluN2B story of the previous section, that sharpen as circuits mature.

Inhibition, once again, is a timekeeper: the maturation of the inhibitory interneurons of Chapter 15 tightens the timing of excitatory firing, and by doing so effectively sharpens the operative plasticity windows, which links the molecular trigger of the critical period to the millisecond rules that do its work.

For the beginner, the essential picture is this: the developing brain is not just noting which cells are active together, it is timing them against each other with millisecond stopwatches, and promoting the connections that consistently arrive on the predictive side of the race.

16.3.3 Synaptic scaling and the stability problem

Hebbian rules have a built-in instability that any engineer would flag immediately.

Strengthening a connection makes the receiving neuron fire more, which produces more coincidences, which strengthens the connection further: a positive feedback loop that, unchecked, would drive every circuit to saturation or silence.

The developing brain, which is simultaneously adding synapses at an enormous rate, growing its cells, and running Hebbian refinement, faces this stability problem in its most extreme form.

The counterweight is homeostatic plasticity, and its best-studied form is synaptic scaling, discovered by Gina Turrigiano, Sacha Nelson, and colleagues, and reported in Nature in 1998.

Recording from cultured cortical neurons, they found that silencing a network's activity for one to two days caused every excitatory synapse on a neuron to strengthen, and artificially elevating activity caused every synapse to weaken, in each case multiplicatively, with each synapse scaled by roughly the same factor.

Multiplicative scaling is the crucial elegance: because every synapse is multiplied by the same factor, the relative differences written by Hebbian learning are preserved, so the neuron can turn its overall volume up or down without erasing what it has learned.

The picture is a neuron with a thermostat: each cell appears to have a target activity range, senses its own average firing through slow calcium signals, and adjusts its total synaptic weight to stay in range, over hours to days rather than the seconds of Hebbian change.

The molecular machinery overlaps with the developmental cast we have already met: scaling up in response to inactivity requires the glial signal tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), described in Chapter 14, and the immediate-early gene Arc, among others, and BDNF signalling participates in the downward direction.

The difference in speed between fast Hebbian learning and slow homeostatic correction is not a flaw but a requirement: theoretical work shows that a homeostat as fast as the learning it constrains would fight and erase that learning, so the brain runs a quick sculptor and a slow stabiliser in deliberate tandem.

Developmentally, scaling and its relatives are believed to keep activity in a workable range while synapse numbers explode in infancy and are pruned in adolescence, and the two-phase ocular dominance story of Chapter 14, depression first, homeostatic recovery second, shows the sculptor and the stabiliser taking turns on a timescale of days in a single developmental episode.

The stability problem also frames disease hypotheses: proposals that some developmental disorders involve failures of homeostatic regulation, leaving networks over-excitable or under-responsive, are an active research area, treated with appropriate caution elsewhere in this corpus.

16.4 Cross-modal plasticity

The final section of this chapter asks what happens to a stretch of cortex when the input it was built for never arrives.

The answer, that it is recruited by other senses, is among the most vivid demonstrations of both the power and the limits of developmental plasticity.

16.4.1 Blindness, Braille, and the recruitment of visual cortex

Braille is the tactile writing system of raised dot patterns read with the fingertips, invented by Louis Braille in the 1820s.

In 1996 Norihiro Sadato, Mark Hallett, and colleagues used positron emission tomography (PET), an imaging method that tracks blood flow as a proxy for brain activity, to scan people blind from early life while they read Braille.

The result overturned textbook assumptions: the primary visual cortex, the region that in sighted people processes input from the eyes, lit up during Braille reading in the blind participants, while in sighted controls the same region quieted during touch tasks.

Correlation again demanded a causal test, and Leonardo Cohen, Hallett, and colleagues provided it in 1997 using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique that briefly and safely disrupts a small patch of cortex with a magnetic pulse through the scalp.

Disrupting the occipital, meaning visual, cortex of early-blind readers induced errors and distorted perceptions in their Braille reading, while the same stimulation did not impair touch in sighted people: the recruited visual cortex was not idling, it was doing the work.

Later imaging showed the recruitment extends beyond touch: the visual cortex of early-blind people responds during Braille and spoken language tasks, verbal memory tasks, and sound localisation, and work by Amir Amedi and colleagues linked stronger occipital recruitment to better verbal memory performance.

Timing matters in exactly the way this chapter predicts: recruitment is strongest and most functionally important in people blind from birth or early childhood, weaker and different in character in those who lose sight as adults, indicating a sensitive period for large-scale cross-modal takeover.

A striking natural experiment underlines the point: case reports describe an early-blind Braille expert who lost Braille reading ability after a stroke that damaged the occipital cortex, despite intact fingers and intact touch sensation.

Two framings of these findings coexist in the literature: one emphasises rewiring, new roles for visual cortex, and the other, associated with the metamodal view of Alvaro Pascual-Leone and colleagues, argues the region was never strictly visual but was always a processor of fine spatial structure that ordinarily wins visual input, and simply accepts the best available input when vision is absent.

On either framing, the practical conclusion stands: the cortex of a person blind from early life is not missing a working region, it has reallocated one, which is a central fact for education, for rehabilitation engineering, and for how this book asks readers to think about disability, as difference in organisation rather than simple absence.

16.4.2 Deafness and the reorganisation of auditory cortex

The mirror-image story unfolds in deafness.

Imaging studies of people deaf from early life show that regions of the auditory cortex, the hearing areas of the temporal lobe, the brain region beneath the temples, respond to visual events, particularly to motion and to sign language, and to touch.

The most rigorous causal evidence comes from congenitally deaf cats, a natural deaf strain studied by Stephen Lomber, Andrej Kral, and colleagues, reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2010.

Deaf cats outperform hearing cats on specific visual tasks, namely detecting motion and localising stimuli in the visual periphery, and Lomber's team showed by reversibly cooling, and thus temporarily switching off, specific patches of deaf auditory cortex that each enhanced visual ability depended on a specific reassigned auditory region: cooling it abolished the advantage, and cooling the same region in hearing cats did nothing to vision.

This established that cross-modal recruitment is functional, specific, and beneficial: the deprived cortex does not decay, it is redeployed, and the redeployment respects the region's original computational speciality, with areas formerly serving auditory localisation now serving visual localisation.

In deaf humans who sign, the recruitment interlocks with language: sign language activates the classic left-hemisphere language network much as speech does, and parts of auditory cortex respond to observed signing, a reminder that the brain's language system is about structured meaning, not sound as such.

The clinical intersection is the cochlear implant, and it returns this chapter to the windows of Chapter 13.

Andrej Kral's animal work and human studies by Anu Sharma and by Dora Hermes-adjacent electrophysiology groups indicate that when auditory cortex has been extensively colonised by vision during years of early deafness, the capacity of implant-delivered hearing to reclaim it diminishes, which is part of why early implantation, within the sensitive period of roughly the first one to three and a half years for the central auditory system, predicts better spoken-language outcomes on average.

The details remain under active study, and the simple story of cross-modal takeover as purely an obstacle has been complicated: studies by Anderson and colleagues in 2017 found that some visual recruitment of auditory cortex in implant users correlates with better audiovisual speech understanding, suggesting the reorganised cortex can be an ally, integrating lip reading with sound, rather than only a squatter.

For deaf children whose families choose sign language, the same science carries a symmetrical message recorded in Section 13.2.3: the developing language network cares about receiving a full language in the window, and a visual language serves that need fully.

Cross-modal plasticity thus closes this chapter where it began: the brain wires itself by activity, whatever the source of the activity, using spontaneous waves before the senses work, sensory experience during the windows, and, when a sense never arrives, the richest remaining input it can find.

CHAPTER 17. THE PRUNING MACHINERY (CORE)

A young brain makes far more connections between its nerve cells than the adult brain will keep.

This chapter is about the machinery that removes the extras, a process called synaptic pruning, where a synapse is the tiny junction through which one nerve cell passes signals to another.

Pruning sounds destructive, but it is one of the most constructive things a brain does, because a circuit sculpted down to its strongest and most useful connections works faster and more precisely than a tangle of every connection ever tried.

The surprise of the last two decades is that much of this sculpting is done not by the nerve cells themselves but by the brain's resident immune cells and support cells, which physically eat the connections that are marked for removal.

Understanding who does the eating, how a connection gets marked, and what happens when the marking system goes wrong turns out to matter for conditions as different as schizophrenia and autism.


17.1 The cellular gardeners

The cells that carry out pruning are best pictured as gardeners moving through a hedge, snipping some branches and leaving others.

Two cell types do most of the work: microglia, which are the brain's own immune cells, and astrocytes, which are star-shaped support cells that feed and regulate nerve cells.

This section introduces each gardener and the chemical conversation that tells it where to snip.


17.1.1 Microglial engulfment and the fractalkine signal

Microglia are small, mobile cells that patrol the brain constantly, and for a century they were thought of mainly as damage-response cells that cleaned up after injury or infection.

The modern view began to form around 2011 and 2012, when time-lapse imaging and electron microscopy showed microglia in healthy young brains with fragments of synapses inside their bellies, caught in the act of engulfment, which simply means swallowing material whole.

A landmark study by Dorothy Schafer, Beth Stevens, and colleagues in 2012 watched this happen in the developing visual pathway of the mouse, in the connection between the eye and a relay station called the lateral geniculate nucleus, and showed that microglia were eating synaptic material during the exact developmental window when that pathway is being refined.

One of the signals that guides microglia to their work is fractalkine, a chemical messenger made by nerve cells, which is detected by a receptor on microglia called chemokine receptor CX3CR1, where a receptor is a molecular antenna on a cell's surface that responds to one specific signal.

Mice engineered to lack the fractalkine receptor show delayed synaptic pruning in early life, with too many immature connections lingering in the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that is central to memory, in work associated with Rosa Paolicelli and Cornelius Gross in 2011.

The fractalkine system seems to act partly as a recruiting and positioning signal, telling microglia where nerve cells are and drawing them into circuits at the right time, rather than marking individual synapses for death.

An honest caveat belongs here: fractalkine signalling is not required for every pruning job in the brain, because for example the removal of surplus climbing-fibre inputs in the cerebellum, the balance and coordination structure at the back of the brain, proceeds normally in mice lacking the receptor.

The picture the field now holds is of multiple partly overlapping pruning systems, each dominant in particular circuits and particular windows, rather than one universal mechanism.


17.1.2 Complement tagging: C1q and C3 as eat-me labels

If microglia are the gardeners, something must mark which branches to cut, and the best-understood marking system is borrowed from the immune system and is called complement.

Complement is a family of blood proteins, discovered over a century ago, whose day job in the body is to stick to bacteria and dying cells and thereby label them for destruction by immune cells, a labelling process immunologists call opsonisation, which is simply the attaching of an eat-me tag.

In 2007 Beth Stevens, working with Ben Barres at Stanford, made the startling discovery that the first protein of this cascade, complement component 1q (C1q), decorates synapses in the developing mouse visual system, and that mice lacking C1q fail to prune the eye-to-brain pathway properly.

C1q sits at the top of a chain reaction: its binding triggers the deposition of a second protein, complement component 3 (C3), on the synapse, and fragments of C3 are recognised by a receptor on microglia called complement receptor 3.

The 2012 study by Schafer and Stevens closed the loop by showing that microglia use exactly this receptor to engulf synaptic material in the developing visual pathway, and that blocking any link in the chain, C1q, C3, or the microglial receptor, leaves the circuit under-pruned and imprecisely wired.

The elegance of the system is that the brain reuses an ancient piece of immune machinery for a completely different purpose, turning a bacteria-labelling kit into a synapse-editing kit.

Here too the field has learned to add caveats, because later work found brain regions and pathways where refinement proceeds normally without C1q, so complement tagging is a major pruning mechanism but not the only one, and its importance varies by circuit and by developmental window.


17.1.3 Astrocytic phagocytosis and the don't-eat-me signals

Astrocytes, the abundant star-shaped support cells of the brain, turn out to be gardeners too.

In 2013 Won-Suk Chung, again from the Barres laboratory, showed that astrocytes actively swallow synapses in the developing mouse visual system using two engulfment receptors called MEGF10 and MERTK, and that mice lacking both receptors keep too many weak connections.

The word for this swallowing is phagocytosis, which literally means cell eating, and it is the same act microglia perform, so the developing brain has at least two independent cell types eating synapses at once.

Later work from the same line of research, published in 2020, showed that astrocytes continue to eat synapses in the adult hippocampus, and that this ongoing housekeeping is needed for normal memory circuitry, so pruning is not only a childhood event.

Because indiscriminate eating would be catastrophic, the system also has protective don't-eat-me signals, and the clearest of these is a surface protein called cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47).

Work by Emily Lehrman and colleagues in Beth Stevens's laboratory in 2018 showed that CD47 sits preferentially on more active synapses, that it engages a receptor on microglia called signal regulatory protein alpha which tells the microglial cell to stand down, and that mice lacking CD47 over-prune and end up with too few synapses.

So the full picture is a two-sided ledger: eat-me tags such as complement and exposed membrane signals push toward removal, don't-eat-me tags such as CD47 push toward protection, and the fate of each synapse is read off the balance.


17.2 The selection rule

Knowing who eats and what the tags are still leaves the deepest question: how does the brain decide which synapses deserve the eat-me tag in the first place.

This section states the selection rule that half a century of work has converged on, which is that use protects and disuse condemns.


17.2.1 Activity dependence: the weaker input is eaten

The rule was first worked out at the simplest synapse in the body, the neuromuscular junction, which is the connection between a nerve fibre and a muscle fibre.

In newborn mammals each muscle fibre receives inputs from several motor nerve cells, but over the first weeks of life all but one are withdrawn, and classic experiments through the 1970s and 1980s, associated with researchers including Jeff Lichtman, showed that the inputs compete and that the more active input wins while the weaker is dismantled.

The same rule was then demonstrated inside the brain, most cleanly in the eye-to-brain pathway, where inputs from the two eyes initially overlap in the lateral geniculate nucleus and are then segregated into eye-specific territories.

The 2012 Schafer and Stevens experiment made the rule visible at the level of the eating itself: when activity in one eye was drugged down, microglia preferentially engulfed the synapses of the quieter eye, and when one eye was made more active, its synapses were spared, so the weaker input is literally eaten.

The molecular translation of the rule is now partly readable, because activity appears to control the tags: less active synapses accumulate eat-me signals such as complement and externalised phosphatidylserine, a fat molecule that flips to a cell's outer surface as a distress flag, while more active synapses display protective CD47.

Spontaneous activity matters as much as experience here, because much of this competition happens before the eyes even open, driven by internally generated waves of activity sweeping across the retina, the light-sensing sheet at the back of the eye.

The beauty of the rule is that it lets experience write itself into anatomy without any overseer, because circuits that are used carry more traffic, more traffic means more protection and fewer tags, and so the wiring diagram gradually comes to mirror the statistics of the child's actual world.

One further honest note: the field still debates how the strength of a synapse is measured and compared at molecular resolution, and how punishment signals from winning inputs reach losing ones, so the rule is secure but its full mechanism is not.


17.3 The clinical shadows

A machine this powerful casts shadows, because a pruning system that runs too hot or too cold could remove connections a person needs or leave in place connections that clutter the circuit.

This section briefly names the two most discussed clinical shadows and points to the chapters where they are treated in full.


17.3.1 Over-pruning and the complement story in schizophrenia, held for Chapter 52

Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric condition, typically emerging in the late teens or twenties, whose features can include hallucinations, delusions, and difficulties with thinking and motivation.

Post-mortem studies have long reported that people with schizophrenia have fewer dendritic spines, the tiny protrusions on nerve cells where most synapses land, especially in the prefrontal cortex, the front-most part of the brain's outer layer that supports planning and reasoning.

Because the illness so often begins during adolescence, exactly when the cortex undergoes its heaviest wave of synapse elimination, Irwin Feinberg proposed as long ago as 1982 that schizophrenia might reflect pruning gone too far.

The genetic era gave that old idea a mechanism, when Aswin Sekar, Steven McCarroll, and colleagues showed in 2016 that the strongest common genetic risk signal for schizophrenia includes variation in the complement component 4 (C4) gene, and that risk versions of the gene produce more C4 protein, which feeds the same complement tagging cascade described above.

The inference that excess complement drives excess pruning in patients is plausible, is supported by mouse and cell-culture experiments, and yet remains an inference rather than a demonstrated fact in living human brains, and it is examined with full care in Chapter 52.


17.3.2 Under-pruning claims in autism, held for Chapter 49

Autism is a developmental condition, present from early life, characterised by differences in social communication alongside focused interests and repetitive behaviours, and it is discussed in this book within a neurodiversity frame that treats it as a difference to be understood rather than simply a defect to be corrected.

The mirror-image claim to the schizophrenia story is that some autistic brains may prune too little, and its best-known evidence is a 2014 post-mortem study by Guomei Tang and David Sulzer, which reported higher dendritic spine density in temporal-lobe cortex from autistic donors and linked it to reduced autophagy, a cellular self-cleaning process.

Supporting threads include the observation that a minority of autistic children show early brain overgrowth, and mouse models of autism-related genes in which spine elimination is reduced.

The honest status of the claim is that it rests on small post-mortem samples, that brain tissue studies of autism are notoriously variable, and that autism is so genetically heterogeneous that no single synaptic story will cover it, so under-pruning is a live hypothesis for some forms of autism rather than an established account of the condition, and the full evidence is weighed in Chapter 49.



================================================================================

PART FIVE. GENES, ENVIRONMENT, AND EPIGENETICS

================================================================================

CHAPTER 18. THE BEHAVIOURAL GENETICS OF DEVELOPMENT (APPARATUS)

This chapter changes altitude, moving from cells and synapses up to whole populations of children, and asks how much of the variation among children, in temperament, in ability, in vulnerability, travels with their genes.

The field that asks this question is behavioural genetics, which uses natural experiments such as twins and adoption to separate the influence of inherited deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecule that carries the genetic instructions in every cell, from the influence of upbringing.

Its findings are among the most replicated in all of psychology and also among the most misunderstood, so this chapter states both the findings and the ways they are commonly misread.

It matters for a book about brain development because every developmental mechanism described elsewhere in these pages runs on genetic parts, in environments the child did not choose, and the two threads cannot be understood separately.


18.1 The designs and the laws

Behavioural genetics rests on a small number of clever research designs and a small number of extremely well-replicated conclusions, sometimes stated as laws.

This section explains the designs, the main objection to them, and the two-sided finding that everything is heritable and nothing is fully heritable.


18.1.1 Twin and adoption logic and the equal-environments debate

The twin design compares identical twins, who develop from one fertilised egg and share essentially all their DNA, with fraternal twins, who develop from two eggs and share on average half of the DNA that varies between people.

Both kinds of twins share a womb, a household, and usually a school, so if identical twins resemble each other more than fraternal twins do on some trait, the extra resemblance is attributed to their extra genetic sharing.

From that comparison researchers compute heritability, which is the proportion of the variation in a trait across a particular population that is statistically associated with genetic differences, and it is worth pausing on that definition because heritability describes differences between people, never the makeup of one person, and it is a property of a population in a time and place, not a fixed constant of nature.

The adoption design uses a different natural experiment, asking whether adopted children resemble their birth parents, who gave them genes but not a home, or their adoptive parents, who gave them a home but not genes, and for most psychological traits the resemblance to birth parents is the stronger by adulthood.

The main objection to the twin design is called the equal-environments assumption, which is the assumption that identical twins are not treated more similarly than fraternal twins in ways that affect the trait being studied, and critics have pointed out that identical twins are in fact dressed alike more often, confused for one another, and encouraged toward similarity.

Defenders reply with several kinds of checks: twins misclassified about their own type resemble each other according to their true genetic type rather than their believed type, degree of similar treatment within pairs does not predict degree of trait similarity well, and identical twins reared apart in different families, studied most famously in the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart led by Thomas Bouchard from 1979, end up about as similar on many traits as identical twins reared together.

The fair summary of the debate is that the equal-environments assumption is probably violated a little for some traits, which would inflate heritability estimates somewhat, but that the broad conclusions survive because they are confirmed by adoption studies, by reared-apart twins, and now by DNA-based methods that need no twins at all.


18.1.2 The replicated findings: everything is heritable, nothing is fully heritable

In 2000 Eric Turkheimer condensed decades of results into what he called the three laws of behaviour genetics, and the first law is that all human behavioural traits are heritable.

The word all is barely an exaggeration, because intelligence, personality, mental illness risk, reading ability, how much television people watch, and even the likelihood of divorce all show heritability in twin and adoption studies, with a sweeping 2015 meta-analysis by Tinca Polderman and Danielle Posthuma, covering fifty years of twin studies of seventeen and a half thousand traits in over fourteen million twin pairs, finding an average heritability across all traits of about 49 percent.

The equally important mirror finding is that nothing psychological is fully heritable, because identical twins, sharing essentially all their DNA and usually a household too, are never perfectly identical in personality, ability, or mental health, so environment in the broadest sense always matters.

Turkheimer's second law states that the effect of being raised in the same family is smaller than the effect of genes for most traits, and the third law states that a substantial portion of variation is explained by neither genes nor shared family environment, falling instead to the puzzling category called non-shared environment, which includes everything from different friendships to different illnesses to plain developmental chance.

Two misreadings must be blocked at once.

Heritable does not mean unchangeable, because height is highly heritable yet average height rose dramatically across the twentieth century as nutrition improved, and the same logic applies to psychological traits.

And a small effect of shared family environment on adult outcomes does not mean parenting is irrelevant, because parents shape their children's languages, values, skills, safety, and daily experience of being loved, even where they do not much shift the child's rank order on standardised trait measures within a given society.


18.2 Heritability across age

One of the least intuitive discoveries in the field is that heritability is not constant across childhood but changes with age, and for intelligence it changes in the opposite direction to what almost everyone guesses.

This section describes that finding, the leading explanation for it, and the evidence that poverty can bend the pattern.


18.2.1 The Wilson effect: heritability of intelligence rising from childhood to adulthood

Most people assume that genes matter most in infancy and that experience takes over with age, but for measured intelligence the data say the reverse.

In longitudinal twin studies, the heritability of intelligence test scores is modest in early childhood, roughly in the region of 20 to 40 percent, rises through the school years and adolescence, and reaches something like 60 to 80 percent by early adulthood.

Meanwhile the influence of the shared family environment on those same scores, clearly present in early and middle childhood, shrinks with age until by early adulthood it accounts for perhaps a tenth of the variation.

Ronald Wilson documented the rising genetic pattern in the Louisville Twin Study in the 1970s and 1980s, tracking twins from infancy onward, and in 2013 Thomas Bouchard, surveying the accumulated twin and adoption evidence in the journal Twin Research and Human Genetics, proposed naming the phenomenon the Wilson effect in his honour, noting that heritability appears to plateau around 0.80 at about 18 to 20 years of age in the samples studied.

Two cautions keep the finding honest.

The high adult estimates come mostly from twin designs in relatively prosperous twentieth-century populations, and newer methods that estimate heritability directly from measured DNA in unrelated people yield lower figures, a gap known as missing heritability that is discussed in Chapter 19.

And a rising heritability of rank order does not mean environments stop mattering with age; it means that within the range of environments those populations actually provided, genetic differences increasingly predicted who scored higher than whom.


18.2.2 Niche-picking as the proposed mechanism

Why would genetic influence grow as a person ages, when no new genes are being added.

The leading explanation is called niche-picking, or active gene-environment correlation, an idea developed most influentially by Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney in a 1983 paper on how people make their own environments.

The proposal is that small initial genetically influenced differences in what a child finds easy and enjoyable lead the child to select, and to be offered, environments that match, so a child who takes early pleasure in reading haunts libraries, chooses bookish friends, and is handed harder books by delighted adults.

Each chosen environment then feeds the trait that did the choosing, so tiny initial differences are compounded, year after year, like interest on a deposit.

On this account, adult heritability is high not because genes act more strongly in adults but because adults have had two decades to build lives that echo and amplify their initial leanings, and the environment, far from opposing genetic influence, has become its instrument.

The idea also explains why shared family environment fades: as children gain freedom, the environments that matter are increasingly the ones they picked rather than the ones their parents imposed.

Niche-picking is a proposed mechanism rather than a demonstrated one, because directly catching the amplification loop in action is hard, but it is consistent with the age trends, with the finding that heritability estimates for adult traits partly reflect gene-environment correlation, and with everyday observation.


18.2.3 Socioeconomic moderation of heritability and its geography

Heritability, being a population statistic, can differ between populations, and the most discussed version of this is its possible dependence on poverty and wealth.

In 2003 Eric Turkheimer and colleagues analysed intelligence scores of seven-year-old twins from the National Collaborative Perinatal Project, an American cohort recruited in the 1960s that included many severely disadvantaged families, and reported a striking interaction: among the poorest families the heritability of the scores approached zero and shared environment dominated, while among affluent families the pattern reversed.

The intuitive reading is that genetic potential needs adequate conditions to express itself, so in environments of deprivation the environment's shortfalls swamp genetic differences, an idea often called the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis after earlier formulations by Sandra Scarr, in 1971, and David Rowe.

The finding, however, has a geography.

A 2016 meta-analysis by Elliot Tucker-Drob and Timothy Bates gathered the relevant studies and found that the interaction appears reliably in United States samples, where the moderation was modest but real, and essentially not at all in studies from Western Europe and Australia.

The favoured interpretation of that split is that countries with stronger safety nets, universal health care, and more equal schooling keep even their poorest children above the threshold where deprivation suppresses the expression of genetic differences, so the interaction is itself evidence that social policy changes what heritability is.

The honest summary is that socioeconomic moderation of heritability is real but context-bound, smaller than the dramatic 2003 estimates suggested, and a standing reminder that no heritability figure travels across societies unchanged.


18.3 Gene-environment interplay

The neat separation of genes and environments that the twin design assumes is, in real development, constantly breached, because genes and environments are correlated and may interact.

This section lays out the vocabulary of that interplay, tells the cautionary tale of the candidate-gene interaction era, and presents the orchid and dandelion idea in its current, chastened form.


18.3.1 Passive, evocative, and active correlation

Gene-environment correlation means that people's genetic makeups and their environments are not dealt independently, and the classic taxonomy, due to Robert Plomin, John DeFries, and John Loehlin in 1977 and elaborated by Scarr and McCartney in 1983, distinguishes three kinds.

Passive correlation arises because children receive both their genes and their early environment from the same parents, so a child of book-loving parents inherits whatever genetic leanings the parents carry and a house full of books, without doing anything at all.

Evocative correlation arises because the child's genetically influenced characteristics draw out responses from other people, so a sunny, easy baby is smiled at, talked to, and carried more, while an irritable baby may exhaust caregivers, and each child thereby receives a different environment partly because of who the child already is.

Active correlation is niche-picking itself, the older child and adult deliberately seeking environments that fit their leanings.

The developmental hypothesis attached to this taxonomy is that passive correlation dominates in infancy, evocative correlation operates throughout life, and active correlation grows as autonomy grows, which meshes with the rising heritability described earlier.

The practical sting is that these correlations complicate every naive causal claim in developmental science, because when children who are read to more become better readers, part of the association can run through the genes the readers and the read-to share, and modern designs, including adoption studies and the DNA-based methods of Chapter 19, exist largely to cut through this knot.


18.3.2 The candidate-gene interaction era and its collapse

The brief tells this book to handle this story honestly, and the honest telling is of a scientific boom that failed.

In the early 2000s technology allowed researchers to measure individual genetic variants cheaply, and the field pinned its hopes on candidate genes, meaning specific genes chosen in advance because their biology seemed relevant, mostly genes affecting the brain's chemical messengers.

Two studies by Avshalom Caspi, Terrie Moffitt, and colleagues, using the Dunedin cohort in New Zealand, defined the era: a 2002 report in the journal Science that a variant of the monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) gene moderated the link between childhood maltreatment and later antisocial behaviour, and a 2003 report, also in Science, that the short form of a variant in the serotonin transporter gene, called 5-HTTLPR, moderated the link between stressful life events and depression.

The findings were biologically plausible, emotionally resonant, and enormous in influence, spawning many hundreds of follow-up studies and a whole vocabulary of genetic vulnerability.

Then the checking began, and it went badly.

A 2009 meta-analysis led by Neil Risch found no reliable interaction between 5-HTTLPR, stress, and depression across the accumulated studies, and a 2011 review by Laura Duncan and Matthew Keller found that claimed candidate-gene interactions were far more likely to appear in small novel studies than in larger replication attempts, the classic fingerprint of a literature built on false positives.

The decisive blow came in 2019, when Richard Border, Matthew Keller, and colleagues, publishing in the American Journal of Psychiatry, tested all eighteen historically favoured candidate genes for depression, including the serotonin transporter, in samples of hundreds of thousands of people, and found that none of them, alone or in interaction with life stress, predicted depression any better than randomly chosen genes.

The autopsy identified the causes of death clearly: the original samples were far too small to detect effects of realistic size, individual common variants turn out to have tiny effects, analytic flexibility let researchers try many statistical routes and report the ones that worked, and journals preferred positive findings.

The collapse does not mean genes are irrelevant to depression or antisocial behaviour, because twin studies and modern genome-wide methods both show genetic influence; it means the influence is spread across thousands of variants of tiny individual effect, and that no single gene of destiny exists to be found.

The era is now taught, as it is taught here, as one of psychology's most instructive cautionary tales about statistical power, publication bias, and the seduction of a good story.


18.3.3 Differential susceptibility: the orchid and the dandelion

Out of the interaction literature came one idea interesting enough to survive its origins, though it must now be held more carefully than its popular image suggests.

The standard vulnerability model, called diathesis-stress, holds that some children carry vulnerabilities that make bad environments worse for them, while robust children shrug the same environments off.

Differential susceptibility, proposed by Jay Belsky in 1997 and developed with Michael Pluess, and in parallel by W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce Ellis in 2005 under the biological sensitivity to context banner, makes a subtler claim: the supposedly vulnerable children are not merely fragile but plastic, more affected by their environments in both directions, doing worst in harsh conditions and best in supportive ones.

Boyce's memorable metaphor, drawn from a Swedish idiom, contrasts dandelion children, who grow much the same anywhere, with orchid children, who wither in poor conditions and flower spectacularly in good ones.

The distinctive prediction is a crossover: the same marker of sensitivity should predict the worst outcomes at one end of the environmental range and the best outcomes at the other, and a number of studies of temperament report exactly that pattern, with behaviourally reactive or difficult infants showing both the poorest outcomes under insensitive care and the richest gains under sensitive care or in intervention trials.

The necessary honesty is that the early genetic versions of this idea were built on the same candidate genes whose general collapse was just described, so claims that specific variants of the serotonin transporter or dopamine receptor D4 genes mark orchid children should be regarded as unproven.

Where the idea currently stands is as a hypothesis with reasonable support at the level of temperament and observed physiological reactivity, active development at the level of genome-wide measures, and an important conceptual legacy: sensitivity to the environment is itself a trait that varies among children, and an intervention that seems weak on average may be working powerfully for the most susceptible subset.


CHAPTER 19. POLYGENIC SCORES AND THE NATURE OF NURTURE (APPARATUS)

The previous chapter used twins to weigh genetic influence without ever reading a single letter of DNA; this chapter is about what happened when the letters themselves became readable at scale.

Its central instrument is the polygenic score, a single number computed from thousands of measured genetic variants that summarises a person's statistical loading for some trait.

Its central lesson is double: these scores genuinely predict developmental outcomes at the level of populations, and they mislead almost everyone about what they can say about an individual child.

Its deepest twist is captured in the phrase the nature of nurture: measured genes turn out to reach children partly through their environments, including through the genes of parents that the children never inherited.


19.1 The genome-wide era

The candidate-gene collapse taught the field to stop guessing which genes matter and to search the whole genome instead, with samples large enough to detect tiny effects.

This section describes the flagship studies of that approach in the developmental domain and then draws, carefully, the line between what a resulting score can and cannot say.


19.1.1 The educational-attainment and cognitive-ability studies at millions of genomes

The workhorse method is the genome-wide association study (GWAS), which measures hundreds of thousands of common genetic variants in each of a very large number of people and tests every variant, one by one, for a statistical association with a trait, using stringent thresholds to guard against false positives.

For developmental psychology the flagship series concerns educational attainment, meaning simply years of schooling completed, chosen not because it is the deepest trait but because it is recorded for millions of people.

The series, run by the Social Science Genetic Association Consortium, grew from about 100 thousand people in 2013, to 294 thousand in 2016, to 1.1 million in a 2018 study led by James Lee, to roughly 3 million people in the 2022 study led by Aysu Okbay, which identified 3,952 independent genetic variants associated with years of schooling.

Each individual variant has a minuscule effect, on the order of weeks of schooling, but summing a person's variants, weighted by their estimated effects, yields a polygenic score, and the 2022 score statistically accounts for about 12 to 16 percent of the variation in educational attainment among people of European ancestries in independent samples.

Parallel work on measured cognitive ability, including a 2018 study led by Gail Davies in over 300 thousand people, produced scores that account for something like 5 to 10 percent of variation in cognitive test performance, and the education and cognition scores overlap heavily.

Two features of these results deserve emphasis: the associated variants are scattered across the entire genome and are concentrated near genes expressed in brain tissue and involved in neural development, which fits the picture of the earlier chapters, and the gap between the roughly 15 percent captured by scores and the far higher twin estimates, part of the missing heritability problem, reflects rare variants the arrays do not measure, effects the samples still cannot detect, and inflation of twin estimates by the complications described below.
