19.1.2 What a polygenic score can and cannot say about a child

A polygenic score is a statistical summary, and everything it legitimately says is population talk, so this sub-section states the translation rules plainly.

The score can say that, across large groups, children with higher scores will on average complete more schooling, and group differences in average outcome across score bands are substantial and replicable.

The score cannot say what an individual child will achieve, because the distributions of outcomes at different score levels overlap enormously, and many children in the lowest band of the education score complete university while many in the highest band do not.

The score is not a measure of the child's fixed potential, because it was trained on a particular society's schools, labour markets, and inequalities, and it partly encodes those circumstances rather than anything inside the child, a point made vivid by the finding, described next, that part of its predictive power runs through parents and family position rather than through the child's own biology.

The score says nothing about causes in the mechanistic sense, because association is not mechanism, and a variant can be associated with schooling through anything from synapse formation to eye colour to the neighbourhood one's ancestors settled in.

And the score's accuracy degrades sharply outside the ancestral population it was built in, which is treated in the portability discussion below.

Kathryn Paige Harden's 2021 book The Genetic Lottery argued that, properly understood, such scores are best treated like measures of luck in a lottery a child did not choose to enter, useful to science and to egalitarian policy precisely because they document unchosen advantage, and that framing, whether or not one accepts her policy conclusions, is a sound antidote to reading the score as a verdict on a child.


19.2 The complications

Between the clean statistics of a genome-wide study and the messy causation of a childhood sit three complications, each discovered by clever family-based designs, and together they justify the chapter's title.

This section takes them in turn: genetic nurture, within-family attenuation, and the portability failure.


19.2.1 Genetic nurture: parental genotypes acting through the environment

The most conceptually startling discovery of the polygenic era is that genes a child never inherited still predict the child's outcomes.

The landmark demonstration came from Augustine Kong and colleagues in Iceland, published in Science in 2018, who exploited the fact that each parent transmits only half of their variants to a given child, so the untransmitted half is a pure test: it sits in the parent, never enters the child's cells, and can influence the child only by shaping the environment the parent provides.

Kong found that a polygenic score built from the parents' untransmitted variants predicted the child's educational attainment with about 30 percent of the strength of the transmitted variants, and he named the phenomenon genetic nurture.

The interpretation is that parental genetic makeup influences parental education, income, reading habits, stability, neighbourhood, and style of care, and those environments then shape the child, so part of what a naive analysis would call the child's genetic effect is actually the environment, built by parental genes, acting on the child from outside.

Subsequent adoption comparisons and parent-child trio studies have confirmed the effect, finding it large for education-related scores and small to negligible for traits such as height, which is exactly the pattern expected if the pathway runs through socially transmitted environments rather than biology.

The finding cuts in an unexpected philosophical direction, because it is a genetic study that ends up demonstrating, with unusual rigour, that family environments matter, which is why the field speaks of the nature of nurture.


19.2.2 Within-family attenuation and the sibling designs

A related check asks what happens to a polygenic score's predictive power when it is tested between siblings within the same family, where the score differences arise purely from the random shuffle of inheritance, and the answer is that it shrinks.

Siblings share their parents, their household, their neighbourhood, and their population ancestry, so comparing the higher-scoring sibling with the lower-scoring one strips away everything those shared factors contribute, leaving something much closer to the direct effect of the child's own inherited variants.

The 2022 educational attainment study quantified the shrinkage: the score's association with schooling roughly halves within families, so approximately half of its ordinary between-family predictive power comes not from the child's own genetic makeup acting in the child but from genetic nurture, from parental resemblance in these scores caused by assortative mating, meaning the tendency of people to pair with partners similar to themselves, and from residual population structure, meaning subtle correlations between ancestry, geography, and circumstance that statistics cannot fully remove.

For height, by contrast, the within-family attenuation is modest, confirming that the heavy shrinkage of the education score reflects the social embedding of educational outcomes rather than a general failure of the method.

The methodological moral has become field-defining: family-based designs, using siblings and parent-child trios, are now regarded as the gold standard for separating direct genetic effects from everything travelling alongside genes, and headline variance figures from studies of unrelated people should always be read with the within-family number beside them.


19.2.3 The portability failure across ancestries

Polygenic scores travel badly.

A score trained in people of European ancestries loses much of its predictive accuracy when applied to people of other ancestries, with the loss increasing with genetic distance, and a widely cited 2019 analysis by Alicia Martin and colleagues estimated that prediction accuracy for various traits in people of African ancestries was reduced by around 70 to 80 percent relative to European-ancestry samples.

The causes are technical rather than mysterious: the measured variants are usually not the causal ones but nearby markers, and the correlation patterns between markers and causal variants differ between populations with different histories; variant frequencies differ; effect estimates carry environmental particulars of the training population; and, overwhelmingly, the great majority of existing genome-wide data comes from European-ancestry participants, a sampling imbalance documented repeatedly since the mid 2010s.

The scientific consequence is that nothing about ancestral group differences in score distributions can be read as evidence about innate group differences, because the scores are not measuring the same thing with the same accuracy in different groups, and reputable statements of the field, including from the American Society of Human Genetics, have said so explicitly.

The practical consequence is an equity problem, because if scores ever become clinically useful, populations missing from the training data will be served worst, and the remedy under way, large genome projects in African, Asian, and admixed populations and new methods that model multiple ancestries jointly, is a matter of scientific priority and simple fairness.


19.3 The ethics, held also for Chapter 68

A number that even weakly predicts a child's future invites uses that science alone cannot police, and this book returns to the full ethical terrain in Chapter 68.

This section treats the one application that most sharply concerns development: the screening of embryos.


19.3.1 Embryo screening and the prediction of children

In vitro fertilisation (IVF), the technique of fertilising eggs outside the body, produces multiple embryos, and cells can be sampled from each embryo and genotyped, so companies now offer to compute polygenic scores for embryos and to help parents choose which to implant.

Several companies, including Genomic Prediction and Orchid Health, began offering such screening for disease risks around 2019 to 2021, the first child selected partly on polygenic risk scores was reported around 2020, and the practice is essentially unregulated in the United States while effectively prohibited for such uses in the United Kingdom and much of Europe.

The scientific case against expecting much from it was set out by Patrick Turley and colleagues in a 2021 New England Journal of Medicine analysis titled Problems with Using Polygenic Scores to Select Embryos, whose core points are quantitative: embryos from the same two parents differ only modestly in polygenic scores, so the expected gain from choosing the top-scoring embryo among a handful is small, uncertain, and often described to customers in relative-risk language that overstates it.

The within-family attenuation described above applies with full force, because embryo selection is precisely a within-family comparison, where scores are at their weakest, and the portability failure means the marketed accuracy applies mainly to customers of European ancestries.

Beyond the arithmetic lie the deeper objections: scores for one outcome are correlated with others, so selecting on one trait shifts others unpredictably; the practice normalises ranking potential children by statistical forecasts of traits like cognition, an echo of eugenics that most ethical commentary, including from the European Society of Human Genetics in 2021, treats as a line requiring extreme caution; and a child born of such a choice inherits not a guaranteed outcome but a parental expectation.

The developmental science position articulated throughout this chapter gives the last word here: a polygenic score is a weak, population-bound, environment-entangled forecast, and treating it as a catalogue description of a future child mistakes both the science and the child.


CHAPTER 20. EPIGENETICS AND EARLY EXPERIENCE (CORE)

Every cell in a child's body carries essentially the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a brain cell behave utterly differently, and the system of molecular switches and dimmers that makes this possible is called epigenetics.

The prefix epi means above or upon, so epigenetics is the layer of control sitting on top of the genetic sequence, deciding which genes are switched on, in which cells, and how strongly, without changing the sequence itself.

This chapter matters for developmental psychology because of a bold and famous hypothesis: that early experience, including the quality of early care, can be written into this control layer and thereby leave lasting marks on stress systems, brain development, and health.

The chapter presents the machinery, the founding experiments, and then, as this book's method requires, an honest appraisal of a literature whose fame ran ahead of its evidence.


20.1 The machinery

Before any claims about experience can be weighed, the molecular hardware has to be on the table.

This section describes the two best-known epigenetic marks, the great erasures that occur early in development, and the special case of imprinted genes.


20.1.1 Methylation, histone modification, and the developmental reprogramming waves

The most studied epigenetic mark is DNA methylation, the attachment of a tiny chemical tag called a methyl group, one carbon atom with three hydrogens, onto the DNA letter cytosine, usually where cytosine is followed by guanine, a pairing written as CpG.

Methylation near the start of a gene, in its promoter region, which is the stretch of DNA that acts as the gene's on-switch, typically dampens that gene's activity, like a dimmer turned down, and the marks are copied when cells divide, which is how a liver cell's daughters stay liver cells.

The second mechanism concerns histones, the spool-like proteins around which DNA is wound for packing, and chemical tags on histone tails, such as acetyl and methyl groups, loosen or tighten the winding, making genes correspondingly easier or harder to read.

Development requires not only writing these marks but erasing them, and mammalian life begins with two dramatic reprogramming waves: in the first days after fertilisation, the embryo strips away most of the methylation inherited on the egg and sperm genomes and then rebuilds a fresh pattern as tissues form, and separately, in the cells that will become the next generation's eggs and sperm, the primordial germ cells, a second and even more thorough erasure occurs around weeks 2 to 7 of human embryonic development.

These waves matter enormously for public claims about epigenetic inheritance across generations, because any mark carrying experience from parent to grandchild would have to survive two near-total wipes, which is why robust transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is well documented in plants and worms but remains unproven in humans.

For brain development specifically, methylation and histone marking are working parts of the story told in earlier chapters, helping to lock in cell identities as neurons are born, guiding the timed switches such as the change in chloride handling and the onset of myelination, and providing one plausible substrate by which experience during sensitive periods could leave durable traces.


20.1.2 Imprinting and its disorders

For almost all genes a child's two copies, one from each parent, are treated identically, but for a small group, on the order of one to two hundred in humans, only the copy from one particular parent is switched on, and the other is silenced by methylation laid down in the egg or sperm.

This parent-of-origin silencing is called genomic imprinting, and the imprinted marks are deliberately spared from the post-fertilisation erasure wave, making them a striking exception to the general reprogramming rule.

The most influential explanation of why imprinting exists, the kinship or parental conflict theory proposed by David Haig in the early 1990s, notes that many paternally expressed imprinted genes push fetal growth harder while many maternally expressed ones restrain it, as expected if paternal and maternal genetic interests over maternal resources differ, though the theory remains debated.

The disorders of imprinting read like controlled experiments of nature.

Deletion of a particular region of chromosome 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome when the deleted copy came from the father, with features including early feeding difficulties followed by intense overeating, and causes the quite different Angelman syndrome when the deleted copy came from the mother, with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, ataxia, which means unsteady movement, and a characteristically happy demeanour, the difference arising purely because the surviving copy is silenced by imprinting in each case.

Angelman syndrome traces to loss of the maternally expressed gene UBE3A in neurons, a gene whose duplication is also among the strongest chromosomal associations with autism, and Beckwith-Wiedemann and Silver-Russell syndromes, disorders of overgrowth and undergrowth respectively, arise from opposite imprinting disturbances on chromosome 11.

For this book the lesson of imprinting is foundational: it is the clearest proof in human biology that methylation marks laid down in one generation can direct brain development and behaviour in the next, which is precisely why the more ambitious claims of the next section seemed plausible.


20.2 The founding experiments

Three studies, one in rats and two in humans, founded the field of behavioural epigenetics and still anchor every review of it.

This section presents them at full strength before the appraisal that follows.


20.2.1 Maternal care and the glucocorticoid receptor in the rat

Rat mothers differ naturally in how much they lick and groom their pups in the first week of life, and Michael Meaney's laboratory at McGill University had shown through the 1990s that pups reared by high-licking mothers grow into calmer adults with better-regulated stress hormones, and that cross-fostering proves the effect is transmitted by care rather than inheritance.

The epigenetic mechanism was reported by Ian Weaver, Meaney, Moshe Szyf, and colleagues in Nature Neuroscience in 2004, in a paper titled Epigenetic programming by maternal behavior, which became one of the most cited papers in behavioural neuroscience.

The chain they described runs as follows: high licking and grooming in the first week of life leads to lower methylation at a specific control region, the exon 1-7 promoter, of the glucocorticoid receptor gene in the pup's hippocampus, where the glucocorticoid receptor is the protein that detects the stress hormone corticosterone, the rat's version of human cortisol, and the hippocampus uses it to tell the stress system to stand down.

Lower methylation means more receptor, more receptor means more sensitive shut-off of the stress response, and so the well-licked pup becomes the calm adult, with the methylation difference emerging in the first week, remaining stable into adulthood, and being partly reversible in adulthood by drugs that alter the epigenetic marks.

The study electrified developmental science because it offered, for the first time, a specific molecular route by which the quality of early care could be biologically embedded, turning a poetic claim into a testable pathway.

Within rat research the core behavioural and endocrine findings are well supported, though later methylation-focused replications have been mixed at the level of the exact sites involved, a caution that belongs in the record.


20.2.2 The human echo in post-mortem hippocampus after childhood abuse

The obvious question was whether anything similar happens in humans, and the closest possible test was carried out by Patrick McGowan, Szyf, Meaney, and colleagues, published in Nature Neuroscience in 2009.

They studied post-mortem hippocampus from the Quebec Suicide Brain Bank, comparing three groups of deceased men: suicide victims with documented histories of severe childhood abuse, suicide victims without such histories, and men who died suddenly of other causes.

The finding echoed the rat work with uncanny precision: only the abused group showed increased methylation at the human equivalent of the same glucocorticoid receptor control region, the exon 1F promoter, together with reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression in the hippocampus.

Because the difference tracked abuse history rather than suicide itself, the authors argued that early adversity, not the final illness, was the marked variable, exactly as the maternal care model predicted.

The study is a landmark and also a study of twelve brains per group, cross-sectional, unable to establish when the marks arose or what caused them, and its specific site-level findings have been followed by a broader literature on this gene region in blood and saliva that a 2016 systematic review judged inconsistent, so it is best held as the founding human echo, suggestive and unrepeatable in kind, rather than as settled fact.


20.2.3 The Dutch Hunger Winter methylation signature six decades on

The third founding study exploited one of history's grimmest natural experiments.

In the winter of 1944 to 1945 the German occupation blockaded the western Netherlands, and official rations fell below 1,000 calories per day and at the worst point to around 400 to 800, so children conceived during those months were exposed to famine at precisely dated stages of gestation, in an otherwise well-nourished and well-documented population.

Decades of follow-up had already shown that people conceived during the famine carried elevated adult rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and schizophrenia, establishing the epidemiology of prenatal programming.

The epigenetic finding came from Bastiaan Heijmans, Lambert Lumey, and colleagues in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2008: individuals exposed to the famine around conception had, some six decades later, less methylation at the imprinted insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene, a key fetal growth gene, in their blood than their own unexposed same-sex siblings.

The design details carry the force: the sibling comparison controls family background, the six-decade interval demonstrates persistence across a human lifetime, and the effect was specific to exposure around conception rather than late gestation, consistent with marks being set during the early reprogramming window when methylation patterns are freshly established.

Later genome-wide follow-ups by the same group found additional famine-associated marks in genes related to growth and metabolism, and work published in 2018 suggested some of these marks statistically mediate part of the link between prenatal famine and adult metabolic health.

The study remains the single most convincing demonstration that a documented prenatal environmental exposure leaves a methylation trace in humans for life, while its own authors note the effects are small, measured in blood, and correlational, which is the bridge to the appraisal that follows.


20.3 The honest appraisal

Few areas of developmental science have had a wider gap between public excitement and evidential strength than behavioural epigenetics, and this book's method requires closing that gap explicitly.

This section names the standard criticisms, states what survives them, and ends with the one epigenetic technology whose predictive claims are currently strongest.


20.3.1 Cross-tissue inference, small effects, and the hype problem

The first structural problem is tissue.

Epigenetic marks are the very mechanism by which tissues differ, so methylation in blood, saliva, or cheek cells, which is what nearly all human studies measure because brains cannot be sampled in the living, is a poor and inconsistent proxy for methylation in the hippocampus or cortex, and blood-brain correspondence at individual sites ranges from moderate to essentially absent depending on the site.

The second problem is size and replication: reported methylation differences associated with adversity are typically tiny, often a few percentage points at single sites, arising from small samples analysed with many researcher choices, and the field has repeated much of the candidate-gene history of Chapter 18, with early candidate-gene methylation findings, including around the glucocorticoid receptor and serotonin transporter, replicating poorly once larger consortium studies with pre-registered pipelines arrived.

The third problem is causal direction, because a methylation difference observed after adversity may be a cause of later outcomes, a consequence of them, a marker of correlated genetic variation, which itself strongly influences methylation, or a signature of changed cell-type proportions in blood, and cross-sectional designs cannot distinguish these.

The fourth problem is the transgenerational leap, because popular accounts moved swiftly from Dutch famine findings to claims that trauma is inherited by grandchildren, when the reprogramming waves described earlier make such inheritance biologically demanding, the famous human datasets, including studies of Holocaust survivors' descendants, are small and contested, and direct exposure of a pregnant grandmother's fetus and that fetus's germ cells can mimic inheritance without any transmitted mark.

Critical reviews making these points, including widely cited pieces by Kevin Mitchell and by John Greally from the mid 2010s onward, coined the working label for the phenomenon: the epigenetics hype problem.

What survives the appraisal is real and worth stating plainly: epigenetic mechanisms indisputably run normal brain development, imprinting disorders prove that methylation differences can shape human minds, the rat maternal care model is a genuine mechanistic discovery in its own species, and the Dutch famine signature shows that prenatal environment can mark the human methylome for decades.

What does not survive is the strong popular claim that early experience is routinely and legibly written into a child's genes, that these marks can be read from a cheek swab, or that trauma is known to be biologically inherited, and an honest sentence for the field is that early adversity certainly gets under the skin, but methylation has not yet been shown to be the main ink.


20.3.2 Epigenetic clocks and the pace of development

Out of the same technology came one genuinely robust discovery, which is that age can be read from methylation with startling accuracy.

In 2013 Steve Horvath at the University of California, Los Angeles showed that a weighted combination of methylation levels at 353 CpG sites predicts a person's chronological age across almost every human tissue, typically within about three and a half years, and such predictors are now called epigenetic clocks.

The developmental interest lies in the gap between clock age and calendar age, because a child or adult whose methylation age runs ahead of their birth certificate is said to show epigenetic age acceleration, and the developmental question is what early life does to the clock.

Later clocks sharpened the tool: a paediatric clock trained on children, and above all DunedinPACE, published by Daniel Belsky, Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi, and colleagues in 2022 from the Dunedin cohort, which estimates not accumulated age but the current pace of biological ageing, calibrated against two decades of repeated physiological measurements in a single birth cohort.

The findings relevant to this book are consistent and sobering: children exposed to serious adversity, including maltreatment, institutional deprivation, and deep poverty, tend as a group to show accelerated epigenetic ageing and faster DunedinPACE in adolescence and adulthood, and faster pace in adults predicts earlier disease, cognitive decline, and death.

A 2020 meta-analysis by Natalie Colich, Maya Rosen, Eileen Williams, and Katie McLaughlin further suggested that threat-type adversity in particular is associated with accelerated cellular ageing and earlier pubertal timing, linking the clock literature to the accelerated development hypothesis discussed elsewhere in this book.

The honest cautions of the previous sub-section still apply, since effects are group averages measured in blood or saliva and no child's future can be read from a clock, but the appraisal here is genuinely more favourable: the clocks replicate across cohorts, were built with the large-sample discipline the earlier literature lacked, and give developmental science its first workable molecular gauge of the suspicion, older than the field itself, that hard beginnings can make a body grow old before its time.

CHAPTER 21. THE SINGLE-GENE TEACHERS (CORE)

This chapter looks at a small set of conditions where a change in a single gene reshapes how the brain develops.

Most of the differences between people arise from many genes working together with the environment, so a single gene rarely tells the whole story.

But a handful of conditions are different, because one gene is enough to set the whole process on a new path.

These conditions are worth studying closely, and not because they are common, since each one is rare.

They are worth studying because they act like teachers.

Each one shows us, in an unusually clear way, how a molecular change ripples upward into the shape of a synapse, then into behaviour, then into a whole life.

A synapse is the tiny junction where one nerve cell passes a signal to the next, and much of this chapter is about how these junctions are built and tuned.

We will meet Fragile X syndrome, Rett syndrome, Williams syndrome, and Down syndrome.

We will see why a drug that cured mice did not help people, why a brain condition once thought permanent could be reversed in adult mice, and why these very different conditions keep pointing back to the same two places in the cell.

Throughout, the register is respectful and plain, because these are descriptions of real people and real families, not puzzles to be solved for their own sake.


21.1 Fragile X syndrome

Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, and it is also a leading single-gene cause of autism.

It gets its name from an odd appearance under the microscope, where the tip of the X chromosome looks pinched or fragile.

This section explains what actually goes wrong at the level of the gene, the protein, and the synapse, and then tells the sobering story of a treatment that worked beautifully in mice and failed in people.


21.1.1 The repeat expansion, the translational repressor, and the spine phenotype

To understand Fragile X syndrome, start with the gene behind it, which is called FMR1, short for Fragile X Messenger Ribonucleoprotein 1.

Near the start of this gene there is a short stretch of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) that repeats a three-letter sequence, cytosine-guanine-guanine, written as CGG.

DNA is the chemical instruction book inside our cells, and a repeat is simply the same short phrase copied over and over.

In most people this CGG phrase repeats somewhere between about five and forty times, and everything works normally.

In Fragile X syndrome the phrase has expanded to more than two hundred repeats, a state called a full mutation.

When the repeat gets that long, the cell responds by chemically silencing the gene, a process called methylation, which is like putting a piece of tape over the instructions so they cannot be read.

With FMR1 switched off, the cell can no longer make the protein it codes for, which is called Fragile X Messenger Ribonucleoprotein, or FMRP.

So the core of the condition is simple to state, which is that a person with Fragile X syndrome makes little or no FMRP.

Now we need to know what FMRP does, because its job explains the whole downstream picture.

FMRP is a translational repressor, and translation is the step where the cell reads a genetic message and builds a protein from it.

A repressor is a brake, so FMRP works as a brake on protein-building at the synapse.

FMRP travels out to the synapses and sits on many messenger molecules, holding them quiet until the neuron actually needs the proteins made.

When FMRP is missing, that brake is gone, and protein-building at the synapse runs too fast and too much.

This overshoot shows up in the physical shape of the synapse itself.

Neurons receive signals on tiny bumps called dendritic spines, which are the little knobs where incoming connections land.

In Fragile X syndrome the spines are unusually long, thin, and immature, and there are too many of them.

This is often called the spine phenotype, and a phenotype is simply the observable form that a genetic change produces.

The picture, then, is of a brain whose connections never fully mature and prune themselves, because the molecular brake that normally shapes them is absent.

This account was built up across the 1990s and 2000s, after the FMR1 gene was identified in 1991 by a large international collaboration.


21.1.2 The mGluR theory and the trial failures: why mouse rescue is not human treatment

Once scientists understood that Fragile X syndrome involved too much protein-building at the synapse, an elegant idea followed, which became known as the mGluR theory.

The letters mGluR stand for metabotropic glutamate receptor, and one particular member of that family, receptor number five, written mGluR5, sits on the receiving side of many synapses.

Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory messenger, meaning the chemical that most often tells a neuron to fire, and mGluR5 is one of the docks that receives it.

When mGluR5 is activated, one of the things it does is trigger local protein-building at the synapse, which is exactly the process that FMRP normally holds in check.

Mark Bear and colleagues proposed in 2004 that in Fragile X syndrome, with the FMRP brake gone, the mGluR5 accelerator was effectively unopposed, so the synapse behaved as though mGluR5 signalling was turned up too high.

The prediction was beautifully clear, which was that turning mGluR5 signalling down should rebalance the system.

In mouse models of Fragile X syndrome, this worked, and it worked repeatedly.

Blocking mGluR5, either with drugs or by genetic tricks, corrected many features of the mice, including aspects of the spine phenotype and various behaviours.

This raised real hope that a drug blocking mGluR5 could treat people.

Two such drugs went into large human trials, one called mavoglurant, made by Novartis, and one called basimglurant, made by Roche.

The mavoglurant trials were reported by Elizabeth Berry-Kravis and colleagues in 2016, and they were serious efforts, enrolling one hundred and seventy-five adults aged eighteen to forty-five and one hundred and thirty-nine adolescents aged twelve to seventeen.

The result was disappointing, because neither trial met its main goal after twelve weeks of treatment, measured on a standard behaviour checklist.

The basimglurant trials likewise did not show the hoped-for benefit.

So a theory that had rescued mice again and again did not help people.

There are several honest lessons here, and the chapter states them plainly rather than glossing over the failure.

One lesson is about timing, because the mouse rescues often began very early in life, whereas the human trials treated adolescents and adults whose brains had already developed for years.

A second lesson is about measurement, because the human outcome was a behaviour rating that may not have captured the biology the drug was changing.

A third lesson is deeper and more general, which is that mouse rescue is not human treatment.

A mouse model captures some of the molecular story but not the whole human condition, and a fix that reverses a mouse phenotype in a dish or a cage may simply not translate to a person's daily life.

This episode is now taught as a cautionary tale across the whole field of single-gene brain conditions, and it tempers the excitement around every new molecular target.


21.2 Rett syndrome

Rett syndrome is a rare condition that overwhelmingly affects girls, and it follows a striking pattern.

A baby girl usually develops normally for the first six to eighteen months, and then enters a period of regression, losing purposeful use of the hands and slowing in other ways.

A hallmark sign is repetitive hand movements, such as wringing or washing motions, that replace skilled hand use.

This section explains the gene behind it, the surprising discovery that the condition could be reversed in adult mice, and where treatments stand now.


21.2.1 MECP2 and the adult-mouse reversal: neurodevelopmental need not mean irreversible

Rett syndrome is caused, in almost all cases, by a change in a gene called MECP2, which stands for methyl-CpG-binding protein two.

This gene sits on the X chromosome, which helps explain why the condition mainly affects girls, and why it is usually severe or lethal early in boys, who have only one X.

The protein made from MECP2 is a reader of the chemical tags on DNA, the same methylation tags we met earlier, and by reading them it helps decide which other genes are switched on or off across the neuron.

So MECP2 is a master regulator, meaning a gene that controls the activity of many other genes, and losing it disturbs the balance of a great many things at once.

For a long time everyone assumed that a condition like this, arising during brain development, must be permanent, because the brain was thought to be built wrong and therefore unfixable.

Then came one of the most important experiments in this whole field.

In 2007, Jacqueline Guy working in Adrian Bird's laboratory in Edinburgh created mice in which the Mecp2 gene was switched off but could be switched back on later by an experimental trigger.

These mice developed Rett-like symptoms as expected.

When the researchers reactivated the gene in fully symptomatic adult mice, many of the neurological features reversed.

This was a genuine shock, because it showed that the neurons had not been destroyed or built wrong beyond repair, but were instead waiting, sick but recoverable, for the missing protein to return.

The headline lesson is that neurodevelopmental need not mean irreversible.

A condition can begin in development and still, in principle, be treatable later, if the underlying molecular cause can be restored.

This finding reframed Rett syndrome from a fixed disability into a target for treatment, and it energised the search for therapies that put MECP2 function back.

A note of caution belongs here, because reversing a gene switch in a specially engineered mouse is far easier than safely restoring a gene in a human brain, and the gap between the two is exactly what the next sub-section is about.


21.2.2 The first approved therapy and the gene-therapy trials

For decades there was no medicine that changed the course of Rett syndrome, only supportive care.

That changed in 2023, when the United States Food and Drug Administration approved a drug called trofinetide, sold as Daybue, as the first treatment specifically for Rett syndrome.

Trofinetide is honestly described as a symptom treatment rather than a cure, because it eases some features of the condition but does not address the root problem, which is the loss of MECP2.

The deeper hope lies in gene therapy, meaning an approach that delivers a working copy of the gene itself into the patient's neurons.

Two such programmes are being tested as this book is written in 2026, and both build directly on the 2007 reversal insight that restoring MECP2 might help even after symptoms appear.

One, developed by Taysha Gene Therapies and called TSHA-102, delivers a shortened working MECP2 gene into the fluid around the spinal cord, and it carries a clever self-regulating switch meant to stop the gene being overproduced.

The other, developed by Neurogene and called NGN-401, delivers a full-length MECP2 gene into the brain's fluid-filled spaces, also with a feedback circuit to control the dose.

The reason both designs fuss so much about not overproducing the protein is important and worth stating plainly.

MECP2 is a Goldilocks gene, because too little of it causes Rett syndrome, but too much of it causes a different serious disorder called MECP2 duplication syndrome.

So a safe gene therapy must deliver an amount that is neither too little nor too much, which is a hard engineering problem.

Early reports from the first handful of patients in both programmes have been cautiously encouraging, with the treatments generally well tolerated and some signs of developmental gains, but the numbers are very small and these are early days.

The honest summary is that Rett syndrome has moved, within a single generation, from an untreatable diagnosis to one with a real approved medicine and genuine experimental cures under test, while none of the gene therapies is yet proven.


21.3 Williams syndrome and Down syndrome

This section pairs two conditions caused not by a single letter change but by missing or extra chunks of chromosome.

Williams syndrome comes from a small deletion, and Down syndrome from a whole extra chromosome.

Each teaches its own lesson, one about how genes and development interact to build a personality and a mind, and one about the long shadow that a genetic dose can cast across a whole lifespan.


21.3.1 The deletion, the phenotype, and the neuroconstructivist lesson

Williams syndrome, sometimes called Williams-Beuren syndrome, is caused by the deletion of a small piece of one copy of chromosome seven, at a location written 7q11.23.

The missing piece contains roughly twenty-six to twenty-eight genes, so unlike Fragile X or Rett syndrome, several genes are lost at once.

The resulting profile is unusual and quite specific.

People with Williams syndrome often have a distinctive warmth and sociability, sometimes described as hypersociability, meaning a strong drive to approach and engage with other people, alongside high anxiety about non-social things.

They frequently have relative strengths in spoken language and face processing, together with marked difficulty in visual and spatial tasks, such as copying a drawing or assembling a puzzle.

This jagged profile, strong here and weak there, made Williams syndrome a famous test case in a long-running argument about how the mind is built.

One older view, sometimes called the nativist or modular view, treated such a profile as evidence that the brain comes pre-divided into independent modules, so that a genetic change could knock out one module, say spatial cognition, while leaving another, say language, intact.

The psychologist Annette Karmiloff-Smith challenged this reading forcefully, and her alternative is called neuroconstructivism.

Neuroconstructivism argues that the adult mind is not pre-divided into modules that genes can switch on or off one at a time.

Instead it holds that genes, brain, cognition, and environment interact back and forth across development, and that specialised abilities are constructed gradually through that interaction rather than being present from the start.

On this view, the uneven Williams syndrome profile is not a snapshot of damaged modules but the end product of a whole development that ran differently from the very beginning.

Karmiloff-Smith made the point sharply in work through the 1990s and 2000s, arguing in a much-cited 1998 paper that development itself is the key to understanding developmental disorders.

The practical upshot is that to understand any of these conditions you have to study the process of development over time, not just the finished adult, and that lesson now shapes the whole field.


21.3.2 Trisomy twenty-one and the early-Alzheimer window

Down syndrome is caused by having three copies of chromosome twenty-one instead of the usual two, a condition called trisomy twenty-one.

Because a whole chromosome is present in triplicate, every gene on it is present in an extra dose, and the effects are wide-ranging, including characteristic facial features, intellectual disability that varies a great deal between individuals, and a higher chance of certain heart and other health conditions.

This sub-section focuses on one particular and poignant consequence, which links Down syndrome to Alzheimer's disease.

Chromosome twenty-one carries a gene called APP, which stands for amyloid precursor protein.

APP is the source of a small sticky fragment called amyloid-beta, and the build-up of amyloid-beta into plaques is one of the defining features of Alzheimer's disease.

In Down syndrome, because there are three copies of chromosome twenty-one, there are three copies of APP, so from birth the person makes extra amyloid precursor protein.

Over decades this extra dose adds up.

Essentially all people with Down syndrome develop the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease, the amyloid plaques and the tangles, by around the age of forty, and a large proportion go on to develop dementia at ages far younger than in the general population.

This is often called the early-Alzheimer window, and it is a striking natural demonstration of the amyloid story, because here a lifelong extra dose of one gene is followed, decades later, by the disease.

The finding matters beyond Down syndrome itself, because people with Down syndrome have become important partners in Alzheimer's research, helping test whether treatments that lower amyloid can delay or prevent the disease.

It must be handled with care and respect, because it describes a real and difficult risk faced by real people and their families, and it is presented here as science, never as a forecast about any particular individual.


21.4 The convergence lesson

Having met four very different conditions, this short closing section asks what they have in common.

The answer turns out to be surprisingly tidy, and it points toward a unifying way of thinking about the genetics of brain development.


21.4.1 The synaptopathies: chromatin and synapse as the common ground of risk genes

When researchers gathered up the long and growing list of genes linked to autism and intellectual disability, they noticed that the genes were not scattered randomly across every possible function.

Instead they clustered, again and again, into two broad jobs.

The first job is building and tuning the synapse, the connection between neurons, and conditions in this group are sometimes called synaptopathies, meaning disorders of the synapse.

Fragile X syndrome fits here cleanly, because FMRP controls protein-building right at the synapse.

The second job is controlling which genes are switched on and off, through the chemical packaging of DNA, which is called chromatin.

Chromatin is the way the long thread of DNA is wound and tagged inside the cell, and adjusting it changes which genes a neuron can read.

Rett syndrome fits here, because MECP2 reads the methylation tags that are part of that packaging.

The striking realisation is that these two jobs are really two ends of one loop.

Experience drives activity at the synapse, that activity signals back to the chromatin in the nucleus to change which genes are read, and the resulting proteins travel back out to reshape the synapse.

So a risk gene that damages the synapse and a risk gene that damages the chromatin machinery can end up disrupting the same loop from opposite sides, and produce overlapping conditions.

This is the convergence lesson, which is that a great many different genetic causes funnel into a small number of shared cellular processes.

It offers a hopeful angle for treatment, because a therapy aimed at the shared process might, in principle, help across several conditions rather than just one.

It also explains why conditions with completely different genetic causes can look so similar in a clinic, since they are different entry points into the same machinery.
