PART SIX. THE PRENATAL ENVIRONMENT AND ITS INSULTS

================================================================================

CHAPTER 22. TERATOLOGY AND ALCOHOL (CORE)

This chapter is about things in the prenatal environment that can harm the developing brain, and how scientists reason about them carefully rather than fearfully.

The word teratology names the study of agents that disturb development before birth, and such an agent is called a teratogen.

The chapter opens with the general rules that govern all such harms, then looks in depth at alcohol, which is the most common preventable cause of developmental disability of this kind, and finally surveys several other exposures, including one famous case where public fear ran far ahead of the actual evidence.

The tone throughout is calm and factual, because this material touches real pregnancies and real families, and the aim is understanding, not alarm.

Nothing here is advice to any particular parent about any particular pregnancy, which is a matter for that family and their own clinicians.


22.1 The principles of teratology

Before looking at any single exposure, it helps to learn the handful of principles that shape how every teratogen acts.

These principles were worked out over the twentieth century, and they let scientists move from vague fear to specific, testable claims.


22.1.1 Timing, dose, and susceptibility, keyed to the timetable of Part Two

The first principle is timing, and it is the most important.

The same exposure can do very different things depending on when in pregnancy it happens, because different parts of the body and brain are being built at different moments.

There is an early window, roughly the first two weeks after conception, that often follows an all-or-nothing pattern, where a large enough hit ends the pregnancy and a smaller one may be fully repaired.

Then comes the period when the major organs form, roughly weeks three to eight, when structural birth defects are most likely, because the body plan is being laid down.

The brain, however, is special, because it keeps developing across the whole of pregnancy and well beyond birth, so it stays vulnerable long after the other organs are largely built.

This is why an exposure late in pregnancy may spare the limbs and heart yet still affect the brain, and it connects directly to the developmental timetable set out earlier in Part Two of this book.

The second principle is dose, meaning that in general more exposure tends to cause more harm.

Many teratogens show a threshold, a level below which harm is hard to detect and above which it climbs, although, as we will see with alcohol, a clear safe threshold is not always established.

The third principle is susceptibility, meaning that the same dose at the same time does not affect every pregnancy equally.

Genes of the mother and of the developing child, along with nutrition and other exposures, all change how vulnerable a given pregnancy is.

This is why some children exposed to a teratogen are seriously affected while others exposed to a similar amount are not, and it warns us against ever reading an individual outcome as if it were guaranteed.

Together these three principles, timing, dose, and susceptibility, form the grammar of the whole chapter, and every exposure below is really a variation on them.


22.2 Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders

Alcohol is the most thoroughly studied teratogen affecting the brain, and prenatal alcohol exposure is among the most common preventable causes of developmental disability.

The umbrella term for the range of resulting conditions is fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, and the word spectrum signals that the effects run from subtle to severe.

This section covers how the condition was first recognised, how common it turns out to be, how alcohol actually harms the developing brain, and why no safe level has been established.


22.2.1 The 1973 recognition and the modern prevalence estimates

Although the idea that drinking in pregnancy might harm a baby is very old, the modern medical recognition has a precise date.

In 1973, Kenneth Lyons Jones and David Weyhe Smith, working in Seattle, published a description in the journal The Lancet of a recognisable pattern in children born to mothers who drank heavily, and they named it the fetal alcohol syndrome.

The pattern they described had three main parts, which are a particular set of facial features, slowed growth, and problems with the brain and nervous system.

Over the following decades it became clear that many affected children did not have the full facial pattern yet still had the brain effects, so the broader umbrella term fetal alcohol spectrum disorders came into use to capture the whole range.

The question of how common this is turns out to be larger than many people expect.

A carefully conducted study led by Philip May and colleagues, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 2018, screened schoolchildren across four communities in the United States.

Depending on the community and on how the estimate was calculated, they found rates ranging from roughly one to five percent of school-aged children, meaning that fetal alcohol spectrum disorders may affect as many as one child in twenty in some populations.

That is far higher than older textbook figures, and it establishes the condition as a major public health issue rather than a rare curiosity.

These numbers describe populations, not any single family, and they are reported here to convey scale, not blame.


22.2.2 The mechanisms: apoptotic neurodegeneration and midline patterning

To understand why alcohol is so damaging, it helps to look at two of the main ways it interferes with the developing brain.

The first mechanism involves cell death, and specifically a form of programmed cell death called apoptosis.

Apoptosis is a normal and necessary process, a kind of built-in self-destruct that the body uses to remove cells it does not need, and healthy brain development uses it in a carefully controlled way.

Alcohol hijacks and amplifies this process, triggering waves of unwanted apoptosis that kill neurons which should have survived, an effect sometimes called apoptotic neurodegeneration.

This was shown vividly in the developing rodent brain by Chrysanthy Ikonomidou, John Olney, and colleagues in a much-cited study published in the journal Science in 2000, where a single episode of alcohol exposure during a sensitive window caused widespread neuronal death.

The second mechanism involves the way the body is patterned down its centre line, called midline patterning.

Early in development a signalling molecule called Sonic hedgehog helps organise structures along the midline, including the middle of the face and parts of the brain.

Alcohol can interfere with this signalling, and this helps explain the characteristic facial features of fetal alcohol syndrome, which sit along the midline of the face, as well as some of the brain effects.

So alcohol harms the developing brain in more than one way at once, killing cells that should live and disturbing the chemical signals that arrange the body plan, which is part of why its effects are so wide-ranging.


22.2.3 Why no safe dose is established

A question families often ask is whether there is some small amount of alcohol that is known to be safe in pregnancy, and the honest scientific answer is that no safe level has been established.

This deserves careful and precise wording, because it is easy to misstate.

To say that no safe level has been established is not the same as saying that every sip certainly causes harm.

It means something more specific, which is that research has not been able to identify a threshold below which harm can be confidently ruled out.

There are several genuine reasons for this uncertainty.

One is the principle of susceptibility from earlier in the chapter, because differences in how a mother and child process alcohol mean the same small amount may be harmless in one pregnancy and not in another.

Another is that the brain is vulnerable across the whole of pregnancy, so timing interacts with dose in complicated ways.

A third is that studying very low levels is genuinely hard, because the effects, if present, are subtle and mixed in with many other influences, and it would be unethical to run an experiment that deliberately assigned pregnant women to drink.

Because a clear safe threshold cannot be drawn, public health bodies in many countries advise that the safest choice is to avoid alcohol entirely in pregnancy, precisely because the lower bound of risk is unknown rather than because every exposure is proven harmful.

This is a case where honest science leads to caution, and the caution follows from the uncertainty itself.


22.3 The other exposures in brief

Alcohol is the most studied prenatal exposure, but it is far from the only one, and this section surveys several others more briefly.

Together they round out the picture, and one of them, the so-called crack baby episode, is an important lesson in how fear can distort science.


22.3.1 Valproate, isotretinoin, and the thalidomide founding disaster

Some medicines are teratogens, which creates hard trade-offs, because the same drug may be genuinely needed to treat the mother.

The founding disaster of modern teratology is thalidomide.

Thalidomide was sold from 1957, first in Germany, as a supposedly safe sedative and a remedy for morning sickness, and it was given to many pregnant women.

It caused a catastrophe, with thousands of babies born with severe limb malformations, most famously a condition called phocomelia, in which the long bones of the arms or legs are very short or absent.

The link was identified in 1961 independently by William McBride in Australia and Widukind Lenz in Germany, and the drug was withdrawn over 1961 and 1962.

More than ten thousand affected children were born worldwide.

In the United States the disaster was largely averted because a Food and Drug Administration reviewer, Frances Oldham Kelsey, refused to approve the drug without better safety data, and her stand became a landmark in the history of drug regulation.

Thalidomide taught the world that a drug can be safe for the mother and devastating for the developing embryo, and that lesson founded the whole modern field of teratology.

A second teratogenic medicine is valproate, an effective treatment for epilepsy and some other conditions, whose risks in pregnancy are now well documented.

Studies have found that prenatal exposure to valproate raises the absolute risk of autism spectrum disorder to somewhere around four to five percent, and it also raises the risk of other neurodevelopmental difficulties and of physical birth defects.

Because valproate can be the medicine that best controls a mother's seizures, its use in pregnancy involves a careful and individual balancing of risks that belongs between a patient and her doctors.

A third example is isotretinoin, a powerful medicine for severe acne, sold under names such as Accutane, which is a potent teratogen.

Isotretinoin is chemically related to vitamin A, and it can cause serious malformations of the brain, face, and heart, which is why its use in people who could become pregnant is governed by strict prevention programmes.

The common thread is that these are real medicines with real benefits, and the science of teratology exists to manage them wisely, not to demonise them.


22.3.2 The crack-baby correction: moral panic against measured effect

In the 1980s and early 1990s, amid a wave of cocaine use in the form of crack in the United States, the media and some experts predicted a generation of permanently damaged crack babies.

The claim was that children exposed to cocaine before birth would grow up biologically ruined, unable to learn, love, or function, and this claim spread widely and shaped public attitudes and even laws.

The science that followed tells a very different and more careful story, and it is one of the clearest examples of a moral panic being corrected by patient measurement.

The key figure is the paediatrician Hallam Hurt, who led a long-term study in Philadelphia that followed children exposed to cocaine before birth alongside a comparison group from the same low-income neighbourhoods, for more than two decades.

The result surprised even the researchers, because they found no significant difference in outcomes between the cocaine-exposed children and the non-exposed children from the same background.

What they did find was that both groups had outcomes shaped powerfully by poverty.

The conclusion, echoed by other researchers such as the paediatrician Deborah Frank, was that poverty was a far more powerful influence on these children's development than prenatal cocaine exposure had been.

This does not mean cocaine in pregnancy is harmless, and the careful researchers were clear that it is not good for a developing baby.

The point is one of proportion, because the measured effect of the drug turned out to be modest and hard to separate from its surroundings, while the predicted catastrophe never materialised.

The crack-baby episode is now taught as a warning about how stigma, race, and class can drive a scientific narrative far past the evidence, harming the very children it claimed to describe, and it is a model of why measured effects must be preferred to frightening predictions.


22.3.3 Lead, mercury, organophosphates, and the silent-pandemic argument

The last group of exposures is environmental pollutants, which reach the developing brain not through medicine or drink but through the air, water, food, and soil.

The clearest case is lead, a metal that has no known safe level of exposure for the developing brain.

Decades of research, including an influential international pooled analysis published by Bruce Lanphear and colleagues in 2005, have shown that even very low blood lead levels are associated with losses in measured intelligence and with problems in learning, attention, and behaviour.

The relationship is unusual in that some of the steepest harm appears at the very lowest levels of exposure, which is part of why scientists say there is no safe threshold for lead.

A second case is methylmercury, a form of mercury that builds up in some fish, which harmed developing brains in notorious poisoning episodes such as Minamata in Japan and which remains a concern from dietary exposure at lower levels.

A third case is organophosphates, a class of pesticides, which several birth cohort studies have linked to poorer neurodevelopment in prenatally exposed children.

The physicians Philippe Grandjean and Philip Landrigan drew these threads together into a broad and deliberately provocative argument.

In a 2006 review in The Lancet and an updated 2014 review in The Lancet Neurology, they argued that industrial chemicals were causing a global, silent pandemic of neurodevelopmental toxicity.

Their 2006 review named five well-established developmental neurotoxicants, which were lead, methylmercury, polychlorinated biphenyls, arsenic, and toluene, and their 2014 update added several more.

The word silent captured their central worry, which is that these harms are invisible, spread thinly across whole populations as small losses of ability rather than dramatic individual cases, and therefore easy to overlook.

The argument is not universally accepted in its strongest form, and some scientists regard the pandemic framing as overstated relative to the certainty of the evidence for the newer chemicals.

What is not seriously disputed is the core of it, that several environmental pollutants, lead most firmly of all, genuinely harm the developing brain, and that reducing exposure protects children.


CHAPTER 23. INFECTION AND MATERNAL IMMUNE ACTIVATION (CORE)

This chapter is about how infections during pregnancy can affect the developing brain, and about a subtle and important idea that grew out of studying them.

Some infections harm the baby directly, when a microbe crosses into the developing body and damages tissue.

But researchers gradually realised that the mother's own immune response, the body's defensive reaction, could itself influence brain development, even when the microbe never reached the baby.

That idea is called maternal immune activation, and it has become one of the most active areas in developmental neuroscience.

The chapter moves from the direct infections, to the population studies linking prenatal infection to later mental illness, to the animal experiments that revealed the immune mechanism.

As with the previous chapter, the material touches real pregnancies and serious conditions, and it is presented plainly, as science about populations, never as a judgement or forecast about any individual.


23.1 The congenital infections

A congenital infection is one that is present from birth because it passed from mother to child during pregnancy.

A handful of these have long been known to affect the developing brain directly, and they set the stage for everything that follows.


23.1.1 Rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, and the Zika microcephaly mechanism

The first of the classic congenital infections is rubella, also called German measles, and its story is a landmark in the whole field.

In 1941, the Australian ophthalmologist Norman Gregg noticed an unusual cluster of babies born with cataracts, a clouding of the lens of the eye, and connected it to their mothers having had rubella during pregnancy.

His observation established, for the first time in a clear way, that a maternal infection could cause birth defects, and the resulting pattern is called congenital rubella syndrome, which classically includes cataracts, deafness, and heart defects.

Rubella has since been largely controlled in many countries through vaccination, which is one of the quiet triumphs of preventive medicine.

The second is cytomegalovirus, usually shortened to CMV, a very common virus that most people catch at some point with few or no symptoms.

When a woman is infected for the first time during pregnancy, however, the virus can cross to the baby, and congenital CMV is in fact the leading non-genetic cause of hearing loss in children, and it can also affect the brain more broadly.

Because it is common and often silent, it receives far less public attention than its impact deserves.

The third is toxoplasmosis, an infection caused by a parasite called Toxoplasma gondii, which can be carried in undercooked meat and in cat faeces.

Congenital toxoplasmosis can damage the brain and the eyes, sometimes producing calcium deposits in the brain, fluid build-up, and inflammation of the retina.

The most recent addition to this list is the Zika virus, whose story unfolded dramatically during an outbreak in Brazil in 2015 and 2016.

Doctors observed a sharp rise in babies born with microcephaly, meaning an unusually small head, which reflects a brain that did not grow to its normal size.

Researchers quickly worked out much of the mechanism, and it is worth understanding because it shows how a virus reaches the specific cells it harms.

The Zika virus has a particular ability to infect neural progenitor cells, which are the stem cells that divide to produce the neurons of the cortex.

By infecting and killing these progenitors, or by disrupting their division, the virus depletes the very population that should have multiplied into billions of cortical neurons, so the brain and therefore the head end up small.

The Zika episode was a vivid modern reminder that the list of congenital infections is not closed, and that a previously obscure virus can become a developmental threat.


23.2 The epidemiology

Epidemiology is the study of how conditions are distributed across populations, and it is the tool that first suggested a link between prenatal infection and later mental illness.

This section covers two of the most important of these population-level findings, one for schizophrenia and one for autism.


23.2.1 Prenatal infection and schizophrenia risk

Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness, usually emerging in late adolescence or early adulthood, involving disturbances of thought and perception.

A striking idea took hold in the twentieth century, which is that some of the risk for this adult illness might be seeded before birth.

An early clue came from Sarnoff Mednick and colleagues, who reported in 1988 that people who had been in the second trimester of gestation during a 1957 influenza epidemic in Finland were more likely to develop schizophrenia later in life.

Studies of this kind, which line up birth dates against past epidemics, are called ecological studies, and they are suggestive but limited, because they cannot confirm that any particular mother was actually infected.

The stronger evidence came later from Alan Brown and colleagues, who used stored blood samples from pregnancies decades earlier to test which mothers had actually been infected, an approach called serological confirmation.

Using these preserved samples, they found that confirmed maternal infections, including influenza and toxoplasmosis, were associated with a raised risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.

The effect is real but should be described with care and proportion.

Prenatal infection appears to raise the risk of schizophrenia modestly, and the great majority of children exposed to maternal infection never develop the illness, so this is one contributing influence among many, not a single cause.

The importance of the finding is less about predicting individuals and more about pointing toward a mechanism, because it suggested that something about the response to infection during pregnancy could nudge brain development in ways that only surface many years later.


23.2.2 Maternal fever and autism risk cohorts

A parallel line of research asked whether prenatal infection might also relate to autism, and here a particularly useful clue turned out to be fever.

Fever is interesting because it is a marker of the immune response itself, the body's reaction, rather than of any one specific microbe.

The strongest evidence comes from large birth cohort studies, meaning studies that enrol many thousands of pregnancies and follow the children forward over years.

A leading example is the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study, often abbreviated MoBa, which includes over one hundred thousand children.

Within that cohort, researchers including Mady Hornig and colleagues reported in 2017 that maternal fever during pregnancy, especially in the second trimester, was associated with an increased likelihood of an autism diagnosis in the child.

The association strengthened with repeated fevers, so mothers who reported three or more fever episodes after the twelfth week of pregnancy had a markedly higher associated risk, although the number of such pregnancies was small.

As always, the effect is a modest shift in risk across a population, and most children whose mothers had a fever in pregnancy are not autistic.

The finding matters because fever points at the immune response rather than at any single germ, which dovetails with the animal experiments in the next section, where it is the immune signalling itself, not the microbe, that turns out to matter.

It is worth adding plainly that this science does not support blame, because fevers in pregnancy are common and usually followed by healthy development, and the register of the neurodiversity discussion elsewhere in this book applies here too, treating autism with respect rather than as a catastrophe to be feared.


23.3 The animal mechanism

The population studies could show that prenatal infection was linked to later conditions, but they could not, on their own, prove how.

For that, researchers turned to controlled experiments in animals, which revealed a surprising and specific mechanism.


23.3.1 The interleukin-6 and interleukin-17a pathway

The central discovery is that the harm from prenatal infection often comes not from the microbe but from the mother's own immune messengers.

When the body fights an infection, immune cells release signalling molecules called cytokines, which are the chemical messengers that coordinate the immune response.

Researchers found that they could reproduce features of the conditions in animals without any real microbe at all, simply by triggering the mother's immune system with a mimic that makes the body think it is infected.

The key figure in this work is Paul Patterson, whose laboratory pioneered the maternal immune activation model in mice.

In a landmark study led by Stephen Smith in Patterson's group, published in 2007, the researchers showed that a single cytokine, called interleukin-6, abbreviated IL-6, was pivotal.

Injecting a pregnant mouse with interleukin-6 alone was enough to produce offspring with behavioural changes relevant to schizophrenia and autism, and blocking interleukin-6 during an immune challenge prevented those changes.

This was a powerful result, because it showed that one specific immune messenger could act as the bridge between a mother's infection and her offspring's brain development.

The story was extended by Gloria Choi, Jun Huh, and colleagues in a study published in the journal Science in 2016, which identified a second key messenger, called interleukin-17a, abbreviated IL-17a.

They showed that interleukin-17a, produced by a particular type of immune cell, acted on the developing fetal brain to produce specific changes in the cortex and in behaviour.

Together the interleukin-6 and interleukin-17a findings sketch a pathway, in which maternal infection raises these cytokines, which then reach and reshape the developing brain.

An important and hopeful implication is that this pathway is a potential target, because interrupting the cytokine signal, rather than the infection itself, might one day reduce the risk.

A necessary caution is that these are experiments in mice, and translating them to human pregnancy is difficult and not yet achieved, so the pathway is far better established in animals than in people.


23.3.2 Two-hit models: immune priming plus adolescent stress

A puzzle runs through this whole chapter, which is that a prenatal event is linked to an illness that often does not appear until adolescence or adulthood, many years later.

The two-hit model is the leading way of making sense of that long delay.

The idea is that a single insult is often not enough on its own to produce the full condition.

Instead, the first hit, such as prenatal immune activation, primes the brain, leaving it more vulnerable but not yet ill.

Then a second hit later in life, such as severe stress during adolescence, or drug use, or another challenge, can tip the primed brain into the disorder.

On this view the prenatal infection sets the stage quietly, and a later event pulls the trigger, which explains both why the timing is so delayed and why not everyone exposed to the first hit becomes ill.

Animal experiments support this picture, showing that offspring exposed to maternal immune activation before birth are more sensitive to stress in adolescence, so that the combination produces effects that neither hit produces alone.

The two-hit model is attractive because it fits a general truth about these conditions, which is that they usually arise from an accumulation of risks over time rather than from any single cause.

It also carries a hopeful message, because if a disorder requires more than one hit, then reducing the later hits, for instance by supporting young people through stressful periods, might help even when the earliest hit cannot be undone.


CHAPTER 24. NUTRITION AND THE FETAL PROGRAMME (CORE)

This chapter turns from harmful exposures to the quieter subject of nutrition, and to the idea that what a developing baby is fed, through the mother, can shape the brain and even set patterns that last a lifetime.

The story has two parts.

The first part is about specific nutrients whose importance for brain development is firmly established, so firmly that supplementing them has prevented disability on a large scale.

The second part is a bigger and more debated idea, that the conditions in the womb can programme the body's long-term settings, a concept known as fetal programming.

The chapter shows both the solid ground and the more speculative frontier, and it keeps the beginner oriented throughout.


24.1 The proven nutrients

Some nutrients matter so clearly for brain development that the evidence is beyond serious dispute, and acting on it has prevented a great deal of harm.

This section covers three of them, folate, iodine, and iron, each with its own well-documented story.


24.1.1 Folate and the neural tube trial

Folate is a B vitamin, also given in a synthetic form called folic acid, and its role in early development is one of the great success stories of preventive nutrition.

Very early in pregnancy the embryo forms a structure called the neural tube, which is the folded-up ridge of tissue that becomes the brain and spinal cord.

If the neural tube fails to close properly, the result is a neural tube defect, such as spina bifida, in which the spine does not close fully, or anencephaly, in which much of the brain fails to form.

Because the neural tube closes in the first four weeks or so after conception, often before a woman even knows she is pregnant, protecting it means having enough folate very early.

The decisive proof came from a large randomised trial, the strongest kind of evidence, in which participants are assigned by chance to receive the treatment or not.

The Medical Research Council Vitamin Study Research Group reported this trial in 1991, and the result was dramatic, because folic acid supplementation prevented about seventy-two percent of neural tube defects among women who had already had an affected pregnancy.

This finding was so strong that many countries went on to add folic acid to staple foods such as flour, a policy called fortification, so that women would have enough folate even before a planned pregnancy.

Fortification has since prevented many thousands of neural tube defects, and the folate story stands as proof that understanding a nutrient's role in development can translate into real prevention on a population scale.


24.1.2 Iodine as the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability

Iodine is a trace element, needed only in tiny amounts, but the developing brain cannot do without it.

The reason is that iodine is an essential ingredient of thyroid hormone, the chemical made by the thyroid gland in the neck, and thyroid hormone is a crucial signal for brain development.

If a pregnant woman lacks iodine, her baby lacks thyroid hormone at a time when the brain most needs it, and the result can be serious and permanent intellectual disability.

The most severe form is called congenital iodine deficiency syndrome, historically known as cretinism, which involves profound intellectual disability along with other effects.

The striking and important fact is that iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the world.

That word preventable is the crucial one, because the remedy is remarkably simple and cheap, which is to add small amounts of iodine to ordinary table salt.

Salt iodisation has been one of the most cost-effective public health measures ever undertaken, and it has protected the developing brains of countless children in regions where the soil, and therefore the food, is naturally low in iodine.

The iodine story is a reminder that a nutrient needed in the smallest quantity can carry the largest consequences, and that a very modest intervention can prevent a very large amount of disability.


24.1.3 Iron, myelin, and dopamine

Iron is the third of the firmly established nutrients, and it matters both before birth and through the early years of life.

Iron is best known for carrying oxygen in the blood, but the developing brain needs it for two further jobs that are central to this chapter.

The first job is myelination, the wrapping of nerve fibres in a fatty insulating sheath called myelin, which lets signals travel quickly and reliably, rather like insulation on an electrical wire.

Building myelin requires iron, so a shortage during the period of rapid myelination can slow this crucial process.

The second job involves the brain's chemical messengers, and in particular dopamine, a neurotransmitter deeply involved in attention, movement, motivation, and reward.

Making and using dopamine depends on iron, so iron deficiency disturbs the dopamine system as well as the myelin.

The developmental psychologist Betsy Lozoff and colleagues studied infants who had iron deficiency anaemia, and their long-term follow-up work carried a sobering message.

They found that children who had been iron deficient in infancy tended to show poorer cognitive, motor, and social-emotional outcomes years later, even after their iron levels had been corrected.

This points to the possibility that iron deficiency during a sensitive early window can have effects that do not fully reverse with later treatment, which is why the timing of iron sufficiency, and not just its eventual correction, appears to matter.

The iron story therefore reinforces a theme running through this whole part of the book, which is that the developing brain has windows during which the right supplies must arrive on time, because catching up later is not always enough.


24.2 Famine and programming

The nutrients above are about having enough of specific ingredients, but there is a broader question about overall nourishment.

What happens to a brain, and a life, when a developing baby is undernourished across the board, as in a famine?

The answer opened up one of the most influential ideas in the whole of developmental science, and this section tells that story.


24.2.1 The Dutch Hunger Winter and its psychiatric sequelae

History occasionally produces a tragic natural experiment, and one of the most studied is the Dutch Hunger Winter.

In the final winter of the Second World War, from late 1944 into 1945, a German blockade caused a severe and precisely dated famine in the occupied western Netherlands.

Because the famine had a clear beginning and end, and because the Dutch kept good records, researchers could later identify exactly which pregnancies had been exposed to starvation and at which stage.

The word sequelae simply means the later consequences that follow from an earlier event, and the psychiatric sequelae of this famine were carefully studied decades afterward.

Ezra Susser and colleagues reported in 1992 that people who had been conceived at the height of the famine, and so exposed to severe undernutrition in early gestation, had roughly double the rate of schizophrenia in adulthood.

Later work on the same population linked early-gestation famine exposure to other outcomes as well, including congenital nervous system anomalies and other psychiatric conditions.

The importance of the Dutch Hunger Winter studies is twofold.

They showed that the effects of prenatal nutrition could reach all the way into adult mental health, many decades later.

And, because the timing of exposure was known so precisely, they showed that early gestation was a particularly sensitive window, since the outcomes depended on when in pregnancy the famine struck.

These findings are presented as population-level science about a historical catastrophe, and they carry no implication about any individual who lived through it.


24.2.2 The developmental origins framework: the Barker hypothesis and predictive adaptation

The famine studies were part of a larger idea that reshaped how scientists think about health across the whole lifespan.

Its central figure is the epidemiologist David Barker, and the idea is often called the Barker hypothesis, or more formally the developmental origins of health and disease.

Barker noticed, from historical records, that people who had been smaller at birth, a sign of poorer nourishment in the womb, had higher rates of heart disease and related conditions in adult life.

From this he proposed that the environment in the womb programmes the body's long-term settings, adjusting its metabolism and physiology in ways that persist for decades.

A helpful way to understand the mechanism is an idea called predictive adaptation, sometimes called the thrifty phenotype.

The suggestion is that a developing baby uses the nutritional conditions in the womb as a forecast of the world it is about to enter, and adjusts its biology accordingly.

If the womb signals scarcity, the baby may set its metabolism to be thrifty, holding on to every calorie, which would be a sensible preparation for a hungry world.

The problem comes when the forecast turns out to be wrong.

If a baby prepared for scarcity is then born into a world of plenty, that thrifty setting becomes a liability, raising the risk of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease later on, because the body is mismatched to its actual environment.

This developmental origins framework has been enormously influential, and it extends the logic of this whole chapter, that early nutrition matters, from specific birth defects all the way to adult chronic disease and mental health.

It should be presented with appropriate care, because it is a broad framework rather than a precise law, and the strength of programming effects, and how far they can be reversed later, remain areas of active research and genuine debate.

What is well supported is the core insight, which is that the developing body is not a passive vessel but an organism actively tuning itself to its earliest environment, for better and sometimes for worse.

CHAPTER 25. PREMATURITY AND THE FIRST ENVIRONMENT OF CARE (CORE)

Most chapters in this book describe a brain developing inside the womb or inside a family home.

This chapter is about babies whose brain development finishes somewhere else entirely - inside an incubator, surrounded by machines.

A baby born very early must complete, in a hospital ward, the delicate wiring work that was supposed to happen in the quiet, dark, fluid-filled world of the uterus.

We will look at what large studies tell us about how these children fare, why the preterm brain is injured in a very particular way, how the intensive care environment itself shapes development, and what a simple act - holding a baby against a parent's bare chest - can do for survival.

25.1 The outcomes by gestational age

Gestational age is the length of a pregnancy, counted in weeks from the mother's last menstrual period, and a full-term pregnancy runs about 40 weeks.

The single most powerful predictor of how a preterm baby will do is how many of those weeks were completed before birth.

This section looks at the big national studies that followed extremely preterm children for years, and at the steep gradient they reveal, where every extra week inside the womb measurably improves the odds.

25.1.1 The extreme-prematurity cohorts and their gradients

Extreme prematurity usually means birth before 28 weeks of gestation, which is roughly three months early.

To find out what happens to these children, researchers have run large cohort studies, meaning studies that identify every baby born in a country or region during a set period and then follow them all as they grow.

The best known is EPICure, a study that registered every baby born at 25 weeks of gestation or less across all 276 maternity units in the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland between March and December of 1995, and then followed the survivors at 2.5 years, 6 years, and 11 years of age.

A second EPICure cohort was collected in 2006, allowing researchers to compare children born extremely preterm a decade apart and to see how changing care changed outcomes.

France ran parallel national studies called EPIPAGE, with a second wave, EPIPAGE-2, enrolling babies born between 22 and 26 weeks in 2011.

These studies agree on a central finding, which is a gradient - a steady, week-by-week slope rather than a cliff edge.

At 22 weeks survival is rare, and among survivors serious disability is common.

By 25 or 26 weeks, most babies who receive active intensive care survive, and most survivors do not have a severe disability.

Each completed week of gestation buys a meaningful improvement in survival, and a meaningful drop in the risk of cerebral palsy, which is a lifelong disorder of movement and posture caused by early brain injury, and in the risk of learning difficulties, attention problems, and psychiatric conditions later in childhood.

EPIPAGE-2 also showed that the intensity of care matters, since hospitals that actively treated babies born at the edge of viability had more survivors without sensorimotor disability, not just more survivors.

The honest picture from these cohorts is neither doom nor false comfort.

Most extremely preterm children grow up without severe disability, yet as a group they carry higher rates of cognitive, motor, attention, and emotional difficulties than children born at term, and those rates climb steeply as gestational age at birth falls.

25.1.2 The encephalopathy of prematurity and the vulnerable pre-oligodendrocyte

Encephalopathy is a general medical word for a disorder or injury of the brain, and the encephalopathy of prematurity is the name the neurologist Joseph Volpe gave to the characteristic pattern of injury and disturbed development seen in the preterm brain.

To understand it, we need one cell type.

The brain's long-distance wiring is made of axons, which are the cable-like fibers that carry electrical signals between nerve cells.

Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating sheath that makes signals travel far faster, and the cells that manufacture myelin are called oligodendrocytes.

Between roughly 24 and 40 weeks of gestation, the white matter - the deep tissue made mostly of these wired connections - is populated largely by pre-oligodendrocytes, which are immature cells that have not yet started wrapping axons in myelin.

These pre-oligodendrocytes turn out to be extraordinarily fragile.

They are far more easily killed than mature oligodendrocytes by three insults that preterm babies commonly face: shortage of oxygen and blood flow, inflammation from infection, and oxidative stress, which is chemical damage from unstable oxygen-derived molecules.

So a baby born at 26 weeks passes through exactly the window when the white matter is stocked with its most vulnerable cells, at exactly the moment when unstable breathing, immature circulation, and infections make injury most likely.

When pre-oligodendrocytes die or stall, myelination fails or is delayed, and the classic result is white matter injury, historically called periventricular leukomalacia, meaning softening of the white matter near the fluid-filled ventricles at the center of the brain.

Volpe's crucial insight was that this is not only destruction but also derailed development.

The injury also involves axons, the thalamus - the deep relay station that routes sensory information to the cortex - the subplate neurons that guide early cortical wiring, and migrating inhibitory neurons, so a single early hit ripples outward into how the whole network assembles.

This is why the signature problems of prematurity are so often problems of connection and coordination - motor control, processing speed, attention - rather than the focal deficits seen after strokes in adults.

25.2 The neonatal intensive care unit as an environment

The neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) is the hospital ward where preterm and sick newborns are cared for.

It saves lives, and it is also, unavoidably, the developmental environment in which a preterm baby's brain does weeks or months of its growing.

This section treats the NICU the way this book treats any environment - as a set of experiences that sculpt a developing brain - and asks what its sounds, lights, and needles cost, and what kinds of care can give back.

25.2.1 Sound, light, and pain, and their developmental costs

The womb is dim, warm, and acoustically muffled, dominated by the mother's heartbeat, digestion, and low-frequency voice.

The NICU, by contrast, can be a place of alarms, ventilator noise, bright overhead lighting, and frequent handling.

Studies measuring the ward directly have found that sudden sound peaks and abrupt changes in light levels produce measurable stress and pain behaviors in very preterm infants, which is why modern units work to keep sound low and to cycle or shield lighting.

The heaviest cost, though, appears to come from pain.

A very preterm baby may undergo hundreds of skin-breaking procedures during a hospital stay - heel pricks for blood tests, intravenous line insertions, suctioning of breathing tubes.

For a long time it was assumed that newborns barely registered pain, but that assumption was wrong, and preterm infants show clear physiological and brain responses to painful procedures.

Work by Ruth Grunau, Steven Miller, and colleagues, following very preterm babies with repeated brain scans, found that a greater number of painful procedures predicted slower maturation of the white matter and of deep gray matter structures, and thinner cortex in frontal and parietal regions, even after statistically accounting for how sick each baby was.

Greater early pain exposure has also been linked to poorer motor, cognitive, and behavioral outcomes in childhood, and these associations appear even in babies with no visible structural brain injury.

The plain conclusion is that pain in the preterm period is not a passing unpleasantness but a developmental exposure, which is why NICUs now count procedures, cluster necessary care to reduce disturbances, and use comfort measures such as sucrose, swaddling, and skin-to-skin contact during procedures.

25.2.2 Kangaroo mother care and the mortality trial of 2021

Kangaroo mother care is the practice of holding a small baby upright against a parent's bare chest, skin touching skin, for as many hours a day as possible, usually combined with breastfeeding support.

It was developed in Bogota, Colombia, in the late 1970s, partly because there were not enough incubators, and it turned out to be far more than a substitute.

Against a parent's chest a small baby stays warmer, breathes more steadily, is colonized by the family's protective microbes rather than the hospital's dangerous ones, and feeds more successfully.

Earlier trials had already shown that kangaroo mother care, started once a baby was medically stable, cut mortality in low birth weight babies by roughly 40 percent compared with conventional incubator care.

The open question was whether it was safe to start immediately at birth, before stabilization, which is precisely when most deaths occur.

A large randomized trial coordinated by the World Health Organization (WHO), run in hospitals in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, answered this.

More than 3,200 infants weighing between 1.0 and 1.8 kilograms were randomly assigned either to immediate continuous kangaroo mother care, with intensive care delivered while the baby stayed on the mother's chest, or to conventional care in an incubator until stable.

The trial was stopped early because the benefit was so clear: babies who received immediate kangaroo mother care were about 25 percent less likely to die in their first 28 days.

The investigators estimated that starting skin-to-skin care at birth rather than after stabilization could save well over 100,000 additional newborn lives each year worldwide.

For a book about the developing brain, the lesson is striking - one of the most powerful neonatal interventions ever tested is not a drug or a machine but the restoration of the biologically expected first environment, a parent's body.

25.3 The imaging window

Because preterm babies are outside the womb during weeks when their peers are still inside it, they offer science a unique, if unwanted, window - the chance to watch the third trimester of human brain development directly with brain scanners.

This section looks at what modern large-scale imaging of newborns has revealed.

25.3.1 What the developing connectome project sees in the preterm brain

The word connectome means the complete map of connections in a brain, the way a road atlas maps every highway between cities.

The Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) is a large European-funded effort, led from London, that has used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a scanning technique that pictures soft tissue in fine detail without radiation, to scan hundreds of fetuses and newborns from about 20 to 44 weeks of gestational age.

Its open dataset lets researchers chart, week by week, how the folds of the cortex form, how white matter pathways mature, and how the brain's resting-state networks - sets of regions whose activity rises and falls together even during sleep - come online.

One of its central findings is that the adult brain's major functional networks are already recognizable, in draft form, around the time of normal birth, with sensory and motor networks looking most mature and the higher-order networks that will support attention and thought still immature.

When the project compared babies born preterm, scanned at the age they should have been born, with babies born at term, it found widespread differences.

Preterm birth was associated with altered functional connectivity, with disruption reported in the connections between the thalamus and the cortex - exactly the relay wiring that is being built during the third trimester, and exactly the circuitry that Volpe's account of the encephalopathy of prematurity predicts should suffer.

White matter pathways in preterm-born babies show lower measures of microstructural maturity, consistent with the pre-oligodendrocyte story told earlier in this chapter.

The importance of this imaging window is twofold.

It shows that being born early changes brain development even in babies with no visible injury on a clinical scan, and it gives medicine a way to test, objectively and early, whether protective care such as reduced pain exposure and kangaroo mother care leaves the developing connectome measurably closer to the path it would have taken in the womb.

PART SEVEN. THE DEVELOPMENT OF PERCEPTION AND ACTION

================================================================================

CHAPTER 26. THE COMPETENT NEWBORN (CORE)

For much of the twentieth century the newborn was described as experiencing, in William James's famous phrase, a blooming, buzzing confusion.

Modern research has demolished that picture.

A newborn arrives having already learned from months of listening in the womb, equipped with biases that point its attention at faces and eyes, and ready to begin the social life on which all later development depends.

This chapter tours that surprising competence, and it also tells a cautionary tale - the story of neonatal imitation, a famous claim about newborn abilities that ran into a major replication failure and is still being argued over.

26.1 Learning before birth

Learning does not wait for birth.

The auditory system begins working months before delivery, and the fetus uses it, so that every baby is born already shaped by the particular voices and language it overheard.

This section covers when fetal hearing starts, what the womb lets through, and the clever experiments that proved newborns remember what they heard inside.

26.1.1 Fetal hearing from mid-gestation and the low-pass filtered womb

The cochlea, which is the snail-shaped organ in the inner ear that converts sound vibrations into nerve signals, becomes functional around the middle of pregnancy, and fetuses begin responding to sounds at roughly 24 to 26 weeks of gestation, with responses becoming reliable and refined over the third trimester.

But the fetus does not hear the world as we do.

The mother's abdominal wall, the uterus, and the amniotic fluid act together as a low-pass filter, which means a filter that lets low-pitched sound through while muffling high-pitched sound.

Frequencies above roughly 600 to 1,000 hertz are attenuated by tens of decibels, so the crisp consonants of speech are largely smeared away.

What survives the filter is the melody of speech - its pitch contours, its rhythm, its stress patterns - and the mother's own voice, which reaches the fetus both through the air and through her body, arrives clearest of all.

So the fetus spends the last trimester bathed in the prosody of its native language, the rise and fall of its mother's sentences, without hearing most of the fine detail.

That particular diet of sound turns out to leave measurable traces.

26.1.2 The newborn's preference for the mother's voice and the prenatally heard story

In 1980, Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer published one of developmental psychology's most elegant experiments.

They gave newborns, some only days old, a pacifier wired to a recording system, and arranged things so that sucking in one rhythm turned on a recording of the baby's own mother reading, while sucking in a different rhythm turned on an unfamiliar woman's voice.

The newborns adjusted their sucking to hear their mother, showing both that they recognized her voice and that they would work to obtain it - a preference that can only have been learned before birth.

Follow-up work sharpened the point: newborns prefer a low-pass filtered version of the mother's voice, the wombs-eye version, and show no such pull toward her whispered voice, which lacks the vocal-cord vibration that carried through her body.

Then DeCasper and Melanie Spence, in a study published in 1986, showed that fetuses learn not just voices but specific sound patterns.

They asked pregnant women to read aloud a particular Dr. Seuss story, The Cat in the Hat, twice a day during the final six weeks of pregnancy.

After birth, the babies sucked to hear the familiar story rather than a novel story, and they did so even when the familiar story was read by a stranger's voice.

Since the babies had never heard the story outside the womb, they must have learned its rhythm and cadence prenatally, and what they retained was the pattern itself, not merely the voice that carried it.

26.1.3 The prenatal exposure experiments and the newborn cry melody

Later experiments pinned down what, exactly, is learned in the womb.

Christine Moon, Hugo Lagercrantz, and Patricia Kuhl, in a two-country study published in 2013, tested 80 newborns in Sweden and the United States at an average age of about 33 hours.

The babies controlled the playback of vowel sounds by sucking on a pacifier, and in both countries they responded differently to native vowels than to vowels from the other language, showing that even individual speech sounds - at least vowels, whose low frequencies pass the womb's filter - begin to be learned before birth.

Related brain-recording work in Finland showed that fetuses exposed repeatedly to a made-up word in late pregnancy showed enhanced neural responses to that word after birth, direct evidence of prenatal memory traces in the brain.

The most charming evidence, though, comes from crying.

Birgit Mampe, Angela Friederici, Anne Christophe, and Kathleen Wermke, in a 2009 study in Current Biology, analyzed the cries of 30 French and 30 German newborns, all just a few days old.

French newborns tended to cry with a rising melody, while German newborns tended to cry with a falling melody, matching the characteristic intonation contours of the two languages.

Newborns, in other words, do not merely recognize their native language's melody - they already reproduce it with the one instrument they can play, the cry.

The sensible caution is that these are group-level tendencies in modest samples, not a claim that any individual baby's cry reveals its nationality, but the converging picture from preference, brain response, and cry production is that language learning begins in the womb.

26.2 The newborn's biases

Learning explains part of newborn competence, but not all of it.

Newborns also arrive with built-in biases, which are simple preferences that aim their limited attention at the most important things in their world - above all, other people.

This section covers the two most studied biases: the pull toward faces, and the pull toward eyes that are looking back.

26.2.1 The face preference and the two-process account

Within hours of birth, before any meaningful visual experience, newborns will turn their eyes and head further to follow a moving face-like pattern - two blobs above a third, arranged like eyes above a mouth - than to follow the same blobs scrambled.

This was shown in classic work by Carolyn Goren and colleagues in 1975 and confirmed by Mark Johnson, John Morton, and colleagues in 1991.

To explain it, Johnson and Morton proposed an influential two-process account in 1991, giving the two processes the memorable names CONSPEC and CONLERN.

CONSPEC is a crude, built-in orienting mechanism, thought to depend on ancient subcortical structures - the brain regions beneath the cortex that handle fast, automatic responses - and it does nothing more sophisticated than steer the newborn's gaze toward anything with the rough top-heavy geometry of a face.

CONLERN is a slower, cortical learning system that, from about 2 months of age, takes over and gradually becomes expert in the particular faces the baby actually sees.

The elegance of the account is its division of labor: a cheap innate bias guarantees that faces dominate the input, and a powerful general learning system does the rest.

The account has been refined over two decades - later research showed that newborns' preference partly reflects general visual biases, such as a liking for top-heavy patterns and for stimuli with the right contrast polarity, dark features on a lighter background, and researchers still debate how face-specific CONSPEC really is.

But the core two-process logic, an initial orienting bias handing off to experience-driven cortical specialization, remains the standard framework, and it recurs throughout this book as a general pattern in development.

26.2.2 Eye contact detection from birth

Among all the parts of a face, the eyes matter most, because gaze tells you where another creature's attention is - and whether it is on you.

Teresa Farroni, Gergely Csibra, and colleagues showed in a 2002 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that sensitivity to eye contact is present from birth.

Newborns between 1 and 5 days old were shown pairs of faces, identical except that one had direct gaze, looking straight at the baby, and the other had averted gaze.

The newborns looked longer, and oriented more often, toward the face that was looking back at them.

The same study found that by 4 months of age, faces with direct gaze evoked enhanced brain responses, measured with electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity through sensors resting on the scalp.

Direct gaze is the opening move of human communication, and the newborn brain appears tuned to catch it from the first days, giving parents' instinctive face-to-face engagement a prepared audience.

26.3 The neonatal imitation dispute

No topic in newborn research better illustrates how science self-corrects, and how messy that correction can be, than neonatal imitation.

For decades textbooks stated that newborns can imitate facial gestures such as sticking out the tongue.

That claim then failed the largest replication attempt ever conducted on it, the original researchers fired back, and the field remains genuinely divided.

This book's policy is to present such disputes plainly, and this section does.

26.3.1 The classic claims, the large failed replication, and the rebuttal

In 1977, Andrew Meltzoff and Keith Moore published a famous paper in Science reporting that infants between 12 and 21 days old imitated an adult's facial and manual gestures - tongue protrusion, mouth opening, lip protrusion, and finger movements.

The claim was sensational, because imitating a face you have never seen your own face make seems to require some inborn ability to map what you see onto what you feel your own body doing.

Neonatal imitation became a foundation stone for theories of social cognition, and later it was widely linked to mirror neurons, which are brain cells, first described in monkeys, that fire both when an animal performs an action and when it watches another perform it.

Replications over the following decades were strikingly inconsistent, with some laboratories finding the effect and others not.

Then in 2016, Janine Oostenbroek, Virginia Slaughter, and colleagues published the largest and most systematic test yet, a longitudinal study of 106 infants, each tested at 1, 3, 6, and 9 weeks of age on 9 modeled gestures plus control conditions.

The design's strength was breadth: by testing many gestures and comparing each response against its rate during other models, it could ask whether babies specifically matched what they saw, rather than simply producing tongue protrusions to anything interesting.

The result was null - infants were no more likely to produce a gesture when it was modeled than when a different gesture was modeled, at any age.

The authors concluded that the evidence for neonatal imitation was, at best, an artifact of designs that used too few comparison conditions.

In 2018, Meltzoff and colleagues published a re-examination in Developmental Science, arguing that the replication's design contained numerous flaws that biased it toward null results - among them very short presentation periods for each gesture and testing conditions that left infants inattentive or fussy - and reporting that their reanalysis of the raw data showed significant tongue-protrusion matching at all four ages.

Oostenbroek and colleagues responded in turn, defending their design and disputing the reanalysis.

That is where the dispute honestly stands: a foundational claim, a large pre-registered-style failure to replicate, a detailed rebuttal, and no consensus.

Readers should treat confident statements in either direction - that newborns clearly imitate, or that neonatal imitation is clearly a myth - as overclaiming.

26.3.2 What survives: the tongue protrusion case and the lesson in measurement

If anything survives from the original claims, most reviewers agree it is tongue protrusion, the single gesture that has shown matching most often across four decades of studies, including in Meltzoff's reanalysis of the 2016 replication data.

But even here there is a deflationary interpretation with real support.

Tongue protrusion is one of the newborn's few readily available motor acts, and newborns produce more tongue protrusions to many kinds of arousing stimuli - flashing lights and lively music among them - which raises the possibility that an interesting face at close range simply excites the baby, and excitement comes out through the tongue.

On that reading, the effect is real but is general arousal, not imitation, and it says little about inborn social mirroring.

On the richer reading, defended by Meltzoff, tongue matching is the visible tip of a genuine, if fragile, capacity to map others' acts onto one's own body.

Current evidence does not decisively separate these readings, and this book will not pretend it does.

The deeper lesson is about measurement.

The original effect was small, the behaviors are low-frequency and easily influenced by infant state, and early studies often compared only one or two gestures, a design that cannot distinguish specific imitation from general excitement.

When a field builds theory on a small effect measured with permissive designs, it accumulates risk, and the neonatal imitation saga - like the infant false-belief literature discussed later in this book - shows what happens when that risk comes due.

The constructive legacy is a set of better standards: many gestures, cross-target comparisons, adequate presentation time, attention to infant state, and large samples, standards that now shape infant research well beyond imitation.


CHAPTER 27. VISION: FROM BLUR TO EXPERTISE (CORE)

A newborn sees the world roughly the way an adult sees it through frosted glass - blurry, low in contrast, and flat.

Within months that picture sharpens, gains depth, and begins to organize itself around the things that matter most, above all faces.

Within years, parts of the visual brain are recruited for an ability evolution never anticipated - reading.

This chapter follows vision from its blurry start to its specialized adult expertise, because vision is the clearest showcase of how experience and built-in timing together tune a sensory system.

27.1 The basic capacities

Before the interesting specializations come the basics: how sharp is a baby's sight, and when does the world gain depth?

This section gives the real numbers and timings.

27.1.1 Acuity from roughly twenty-four-hundredths of adult at birth to adult levels by three to five years

Visual acuity is the sharpness of vision, the ability to resolve fine detail, and it is what an eye chart measures.

Newborn acuity is estimated at around 20/600 in the notation used for eye charts, meaning that a newborn at 20 feet resolves only what an adult with normal sight could resolve from 600 feet - only a few percent of adult sharpness, though estimates vary with the method used.

Since babies cannot read eye charts, researchers measure acuity with preferential looking, exploiting the fact that infants would rather look at stripes than at a blank field, so the finest stripes a baby reliably prefers reveal the finest detail the baby can see, or with visual evoked potentials, which are the brain's electrical responses to patterned stimuli recorded from the scalp.

The early gains are fast: acuity improves severalfold in the first 6 months, reaching very roughly 20/200 by about 1 year.

Full adult acuity, however, arrives only around 3 to 5 years of age, with some measures maturing even later.

The limiting factors are mostly in the brain and retina rather than the optics - the fovea, the central pit of the retina responsible for sharp vision, is still immature at birth, and the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain that processes sight, is still wiring itself.

This long tail of maturation matters clinically, because it is exactly the period during which unequal input to the two eyes, from a cataract or a chronically unfocused eye, can produce amblyopia, a lasting loss of acuity caused by the brain rather than the eye - a topic this book treats fully in its critical-period chapters.

27.1.2 Stereopsis switching on at three to five months

Stereopsis is depth perception from binocular disparity, meaning the small differences between the two eyes' images that the brain uses to compute three-dimensional structure - it is what 3D glasses exploit at the cinema.

Unlike acuity, which improves gradually, stereopsis switches on abruptly.

Infants show essentially no sensitivity to binocular disparity before about 3 months, and then, at some point between roughly 3 and 5 months of age, an individual infant goes from stereoblind to stereoscopic within a matter of weeks, a finding established in the 1980s by researchers including Richard Held, Eileen Birch, and Jane Gwiazda.

After onset, stereo sensitivity sharpens very rapidly toward adult-like fineness over the following weeks and months.

The abruptness is thought to reflect a specific wiring event in the visual cortex - the segregation of inputs from the two eyes into alternating columns, which gives cortical neurons the clean two-eye comparison that disparity computation requires.

Stereopsis then depends on the two eyes staying aligned and balanced, which is why strabismus, the condition in which the eyes point in different directions, can permanently prevent fine stereo vision if not corrected early, and why this system became neuroscience's textbook example of a critical period.

27.2 The face pathway

Faces get special treatment from the visual system, and the infant's first year shows us that specialization being built.

This section follows three findings on one theme: tuning to the faces you actually see, at the cost of the faces you do not.

27.2.1 Perceptual narrowing: losing the monkey faces between six and nine months

Perceptual narrowing is the process by which an infant's initially broad perceptual abilities sharpen around the categories in its environment while sensitivity to unencountered categories fades.

Its most famous demonstration used monkey faces.

Olivier Pascalis, Michelle de Haan, and Charles Nelson, in a 2002 study in Science, tested infants with a visual paired-comparison task, which relies on babies looking longer at something new: if a baby looks longer at a new face than at a face just studied, the baby must be able to tell them apart.

Six-month-old infants discriminated individual monkey faces as well as individual human faces.

Nine-month-olds and adults discriminated human faces easily but failed with the monkeys.

Somewhere between 6 and 9 months, then, the face system commits to the faces it actually meets - human ones - and lets the unused ability go.

Crucially, the narrowing is experience-dependent and, at that age, reversible: a follow-up study by Pascalis and colleagues in 2005 showed that infants given picture books of monkey faces to view at home between 6 and 9 months retained the ability to discriminate monkey faces at 9 months.

Narrowing is not decay but tuning - the system allocates its resolution where the input says it will be needed.

27.2.2 The other-race effect on the same calendar

The other-race effect is the well-documented finding that people recognize faces of their own racial group more easily than faces of less familiar groups - an experience effect, not anything deeper, and one with real-world consequences for eyewitness reliability.

David Kelly, Paul Quinn, Alan Slater, Kang Lee, Liezhong Ge, and Olivier Pascalis showed in 2007 that this effect is built in infancy, on the same calendar as the monkey-face narrowing.

They tested Chinese infants in China with faces from their own and other groups.

Three-month-olds discriminated individual faces from all the groups tested.

Six-month-olds discriminated some other-group faces but not all.

Nine-month-olds discriminated only own-group faces.

The same 6 to 9 month window, in other words, tunes the face system not just to the human species but to the particular faces in the baby's daily life.

And as with monkey faces, exposure changes the outcome - infants who see many faces from other groups, in the family or in picture-book training studies, keep broader discrimination - which is a concrete reminder that this effect indexes experience, not race in any biological sense.

27.2.3 The fusiform face area's long childhood

In adults, faces are processed by a network centered on the fusiform face area (FFA), a region on the fusiform gyrus, a fold on the underside of the temporal lobe, that responds far more strongly to faces than to objects, as characterized by Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues in 1997.

Given how early infants prefer faces, one might expect the FFA to be finished early.

It is not.

Functional MRI studies by Golijeh Golarai and colleagues in 2007, and by Kalanit Grill-Spector, Jesse Gomez, and colleagues through 2017, found that the face-selective territory in the fusiform gyrus is markedly smaller in children of 7 to 11 years than in adults, and that it continues to expand and sharpen its selectivity through adolescence.

Gomez's 2017 work added a startling anatomical finding: the tissue itself keeps developing, with measures suggesting continued microstructural growth in the face region across childhood, in step with improving face-recognition ability.

Infant brain-imaging studies have found face-preferring responses in roughly the right cortical neighborhood within the first months of life, so the region does not appear from nothing - but its adult size, selectivity, and expertise take well over a decade of face experience to build.

Face perception is thus a lifelong showcase of the pattern this book keeps meeting: early biases guarantee the input, and prolonged cortical development turns input into expertise.

27.3 The streams and their vulnerability

Beyond the early visual areas, visual information travels through two great processing streams, and they do not mature or fail equally.

This section introduces them and a hypothesis about why one of them keeps turning up damaged.

27.3.1 Dorsal-stream vulnerability across disorders

Visual cortex feeds two broad pathways.

The ventral stream runs down into the temporal lobe and handles what things are - object identity, faces, and eventually words.

The dorsal stream runs up into the parietal lobe and handles where things are and how to act on them - motion, spatial relations, and the visual guidance of reaching, grasping, and attention.

Oliver Braddick and Janette Atkinson, in an influential body of work from the early 2000s onward, noticed a recurring pattern: across a remarkable range of developmental conditions, tests of dorsal-stream function are impaired more than matched tests of ventral-stream function.

Their standard comparison sets global motion perception, detecting coherent movement among noise dots, which taxes the dorsal stream, against global form perception, detecting coherent patterns among static elements, which taxes the ventral stream.

Deficits in global motion relative to global form have been reported in children born very preterm, in Williams syndrome, which is a genetic condition affecting spatial cognition, in developmental dyslexia, in autism, in congenital hemiplegia, and after early treated cataract or amblyopia.

Braddick and Atkinson named this pattern dorsal-stream vulnerability.

Why the dorsal stream should be the fragile one is not settled, and proposed explanations include its more protracted developmental timetable, its dependence on precise timing signals carried by the fast magnocellular pathway from the retina, and its reliance on long-range connections of the kind most at risk from the white matter injury of prematurity described in Chapter 25.

The idea should be held as a well-supported generalization rather than a law, since not every study of every disorder finds the dissociation, but it usefully predicts that spatial, motion, and visuomotor skills are where early-injured visual systems most often struggle.

27.4 The reading window into cortex

Reading is only a few thousand years old, far too recent for evolution to have built reading circuitry.

Yet every literate brain has a patch of cortex specialized for print.

Watching that patch appear in children is one of neuroscience's clearest views of how culture installs itself in the brain, and this section tells that story.

27.4.1 The visual word form area emerging within months of schooling

The visual word form area (VWFA) is a region of the left ventral visual stream - sitting among the object and face areas of the fusiform region - that in literate people responds selectively to written words and letter strings, a characterization developed by Stanislas Dehaene, Laurent Cohen, and colleagues from 2000 onward.

Its location is strikingly consistent across individuals and across writing systems, from alphabets to Chinese characters.

Longitudinal studies have caught its birth.

In a 2018 study led by Dehaene-Lambertz, Monzalvo, and Dehaene, ten 6-year-old children were scanned with functional MRI six or seven times across their first year of school.

Before reading instruction, the future word area showed no special response to print.

Within the first months of schooling, a robust response to written words emerged at the classic left ventral site, and its strength tracked the children's growing reading skill.

Studies of adults who learned to read late, including work with unschooled adults in Brazil and Portugal, show the same region gaining print responsiveness whenever literacy is acquired, though childhood learning appears to produce the strongest specialization.

Cortex, in short, can be visibly re-purposed by classroom experience within months, and the VWFA is the best-documented case of culture writing itself into the brain.

27.4.2 Neuronal recycling as the general principle

Why does reading always land in that particular patch of cortex?

Dehaene's answer is the neuronal recycling hypothesis, proposed in the mid-2000s.

The idea is that cultural inventions such as reading and arithmetic cannot conjure new brain tissue, so they must invade existing circuits whose natural function is close enough to the new demand to be re-trainable.

The VWFA's neighborhood is high-resolution, shape-analyzing cortex with strong connections to the left hemisphere's language network - precisely the combination reading needs, since reading means mapping fine visual shapes onto spoken language.

The 2018 longitudinal study added an important refinement: in those children, print responses grew mainly in cortex that had been only weakly specialized beforehand, next to but not on top of the face- and object-selective patches, which largely kept their prior tuning.

Recycling, on this evidence, is less a hostile takeover than a settlement of weakly claimed territory, though there is also evidence that heavy literacy competes with face processing at the margins, and researchers still debate how much displacement occurs.

The principle generalizes well beyond reading.

Arithmetic settles into parietal circuits for quantity and space, and every classroom subject must likewise negotiate with the cortical maps evolution provided.

Neuronal recycling is thus this book's bridge between brain development and education: schooling works precisely because the developing cortex retains, for years, the capacity to re-tune inherited circuits to invented skills.


CHAPTER 28. HEARING AND SPEECH: THE NARROWING EAR (CORE)

A newborn can hear the difference between speech sounds used in any of the world's roughly 7,000 languages, including differences its parents can no longer hear.

By the first birthday, much of that universal ear is gone, traded for something better - exquisite tuning to the native language.

This chapter follows that trade: the infant's early universal abilities, the narrowing that commits the ear to one language, the astonishing statistical learning that finds words in the stream of speech, and the brain measures that let scientists watch it all happen.

28.1 Universal then native

The infant speech-perception story has a famous arc - universal listener first, native-language specialist by twelve months.

This section walks through that arc, experiment by experiment.

28.1.1 Categorical perception in the first months

Speech sounds vary continuously, but we hear them in categories.
