Acoustically, the difference between the syllables ba and pa is a graded dimension called voice onset time, the delay between the lips opening and the vocal cords starting to vibrate, yet adults hear a sharp boundary - everything on one side is ba, everything on the other is pa, and two sounds that differ by the same acoustic step are easy to distinguish across the boundary and hard to distinguish within a category.

This phenomenon is called categorical perception.

In 1971, Peter Eimas, Einar Siqueland, Peter Jusczyk, and James Vigorito published a landmark study in Science showing that infants of 1 and 4 months already perceive speech this way.

They used high-amplitude sucking, a method in which an infant's sucking on a pacifier controls sound presentation: the baby sucks eagerly to a new sound, the sucking declines as the sound repeats and becomes boring, and a renewed burst of sucking when the sound changes proves the baby noticed the change.

Infants noticed acoustic changes that crossed the adult ba to pa boundary but largely ignored equal-sized changes within a category.

Speech perception, in other words, is organized into categories from the earliest months, long before babies understand a single word - a foundation that later theorists have interpreted in different ways, since some categorical-like discrimination also appears in non-speech hearing and in other species, suggesting the infant starts from general auditory boundaries that language then reshapes.

28.1.2 The loss of non-native contrasts by ten to twelve months, vowels before consonants

The young infant's categories are not limited to the native language.

Janet Werker and Richard Tees, in a classic 1984 study, tested English-learning infants on consonant contrasts that matter in Hindi and in Nthlakampx, a Salish language of British Columbia, but not in English.

Infants of 6 to 8 months discriminated these foreign contrasts readily, even though English-speaking adults could not.

By 10 to 12 months, the same test found the ability largely gone: the English-learning infants now failed the Hindi and Salish contrasts, while infants learning those languages retained them.

This decline between roughly 6 and 12 months, confirmed many times since across languages and contrast types, is perceptual narrowing in hearing - the auditory twin of the monkey-face effect in Chapter 27, and on almost the same calendar.

Vowels narrow before consonants.

Work by Patricia Kuhl and colleagues in 1992 and by Linda Polka and Janet Werker in 1994 showed that native-language effects on vowel perception are already present by about 6 months, several months before the consonant reorganization at 10 to 12 months.

A plausible reason is exposure: vowels are longer, louder, and carried by the low frequencies that even the womb transmits, so the statistics of native vowels accumulate earlier.

Two clarifications keep the story honest.

The decline is a reorganization rather than a deletion, since with training, adults can partially relearn foreign contrasts, though rarely to native level.

And narrowing is accompanied by improvement, because over the same months, discrimination of native contrasts sharpens - the ear is not losing ability so much as spending its resolution where its language needs it.

28.1.3 The native language magnet and the social gating experiment: the live tutor against the video

Patricia Kuhl's native language magnet theory, first proposed in the early 1990s and expanded since, offers a mechanism for narrowing.

The proposal is that as an infant hears thousands of examples of each native speech sound, the brain forms prototypes, meaning stored best examples of each category, and each prototype then acts like a perceptual magnet, pulling nearby sounds toward itself so that differences close to the prototype become harder to hear.

Native prototypes thus simultaneously sharpen native categories and swallow foreign distinctions that fall within their pull.

Kuhl's most famous experiment, published with Feng-Ming Tsao and Huei-Mei Liu in 2003, asked whether the narrowing could be reversed by fresh experience, and what kind of experience counts.

Nine-month-old American infants received 12 sessions of exposure to Mandarin Chinese over about 4 to 5 weeks, at exactly the age when their perception was committing to English.

Infants exposed to live Mandarin speakers, who played with them and read to them, discriminated a Mandarin consonant contrast afterward about as well as infants raised in Taiwan.

Infants given the same material by television or by audio recording learned essentially nothing, performing like unexposed controls.

The identical sounds, delivered without a person, failed.

Kuhl drew from this the social gating hypothesis - the idea that social interaction gates language learning, perhaps because a live partner drives attention and arousal, provides eye gaze and contingent responses, and marks what matters.

Later work by Barbara Conboy, Andrew Meltzoff, and Kuhl showed that infants who engaged more with the tutors, tracking gaze and shifting attention, learned more, strengthening the interpretation.

The finding is among the most cited in developmental science and its broad lesson, that infant language learning feeds on interaction rather than exposure alone, is widely accepted, though its boundary conditions are still being mapped - somewhat older children can learn some things from well-designed contingent video such as live video chat, so the gate appears to be about contingency and engagement more than about screens as such.

28.2 The statistical infant

Before an infant can learn words, it must solve a problem adults never notice: spoken sentences have no spaces.

Where does one word end and the next begin?

This section describes the discovery that infants crack this problem with statistics, and that the ability is running from the first days of life.

28.2.1 Word segmentation from transitional probabilities in two minutes of exposure

In fluent speech the syllables of a word reliably follow one another, while the syllable that ends one word can be followed by the first syllable of almost any next word.

The transitional probability - the likelihood that syllable B follows syllable A - is therefore high inside words and low across word boundaries, so a listener who tracked these probabilities could find the words without knowing any of them.

Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin, and Elissa Newport, in a celebrated 1996 study in Science, showed that 8-month-old infants do exactly this.

The infants heard 2 minutes of a continuous stream of synthesized syllables - a made-up language of four three-syllable words repeated in random order, spoken in a flat monotone with no pauses, no stress, and no melody, so that transitional probabilities were the only cue to word boundaries.

Afterward, the infants were tested with the stream's words against part-words, meaning syllable sequences that had also occurred in the stream but spanned a word boundary and therefore had lower internal probabilities.

The infants listened differently to words than to part-words, showing they had segmented the stream - from 2 minutes of passive listening, with no rewards, no repetition of isolated words, and no help.

This result founded the modern study of statistical learning, the brain's automatic extraction of patterns from experience, and later work extended it beyond speech to tones, visual sequences, and other species, establishing it as a general learning mechanism that language exploits rather than a language-only trick.

28.2.2 Newborn neural statistical learning

Is statistical learning something infants develop by 8 months, or is it running from the start?

Brain recordings answered: from the start, and even in sleep.

Tuomas Teinonen and colleagues, in a 2009 study in BMC Neuroscience, played sleeping newborns a continuous syllable stream of the Saffran type while recording event-related potentials, which are the brain's electrical responses to specific events measured with electroencephalography (EEG), the scalp-recording technique introduced earlier.

The sleeping newborns' brains responded differently to syllables depending on their statistical position within the hidden words, evidence that the neonatal brain was tracking transitional probabilities and detecting word boundaries with no behavioral involvement at all.

Related newborn work using brain imaging by Judit Gervain and colleagues showed sensitivity to repetition patterns in speech in the first days of life, and a 2022 study found that sleeping neonates track transitional probabilities though their retention of the resulting word forms is still fragile.

The picture is that the statistical machinery is factory-installed and always on, silently turning the speech stream into candidate words months before the first word is understood - and, combined with the prenatal learning of Chapter 26, it means language acquisition has been running for months by the time a baby is born.

28.3 The neural indices

Behavioral tests tell us what infants discriminate, but brain measures let researchers watch the narrowing itself, and even use it to forecast a child's language future.

This section covers the main tool and the predictive findings.

28.3.1 Mismatch responses as the tracker of narrowing

The workhorse measure is the mismatch response.

In this method, an infant - often asleep or watching a silent toy - hears a repeating standard sound with occasional deviant sounds mixed in, and if the brain distinguishes the two, the deviants evoke a characteristic electrical signature in the EEG.

In adults this signature is the mismatch negativity (MMN), a negative voltage deflection peaking roughly 150 to 250 milliseconds after the change, discovered by Risto Naatanen in the 1970s.

In young infants the response often appears first as a positive deflection, a mismatch response that shifts toward the adult negative form as the auditory cortex matures, and the timing of that shift varies across sound features and across studies.

Because it requires no attention and no behavior, the mismatch response can be recorded at any age, making it the ideal tracker of perceptual narrowing.

Longitudinal and cross-sectional studies show exactly the pattern the behavioral work predicts: mismatch responses to native contrasts grow stronger between 6 and 12 months, while responses to non-native contrasts weaken over the same window, with work by Kuhl's group and by Maritza Rivera-Gaxiola and colleagues in the mid-2000s among the anchors.

Bilingual infants show the same tuning process for both of their languages on a somewhat extended timetable, and enriched experience, such as the live-exposure sessions of the Mandarin experiment, measurably restores the neural response to the trained foreign contrast.

28.3.2 Native discrimination at seven months predicting later language

The most consequential findings connect these infant brain responses to the child's language years later.

Behavioral work by Feng-Ming Tsao, Huei-Mei Liu, and Patricia Kuhl in 2004 first showed that infants who were better at discriminating native speech sounds at 6 months had larger vocabularies and more advanced language at 13 to 24 months.

Kuhl and colleagues then showed, in studies published across 2005 to 2008 using both behavioral and brain measures around 7 months of age, that the direction of an infant's tuning matters.

Stronger neural discrimination of native contrasts at about 7 months predicted faster language growth in the second and third years.

Strikingly, stronger responses to non-native contrasts at the same age predicted slower later language - not because foreign sensitivity is harmful, but because it marks an infant whose system has not yet committed to the native categories, and later commitment forecasts slower progress.

Narrowing itself, in other words, is a milestone, and its timing carries information.

Later magnetoencephalography work - magnetoencephalography (MEG) is a technique that measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by brain activity, offering better localization than EEG - has extended these predictions, with infant speech responses forecasting language skills into the preschool years.

These are group-level statistical predictions with plenty of individual scatter, and they are not a screening test for any individual baby.

Their scientific weight lies elsewhere: they establish that the quality of speech processing in the first year is not a curiosity of the laboratory but an early, measurable foundation on which the whole edifice of language - words, grammar, and eventually reading - will be built, which is exactly where the next chapters go.

CHAPTER 29. MOTOR DEVELOPMENT: FROM REFLEX TO SKILL (CORE)

This chapter follows the body's story, from the automatic movements a newborn arrives with to the smooth, deliberate skills of a walking, reaching, tool-using child.

Movement might seem like the simple part of development, but it turns out to be one of the richest windows we have into how the brain, the body, and the environment build each other.

Along the way we will meet a famous scientific mystery about a disappearing reflex, a spinal highway that must be pruned, and a theory that changed how developmental science thinks about change itself.

29.1 The reflex calendar and its reinterpretation

Newborn babies come equipped with a set of automatic movement patterns called reflexes, and for most of the twentieth century their appearance and disappearance were read as a simple calendar of brain maturation.

This section tells that classic story first, and then the modern experiments that overturned its simplest version.

29.1.1 The primitive reflexes and their disappearance

A reflex is an automatic movement that happens in response to a trigger, without any decision or learning.

The primitive reflexes are the set of these automatic patterns that are present at birth, wired mostly in the spinal cord and the brainstem, the ancient stalk at the base of the brain that handles life support and basic movement.

The rooting reflex makes a newborn turn the head toward a touch on the cheek, which helps the baby find the breast, and it typically fades by about 4 months.

The sucking reflex turns anything that touches the roof of the mouth into a trigger for rhythmic sucking, and it gradually comes under voluntary control over the first months.

The palmar grasp reflex makes the fingers close tightly around anything placed in the palm, and it usually disappears between about 3 and 6 months.

The Moro reflex, described by the Austrian paediatrician Ernst Moro in 1918, is the startle pattern in which a sudden drop or loud sound makes the baby fling the arms outward and then draw them back in, and it typically vanishes by about 4 to 6 months.

The asymmetric tonic neck reflex, sometimes called the fencing posture, extends the arm on the side the head is turned toward, and it fades by roughly 4 to 6 months.

The Babinski response, in which stroking the sole of the foot makes the toes fan upward and outward instead of curling down, can persist into the second year before switching to the adult downward curl.

The classic interpretation, championed by early observers such as Myrtle McGraw in the 1930s and 1940s, was that these reflexes disappear because the cerebral cortex, the brain's folded outer sheet where voluntary control lives, matures and actively inhibits the older circuits below it.

There is real truth in that picture, and doctors still use the reflex calendar clinically, because a primitive reflex that persists far past its usual window, or one that is absent or asymmetric early on, can signal a problem in the nervous system.

But the next sub-section shows why the pure maturation story is too simple.

29.1.2 The stepping reflex and the biomechanical lesson

If you hold a newborn upright with the feet touching a surface, the baby performs surprisingly coordinated stepping movements, as if walking in place.

This stepping reflex normally cannot be elicited after about 2 months of age, and the traditional explanation was cortical inhibition, the maturing brain switching the primitive pattern off.

The developmental psychologist Esther Thelen noticed something odd, which is that babies lying on their backs keep producing kicking movements that are essentially identical to stepping in their muscle timing and mechanics, and this kicking does not disappear at 2 months.

If the brain had switched the pattern off, it should be off in every posture.

In work published in the early 1980s, Thelen and her colleagues, including a much-cited 1982 explanation of the disappearing reflex with Donna Fisher, showed that the real culprit was the body, not the brain.

In the early months, infants gain fat much faster than muscle, so the legs become heavier without becoming proportionally stronger, and lifting them against gravity in the upright posture becomes too hard.

The experiments were elegant and simple.

When the researchers attached small weights to the legs of young infants who still stepped, the stepping weakened or vanished.

When they submerged the legs of older infants in warm water, so that buoyancy cancelled some of the weight, the vanished stepping came back, with faster stepping rates and larger joint flexions.

Later work, such as a 2002 study by Karen Adolph and colleagues, added the caution that leg mass is not the whole story, since factors like the older infant's bias toward keeping the legs flexed also matter, but the central lesson stands.

That lesson is that a change in behaviour is not automatically a change in the brain, because development is a conversation among the nervous system, the growing body, and the physical situation.

This single finding became the seed of the dynamic systems view described in section 29.3.

29.2 Reaching, grasping, walking

This section covers the visible milestones every family watches for, what the worldwide data say about when they happen, and the slow construction of the brain-to-muscle wiring that makes skilled movement possible.

29.2.1 The milestone windows and their cultural variation

A milestone is simply a skill, such as sitting or walking, whose first appearance can be dated.

The most careful worldwide dataset comes from the World Health Organization (WHO) Multicentre Growth Reference Study, published in 2006, which followed healthy children in Ghana, India, Norway, Oman, and the United States.

That study reported windows of normal achievement, not single ages, and the windows are wide.

Sitting without support was achieved between about 3.8 and 9.2 months, crawling on hands and knees between about 5.2 and 13.5 months, standing alone between about 6.9 and 16.9 months, and walking alone between about 8.2 and 17.6 months.

Roughly half of children walk independently by about 12 months, but a healthy child can walk at 9 months or at 17 months, and both are normal.

About 4 percent of healthy children in the WHO study never crawled on hands and knees at all, moving instead by scooting or going straight to standing, which is why crawling is no longer treated as an obligatory stage.

Culture shifts the windows in measurable ways.

In several African and Caribbean communities, caregivers traditionally exercise infants with stretching and stepping routines, and studies going back to Charles Super's 1976 work in Kenya found sitting and walking arriving weeks earlier in communities that deliberately practise those skills.

In the other direction, cultural practices that reduce practice delay milestones without harming the endpoint, as shown by Dennis and Dennis in their 1940 study of Hopi cradleboard rearing and by later work on infants who spend long periods lying flat.

A striking natural experiment came from the Back to Sleep campaign against sudden infant death, launched in the United States in 1994, after which infants who slept on their backs and got less tummy time reached crawling slightly later, while walking age stayed essentially unchanged.

The overall picture is that experience tunes the timetable, while the destination of independent walking is robust across an enormous range of childrearing customs.

29.2.2 The corticospinal system's protracted maturation and the withdrawal of ipsilateral projections

The corticospinal tract is the great cable of nerve fibres running from the motor cortex, the strip of the brain's outer sheet that commands movement, down into the spinal cord.

It is the main highway for skilled, voluntary movement, especially of the hands and fingers.

At birth this highway exists but is slow, weakly connected, and surprisingly unspecific.

Each side of the newborn brain sends fibres not only to the opposite side of the body, the contralateral projections, but also substantial fibres to the same side of the body, the ipsilateral projections.

Janet Eyre and her colleagues in Newcastle showed this directly, using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a safe technique that uses a magnetic pulse on the scalp to activate the motor cortex and measure the responses in the muscles.

In their 2001 study in the journal Neurology, newborn responses on the same side of the body were fast and strong, but by about 15 months the same-side responses had become weaker, slower, and harder to evoke, while the opposite-side responses strengthened.

The interpretation is activity-dependent competition, meaning that the two sets of fibres compete for connections in the spinal cord, and the busier contralateral projections win while most ipsilateral ones withdraw.

The clinical evidence is telling, because in children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, a condition in which brain injury around birth weakens one side of the body, the injured hemisphere falls silent in the competition and the healthy hemisphere abnormally keeps its same-side projections.

The whole system matures slowly, with the fatty insulation called myelin thickening along the tract and conduction speeds not reaching adult values until roughly mid-childhood.

Fine finger control, called fractionated finger movement, follows this slow build, which is why precision grip appears around 9 to 12 months but keeps improving for a decade.

This protracted construction is also why the first years are a sensitive time for motor rehabilitation, since the spinal wiring is still being decided by use.

29.3 The dynamic systems reading

This section introduces the theoretical framework, built largely by Esther Thelen and Linda Smith in the 1980s and 1990s, that treats motor development not as the unfolding of a fixed brain programme but as the self-organising product of many interacting parts.

29.3.1 Soft assembly and massive variable practice

Soft assembly is the idea that a movement is not stored as a rigid programme but is assembled fresh each time from whatever the child's body, energy, surface, and goal afford at that moment.

A softly assembled skill bends to circumstances, which is why the same baby steps in water but not in air, and why a new walker moves differently on carpet, grass, and a slope.

The evidence for how such flexible skill is built comes from Karen Adolph's laboratory at New York University, which put sensors and video on ordinary infants and simply counted.

In a 2012 study, Adolph and colleagues reported that toddlers in free play take an enormous number of steps, in the range of 2,000 or more steps per hour, travelling the length of several football fields, and falling frequently, with new walkers falling on the order of 17 times per hour.

Across weeks this adds up to millions of steps, and crucially the practice is variable, spread across surfaces, speeds, directions, and postures, rather than repetitive drilling.

Adolph's earlier work on slopes and cliffs showed that what infants learn is not a general rule like avoid drop-offs but a posture-specific mapping between their current body and the world, so that an experienced crawler who wisely refuses a steep slope will, on becoming a novice walker, march straight over the same edge and must learn again.

The dynamic systems reading is that development is this ongoing loop, in which massive variable practice generates experience, experience retunes perception and action together, and each new posture opens a new learning problem.

The brain matters enormously in this story, but as one component among several, alongside leg fat, muscle strength, balance, motivation, and the layout of the living room.

29.3.2 Locomotion reorganising cognition: travel broadening the infant mind

Moving through the world on your own turns out to change how you think about the world.

The classic evidence involves the visual cliff, an apparatus built by Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk in 1960, which is a sturdy glass table with a shallow-looking side and an apparent drop-off under the glass.

Joseph Campos and his colleagues showed across the 1980s and 1990s that wariness of the drop is not simply a matter of age but of locomotor experience, since infants with weeks of crawling experience show fear responses at the cliff while same-aged non-crawlers do not, and giving pre-crawling infants powered mobility in a little cart accelerates the wariness.

Campos summarised the broader case in a 2000 paper wonderfully titled Travel Broadens the Mind.

Crawling experience is associated with better performance on hidden-object search tasks, improved understanding of distance and heights, more sophisticated use of the caregiver's emotional signals when deciding whether a situation is safe, and changes in attention to the spatial layout.

The proposed mechanism is straightforward, which is that self-produced movement forces the infant to update position constantly, to attend to distant goals, to coordinate vision with action, and to check back with caregivers, and this new information economy retunes many cognitive systems at once.

Walking then repeats the trick at a higher level, and work from Adolph's and Campos's traditions shows that new walkers carry objects more, approach caregivers to share things more, and receive different language from adults, so a motor milestone cascades into social and linguistic experience.

The honest caution is that much of this evidence is correlational, and the powered-mobility experiments, while pointing toward causation, are small, so the field treats locomotion as one strong driver among several rather than a magic switch.

29.4 The cerebellum's long build

This final section turns to the brain structure most tightly linked to coordination, and to why smooth skill keeps improving into the teenage years.

29.4.1 Late growth, internal models, and coordination into adolescence

The cerebellum is the densely folded structure tucked under the back of the brain, and despite taking up about a tenth of the brain's volume it contains most of the brain's neurons, thanks to its tiny, tightly packed granule cells.

Its developmental schedule is unusual at both ends.

It grows explosively late in pregnancy and in the first year, with imaging studies showing cerebellar volume increasing around 240 percent across the first year in some reports, which makes it especially vulnerable to premature birth.

It then keeps maturing for a very long time, and a longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study by Tiemeier, Giedd, and colleagues in 2010 found total cerebellar volume peaking at about 11.8 years in girls and about 15.6 years in boys, later than the cerebral cortex on average, with different lobes on different timetables.

Functionally, the cerebellum is the brain's specialist in internal models, which are little learned simulations that predict the sensory consequences of a command, such as what your arm will feel like a fraction of a second after you start a reach.

With good internal models, movement can be smooth and anticipatory rather than a series of corrections, which is why cerebellar damage produces clumsy, jerky, poorly timed movement called ataxia.

Children's reaching starts out as exactly the kind of multi-corrected, segmented movement you would expect before the models are trained, and studies of reaching kinematics show movement smoothness improving steadily through childhood, with adult-like anticipatory control of grip forces and timing not fully in place until adolescence.

The cerebellum's long build also matters beyond movement, because it is heavily interconnected with the prefrontal cortex, the forward part of the brain's outer sheet that handles planning, and modern work implicates the cerebellum in the fine timing of language, attention, and social prediction.

Its late schedule means it remains open to experience, from sport to musical instruments, deep into the second decade, and it also means it remains exposed to insult, which is one thread in research on developmental coordination disorder and on the motor features seen in some autistic people.

The chapter's overall message is that motor development is slow, statistical, and embodied, a decade-long apprenticeship in which reflexes are re-explained, highways are pruned by use, and millions of variable steps teach a brain and a body to move as one.



================================================================================

PART EIGHT. LANGUAGE AND LITERACY

================================================================================

CHAPTER 30. WORD LEARNING AND THE GROWING LEXICON (CORE)

This chapter is about one of the most astonishing feats a human ever performs, which is learning words, thousands of them, mostly without being taught.

We will look at when understanding begins, whether there is really a vocabulary explosion, what mental machinery makes word learning possible, and the heated modern debate about how much the amount of talk a child hears matters.

30.1 The first words

This section asks when word knowledge actually starts, and the answer has moved earlier and earlier as methods improved.

30.1.1 Comprehension before production: known nouns by six to nine months

Comprehension means understanding a word, and production means saying it, and comprehension runs months ahead of production throughout early childhood.

Most children say their first recognisable word around 12 months, but understanding is demonstrably present far earlier.

The landmark study is by Elika Bergelson and Daniel Swingley, published in 2012 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), titled At 6 to 9 months, human infants know the meanings of many common nouns.

They used eye tracking, a method that measures exactly where a baby is looking, and showed infants pairs of pictures or natural scenes while a parent said sentences like where is the apple.

Infants aged 6 to 9 months looked reliably more at the named object for a set of common food and body-part words, such as apple, banana, hand, and mouth, even though these babies would not speak for months.

The effects at 6 to 9 months are real but small, comprehension strengthens markedly around 13 to 14 months in the same paradigm, and later work by Bergelson showed that words whose referents are visually present and distinct in daily life are learned first.

This finding rewrote the timeline, because it means word learning begins during the same window in which infants are still perceptually tuning to the sounds of their native language, rather than after it.

It also means that by the first birthday party, the quiet baby in the high chair is already a listener with a small dictionary, built purely from overheard daily life.

30.1.2 The vocabulary spurt and the debate over whether it is a spurt

Around 18 months, many children's productive vocabulary seems to take off, jumping from slow accumulation to several new words a day, and this classic observation is called the vocabulary spurt or naming explosion.

Typical figures are around 50 produced words at 18 months and roughly 200 to 300 or more by the second birthday, with enormous individual variation documented by the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories, the standard parent-report checklists developed by Larry Fenson and colleagues in the 1990s.

Older theories treated the spurt as a discontinuity revealing some new insight, such as the child suddenly grasping that everything has a name, or a categorisation breakthrough.

The modern debate is over whether there is any discontinuity at all.

Bob McMurray's 2007 paper in Science, Defusing the childhood vocabulary explosion, showed with simple simulations that an apparent explosion is exactly what you get from steady parallel learning, with no special mechanism, as long as two ordinary things are true.

The first is that words vary in difficulty, and the second is that the child is learning many words at once, so after a slow start the many medium-difficulty words all cross the finish line in a bunch, producing an acceleration that looks like a spurt.

Careful longitudinal analyses agree that only a minority of children show a statistically sharp inflection in their own growth curves, and that most curves are smoothly accelerating.

The fair summary for a beginner is that the experience of a spurt is real for many families, but it probably reflects the mathematics of learning many things in parallel rather than a switch flipping in the brain.

The variation is also worth stating plainly, because late talkers with small vocabularies at age 2 often catch up, while a minority go on to language disorder, and vocabulary at this age is a weak individual predictor precisely because the normal range is so wide.

30.2 The learning machinery

This section opens the hood and asks how a learner who cannot ask for definitions manages to attach the right meanings to the right sounds.

30.2.1 The constraints: mutual exclusivity and the whole-object bias

The philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine famously posed the puzzle in 1960, which is that when a speaker of an unknown language points at a rabbit and says gavagai, the word could logically mean rabbit, fur, ears, hopping, or undetached rabbit parts, so how does any learner ever narrow it down.

Children appear to solve this by bringing default assumptions to the task, called word-learning constraints or biases.

The whole-object bias, described by Ellen Markman in the late 1980s, is the assumption that a new word refers to a whole object rather than to its parts, its colour, or its substance, so gavagai means the rabbit, not the ears.

Mutual exclusivity, studied in detail by Markman and Gwyn Wachtel in 1988, is the assumption that each object has one name, so if a child who knows cup hears where is the dax while looking at a cup and a strange object, the child concludes that dax must be the strange object.

This use of a known name to infer a new one is sometimes called disambiguation, and it is measurable by around 17 to 18 months in many studies, with some evidence of earlier precursors.

These biases are best understood as helpful defaults rather than unbreakable rules, since children happily learn second labels like animal and dog when the evidence demands it.

There is also an important cultural and bilingual wrinkle, because a bilingual child's world genuinely contains two names for everything, and studies by Krista Byers-Heinlein and others show that bilingual infants rely on mutual exclusivity less strongly than monolinguals, which is exactly what you would expect if the bias is learned from the statistics of experience rather than innately fixed.

30.2.2 Fast mapping and cross-situational learning

Fast mapping is the ability to form a quick, rough idea of a new word's meaning from a single exposure or a handful of exposures.

The term comes from Susan Carey and Elsa Bartlett's 1978 study, in which preschoolers were casually asked to bring the chromium tray, not the blue one, from a pair of trays, and a week later many still had some memory that chromium was a colour word for that odd olive shade.

The key modern refinement is that fast mapping is fast but shallow, giving a fragile initial guess that needs consolidation, and sleep research shows that new word memories are strengthened overnight, while follow-up studies show single-exposure mappings decay quickly without further encounters.

Cross-situational learning is the complementary slow engine, which is the ability to average across many ambiguous situations.

Linda Smith and Chen Yu showed in experiments from 2007 onward that both adults and 12 to 14 month old infants can learn word-object pairings even when every individual scene is ambiguous, simply by tracking which object keeps co-occurring with which word across scenes.

If ball is heard around a ball, a dog, and a cup in one scene, and around a ball, a shoe, and a hat in another, only the ball survives the intersection.

Head-camera studies from Yu and Smith added a beautiful twist, which is that from the toddler's own point of view the world is often less ambiguous than it looks, because when a toddler holds an object it looms large and alone in the visual field, and naming events timed to those moments are especially effective.

The consensus picture is a partnership, in which biases narrow the possibilities, fast mapping plants a quick guess, and cross-situational statistics plus sleep slowly firm the guess into knowledge.

30.2.3 The social-pragmatic route

The social-pragmatic account, associated above all with Michael Tomasello, argues that the deepest word-learning tool is not a statistical filter but the child's reading of other minds.

Words are used by people to direct attention, so a learner who can work out what a speaker is attending to and intending can crack meanings that no statistic could.

The foundational skill is joint attention, the three-way state in which child and adult are attending to the same thing and know it, which consolidates between about 9 and 12 months and whose amount predicts later vocabulary, as shown in longitudinal work by Tomasello and Michael Farrar in 1986.

Dare Baldwin's experiments around 1991 to 1993 provided the crucial demonstration, because when an experimenter said a new word while the toddler was looking at one toy but the experimenter was looking at a different toy, 18 to 19 month olds did not attach the word to their own focus of attention, but followed the adult's gaze and attached the word to the adult's object.

That is not passive association, it is inference about a speaker's intention.

Later studies showed toddlers using an adult's excitement, previous behaviour, and even what is new for the adult versus for themselves to figure out intended referents.

The modern synthesis is not a war between statistics and social insight but a layered account, in which social cues are themselves powerful statistical signals about reference, and children weight all of these sources, with the social route becoming increasingly dominant as understanding of other minds grows across the second year.

30.3 The input matters

This section faces the question with the largest social stakes in this chapter, which is how much the sheer quantity and quality of talk directed to a child shapes the growing lexicon, and what happened when a famous number was challenged.

30.3.1 The thirty-million-word claim and its replication critique

In 1995, Betty Hart and Todd Risley published Meaningful Differences in the Everyday Experience of Young American Children, based on monthly hour-long home recordings of 42 families in Kansas followed for about two and a half years.

Extrapolating their samples across four years, they estimated that children in the professional families would hear about 45 million words addressed to them, while children in the families receiving welfare would hear about 13 million, a difference popularised as the 30 million word gap.

The number became one of the most quoted figures in education policy, driving campaigns and interventions aimed at getting parents to talk more.

This corpus records the claim as contested, and the story of the challenge matters as much as the original.

In 2019, Douglas Sperry, Linda Sperry, and Peggy Miller published a study in Child Development using recordings from five American communities, and they counted not only speech addressed directly to the child but also speech around the child.

They found enormous variation within every income group, and some low-income communities in their data, such as families in rural Alabama, produced far more speech than Hart and Risley's lowest group, which led to headlines announcing that the word gap had been debunked.

The rebuttals came quickly, notably from Roberta Golinkoff, Erika Hoff, Meredith Rowe, Catherine Tamis-LeMonda, and Kathy Hirsh-Pasek in 2019, who pointed out that the Sperry study included no high-income professional group at all, so it could not test the original comparison, and that overheard speech is known from other research to contribute much less to vocabulary than child-directed speech.

Where does the evidence honestly stand.

Average differences in child-directed speech associated with socioeconomic status are real in many datasets, but the original number was an extrapolation from a small sample, the variation within every income group is huge, the deficit framing has been criticised as stigmatising low-income and minority families whose rich verbal traditions differ in form, and simple word counting misses what the next sub-section shows actually matters most.

The responsible summary is that input matters, the specific figure of 30 million should not be treated as a measured fact, and quality of interaction has overtaken quantity of words as the scientific headline.

30.3.2 Conversational turns and the child's Broca activation

A conversational turn is a simple back-and-forth exchange, an adult speaks and the child responds, or the reverse, within a few seconds.

Modern studies count turns automatically using small wearable recorders, most famously the Language Environment Analysis (LENA) system, which records a full day of a child's audio and estimates adult words, child vocalisations, and turns.

The pivotal study is by Rachel Romeo, John Gabrieli, and colleagues, published in Psychological Science in 2018 under the title Beyond the 30 Million Word Gap.

They recorded the home language environments of 36 children aged 4 to 6 from a wide range of family incomes, and then scanned the children with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that maps brain activity by tracking blood flow, while the children listened to stories.

The number of conversational turns, not the sheer number of adult words, predicted the children's language skills and predicted stronger activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus, the region commonly called Broca's area after the nineteenth-century physician Paul Broca, which is central to producing and processing language.

Strikingly, these relationships held independently of socioeconomic status, and children from lower-income homes who experienced many turns showed language skills and Broca activation resembling those of children from higher-income homes.

A companion study by the same group in 2018 found that more turns were also associated with stronger white matter connectivity in the left arcuate fasciculus, the fibre bundle linking the frontal and temporal language regions, and a 2021 follow-up found that a parent-coaching intervention that increased turns changed children's language outcomes, pushing the evidence gently toward causation.

The beginner's takeaway is warm and practical at the level of populations rather than prescriptions, which is that serve-and-return conversation, responding to a child and giving the child room to respond back, is the form of language experience most tightly linked to the developing language brain that science can currently measure.

These were small studies, replication and extension are ongoing, and no one should read a brain scan as a verdict on any individual family, but the shift from counting words at children to counting exchanges with children is one of the field's healthiest corrections.


CHAPTER 31. SYNTAX, THE LANGUAGE NETWORK, AND THE WINDOWS (CORE)

This chapter moves from single words to grammar, the system that lets a finite mind produce unlimited sentences, and to the brain network that carries it.

It then confronts one of the oldest and most emotionally charged questions in the field, which is whether there are windows in development after which language, or a second language, can no longer be learned to the same level.

31.1 The grammar calendar

This section lays out the remarkably regular timetable by which grammar emerges in children's speech, and what children's errors reveal about the machinery underneath.

31.1.1 Two-word speech near twenty-four months and the morpheme sequence

Syntax means the rules for combining words into phrases and sentences.

After the one-word stage, children begin combining two words, typically somewhere between 18 and 24 months, with combinations like more juice, daddy go, and mummy sock.

Researchers called this telegraphic speech, because like an old telegram it keeps the content words and drops the little grammatical pieces, though the term is used more cautiously now because children's comprehension shows sensitivity to those little pieces earlier than their speech does.

A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning, so dogs has two morphemes, dog and the plural s, and walked has walk plus the past-tense ending.

The classic study of how these grammatical morphemes arrive is Roger Brown's 1973 book A First Language, which followed three children, given the pseudonyms Adam, Eve, and Sarah, in extraordinary longitudinal detail.

Brown found that 14 grammatical morphemes of English are acquired in a strikingly consistent order across children, even though the children differed in speed.

The present progressive ing, as in daddy running, comes early, followed by the prepositions in and on and the regular plural s, while forms of the verb to be and the third-person endings arrive late.

The order is explained not by how often parents use the forms but by their semantic and grammatical complexity, which was an early, striking sign that children are building a system, not parroting.

Sentence complexity then climbs steeply, with questions, negations, and embedded clauses appearing across ages 2 to 4, so that a typical 4 year old commands most of the core grammar of the native language without a single lesson.

Researchers index this growth with mean length of utterance (MLU), the average number of morphemes per utterance, which Brown introduced as a better yardstick than age.

31.1.2 Overregularisation as a window on rules

Overregularisation is the charming error in which children apply a regular rule to an irregular word, producing goed, comed, foots, and mouses.

These errors are precious evidence, because a child who says goed has never heard an adult say it, so the child cannot be imitating and must be generating from a rule.

The definitive count comes from Gary Marcus, Steven Pinker, and colleagues in a 1992 monograph, which analysed thousands of child utterances and found that overregularisation is real but rare, occurring in roughly 2.5 percent of irregular past-tense uses on average, scattered across a long period rather than dominating any stage.

The developmental path is often described as U-shaped, because children may first produce correct irregulars like went as memorised items, then produce occasional goed once the rule is extracted, then return to went as the memorised form wins the competition.

Two broad theoretical camps have fought over these errors for decades.

The words-and-rules view, argued by Pinker, holds that regulars are computed by a genuine mental rule while irregulars are stored in memory, with the error occurring when memory retrieval momentarily fails and the rule fills the gap.

The connectionist view, launched by David Rumelhart and James McClelland's 1986 network model, holds that a single associative system learning statistical patterns can produce the same U-shaped behaviour without any explicit rule, and later models improved on the first one's shortcomings.

The debate is genuinely unresolved as a matter of mechanism, but both camps agree on the developmental headline, which is that children generalise beyond their input, and that grammar acquisition is an act of pattern extraction, not recording.

31.2 The network's construction

This section turns to the brain, asking where language lives, how early the machinery is biased toward it, and which wiring matures last.

31.2.1 Left-lateralised speech response at three months

In most people, language is left-lateralised, meaning the left hemisphere of the brain does most of the work, a fact known since Paul Broca's patients in the 1860s.

A central developmental question was whether this asymmetry is built by years of language experience or is present from the start.

Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz, Stanislas Dehaene, and Lucie Hertz-Pannier answered a large part of it in a 2002 study in Science, which placed awake and sleeping 3 month old infants in an fMRI scanner and played them speech.

The infant brain responded to speech in the left superior temporal regions, overlapping the classic adult language areas, with stronger left-sided activation, and forward speech engaged additional regions compared with backward speech, which shares the acoustics but not the linguistic structure.

Later work pushed sensitivity even earlier, since near-infrared spectroscopy studies of newborns by Marcela Peña and colleagues in 2003 found stronger left temporal responses to forward speech within days of birth, and studies of premature infants by Fabrice Wallois's group found the temporal cortex already discriminating syllables weeks before full term.

The careful conclusion is that the language network does not wait for language, because a structural and functional bias toward speech in the left temporal cortex is present at or before birth, providing a prepared scaffold.

Experience then does the actual construction on that scaffold, which is why the same regions end up handling Japanese, Swahili, or sign language depending on what the child meets, and why sign languages in deaf children engage substantially the same left-hemisphere network.

31.2.2 The dorsal pathway's late myelination tracking syntax

The adult language network is organised into two great fibre systems, described in influential form by Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel and, developmentally, by Angela Friederici.

The ventral pathway runs along the bottom of the temporal lobe and links sound to meaning, and the dorsal pathway arcs up and over, most prominently as the arcuate fasciculus, the fibre bundle connecting the temporal cortex with Broca's area in the frontal lobe.

Myelination is the wrapping of nerve fibres in myelin, the fatty insulation that makes signals fast, and the two pathways myelinate on different schedules.

Jens Brauer, Alfred Anwander, and Angela Friederici showed in work published around 2011 to 2013, using diffusion imaging that maps fibre bundles by tracking water movement, that the ventral pathway and a dorsal branch to the premotor cortex are already in place in newborns, while the dorsal branch connecting directly to Broca's area is immature at birth and strengthens slowly across childhood.

Friederici's group has argued across several studies that the maturation of this dorsal tract tracks the child's mastery of complex syntax, since children's ability to understand sentences with demanding structures, such as object-first sentences in German, correlates with the microstructural maturity of the arcuate fasciculus, and full adult-like processing of complex sentences is late, continuing to sharpen past age 7 and into adolescence.

Michael Skeide and Friederici summarised this in a 2016 account of the ontogeny of the cortical language network, proposing that meaning-related processing matures earlier along the ventral route while hierarchical grammar rides the slow dorsal route.

A fair caution for the reader is that these are correlations between anatomy and ability in modest samples, and the strict mapping of syntax to one tract is debated, but the broad picture of a late-maturing dorsal connection setting the pace for complex grammar is one of the better-supported stories in developmental neurolinguistics.

31.3 The windows

This section addresses sensitive periods for language, meaning stretches of development when learning is easiest and after which some aspects rarely reach native levels, and it handles two famous bodies of evidence and one famous number with the caution this corpus requires.

31.3.1 The deprivation cases and late first language

The harshest evidence about windows comes from the rare, tragic cases of children who grew up without language.

The most cited case is Genie, a girl discovered in Los Angeles in 1970 at age 13 after years of extreme isolation and abuse, who had heard almost no language.

Studied by Susan Curtiss and colleagues, Genie learned many words and could combine them meaningfully, but her grammar never approached normal, with function words, verb endings, and sentence structure remaining profoundly impaired, and her case is documented in Curtiss's 1977 book.

Such cases are scientifically compromised, because the children suffered malnutrition, trauma, and total social deprivation alongside the language deprivation, so no clean conclusion about language alone is possible.

The cleaner natural experiment involves deaf children born to hearing families, who are often cognitively healthy and loved but simply not exposed to an accessible language early, because they cannot hear speech and no one around them signs.

Rachel Mayberry's studies of deaf adults who first met American Sign Language at different ages show a clear gradient, since those exposed from birth sign like natives, those first exposed in later childhood or adolescence show lasting deficits in grammar even after 30 years of daily use, and the deficits centre on exactly the structural machinery that Genie lacked.

Mayberry's work also shows that late first-language learners are measurably worse off than late second-language learners, meaning that having any language early protects the capacity to learn languages later.

Neuroimaging of late first-language learners shows atypical recruitment of the language network, consistent with the idea that the early years install the scaffolding on which all later language rests.

The consensus is that a first language should reach a child as early as possible, in whatever modality is accessible, and this is why early sign exposure and early hearing screening are public-health priorities.

31.3.2 The age-of-arrival evidence and the seventeen-year window finding, with this corpus's recorded caution about it

For second languages, the classic evidence is about age of arrival in a new language community.

Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport's 1989 study of Chinese and Korean immigrants to the United States found that grammatical test performance declined steadily with age of arrival after early childhood, with those arriving before about age 7 performing like natives and later arrivals showing increasing, permanent variability.

Accent shows the tightest window, with native-like pronunciation becoming rare after early adolescence, while vocabulary learning remains strong for life.

The famous recent number comes from Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum, and Steven Pinker, who in 2018 analysed a grammar quiz that went viral online and was completed by about two thirds of a million people.

Their computational model concluded that the underlying ability to learn grammar stays high until about 17.4 years of age and then declines, a figure widely reported as evidence that the window for grammar closes at the end of adolescence.

This corpus records a specific caution about that figure, and it must be taught as contested.

A 2022 reanalysis of the same dataset by Frans van der Slik and colleagues in the journal Language Learning argued that the sharply defined 17.4 year cliff is an artefact of the modelling choices, because when learner groups are analysed separately, monolinguals, bilinguals, and early immersion learners are fitted better by a continuous, steady decline with no cliff at all, while only non-immersion and later immersion learners show a discontinuity, and there at about 18.6 to 19.0 years.

The reanalysts suggested that social life events around the end of schooling, such as leaving the classroom and changing immersion environments, could produce an apparent cliff without any biological window slamming shut.

The honest summary for the beginner is layered.

Earlier is reliably better for second-language grammar and especially accent, the decline with age is real and gradual, but the existence of a single sharp biological deadline, and certainly the specific number 17.4, is not settled science, and adults do learn second languages to high levels, just rarely to native-indistinguishable levels in grammar and accent.

31.3.3 The bilingual infant: two systems without confusion, and the disputed executive advantage

A persistent folk worry is that hearing two languages confuses babies or delays language, and the evidence says otherwise.

Bilingual infants distinguish their two languages from very early, since newborns already discriminate rhythmically different languages, and work by Janet Werker, Krista Byers-Heinlein, and Núria Sebastián-Gallés shows bilingual infants tracking the sound systems and even the visual mouth movements of both languages, keeping them functionally separate.

Bilingual children hit the major milestones, babbling, first words near 12 months, and word combinations near 24 months, on essentially the same schedule as monolinguals.

Their vocabulary in each single language tends to be smaller than a monolingual's, because experience is divided, but their total conceptual vocabulary across both languages is comparable, and code-mixing, using words from both languages in one sentence, is grammatically structured and normal, not confusion.

The genuinely disputed question is whether bilingualism gives a bonus outside language.

Ellen Bialystok and colleagues reported from the early 2000s that bilingual children and adults outperform monolinguals on executive function tasks, which are tasks measuring attention control and switching, the idea being that a lifetime of managing two competing languages trains the brain's control systems.

The claim became famous, and then the replication era arrived.

Large studies and meta-analyses, including work by Kenneth Paap from 2013 onward and a 2018 meta-analysis by Minna Lehtonen and colleagues, found effects that are tiny or absent once publication bias, the tendency of journals to publish positive results, is corrected, and a 2015 analysis by Angela de Bruin documented that conference results showing no advantage were less likely to be published.

Defenders reply that the advantage may be real but conditional, appearing in some populations, ages, and task types, and the debate remains genuinely open.

What is not disputed is the null of harm, meaning that raising a child bilingual carries no cognitive cost, delivers two languages, and in the case of children in migrant families preserves the home language that connects them to family and heritage.

The chapter closes with the windows in perspective, since the strongest sensitive-period evidence in this whole area concerns having a first language early, the second-language evidence shows gradients rather than proven cliffs, and the famous 17.4 year figure is a contested model output, not a biological constant.


CHAPTER 32. READING, DYSLEXIA, AND THE EDUCATED BRAIN (CORE)

This chapter is about something evolution never planned for, which is reading.

Writing is only about 5,000 years old and mass literacy far younger, so there is no reading organ in the brain, and every reader you know performed a feat of neural recycling, rewiring ancient visual and language circuitry for an invented code.

We will follow how the circuit is built, what literacy does to the cortex, and what happens in dyslexia, where a capable mind meets an unusually resistant code.

32.1 The reading circuit

This section describes the skill that predicts reading before reading exists, and the three-region brain circuit that every skilled reader assembles.

32.1.1 Phonological awareness as the precursor

Phonological awareness is the ability to notice and mentally manipulate the sounds inside spoken words, for example knowing that cat and hat rhyme, that sun and sock start the same way, or that removing the first sound of stop leaves top.

It is entirely about spoken language, and yet it is one of the strongest known predictors of how easily a child will learn to read, because alphabetic writing is a code that maps letters onto exactly these sound units, called phonemes.

The landmark longitudinal and experimental evidence comes from Lynette Bradley and Peter Bryant, whose 1983 study in Nature followed hundreds of British children and found that preschool skill at detecting rhyme and alliteration predicted reading years later, and crucially that training sound categorisation, especially when combined with letters, improved later reading, which is the experimental step that turns a correlation into a cause.

Decades of replication built on this, and the United States National Reading Panel's 2000 review concluded that explicit teaching of phonemic awareness and phonics reliably improves reading, a conclusion at the heart of what is now called the science of reading movement.

Development follows a coarse-to-fine path, since children first notice syllables and rhymes in the preschool years, while full phoneme-level awareness, such as counting the three sounds in cat, typically arrives with, and partly because of, instruction in an alphabet, showing that the street runs both ways between sound awareness and literacy.

Phonological awareness in the preschool years, together with rapid naming speed and letter knowledge, forms the screening trio used to spot children at risk for reading difficulty before they fail.

32.1.2 The three-region circuit and the print tuning of the N170

Skilled reading in alphabetic scripts runs on a mostly left-hemisphere circuit with three principal hubs, a description consolidated by researchers including Sally Shaywitz, Bennett Shaywitz, Kenneth Pugh, and Stanislas Dehaene.

The first hub is the left occipito-temporal region on the underside of the brain toward the back, home of the so-called visual word form area, described by Laurent Cohen and Dehaene in 2000, which learns to recognise letters and letter strings rapidly regardless of size, font, or position.

The second hub is the left temporo-parietal region, toward the upper back of the left side, which does the slow assembly work of mapping letters onto sounds and is the workhorse of beginning reading.

The third hub is the left inferior frontal region around Broca's area, which supports pronunciation, articulation-based decoding, and meaning.

Development shifts the balance, because beginners lean on the temporo-parietal assembly route, reading slowly and piece by piece, while practice trains the occipito-temporal region into a fast whole-word recogniser, which is why an adult cannot help but read a word placed in front of them.

The construction of this fast recogniser can be watched electrically.

The N170 is a negative brain wave measured by electroencephalography (EEG), the technique that records brain electricity from the scalp, appearing about 170 milliseconds after something is seen, and in literate people it becomes larger over the left visual cortex for written words than for scrambled or unfamiliar symbols, a signature called print tuning.

Urs Maurer, Daniel Brandeis, and colleagues showed in studies around 2005 to 2007 that this print-tuned N170 is absent in kindergarten non-readers, emerges rapidly within the first year or two of reading instruction, is initially coarse and strong, and later becomes more refined in expert readers, and that its emergence tracks learning the letter-sound code rather than mere visual familiarity.

The N170 story gives the beginner a concrete image, which is that within about two hundred milliseconds of your eyes landing on this sentence, a patch of your left visual cortex, trained by years of practice, has already flagged these shapes as language.

32.2 Literacy remakes cortex

This section asks what learning to read does to a brain, using the most direct evidence available, which is comparing people who read with otherwise similar people who never had the chance to learn.

32.2.1 The illiterate-to-literate comparisons

The decisive study was led by Stanislas Dehaene, Laurent Cohen, Régine Kolinsky, José Morais, and colleagues, published in Science in 2010 under the title How learning to read changes the cortical networks for vision and language.

They scanned 63 adults in Portugal and Brazil, including illiterate adults, ex-illiterates who had learned to read as adults, and people literate since childhood, which allowed the effects of literacy to be separated from the effects of schooling and childhood.

Literacy changed the brain in several measurable ways.

Reading ability was associated with stronger responses to written words in the left occipito-temporal cortex at the visual word form site, and the effect appeared even in ex-illiterates, proving that the adult brain retains the capacity for this reorganisation.

Literacy also boosted responses in early visual cortex, sharpened the precision of visual analysis, and, remarkably, changed the processing of spoken language, because literate brains showed stronger activation of speech regions and online activation of spelling knowledge when merely listening, which is why literate people can play alphabet games with heard words that illiterate adults find nearly impossible.

Behavioural work by Morais and Kolinsky going back to 1979 had already shown that illiterate adults struggle to delete or add single phonemes in spoken words, demonstrating that fine phoneme awareness is largely a product of alphabetic literacy, not a precondition sitting ready in everyone.

Follow-up work, including a 2017 longitudinal study by Michael Skeide, Falk Huettig, and colleagues that taught reading to illiterate adults in rural India, found that learning to read reshaped not only cortex but also the responses and connectivity of deep structures including the thalamus, the brain's central relay station, and the brainstem, showing the reach of literacy runs deeper than the cortical surface.

The general lesson is called neuronal recycling, Dehaene's term for the way a cultural invention colonises evolutionarily older circuits that have the right properties, in this case the ventral visual system's shape expertise.

32.2.2 The trade-offs in the fusiform

The fusiform gyrus is the ridge of cortex on the underside of the temporal lobe where the ventral visual system houses its specialists, including regions preferring faces, and the visual word form site sits within this territory.

Cortex is finite, and the recycling account predicts that installing a word specialist should carry a cost for whatever occupied the neighbourhood first.

The 2010 illiterate-to-literate comparisons found exactly this signature, because at the left visual word form site, responses to faces and to checkerboard patterns were higher in illiterates and decreased as literacy increased, while responses to faces shifted rightward, strengthening in the right fusiform.

In other words, learning to read appears to nudge face processing toward the right hemisphere, and this is one proposed explanation for why face recognition is right-lateralised more strongly in literate adults.

Developmental studies support the competition picture, since work by Dehaene-Lambertz, Monzalvo, and Dehaene following children through the first year of school in a 2018 study in PLOS Biology found that the word-selective region emerges within months of reading instruction, appearing in cortex that had been weakly specialised, and that face-selective growth in the left hemisphere is correspondingly constrained, with face specialisation expanding more on the right in readers.

The size and permanence of the cost are debated, and it is important to say plainly that literate people are not measurably worse with faces in everyday life, since the reorganisation is a shifting of territory and lateralisation rather than a loss of ability.

Behavioural hints of trade-offs exist, such as findings that strong literacy is associated with reduced mirror-image generalisation, the ancient visual habit of treating b and d shapes as the same object seen from different sides, which reading must actively suppress and which explains why young children so commonly mirror-write letters.

The fusiform story is the clearest case we have of a cultural technology visibly renegotiating the map of the human cortex within a single childhood.

32.3 Dyslexia

This final section turns to developmental dyslexia, the common, lifelong condition in which reading is unexpectedly hard despite adequate intelligence, senses, motivation, and instruction, affecting somewhere around 5 to 10 percent of children depending on the cutoff used.

32.3.1 The phonological core and the multiple-deficit model

The dominant account for four decades has been the phonological deficit hypothesis, which holds that the core problem in dyslexia lies in the brain's representation and manipulation of speech sounds, so that mapping letters onto phonemes, the very heart of alphabetic reading, is laborious and error-prone.

The evidence is broad, since people with dyslexia as a group show weaknesses in phonological awareness tasks, in verbal short-term memory for sounds, and in rapid automatised naming, the speeded naming of familiar items that indexes how quickly sound-based codes can be retrieved.

Sally and Bennett Shaywitz's Connecticut Longitudinal Study, running since 1983, showed additionally that reading ability is a continuum, with dyslexia as the lower tail of a normal distribution rather than a discrete disease category, and that the condition persists rather than being outgrown.

But a single-cause account fails in both directions, because some children with poor phonology read adequately, and some people with dyslexia have measurably normal phonological skills.

Bruce Pennington's multiple-deficit model, articulated in 2006, reframes dyslexia as the outcome of several probabilistic risk factors, phonological weakness usually the largest among them, combining with weaknesses in processing speed, oral language, and attention, and interacting with protective factors, which explains why dyslexia so often co-occurs with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and with language disorders.

Rival and supplementary theories exist, including visual and attentional accounts, temporal auditory processing accounts associated with Paula Tallal, and cerebellar accounts, and the field's current consensus is that these may contribute in subsets of people while the phonological pathway remains the best-supported central route.

It is also a matter of record and of respect that dyslexia is unrelated to intelligence, that many people with dyslexia thrive intellectually and professionally, and that the condition looks different across writing systems, being easier to compensate in highly regular spelling systems like Finnish or Italian and harder in deep ones like English.

32.3.2 The hypoactivation signature, present before reading begins

Neuroimaging of dyslexia converges on a signature, which is hypoactivation, meaning reduced activation, of the left temporo-parietal and left occipito-temporal reading regions during reading and sound-based tasks, often accompanied by extra compensatory activity in frontal regions and the right hemisphere.

This signature appears across languages and writing systems, as shown in cross-cultural work by Eraldo Paulesu and colleagues in 2001 comparing English, French, and Italian readers.

The decisive developmental question was whether the signature is a cause or merely a consequence of struggling to read, since a brain that reads less might simply develop less reading activation.

Studies of pre-readers answered it, because children can be identified before school through familial risk, given that dyslexia runs strongly in families and a child with an affected parent carries roughly a 30 to 50 percent chance of reading difficulty.

Nora Raschle, Nadine Gaab, and colleagues reported in 2012 that pre-reading kindergarten children with a family history of dyslexia already showed reduced activation in left temporo-parietal and occipito-temporal regions during sound-processing tasks, before a single word had been formally taught.

Structural differences also precede reading, and the Boston and Jyväskylä longitudinal projects, along with work by Ozernov-Palchik and Gaab, found differences in left-hemisphere white matter and in the arcuate fasciculus in at-risk pre-readers that predicted later reading outcomes.

Even infancy is informative, since Dennis Molfese's 2000 study found that newborn EEG responses to speech sounds predicted reading group membership at age 8 with striking accuracy in a small sample, and Finnish infant studies found atypical auditory brain responses in newborns at familial risk.

The conclusion is that dyslexia is a developmental difference in brain organisation that predates and produces the reading difficulty, not a scar left by failure, which strengthens the case for early screening and early support rather than the traditional approach of waiting for a child to fail for two or three years before acting.

32.3.3 The intervention findings: remediation normalising the left-hemisphere response

The hopeful chapter of the dyslexia story is that intensive, well-designed teaching changes both reading and the brain.

Effective programmes share a core, which is explicit, systematic instruction in phonemic awareness and letter-sound decoding, delivered intensively, and their behavioural effectiveness is documented in meta-analyses going back to the National Reading Panel in 2000, with the caution that gains are real but often modest and that early intervention outperforms late.

Elise Temple, Michael Merzenich, John Gabrieli, and colleagues published a landmark fMRI study in 2003, scanning children with dyslexia before and after eight weeks of intensive remediation, and found that the children improved in reading and that activation in the left temporo-parietal cortex and left frontal regions increased toward the levels seen in typical readers, a pattern the authors described as partial normalisation.

Panagiotis Simos and colleagues reported converging results in 2002 using magnetoencephalography (MEG), a technique that maps brain activity by measuring the tiny magnetic fields of neurons, showing that successful intervention shifted children's processing from atypical right-hemisphere patterns to the typical left temporo-parietal pattern.

Barbara Shaywitz and colleagues showed in 2004 that a year of explicit phonics-based intervention in young children increased left occipito-temporal activation, with gains persisting at follow-up.

Brain measures even hold some promise for prediction, since a 2011 study by Fumiko Hoeft and colleagues found that patterns of right frontal activation and right-hemisphere white matter predicted which adolescents with dyslexia would improve over two and a half years better than any behavioural measure did.

The honest boundaries deserve statement, because these neuroimaging studies are small, normalisation is partial and not universal, some studies find compensatory rather than normalised patterns, reading fluency often remains slow even when accuracy is repaired, and no commercial programme deserves the label brain-based simply for existing.

The robust core is this, which is that the dyslexic brain is teachable, the earlier the better, and the changes teaching produces are visible in the very circuits where the difference began.

32.3.4 The genetics and the at-risk longitudinal studies

Dyslexia is among the most heritable of common learning conditions, with twin studies, including the long-running Colorado twin project led by Richard Olson and John DeFries, estimating heritability of reading difficulty at roughly 40 to 70 percent, meaning that in the studied populations a large share of the variation among children traces to genetic variation.

Heritability does not mean destiny, and it does not mean a single gene, because reading difficulty, like height, reflects thousands of genetic variants of tiny effect combined with environment and instruction.

The first wave of molecular work identified candidate genes through affected families, including DYX1C1, DCDC2, KIAA0319, and ROBO1, several of which participate in neuronal migration, the prenatal process by which new neurons travel to their proper cortical layer, and imaging genetics studies linked variants in these genes to differences in left temporo-parietal white matter.

The candidate-gene era must be reported with its correction, because large modern datasets have failed to confirm several of these specific genes cleanly, and the field has moved to genome-wide association studies, with a 2022 study of over one million people led by Catherine Doust and Michelle Luciano identifying 42 genome-wide significant variants associated with dyslexia, each of tiny effect, many shared with general cognitive and educational traits.

The longitudinal at-risk studies are the developmental jewel of this literature.

The Jyväskylä Longitudinal Study of Dyslexia in Finland, led by Heikki Lyytinen, followed roughly 200 children, half with a dyslexic parent, from birth to adulthood, and found atypical newborn auditory brain responses, later small delays in speech perception and vocabulary, and letter-knowledge differences by preschool in the children who went on to reading difficulty.

The Dutch Dyslexia Programme and the Boston longitudinal work of Gaab and colleagues found convergent results, and across studies roughly a third to a half of familial at-risk children develop reading difficulty, while risk expresses itself continuously across the whole group rather than splitting children into the affected and the untouched.

The practical meaning of the genetics is often misread, so it should be said plainly that genetic risk shifts probabilities rather than issuing sentences, that the environment of instruction is precisely the lever that intervention studies show works, and that family history is currently the single most useful early warning sign a school can ask about, costing nothing and available years before failure.

The chapter ends where the educated brain begins, with the recognition that reading is a cultural gift that must be built in every child anew, that the building follows knowable neural rules, and that when the building goes hard, science now offers earlier warning and better tools than at any time in the history of literacy.

PART NINE. THE DEVELOPMENT OF COGNITION

================================================================================
