CHAPTER 33. ATTENTION: THE THREE NETWORKS COME ONLINE (CORE)

Attention is the mind's ability to select some things for processing and set other things aside.

This chapter tells the story of how that ability is built during the first years of life, and it matters because almost every other mental skill, from learning words to controlling impulses, rides on top of it.

The guiding framework comes from the psychologist Michael Posner, who proposed that attention is not one thing but three cooperating brain networks: an alerting network that achieves and holds a state of readiness, an orienting network that points the mind at a location or object, and an executive network that resolves conflict between competing responses.

The developmental finding at the heart of the chapter is that these three networks do not arrive together but come online in a sequence, each with its own timetable.


33.1 The sequence

This section lays out the order in which the three attention networks appear, from the drowsy alertness of the newborn to the deliberate, conflict-resolving attention of the toddler.

33.1.1 Alerting early, orienting from three to four months, executive attention from the first birthday

The alerting network, which depends heavily on the brainstem chemical norepinephrine (a signalling molecule that raises the brain's readiness), is the first to function, because a newborn can already be roused into an awake, receptive state, although newborns can hold that state only briefly and spend most of the day asleep.

Across the first months, the periods of calm alertness lengthen, and by around three months an infant can sustain alert attention long enough to study a face or a toy for many seconds at a time.

The orienting network, which links parietal cortex (the brain region on the upper back of each hemisphere that maps space) with midbrain structures that move the eyes, undergoes a dramatic improvement between roughly three and four months, when infants become able to shift their gaze flexibly from one interesting thing to another and even to anticipate where something will appear.

Research by Posner, Mary Rothbart, and colleagues, summarised in reviews such as Posner, Rothbart, Sheese, and Voelker in 2014, showed that during infancy it is largely this orienting system, often steered by caregivers who attract and redirect the baby's gaze, that does the work of calming and regulating the infant.

The executive attention network, centred on the anterior cingulate cortex (a curved strip of cortex on the inner face of each hemisphere that monitors conflict between competing signals) together with lateral prefrontal cortex, begins to show its first clear signs of function near the end of the first year and into the second.

Around the first birthday, infants begin to resolve simple conflicts, for example looking towards a learned target location rather than towards a flashy distractor, and longitudinal work by Posner's group found that individual differences in such conflict resolution in infancy predict later self control.

From that point onward, a slow handover takes place in which control of behaviour passes from the orienting network to the executive network, a handover that continues across the whole of childhood.

33.1.2 Sticky fixation and the birth of disengagement

Between roughly one and three months of age, infants show a striking limitation that researchers call sticky fixation: once the baby's gaze locks onto a salient object, the baby can find it very hard to pull the eyes away, sometimes staring for long stretches and even becoming distressed.

The standard laboratory test is the fixation shift or gap and overlap paradigm, in which a central picture either disappears before a peripheral picture appears (the gap or non competition condition) or stays on while the peripheral picture appears (the overlap or competition condition).

Work by Janette Atkinson, Oliver Braddick, and colleagues, and by Mark Johnson, showed that one to two month olds are often unable to disengage in the competition condition at all, whereas by around four months most infants shift gaze quickly and reliably even when the central picture stays on.

Michael Johnson's influential 1990 account explained the change in terms of maturing cortical circuits, particularly parietal and frontal eye movement pathways, gaining control over the superior colliculus (a midbrain structure that drives reflexive eye movements).

The birth of disengagement matters far beyond eye movements, because being able to look away is the infant's first tool for regulating emotion: a four month old who can break gaze from something overwhelming has a primitive way to turn down distress, and caregivers instinctively exploit this by redirecting an upset baby's attention.

Slow disengagement past the usual age has also been studied as an early marker of later attention and social communication difficulties, although as a single measure it is far too noisy to say anything about an individual child.


33.2 The executive network's childhood

This section follows the youngest network, executive attention, through its main growth years, and connects it to temperament, the child's built in style of reacting and self regulating.

33.2.1 The child attention-network task and the growth years from two to seven

To measure the three networks in one sitting, Jin Fan, Posner, and colleagues created the Attention Network Test (ANT) in 2002, and Rueda, Fan, Posner, and colleagues built a child friendly version in 2004 in which the arrows of the adult test become a row of cartoon fish, and the child must feed the middle fish by pressing the button for the direction it faces.

When the flanking fish point the opposite way from the middle fish, the child must resolve a conflict, and the extra time this costs is the measure of executive attention efficiency.

Cross sectional studies with the child ANT, beginning with Rueda and colleagues in 2004, found that alerting is present early but continues to improve into the school years, orienting is fairly stable across middle childhood, and executive attention shows its steepest improvement between roughly ages two and seven, after which the conflict cost measured in this simple task changes relatively little, with finer improvements continuing into adolescence on harder measures.

Brain imaging and scalp electrophysiology tie this behavioural curve to the anterior cingulate cortex and its connections, which become faster and more efficient across the preschool years as the connecting fibres gain myelin (the fatty insulation that speeds electrical signals).

The practical meaning is that the preschool years, roughly ages two to seven, are the season in which the brain's conflict resolving machinery does most of its growing, which is precisely when children are learning to follow rules, take turns, and hold back impulses.

33.2.2 Training effects and the temperament link to effortful control

Rueda, Rothbart, McCandliss, Saccomanno, and Posner reported in 2005 that five days of computerised attention exercises improved four and six year olds' executive attention and shifted the associated brain electrical responses towards a more mature pattern, and a 2012 follow up study found some effects still present two months after training.

At the same time, the wider literature on cognitive training urges caution, because trained gains often stay near the trained task, and transfer to school achievement or general intelligence has been small and inconsistent across studies, so the honest summary is that executive attention is trainable in the narrow sense while broad transfer remains unproven.

The temperament connection runs through a trait that Rothbart named effortful control, which is the questionnaire measured capacity of a child to voluntarily suppress a dominant response in order to perform a subdominant one, for example whispering when shouting would be easier.

Studies by Rothbart, Posner, and colleagues found that parent reported effortful control correlates with laboratory measures of executive attention, so the temperament trait and the brain network appear to be two views of the same underlying system.

Effortful control measured in early childhood predicts conscientiousness, school success, and social competence years later, which is one reason developmental scientists regard the executive attention network's childhood as consequential.


33.3 The social attention system

This section turns from attention to things towards attention to people, which follows its own timetable and recruits additional brain machinery for faces, eyes, and shared experience.

33.3.1 Gaze following and joint attention at nine to twelve months

Gaze following means noticing where another person is looking and turning one's own attention to the same place, and it was first brought into the laboratory by Michael Scaife and Jerome Bruner in 1975, who showed that infants in the first year will follow an adult's head and eye turn.

Simple, fragile forms of gaze following appear earlier, but between roughly nine and twelve months the skill becomes reliable, flexible, and genuinely referential, meaning the infant seems to grasp that the adult's eyes are directed at something.

The same window brings joint attention, the three way state in which infant and adult attend to the same object and both know it, shown when a twelve month old points at a dog, looks back at the parent's face to check, and looks at the dog again.

Michael Tomasello has argued that this nine month revolution is the gateway to human culture, because sharing attention is what allows word learning, imitation of intentions, and cooperation, and studies confirm that the amount of joint attention an infant experiences predicts later vocabulary size.

At the brain level, work by Mark Johnson, Teodora Gliga, and colleagues implicates a cortical network including the superior temporal sulcus (a groove along the side of the brain that responds to biological motion and gaze) and medial prefrontal regions, with electroencephalography (EEG), the recording of the brain's electrical activity from the scalp, showing distinctive responses to direct versus averted gaze already in early infancy.

33.3.2 The declining eye fixation finding in infants later diagnosed with autism

In 2013, Warren Jones and Ami Klin published in the journal Nature a prospective study that followed infants at high and low familial likelihood of autism from birth, tracking their eye movements while they watched videos of a caregiver's face.

The infants who were later diagnosed with autism did not lack eye contact from the start; instead, their fixation on the caregiver's eyes began at typical levels and then declined steadily from about two months to six months of age, a downward slope not seen in the other infants.

This mattered theoretically because it suggested that some early social machinery is initially present in autism and that the divergence is a developmental derailment rather than an absence from birth, which in turn raised the possibility of a window for very early support.

It matters to state the limits plainly: the study was small, eye tracking measures vary greatly from child to child, and a declining group average cannot diagnose any individual infant, so this is a scientific clue about developmental timing, not a screening test.

Later and larger work by the same group, including a 2023 study in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) of eye tracking as a diagnostic aid in toddlers aged 16 to 30 months, has pushed the approach towards clinical use at older ages, while the infant decline finding remains a research result.

Framed in the register of neurodiversity, the value of this line of work is understanding how autistic development unfolds and how support can meet a child early, not the framing of autistic attention as merely a deficit.


CHAPTER 34. MEMORY: FROM RECOGNITION TO REMEMBERING (CORE)

Memory is the brain's ability to carry the past into the present, and in development it does not arrive all at once but in layers.

A newborn can recognise, a one year old can recall and re enact, a four year old can tell you a story about yesterday, and yet the adult that child becomes will remember almost nothing from before age three.

This chapter walks through those layers, visits the century old puzzle of infantile amnesia, and follows episodic memory, the memory for specific personally experienced events, on its long climb through childhood.

The central brain structure throughout is the hippocampus, a seahorse shaped structure deep in each temporal lobe that binds the pieces of an experience into a retrievable whole.


34.1 What infants retain

This section asks what memory a baby actually has, and the answer, uncovered by some famously clever experiments, is far more than early psychology assumed.

34.1.1 Recognition from birth and the conditioned-mobile time windows

Recognition, the sense that something now present has been encountered before, is demonstrably working at birth, since newborns prefer their mother's voice, as Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer showed in 1980, and prefer a story that was read aloud to them repeatedly during the final weeks of pregnancy, as DeCasper and Melanie Spence showed in 1986.

Newborns also habituate, meaning they look less and less at a repeated picture and perk up for a new one, which is a basic form of recognition memory that researchers exploit constantly.

The landmark measurement of how long infant memory lasts came from Carolyn Rovee-Collier's mobile conjugate reinforcement paradigm, introduced in the 1960s and developed over decades, in which a ribbon connects a baby's ankle to an overhead mobile so that kicking makes the mobile move.

Infants between about two and six months quickly learn the contingency, kick vigorously, and can be tested later by reattaching the ribbon loosely and seeing whether they kick above baseline, which reveals whether the earlier learning is retained.

The retention windows grow with age in an orderly way: two month olds remember the task for a day or two, three month olds for about a week, and six month olds for around two weeks, and with the related train moving paradigm for older infants the window stretches to weeks and then months across the first year and a half.

Rovee-Collier's most surprising finding was reactivation: a brief reminder, such as merely seeing the mobile move the day before the test, could restore a memory that seemed completely gone, showing that infant memories often become inaccessible rather than erased, a theme that will return in the infantile amnesia debate.

Her work also showed that these early memories are tightly bound to context, since a three month old trained with one crib liner pattern may fail to kick when the liner is changed, which tells us infant memory is real but highly specific.

34.1.2 Deferred imitation and long-term recall by the first birthday

Deferred imitation means watching someone perform a novel action, waiting, and reproducing the action later from memory alone, and it is treated as an early index of recall, the active retrieval of a stored representation, rather than mere recognition.

Andrew Meltzoff showed in studies from 1985 and 1988 that nine and fourteen month olds could reproduce novel actions, such as leaning forward to touch a panel with the forehead to make it light up, after delays of a day to a week, and in a large 1995 study with 192 infants he found significant deferred imitation in 14 and 16 month olds after delays of two and even four months.

Patricia Bauer built the elicited imitation method into a systematic mapping of early recall, using multi step event sequences such as making a rattle by putting a ball in a cup, covering it, and shaking, and her work showed that by the first birthday infants can reproduce ordered sequences after long delays, with the length and robustness of recall growing steeply across the second year.

Bauer's group found, for example, that a substantial share of infants who experienced events at 13 months could still reproduce something of them months later, and that 20 month olds recall ordered sequences after intervals as long as a year, although younger infants need more exposures and more retrieval cues.

Because deferred imitation is impaired in adult patients with damage to the hippocampal system, as work by Loretta McDonough, Jean Mandler, and colleagues showed in 1995, developmental scientists take successful deferred imitation in the first year as evidence that a declarative, hippocampus dependent memory system is already operating in infancy, well before language.


34.2 Infantile amnesia

This section confronts the puzzle those infant abilities create: if babies can form memories that last months, why do adults remember essentially nothing from their first years?

Infantile amnesia, also called childhood amnesia, is the near universal inability of older children and adults to retrieve autobiographical memories, meaning memories of specific personally experienced events, from roughly the first three years of life.

34.2.1 The offset near ages three to four and its cultural variation

When adults are asked for their earliest memory, the average answer across many studies in Western samples falls between ages three and four, commonly summarised as an offset near three and a half years, with very few verifiable memories dating from before age two.

The boundary is soft rather than sharp, since memories from ages three to seven are also sparser than a simple forgetting curve would predict, a stretch some researchers treat as a second, partial phase of childhood amnesia.

The offset moves with culture, which is a vital clue that memory retrieval is shaped by the social practices wrapped around it.

Research by Qi Wang comparing American and Chinese adults found that Americans' earliest memories dated on average from around three and a half years while Chinese adults' earliest memories came several months to a year later, and work by Harlene Hayne and Shelley MacDonald found that Maori adults in New Zealand, whose culture places high value on narrating the past, reported earliest memories from around age two and a half, earlier than either European New Zealanders or Asian comparison groups.

Katherine Nelson and Robyn Fivush's social cultural developmental theory explains this pattern by proposing that autobiographical memory is built in conversation: parents who reminisce with their children in a rich, elaborative style give the child a narrative scaffold for encoding and retrieving events, and cultures differ systematically in how much such reminiscing they do.

Culture and conversation clearly move the boundary by a year or so, but they do not abolish it anywhere, so the field's consensus is that infantile amnesia has both a social linguistic layer and a biological layer, and the next two sub sections concern the biology.

34.2.2 The neurogenic hypothesis: new dentate neurons overwriting old traces

The dentate gyrus, the input gate of the hippocampus, is one of the very few brain regions that keeps producing new neurons after birth, a process called neurogenesis, and in infancy the rate of this production is at its lifetime high.

The neurogenic hypothesis of infantile amnesia proposes that this flood of new neurons, wiring themselves into existing hippocampal circuits, physically remodels the circuits that store recent memories and thereby degrades or overwrites them, so the very plasticity that lets the infant brain learn fast also makes its stored episodes unstable.

The key experimental support came from Katherine Akers, Paul Frankland, Sheena Josselyn, and colleagues in a 2014 paper in the journal Science, who showed that increasing neurogenesis in adult mice, for example by exercise, accelerated forgetting of a learned fear memory, while decreasing neurogenesis in infant mice reduced their normally rapid forgetting.

They also reported the complementary comparative point that guinea pigs and degus, rodent species born with more mature brains and lower infant neurogenesis, do not show the same rapid infant forgetting.

The hypothesis is attractive because it explains why infantile amnesia is found across mammals, long before language or self concept could be responsible, but it is a causal account established in rodents, and directly testing it in humans is not possible with current methods, so in humans it stands as a plausible mechanism rather than a demonstrated one.

34.2.3 The latent-trace alternative and the awake-infant hippocampal encoding finding of 2025

The main alternative holds that infant memories are not destroyed but become latent, meaning the trace still exists in the brain but can no longer be found by adult retrieval processes.

Rodent work supports this too: Alessio Travaglia and Cristina Alberini showed in 2016 that infant rats' apparently forgotten memories leave a dormant trace that reminders can reinstate, and a 2018 study from Frankland's group and a 2023 study by Tomás Ryan's group used optogenetics, a technique that uses light to activate genetically tagged neurons, to directly reactivate the engram cells (the specific neurons that stored the memory) in adult mice and recover infant memories that behaviour said were lost.

Into this debate arrived a striking human finding: in March 2025, Tristan Yates, Nicholas Turk-Browne, and colleagues at Yale and Columbia published in Science a study titled Hippocampal encoding of memories in human infants, which scanned awake infants aged about four months to two years with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a method that images brain activity through blood flow, which is extraordinarily difficult in awake babies and required years of method development.

The infants viewed a stream of new photographs and were later shown a previously seen photograph next to a new one while their looking was tracked, and the researchers found that greater hippocampal activity at the moment a picture was first seen predicted the infant looking longer at that picture later, the classic subsequent memory effect used in adults.

The effect was reliable in the infants older than about twelve months, indicating that the hippocampus is encoding individual episodic like memories within the very period that adult autobiography will later leave blank.

The natural reading, which the authors themselves drew, is that infantile amnesia is at least partly a failure of later retrieval or of post encoding stabilisation rather than a failure of encoding, which fits the latent trace view and Rovee-Collier's old reactivation results, while remaining fully compatible with neurogenesis making those traces hard to keep addressable.

The honest bottom line for a beginner is this: babies do form memories, the adult inaccessibility of those memories is real, and the field's live question has shifted from whether infant brains encode to why the encoded traces become unreachable, with circuit remodelling, retrieval mismatch, and the late arrival of narrative scaffolding all still on the table.


34.3 The long climb of episodic memory

This section follows memory across childhood, when the ability to recall does not simply exist or not exist but slowly gains precision, context, and self awareness.

34.3.1 Binding what, where, and when across ages four to ten

An episodic memory is not a single item but a bound package: what happened, where it happened, and when it happened, tied together so that retrieving one piece brings back the others.

Behavioural studies show that this binding improves markedly between about ages four and ten, since young children often recognise an item perfectly well yet misremember which background it appeared on, which list it came from, or which day it happened, and tasks that require remembering item plus context show much steeper age curves than item recognition alone.

The neural account ties this to the protracted development of the hippocampus, whose subfields mature on different schedules, with work by Joshua Lee, Simona Ghetti, and colleagues showing that the dentate gyrus and the CA3 region (an internal hippocampal subfield that supports pattern completion) continue changing structurally through middle childhood and that their development tracks gains in associative memory.

Longitudinal imaging by Ghetti's and Noa Ofen's groups shows that during successful encoding, children increasingly recruit the same hippocampal prefrontal circuitry as adults, with the connections strengthening across ages four to ten, so the climb of episodic memory is the slow knitting together of a network rather than the switching on of a part.

By around age ten, binding of what, where, and when approaches adult levels on simple laboratory tasks, though memory for the temporal order of complex real events keeps improving into adolescence.

34.3.2 Source memory and strategy late, with prefrontal cortex

Source memory is memory for where a piece of knowledge came from, for example whether you saw an event yourself, were told about it, or imagined it, and it is one of the last components of episodic memory to mature.

Experiments by Kathleen Drummey and Nora Newcombe in 2002 found that four year olds frequently attributed facts they had just learned in the laboratory to their parents or to television, a source error that dropped sharply by ages six to eight.

Source monitoring depends on the prefrontal cortex, the front most part of the brain that supports control, evaluation, and strategy, and the prefrontal cortex is among the slowest maturing brain regions, which is why source judgement lags item memory by years.

The same prefrontal timetable governs memory strategies, the deliberate techniques such as rehearsal, grouping items into categories, and elaboration: John Flavell's classic work in the 1960s showed that five year olds rarely rehearse spontaneously, ten year olds usually do, and children in between often show a production deficiency, meaning they can use a strategy when taught but do not summon it on their own.

Alongside strategies grows metamemory, the child's knowledge about memory itself, such as knowing that a long list is harder than a short one, and improvements in metamemory, strategy use, and prefrontal function travel together through the school years.

34.3.3 Suggestibility and the eyewitness child

Suggestibility is the degree to which a person's memory report can be altered by leading questions, social pressure, or misinformation, and its developmental study became urgent in the 1980s when daycare abuse prosecutions rested on the testimony of very young children.

Stephen Ceci and Maggie Bruck's 1993 review in Psychological Bulletin synthesised a century of research and a wave of new experiments, concluding that preschool children, roughly ages three to five, are reliably more suggestible than older children and adults, especially under repeated suggestive interviewing.

In Ceci's famous mousetrap studies, preschoolers who were repeatedly asked to think about fictitious events, such as getting a hand caught in a mousetrap, came to produce detailed, emotionally convincing false narratives that trained professionals could not distinguish from true ones.

The developmental mechanics connect directly to the previous sub section: weak source monitoring lets an imagined or suggested event be mistaken for an experienced one, and an immature grasp of the interviewer's social intent makes a young child prone to give the answer the adult seems to want.

The crucial balancing fact is that young children questioned once, neutrally, and in their own words can be accurate witnesses, so the research reshaped forensic practice through structured protocols such as the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) interview protocol, which uses open prompts and avoids suggestion.

This literature is a rare case where developmental cognitive neuroscience directly changed courtroom procedure, and it is discussed here as science about memory systems, not as guidance for evaluating any particular child's account.

34.4 Working memory

This section turns from memory for the past to working memory, the mental workspace that holds and manipulates information over seconds, which behaves developmentally like a capacity that grows rather than a skill that switches on.

34.4.1 The linear growth of span from four to fifteen

Working memory is classically measured as span, the number of items a person can hold and use, for example repeating back a list of digits (simple span) or repeating it backwards (complex span, which requires manipulation as well as storage).

Susan Gathercole, Susan Pickering, Ben Ambridge, and Hannah Waring published in 2004 a large cross sectional study of children from four to fifteen years and found that performance on every working memory measure rose in a strikingly steady, broadly linear fashion across that whole range, with no sudden jumps.

In round numbers, a typical four year old manages a forward span of about two to three items, a school aged child four to five, and a teenager approaches the adult range of around six to seven, with backward and complex spans following the same slope at lower absolute levels.

Gathercole's study also showed that the architecture of working memory, in the sense of Alan Baddeley's model with separable verbal storage, visuospatial storage, and a central executive coordinating them, is already in place by about age six, so what changes over childhood is mainly the capacity and efficiency of the components, not the basic structure.

Working memory capacity matters enormously in practice, because it constrains mental arithmetic, following multi step instructions, and reading comprehension, and low working memory is a common thread across many learning difficulties.

34.4.2 The fronto-parietal correlates

In adults, working memory reliably engages a fronto parietal network, meaning coordinated activity between the lateral prefrontal cortex and the intraparietal and superior parietal cortex, and developmental imaging shows children recruit the same network from at least middle childhood.

Studies by Torkel Klingberg and colleagues in the early 2000s found that activity in frontal and intraparietal regions during visuospatial working memory tasks increases with age from childhood to adolescence and correlates with capacity, and that the maturation of the white matter tracts (the myelinated fibre bundles) connecting these regions tracks span as well.

Later longitudinal work, including studies by Ulman Lindenberg's and Klingberg's groups and by the large Philadelphia and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohorts, supports a picture in which increasing capacity reflects stronger, more selective fronto parietal activation, better suppression of activity in the default mode network (the network active during rest and mind wandering), and faster long range connections.

So the linear behavioural growth of span from four to fifteen has an equally gradual neural story underneath it: the workspace gets bigger mainly because its long distance wiring gets faster and its control signals get cleaner, a theme that the next chapter, on executive function, develops at full length.


CHAPTER 35. EXECUTIVE FUNCTION: THE PREFRONTAL DECADES (CORE)

Executive function is the umbrella term for the mental abilities that control other abilities: holding goals in mind, resisting impulses, and shifting flexibly between rules.

These abilities depend on the prefrontal cortex, the large front region of the brain, together with its dopamine supply and its long range connections, and their development is the slowest in all of cognition, stretching from the first year of life into the third decade.

This chapter follows that long arc in three movements: the surprising executive achievements of infancy, the dramatic leap of the preschool years, and the extended adolescence of cognitive control.

The practical stakes are high, because childhood executive function predicts school achievement, health, and wellbeing, and because the field has learned hard lessons about what such predictions do and do not mean.


35.1 Infancy

This section shows that executive function does not wait for childhood: its first machinery is testable, and lesionable in animal models, before the first birthday.

35.1.1 A-not-B, delayed response, and the dorsolateral prefrontal link

The A-not-B task comes from Jean Piaget's observations in the 1950s: an object is hidden repeatedly at location A, the infant retrieves it, and then, in full view, the object is hidden at location B, yet infants of around eight to ten months often reach back to A.

Adele Diamond's doctoral work in the 1980s turned this curiosity into a precision instrument by showing that the error depends on the delay between hiding and reaching, with the delay an infant can withstand growing from about two to five seconds at seven and a half to nine months to more than ten seconds by twelve months.

The decisive link to the brain came from Diamond's collaboration with Patricia Goldman-Rakic, published in 1989, comparing infants, adult monkeys, and monkeys with surgical removal of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the upper side portion of the prefrontal cortex that holds information over delays.

Monkeys without dorsolateral prefrontal cortex made the A-not-B error at the same short delays as human seven and a half to nine month olds, while intact monkeys performed like twelve month olds, and the same lesion impaired the closely related delayed response task that Goldman-Rakic's laboratory had tied to sustained neuronal firing during the delay.

The conclusion, now standard, is that the improvement between roughly seven and twelve months reflects the functional coming online of dorsolateral prefrontal circuits that combine working memory (holding where the toy is) with inhibition (suppressing the practised reach to A), the two ingredients that define executive function ever after.

35.1.2 The dopamine dependence and the phenylketonuria lesson

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter, a chemical messenger between neurons, and the prefrontal cortex is exquisitely dependent on receiving the right amount of it to sustain the delay period firing that working memory requires.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a genetic disorder in which the enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine is deficient, and untreated it causes severe intellectual disability, which a low phenylalanine diet largely prevents.

Diamond noticed a puzzle in treated children: even with the diet, children whose blood phenylalanine ran at the high end of the accepted range showed selective difficulty on exactly the tasks that need dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, such as A-not-B with delay and tapping tasks requiring inhibition, while other cognitive abilities were spared.

Her explanation, supported by an animal model she published with colleagues in the 1990s, is biochemical: moderately raised phenylalanine competes with tyrosine, the raw material for dopamine, at the transport step into the brain, and the prefrontal dopamine neurons, which fire fast and lack strong reuptake, are the first and hardest hit by a modest shortfall.

The PKU story earned its place in every textbook for two reasons: it demonstrated in humans that early executive function depends on prefrontal dopamine specifically, and it changed clinical practice by motivating stricter phenylalanine targets for infants and children.

It is also a model example of how a metabolic detail, one enzyme, one transporter, one neurotransmitter, can produce a sharply selective cognitive signature in a developing brain.


35.2 The preschool leap

This section covers ages three to six, when executive abilities improve faster than at any other time of life, and when some of psychology's most famous, and most misread, experiments were run.

35.2.1 Inhibition, the card sort, and graded representations

The signature preschool test is the Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS), standardised by Philip Zelazo and published as a protocol in 2006, in which children sort cards showing, say, red rabbits and blue boats first by colour and then are asked to switch and sort the same cards by shape.

Most three year olds sort the first dimension perfectly, can state the new rule aloud, and then go on sorting by the old rule anyway, while most four and five year olds switch successfully, and a meta analysis found roughly four in ten three year olds switching against nearly nine in ten five year olds.

This dissociation between knowing and doing is the purest demonstration that executive control is a separate, later developing layer on top of knowledge, and the same years bring parallel gains in inhibition tasks such as day night (say night to a picture of the sun) and grass snow.

Theories differ on what exactly matures: Zelazo's cognitive complexity and control theory says children become able to represent higher order rules, rules about rules, while the graded representations account of Yuko Munakata and colleagues holds that the change is quantitative, a gradual strengthening of active goal representations in prefrontal cortex until they can overcome the latent pull of recent habits, and computational models show that such graded strengthening reproduces the three year old's knowing but failing pattern without any discrete new capacity.

The graded view fits the neuroscience comfortably, since nothing in prefrontal maturation is switch like across this period, and it predicts, correctly, that small changes in task support, such as labelling the relevant dimension, can shift a three year old into success.

35.2.2 Delay of gratification and what its follow-ups did and did not show

In Walter Mischel's delay of gratification studies at Stanford around 1970, popularly the marshmallow test, preschoolers chose between one treat now and two treats if they waited alone for up to about fifteen minutes, and the children's strategies, such as looking away or covering their eyes, revealed early self regulation in action.

Follow ups published by Mischel, Yuichi Shoda, and Philip Peake in 1988 and 1990 reported that seconds of preschool waiting predicted adolescent competence and Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT) scores, a result that made the test a cultural icon and fed a narrative that a single early willpower measure foretells life outcomes.

The modern correction came from Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan, and Haonan Quan in 2018, who ran a conceptual replication in a much larger and more diverse sample of around nine hundred children and found that the correlation between waiting at age four and achievement at age fifteen was about half the original size, and shrank by roughly two thirds more, to a very small value, once family background and early cognitive ability were controlled.

The fair reading, echoed in subsequent exchanges between the original and replication teams, is not that delay ability is meaningless but that much of its predictive power rides on the circumstances a child grows up in, since waiting for a promised second treat is also a rational bet about whether adults in your environment keep promises, a point made vivid by Celeste Kidd's 2013 experiment in which children waited far longer for a researcher who had just proven reliable.

The lesson this corpus draws is methodological and humane at once: single snapshot measures of a developing control system are weak crystal balls, and early executive behaviour is entangled with the child's economic and social world rather than being a fixed trait of the child alone.

35.2.3 Hot against cool executive function

Developmental scientists distinguish cool executive function, control exercised over neutral material such as sorting cards, from hot executive function, control exercised when rewards, emotions, or desires are directly at stake, as in delaying gratification or gambling style choice tasks.

The distinction has an anatomical shadow: cool tasks lean on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and its parietal partners, while hot tasks additionally engage the orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, the lower and middle prefrontal territories connected to the amygdala and the reward system.

Zelazo and colleagues, who articulated the distinction in the early 2000s, showed that hot and cool measures in preschoolers correlate only modestly with each other and follow partly separate developmental timetables, and children's versions of reward based tasks such as the children's gambling task show competence emerging later than matched cool tasks.

The distinction should be held lightly, because meta analytic and factor analytic work has found the hot cool separation to be blurrier than the labels suggest, with task specific factors often swamping the hot cool difference, so it is best treated as a useful organising axis rather than two distinct modules.

Its developmental importance returns at full strength in adolescence, where control in cool laboratory conditions can look mature years before control in emotionally charged, peer saturated conditions does.


35.3 The long adolescence of control

This section follows executive function through its final and longest act, the slow consolidation of cognitive control across the second decade and into the third.

35.3.1 The antisaccade curve and the network segregation story

The antisaccade task asks a person to look away from a light that suddenly appears, pitting a deliberate goal directly against a powerful reflex, and it is a favourite of developmental science because it needs no language and works from childhood to old age.

Beatriz Luna and colleagues, in cross sectional and longitudinal studies beginning in 2004, charted the antisaccade curve: error rates fall steeply through childhood and adolescence and reach adult levels in the mid teens by some measures, with the consistency and speed of correct performance continuing to improve into the early twenties.

Luna's imaging work showed that adolescents can generate adult level single trial performance but do so with more effortful and more variable recruitment of prefrontal circuitry, while adults achieve the same control more cheaply through distributed, well integrated networks.

The wiring level account is the network segregation story: as myelination and synaptic pruning proceed, the brain's large scale networks become more internally coherent and more cleanly separated from one another, and Graham Baum, Theodore Satterthwaite, and colleagues showed in 2017, in 882 people aged eight to twenty two, that this modular segregation of structural networks directly mediates the age related improvement in executive performance.

A necessary caution recorded throughout this corpus applies here: the popular claim that the brain, or the prefrontal cortex, matures at twenty five is an artefact of studies whose samples stopped in the mid twenties, since different measures plateau at different ages, some in the teens, some around thirty, and change never fully stops, so the honest statement is that executive control undergoes protracted refinement into the twenties without any single finish line.

35.3.2 Unity and diversity emerging with age

The adult architecture of executive function was mapped by Akira Miyake, Naomi Friedman, and colleagues in 2000 using latent variable analysis, a statistical method that extracts what many tasks share, and they found unity and diversity: three separable factors, inhibition, updating of working memory, and shifting between task sets, all riding on a substantial common core.

Developmentally, this structure is not present from the start: in preschoolers, executive tasks tend to load on a single undifferentiated factor, and studies across childhood and adolescence find the structure gradually differentiating, from one factor in early childhood towards the two to four factor solutions seen by adolescence, although exact factor solutions vary across studies and measurement of young children is noisy.

Friedman and colleagues' twin studies added that both the common core and the specific factors are strongly heritable by adolescence and remarkably stable across time, while remaining, as the training literature shows, responsive to context and load.

The emerging picture is of an executive system that begins as one general purpose, effortful capacity and specialises with age, in step with the same network segregation described above, so unity comes first in development and diversity is grown.

35.3.3 Training and its transfer limits

Because executive function predicts so much, enormous effort has gone into training it, through computerised working memory programs, executive loaded school curricula, aerobic exercise, mindfulness practices, music, and martial arts.

The reliable finding, established across hundreds of studies, is near transfer: practising a working memory or inhibition task makes you better at that task and close variants, with gains that can persist for months.

The equally reliable disappointment is limited far transfer: meta analyses by Monica Melby-Lervag and Charles Hulme in 2013 and 2016, and by Giovanni Sala and Fernand Gobet, found that gains from working memory training do not convincingly transfer to fluid intelligence, reading, or arithmetic, and the once celebrated commercial brain training industry was formally rebuked when Lumos Labs settled deceptive advertising charges with the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in 2016.

Adele Diamond's 2011 review in Science of school based approaches, including the Tools of the Mind curriculum, argued that the most promising route is not isolated drilling but embedding executive challenge in meaningful, emotionally engaging, physically active practice, with the largest benefits for the children starting lowest, although later randomised trials of such curricula have themselves produced mixed results.

The balanced conclusion is that executive function is experience dependent and can be supported, especially where poverty and stress load it down, but that no known program installs a generally better prefrontal cortex, and claims of broad transfer should be met with the same scrutiny this chapter applied to the marshmallow test.


CHAPTER 36. NUMBER AND MATHEMATICAL COGNITION (CORE)

Number is a domain where the developmental story runs unusually cleanly from newborn instinct to schooled expertise, which is why it has become a model system for developmental cognitive neuroscience.

This chapter begins with the approximate number system, the built in ability to estimate quantities without counting, follows the construction of number circuitry in the parietal lobe, watches children bootstrap their way into exact symbolic number, and ends with dyscalculia, the specific learning difficulty of mathematics.

The recurring brain region is the intraparietal sulcus, a long groove on the upper side surface of each hemisphere that houses the brain's core quantity code in monkeys, human adults, and, as we will see, young children.

The recurring theme is interaction: a coarse inherited sense of quantity meets a cultural symbol system, and education literally rewires the cortex that joins them.


36.1 The approximate number system

This section introduces the evolutionarily ancient estimation sense that humans share with many animals, and the evidence that it is running in the first days and months of life.

36.1.1 Ratio-dependent discrimination in the first year and at birth

The approximate number system (ANS) represents quantities imprecisely, like a mental fog gauge, and its defining signature is ratio dependence, meaning that telling two quantities apart depends on their ratio rather than their absolute difference, a property known in psychophysics as Weber's law.

Fei Xu and Elizabeth Spelke showed in 2000 that six month old infants, habituated to displays of dots, look longer at a new numerosity when the ratio is two to one, discriminating eight from sixteen, but fail at a three to two ratio, eight against twelve, with careful controls ruling out area, density, and other non numerical cues.

Precision sharpens on a slow schedule: by nine to ten months infants succeed at three to two, preschoolers manage four to three, and adult precision, typically around ten to nine or a little finer, is not reached until adolescence, with wide and stable individual differences at every age.

The system is present at birth: Veronique Izard, Coralie Sann, Spelke, and Arlette Streri reported in 2009 that newborns only hours to days old, familiarised with sequences of sounds of a given number, looked longer at visual displays matching that number, succeeding at a three to one ratio, which shows the newborn representation is not only present but abstract, linking number across hearing and vision.

Because ratio dependent numerosity discrimination is also found in monkeys, rats, fish, and chicks, the ANS is taken to be an evolutionarily ancient endowment, the starting capital on which human mathematics is later built.

36.1.2 The two-systems view: tracking small sets against estimating large ones

A curious failure complicates the story: infants who discriminate eight from sixteen often fail to discriminate two from four, an easy two to one ratio, when the sets are small.

The accepted resolution, articulated in Lisa Feigenson, Stanislas Dehaene, and Spelke's influential 2004 review, is that two core systems handle quantity: the ANS for larger sets, and a distinct object tracking system, also called the parallel individuation system, which represents each item in a small set as a separate object file but holds only about three such files in infancy.

Small sets are captured by the exact object tracking system, large sets by the approximate estimator, and infant failures occur exactly where a comparison would force the two incompatible codes to talk to each other, such as two against four.

Feigenson's crawling and cracker choice experiments show the small system's sharp limit: ten to twelve month olds reliably choose two crackers over one and three over two, but fall to chance at three against four and even one against four, because four items overflow the object files and the representation collapses.

The two systems view is the majority position but not unanimous, since some researchers, including Susan Carey on the conceptual side and others on the psychophysical side, debate whether small numbers are ever handled by the ANS and how the two codes interact, and this book records it as a well supported framework with active edges rather than settled law.

For development, the two systems matter because each contributes something different to later mathematics: the object tracking system gives exactness over tiny sets, the ANS gives comparability over all sets, and neither alone can represent exactly seven, which is the gap that language and counting will close in section 36.3.


36.2 The parietal construction

This section moves into the brain, asking when and how the parietal cortex, and specifically the intraparietal sulcus, becomes the home of number.

36.2.1 Intraparietal number responses by age three to four

In adults, the horizontal segment of the intraparietal sulcus responds to number across notations and senses, and single neurons tuned to particular numerosities were found in the monkey homologue by Andreas Nieder and Earl Miller in 2002, so the question for development is how early this parietal number code exists.

Jessica Cantlon, Elizabeth Brannon, and colleagues showed in 2006 with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) that four year olds watching numerosity changes activate the intraparietal sulcus in the same right lateralised way adults do, and Daniel Hyde, Nathan Boas, and colleagues, using near infrared spectroscopy (a method that measures brain activity with gentle light through the scalp), found number specific parietal responses in six month old infants.

Electroencephalography work by Izard and colleagues in 2008 likewise found distinct parietal responses to number changes in three month olds, so converging methods place at least a coarse parietal quantity signal in the first year, with clear adult like intraparietal responses demonstrable by age three to four.

The developmental refinement that follows is tuning: behavioural and imaging work by Manuela Piazza and colleagues shows the parietal number code becoming progressively sharper from childhood to adulthood, in parallel with the behavioural sharpening of ANS precision described above.

The take home for a beginner is that the parietal number region is not created by schooling; a rough version is present in infancy, and development is a long process of sharpening it and connecting it to everything else.

36.2.2 The frontal-to-parietal shift with schooling

A classic finding holds that as children learn arithmetic, the brain's workload shifts backwards: Susan Rivera, Vinod Menon, and colleagues reported in 2005 that during addition and subtraction, older subjects in a sample aged eight to nineteen showed more activation in the left inferior parietal cortex, around the supramarginal gyrus and intraparietal sulcus, while younger subjects leaned more on prefrontal cortex, the anterior cingulate, and the hippocampus.

The standard interpretation is efficiency: novices must assemble each answer with effortful, general purpose executive machinery in the front of the brain, while practice hands the job to specialised parietal circuits that retrieve and manipulate quantities directly, so the frontal to parietal shift is the neural signature of arithmetic becoming fluent.

Honesty requires reporting that this textbook shift has recently been contested: the original evidence was cross sectional and modest in size, some later training studies found reduced frontal activity without any increased parietal activity, and a large preregistered registered report published in 2025, following a 2021 protocol in the journal Public Library of Science One (PLOS ONE), reported no developmental frontal to parietal shift in brain activation during mental arithmetic across the lifespan.

The fair current summary is that frontal engagement clearly decreases as arithmetic becomes practised, that parietal cortex clearly matters for calculation at every age, but that the simple picture of activity migrating from front to back with schooling is now uncertain and may have been an artefact of small cross sectional samples, and this outline teaches it as a contested claim.

What is not contested is that schooling changes number cortex: literacy and arithmetic instruction measurably reorganise parietal and visual regions, including the emergence of specialised responses to written digits in ventral visual cortex during the early school years.

36.3 Symbols and bootstrapping

This section covers the uniquely human step: how a child converts the fuzzy quantities of the ANS and the tiny exact sets of object tracking into the infinite, exact system of counting numbers.

36.3.1 The counting principles and the knower levels

Rochel Gelman and Randy Gallistel proposed in their 1978 book The Child's Understanding of Number that counting is governed by principles, most importantly one to one correspondence (each item gets exactly one tag), stable order (tags come in a fixed sequence), and cardinality (the last tag names the size of the whole set).

Children recite the count list long before they understand it, and the tool that revealed the hidden stages is the give N task, in which a child is simply asked to give a puppet one, two, three, or more items from a pile.

Karen Wynn's longitudinal work in 1990 and 1992 discovered the knower levels: children first succeed only for one (one knowers), then after some months for two (two knowers), then three, and sometimes four, each level taking weeks to months, before an abrupt transition to cardinal principle knowers who can give any number within their count list.

Barbara Sarnecka, with Susan Gelman and later with statistical modelling by Michael Lee, confirmed that these levels are real, discrete, and ordered rather than noise, and that the whole climb typically spans roughly ages two to four, with the cardinal principle usually grasped between three and four in children learning number rich languages.

Susan Carey's bootstrapping theory interprets the sequence: the early knower levels are powered by the small exact object tracking system mapped onto the first few words, and the leap to cardinal principle knowledge happens when the child induces the pattern that moving one step in the count list means adding exactly one, thereby constructing a genuinely new representational capacity, exact large number, that neither core system provides.

Bootstrapping is debated, with critics including Gallistel arguing the ANS plays a bigger role and others questioning how induction over a small list can yield the concept of exactness, but the knower level data themselves are among the most replicated facts in cognitive development, and cross cultural work with the Piraha and Munduruku peoples of the Amazon, by Peter Gordon in 2004 and Pierre Pica and colleagues in 2004, shows that without a count list, exact large number does not appear, confirming that the symbol system is doing real constructive work.

36.3.2 The hippocampal moment in arithmetic learning

When children first learn arithmetic facts, they count; with practice, they retrieve, answering three plus four from memory, and the transition between these strategies has a specific neural chaperone.

Shaozheng Qin, Vinod Menon, and colleagues showed in a 2014 longitudinal study in Nature Neuroscience that as seven to nine year olds shifted from counting to memory based retrieval over about a year, engagement of the hippocampus increased while prefrontal and parietal engagement decreased, and the children whose hippocampal to neocortical functional connectivity increased most showed the greatest gains in retrieval fluency.

This is the same hippocampus that chapter 34 introduced as the binder of episodic memories, and its role here follows standard memory systems logic: the hippocampus rapidly stores new associations, such as a problem and its answer, and then trains the neocortex over time, after which fluent adults can retrieve well practised facts with little hippocampal involvement.

Menon's group also found that in adolescents and adults the hippocampal contribution recedes as facts consolidate into cortical networks, so the hippocampal moment is exactly that, a developmental waypoint rather than the permanent home of arithmetic.

The finding has a practical echo: retrieval practice, spacing, and sleep, the classic supporters of hippocampal consolidation, are the same ingredients that build arithmetic fluency, linking the neuroscience of memory directly to the mathematics classroom.

36.4 Dyscalculia

This section addresses developmental dyscalculia, the specific and persistent difficulty with number and arithmetic that affects an estimated three to six percent of children despite adequate schooling and general ability.

36.4.1 The intraparietal signature and the core-deficit against access-deficit debate

Dyscalculia has a reasonably consistent neural signature centred on the intraparietal sulcus: children with dyscalculia show reduced intraparietal activation during number comparison and arithmetic, and structural studies, including work by Elena Rykhlevskaia, Menon, and colleagues in 2009 and studies of dyscalculia of genetic origin such as Turner syndrome by Nicolas Molko and colleagues in 2003, find reduced grey matter and altered connectivity in the same territory.

The causal question splits the field into two hypotheses.

The core deficit hypothesis, championed by Brian Butterworth and supported by findings from Piazza and colleagues in 2010 that children with dyscalculia have markedly less precise ANS acuity, holds that the inherited quantity system itself is weak, so everything built on it, from comparison to arithmetic, inherits the weakness.

The access deficit hypothesis, proposed by Laurence Rousselle and Marie-Pascale Noel in 2007, holds that the core quantity system is intact and the problem lies in connecting symbols to it, based on their finding that children with mathematics difficulties were impaired at comparing digits but not at comparing dot arrays.

Two decades of studies have split between these results, with meta analyses finding that symbolic comparison deficits are larger and more consistent than non symbolic ones, and the emerging view is that dyscalculia is heterogeneous: some children show genuine ANS imprecision, others mainly a symbol to quantity access problem, and still others primarily working memory or attention loads on arithmetic, so a single core deficit for all cases now looks unlikely.

As with the other developmental conditions in this corpus, the neurodiversity framing applies: dyscalculia is a difference in a specific learned and inherited system, it says nothing about general intelligence, and identifying which component is weak in a given learner is precisely what makes targeted, effective support possible, with intervention studies showing that adaptive number training can improve arithmetic and partially normalise parietal responses.

CHAPTER 37. CORE KNOWLEDGE AND THE SPATIAL BRAIN (CORE)

This chapter asks what a baby knows before anyone has taught it anything.

A long tradition in developmental psychology argues that infants arrive with a small set of starter systems - rough, early-working expectations about objects, people, numbers, and space - and that all later learning is built on these foundations.

The chapter lays out that core knowledge proposal, walks through the famous experiments that support it, and then does something a responsible science book must do: it tells you which of those famous findings have held up when other laboratories tried to repeat them, and which have not.

It also descends into the brain itself, following the maturation of the specialised spatial cells that give an animal its sense of place and direction.

The chapter matters because it sits at the centre of the oldest question in the field - how much of the mind is grown from within and how much is written in by experience - and because it is where developmental psychology has faced its own reproducibility reckoning most directly.


37.1 The core systems

This section introduces the core knowledge hypothesis, the idea most closely associated with the psychologist Elizabeth Spelke.

The claim is that human infants, like the young of many other species, come equipped with a handful of ancient, specialised systems of expectation, each tuned to one domain of the world.

The usual list has four members: a system for objects, a system for agents, a system for number, and a system for geometry.

Each system is limited, each works from very early in life, and each is proposed to be shared in some form with other animals, which is part of the evidence that it is built by evolution rather than assembled from scratch by each child.


37.1.1 Objects, agents, number, and geometry

The object system carries expectations that solid things are cohesive, that they move on connected paths, and that they do not pass through one another.

The agent system treats certain moving things - things that start their own motion and act toward goals - as fundamentally different from billiard balls, and expects them to act efficiently.

The number system gives infants an approximate feel for quantity, so that a six-month-old can tell eight dots from sixteen but not eight from nine, a ratio-limited sense that sharpens across childhood.

The geometry system encodes the shape of the surrounding space - the lengths of walls and the directions of corners - and is used for reorienting after being turned around.

A classic demonstration of the geometry system comes from Linda Hermer and Elizabeth Spelke in 1994, who showed that disoriented toddlers search for a hidden toy using the room's rectangular shape, even ignoring an obvious coloured wall that adults would use.

Spelke and Katherine Kinzler laid out the mature statement of the framework in a 2007 paper titled Core Knowledge, adding a possible fifth system for social group membership.

The evidence for each system rests mainly on looking-time methods, which measure how long an infant stares at an event, on the logic that babies look longer at things that surprise them.

That method is powerful but indirect, and how much rich knowledge one may read into a few extra seconds of staring is exactly the dispute that runs through the rest of this chapter.

Critics such as the dynamic-systems theorists Esther Thelen and Gregor Schoner have argued that looking-time differences show only that infants notice a difference between two displays, not that they hold anything like a concept.

The honest summary is that the existence of early, domain-tuned expectations is well supported, while the richness of what those expectations amount to remains genuinely contested.


37.1.2 The drawbridge findings and what infants expect of matter

The single most famous core knowledge experiment is the drawbridge study of Renee Baillargeon, Elizabeth Spelke, and Stanley Wasserman, published in 1985.

Infants of about five months watched a flat screen rotate up and back like a drawbridge through a 180 degree arc until the motion became boring, a process called habituation, which simply means letting the infant get used to a display until interest fades.

Then a solid box was placed behind the screen.

In the possible event, the screen rotated up and stopped where the hidden box should be.

In the impossible event, the screen appeared to rotate straight through the space the box occupied.

The infants looked reliably longer at the impossible event, which Baillargeon read as evidence that they represented the hidden box as still existing and as solid - object permanence far earlier than Jean Piaget's classic account, which placed it at around eight to nine months and full mastery later still.

Baillargeon then pushed the age downward, reporting related effects in infants as young as three and a half months in a 1987 follow-up.

The interpretation has been challenged from the start.

The impossible event contains more motion than the possible event, and later work showed that infants sometimes prefer the full rotation even with no box present, suggesting that raw perceptual preference could contribute to the looking pattern.

Replications of the basic looking difference exist, but the debate about what the looking difference means - rich hidden-object knowledge or simpler perceptual processing - has never fully closed, and this book presents it as a live interpretive dispute rather than a settled fact.

What is not in dispute is narrower and still remarkable: well before their first birthday, infants respond systematically to events that violate solidity and continuity, and they do so months before they can reach for a hidden object.


37.1.3 Violations driving exploration and learning

A newer line of work asks what a violated expectation is for.

In 2015, Aimee Stahl and Lisa Feigenson published a study in the journal Science showing that eleven-month-old infants who had just seen an object behave impossibly - for example, appearing to pass through a wall or float in mid-air - subsequently learned new information about that object better than about an ordinary object.

The surprised infants also explored the strange object in targeted ways, banging an object that had seemed to defy solidity and dropping an object that had seemed to defy gravity, as if testing the specific rule that had been broken.

The proposal is elegant: core knowledge does not just describe the world, it flags the places where the world disagrees with the description, and those flags direct the child's learning budget to exactly the events with the most to teach.

Later work by the same group extended the effect to preschoolers, who ask more questions and explore longer after witnessing impossible events.

Follow-up research and theoretical commentary, including a 2021 paper in the journal Cognition, argues that violations trigger an active search for explanations rather than mere arousal.

This work matters for the replication debates below, because it gives surprise a functional job in learning rather than treating it as a mere laboratory curiosity.

At the same time, the field notes that these are still looking-time and brief-exploration measures in small samples, and the enthusiasm is tempered by the measurement humility that section 37.4 describes.


37.2 Agents

This section turns from matter to minds, asking when infants begin to treat other beings as actors with goals rather than as objects with trajectories.

The findings here include some of the most charming results in the field and also some of its most sobering replication failures, and both halves are told in full.


37.2.1 Goal attribution and rational action

Amanda Woodward's 1998 habituation study is the anchor for goal attribution.

Infants of five to nine months watched a hand repeatedly reach for one of two toys, then the toys swapped positions.

Infants looked longer when the hand reached for a new toy in the old location than when it reached for the old toy in a new location, suggesting they had encoded the reach in terms of its goal object, not its physical path.

Crucially, the effect was much weaker when the reaching thing was a mechanical claw instead of a hand, hinting that infants restrict goal talk to plausible agents.

The second pillar is the rational action work of Gyorgy Gergely, Gergely Csibra, and colleagues, beginning with a 1995 study in the journal Cognition.

Twelve-month-olds watched an animated ball repeatedly jump over a barrier to reach another ball.

When the barrier was removed, infants looked longer if the ball still took the now-pointless jumping path than if it went straight, suggesting they expected agents to pursue goals efficiently given the constraints - what Gergely and Csibra called the teleological stance, meaning an interpretive habit of explaining actions by their goals.

A related and much-cited demonstration is the 2002 rational imitation study by Gergely, Harold Bekkering, and Ildiko Kiraly, in which fourteen-month-olds copied a head-touch on a lamp more often when the adult's hands had been free than when her hands were occupied, as if reasoning about why she had used her head.

That particular finding failed to replicate cleanly in later work, including a large 2016 multi-laboratory effort led by David Buttelmann's critics and colleagues, and simpler motor-based explanations have been offered, so it is taught here as contested.

An adjacent literature deserves its explicit flag: the claim that preverbal infants pass implicit false-belief tests.

A false-belief test asks whether a child understands that another person can hold a belief that is wrong, such as thinking a toy is in a box after it has secretly been moved.

Children reliably pass verbal versions at around four years of age, but Kristine Onishi and Renee Baillargeon reported in 2005 that fifteen-month-olds' looking times tracked an actor's false belief, and Victoria Southgate, Atsushi Senju, and Gergely Csibra reported in 2007 that two-year-olds' anticipatory eye movements did the same.

These findings launched a decade of theorising about innate mindreading, and then the replication attempts arrived.

The anticipatory-looking paradigms have failed repeatedly in direct replications, including large efforts by Louisa Kulke and Hannes Rakoczy from 2018 onward, and violation-of-expectation versions have produced a mixed ledger, with independent laboratories such as those of Diane Poulin-Dubois, Ulf Liszkowski, and Rebecca Saxe reporting failures or partial results alongside the original group's successes.

A tally published in a 2019 meta-analytic review counted roughly ten positive, four negative, and two ambiguous violation-of-expectation reports, which is not the profile of a secure phenomenon.

Baillargeon and colleagues replied in 2018 that many failures altered procedures in consequential ways, and critics replied to the reply that a robust effect should not be so fragile.

This book's verdict, stated plainly: infant implicit false-belief understanding is in a genuine replication crisis, the field does not currently know whether infants represent beliefs, and any confident claim in either direction outruns the evidence.


37.2.2 The helper-hinderer evaluations and their mixed replications

In 2007, Kiley Hamlin, Karen Wynn, and Paul Bloom published a study in the journal Nature that became one of the most celebrated findings in developmental psychology.

Infants of six and ten months watched a puppet show in which a character struggling up a hill was either pushed up by a helper shape or pushed down by a hinderer shape.

Offered the two shapes afterward, the great majority of infants reached for the helper, which the authors interpreted as evidence for a preverbal, perhaps innate, capacity for social evaluation - a first draft of moral sense.

The finding inspired a large literature on infant sociomoral evaluation, including preferences for fair distributors and punishers of wrongdoers.

Replication has been genuinely mixed, and this must be taught as such.

Some independent laboratories reproduced helper preferences, and a 2011 critique by Damian Scarf and colleagues arguing the effect was an artefact of a bouncing collision event was answered experimentally by Hamlin's group.

But a 2020 direct replication attempt with fifteen-month-olds by Megan Salvadori and colleagues, published in Royal Society Open Science, found no helper preference.

The decisive test was ManyBabies4, a coordinated replication in which thirty-seven laboratories on five continents tested over one thousand infants aged five and a half to ten and a half months using a shared, preregistered protocol developed with input from the original authors.

Its result, published by Kelsey Lucca and colleagues in the journal Developmental Science in 2025, was null: about 49 percent of infants chose the helper, which is chance.

Interpretation remains contested even now.

Hamlin and colleagues note that the video-based, standardised procedure differed from the original live puppet shows, and a 2025 commentary in the journal Open Mind argues for contextualising rather than simply discarding the earlier evidence.

Sceptics answer that an effect which survives only under unstandardised conditions in its home laboratory is exactly what a false positive looks like.

The fair current summary is that infant helper preference is unproven at scale, the original strong claim of an early moral sense should not be asserted as fact, and the question of what infants take from these displays is open.


37.3 The spatial circuit's calendar, from the rodent

This section leaves looking times behind and enters the skull, because for spatial cognition we possess something rare in developmental psychology: recordings from the very neurons that do the work, taken while the system is still growing.

The recordings come from rat pups, whose spatial brain is organised like ours in its essentials, and they reveal that the sense of place is assembled in a strict order.


37.3.1 Head direction cells first, place cells next, grid cells last

Three famous cell types make up the rodent positioning system, the discovery of which earned John O'Keefe, May-Britt Moser, and Edvard Moser the 2014 Nobel Prize.

Place cells, found by O'Keefe in 1971 in the hippocampus - a curved structure deep in the temporal lobe that serves memory and navigation - fire when the animal occupies one particular location.

Head direction cells, described by James Ranck and Jeffrey Taube in the 1980s, fire whenever the animal's head points a particular way, like an internal compass.

Grid cells, discovered by the Mosers' laboratory in 2005 in the entorhinal cortex - the gateway region feeding the hippocampus - fire at multiple locations arranged in a strikingly regular hexagonal lattice, providing a metric for space.

In 2010 the journal Science published two back-to-back studies of how these cells come online: one by Tom Wills, Francesca Cacucci, Neil Burgess, and John O'Keefe in London, and one by Rosamund Langston, Edvard Moser, May-Britt Moser, and colleagues in Trondheim.

Both groups recorded from rat pups from postnatal day 16, the age at which pups first leave the nest and explore, and both found the same sequence.

Head direction cells are essentially adult-like from the first recordings at postnatal day 16, present in adult proportions with strong directional tuning.

Place cells exist in rudimentary form at the same age but are fewer, less stable, and less precise, improving gradually over the following weeks.

Grid cells come last: clean hexagonal firing is largely absent at first and emerges abruptly at around postnatal day 20 to 21, reaching near-adult prevalence by about postnatal day 22, roughly three to four weeks of age.

The order is theoretically loaded, because grid cells had been proposed as the source of place cell firing, yet place cells work, roughly, before grid cells do - so the compass and a rough place sense precede the metric map, not the reverse.

Later work from the Cacucci and Wills laboratory in 2014 showed that border cells, which fire along the walls of an environment, are present by around postnatal day 17, and a 2023 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that grid firing develops even in animals raised without normal geometric experience, underlining a strong maturational component.

The whole sequence unfolds mostly after eye opening but before puberty, making it a model case of a brain system whose parts mature on staggered internal timetables.


37.3.2 The human counterpart: allocentric navigation across childhood

The human parallel is measured with behaviour and imaging rather than electrodes.

Two frames of reference matter here.

Egocentric coding locates things relative to your own body, as in "the toy is to my left".

Allocentric coding locates things relative to the world itself, as in "the toy is by the window, whichever way I am facing", and it is allocentric coding that depends on the hippocampal system described above.

Human infants show mostly egocentric responding in the first year, and simple allocentric abilities - using a landmark that stays put while you move - appear in rudimentary form toward the end of the second year.

Virtual-environment and real-space studies, such as those of Almut Hupbach, Lynn Nadel, and later Joshua Newcombe-tradition researchers, find that flexible viewpoint-independent place learning strengthens markedly between about three and a half and seven years of age.

Full adult-like allocentric competence, including combining distant landmarks into a survey-style map and switching smoothly between strategies, continues improving through roughly ten to twelve years of age, with some studies finding refinement into adolescence.
