This slow arc matches the anatomy, because the human hippocampus shows protracted development of its subregions across childhood, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the technique that maps brain activity through blood flow, shows grid-like signals in entorhinal cortex that have been detected in adults and are only beginning to be studied developmentally.

The slow maturation also connects to infantile amnesia, the near-universal inability of adults to recall episodes from the first years of life, which many researchers attribute in part to the late assembly of this same hippocampal machinery.

The rodent order - compass early, places next, metric grid last, all refined by experience - appears to be conserved in outline in the human child, though the human timetable is stretched across years rather than days.

Precise human ages for each component remain less settled than the rodent data, and where studies disagree this book reports the range rather than a false single number.


37.4 The replication lesson

This section steps back from any single finding to the methodological storm that has reshaped infant research over the past decade.

Psychology's broader replication crisis - the discovery, dramatised by the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 report that only around 36 to 39 percent of sampled findings replicated - hit infant studies with special force, because infant studies are expensive, samples are small, and the measures are indirect.


37.4.1 The ManyBabies consortium and measurement humility

The constructive response has been big-team science.

The ManyBabies consortium, founded around 2015 with Michael Frank of Stanford University among its central organisers, pools dozens of laboratories worldwide to run the same preregistered infant experiment at a scale no single laboratory can reach.

Preregistration means publicly committing to the hypothesis, method, and analysis before collecting data, which prevents quietly adjusting the analysis until something looks significant.

The first project, ManyBabies1, published in 2020, tested infants' preference for infant-directed speech - the melodic speech style adults use with babies - across 67 laboratories and more than 2,300 infants.

The preference replicated, but the effect was meaningfully smaller than the original literature implied and varied with age, language background, and method, a lesson in how published literatures overstate effects.

ManyBabies2 has been probing the implicit false-belief paradigms described in section 37.2.1, and its early reports reinforce the doubt already described there.

ManyBabies4, described in section 37.2.2, returned a null result for the helper-hinderer effect across 37 laboratories.

The running scorecard is therefore mixed by design: some pillars stand at reduced height, and some fall.

Alongside replication, the consortium and critics such as Martin Zettersten and colleagues have documented that looking time itself is a noisy instrument, with test-retest reliability for many infant measures far below what would be accepted in adult psychometrics.

The lesson this book draws is called measurement humility.

It means that a single clever study with sixteen infants per condition can suggest but cannot establish, that effect sizes from small first reports should be treated as upper bounds, and that theory built on unreplicated looking-time findings is scaffolding, not stone.

It does not mean nihilism, because the large collaborative studies show that real infant phenomena - speech preferences, habituation itself, violation-of-expectation responses to solidity - do replicate when tested properly.

The core knowledge programme survives this reckoning in its modest form, as a claim about early domain-tuned expectations, while its most spectacular extensions, infant mindreading and infant morality, remain open cases under active retrial.

PART TEN. THE SOCIAL AND EMOTIONAL MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 38. ATTACHMENT AND THE NEUROBIOLOGY OF CAREGIVING (CORE)

This chapter is about the first relationship: the bond between an infant and the people who care for it.

Attachment theory began as a claim about behaviour and feeling, and over seventy years it has acquired a biology - hormones, circuits, and physiological rhythms that run beneath the visible tenderness.

The chapter presents the classic theory and its measuring instruments, then the caregiving brain of the mother and the father, and finally the infant's side of the loop, where a parent's presence acts directly on the child's fear and stress systems.

It matters because this early bond is the environment in which every system described elsewhere in this book does its growing.


38.1 The theory and its instruments

This section introduces attachment theory itself and the tools that turned a warm intuition into a measurable science.

It also reaches back to the animal experiments that overturned the older view that infants love whoever feeds them.


38.1.1 Bowlby's internal working models and the Strange Situation classifications

John Bowlby, a British psychiatrist working from the 1950s onward, proposed that human infants possess an evolved attachment system whose function is to keep a vulnerable child close to a protective adult.

Drawing on ethology, the study of animal behaviour in natural settings, Bowlby argued in his trilogy Attachment and Loss, published between 1969 and 1980, that the infant builds internal working models - mental summaries of how available and responsive caregivers are - and that these models become templates carried forward into later relationships.

Bowlby's collaborator Mary Ainsworth gave the theory its instrument.

After observational studies in Uganda and Baltimore, Ainsworth and colleagues published the Strange Situation procedure in 1978.

It is a roughly twenty-minute laboratory sequence for infants of about twelve to eighteen months, involving two brief separations from the caregiver and two reunions, sometimes in the company of a friendly stranger.

The infant's behaviour at reunion, more than its distress at separation, determines the classification.

Secure infants, about 60 to 65 percent in typical low-risk samples, seek contact at reunion and settle quickly.

Insecure-avoidant infants, roughly 15 to 20 percent, ignore or turn away from the returning caregiver despite physiological signs of stress.

Insecure-resistant or ambivalent infants, roughly 10 to 15 percent, cling and protest but fail to be soothed.

A fourth category, disorganised attachment, was added by Mary Main and Judith Solomon in 1990 for infants showing contradictory or frozen behaviour, and it is the classification most strongly associated with frightening caregiving and with later mental health risk.

Longitudinal studies such as the Minnesota Longitudinal Study of Risk and Adaptation, led by Alan Sroufe and Byron Egeland, find that early security predicts later social competence modestly but reliably, while also showing that attachment classifications can change when life circumstances change.

Two honest cautions belong here: the classifications describe a relationship, not a fixed property of the child, and their distribution varies across cultures in ways still being interpreted, so the categories are a scientific instrument rather than a verdict on any family.


38.1.2 Contact comfort and the hidden regulators

In the 1950s the dominant view, shared by behaviourists and psychoanalysts alike, was that infants attach to their mothers because mothers provide food.

Harry Harlow's experiments at the University of Wisconsin, reported from 1958, tested that claim directly in infant rhesus monkeys.

Given a choice between a bare wire surrogate mother that dispensed milk and a soft cloth surrogate that gave no food, the infant monkeys spent the great majority of their time clinging to the cloth mother, visiting the wire mother only to feed.

When frightened, they ran to the cloth mother, and with her present they explored a strange room instead of freezing.

Harlow named the crucial ingredient contact comfort, and the cupboard-love theory of attachment did not survive the demonstration.

It should be said plainly that Harlow's later isolation experiments inflicted severe suffering on his animals, and they are part of why modern animal research operates under far stricter ethical review.

The second half of this sub-section belongs to Myron Hofer, who asked what, physiologically, a mother actually is to an infant.

In rat studies through the 1970s and 1980s, Hofer separated pups from their mothers and found that the pup's physiology did not fall apart all at once but system by system, each tied to a specific feature of the mother that had been regulating it.

Her warmth regulated the pup's activity level, her milk regulated heart rate, her touch and licking regulated growth hormone release, and her rhythms entrained the pup's sleep.

Hofer called these hidden regulators: the relationship is not one bond but a bundle of sensory channels, each quietly tuning an infant physiological system.

The concept reframed separation and loss, because what looks like grief is partly the simultaneous withdrawal of many regulators at once.

It also built the bridge this chapter walks across, from attachment as felt experience to attachment as biology, and it anticipated the human findings on maternal buffering described in section 38.3.2.


38.2 The caregiving brain

This section turns the microscope around and looks at the parent.

Caring for an infant is a demanding, learned, motivated behaviour, and the brain reorganises to support it - hormonally, structurally, and functionally - in mothers and in fathers.


38.2.1 Oxytocin, the maternal circuit, and the pregnancy grey-matter changes

Oxytocin is a small peptide hormone made in the hypothalamus, the brain's deep regulatory hub, and released both into the bloodstream and within the brain itself.

It triggers labour contractions and milk letdown, and within the brain it modulates social approach, recognition, and the motivation to nurture.

The animal groundwork runs from Terkel and Rosenblatt's 1972 blood-transfer experiments, in which plasma from a new mother rat hastened maternal behaviour in a virgin, to Cort Pedersen and Arthur Prange's 1979 demonstration that oxytocin delivered into the brain could induce maternal behaviour directly.

Michael Numan's decades of work mapped the core maternal circuit: the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, primed by the hormone pattern of late pregnancy, acts through the brain's dopamine reward pathway to make pup care actively rewarding rather than merely tolerated.

In 2014, Robert Froemke's laboratory showed that oxytocin acting in the left auditory cortex of mother mice sharpens the neural response to pup distress calls, a mechanistic picture of a hormone teaching a sensory system to care.

In humans, Ruth Feldman and colleagues have shown that maternal blood oxytocin rises across pregnancy and that its levels track affectionate contact after birth.

The structural headline is the 2017 study by Elseline Hoekzema and colleagues in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

Scanning women before and after a first pregnancy, they found consistent reductions in grey matter volume - the tissue rich in neuron cell bodies - concentrated in the network used for social understanding.

The pattern was so consistent that a computer algorithm could classify every woman correctly as having been pregnant or not from her scan alone.

Reduction sounds like damage, but the authors' interpretation, by analogy with adolescent synaptic pruning, is refinement: the affected regions overlapped with the areas that responded most strongly to the woman's own baby, and the magnitude of change predicted maternal attachment measures after birth.

Follow-up work found the changes still present two years later, and a 2025 dense-scanning study by Emily Jacobs' group charted the trajectory across an entire pregnancy in fine detail.

These are small samples in a young literature, and long-term functional consequences are still being worked out, so the findings are presented as a robust structural observation with an interpretation that remains under study.


38.2.2 The paternal brain and biobehavioural synchrony

Fathers do not undergo pregnancy, yet the caring father's brain and hormones change too.

Studies by Anne Storey and Katherine Wynne-Edwards from 2000 found that expectant and new fathers show raised prolactin and lowered testosterone, and Lee Gettler's 2011 longitudinal study in the Philippines showed that becoming an involved father lowers a man's testosterone over years, with the most hands-on fathers showing the largest declines.

Ruth Feldman's group has shown that fathers' oxytocin levels rise with infant contact and are comparable to mothers', but are released most strongly by different interactions: mothers' oxytocin tracks affectionate cuddling, fathers' tracks stimulating, playful contact.

A 2014 functional imaging study by Eyal Abraham, Feldman, and colleagues compared mothers, secondary-caregiving fathers, and primary-caregiving fathers raising infants without a female partner.

Mothers showed strongest activation in amygdala-centred emotional vigilance circuitry, secondary fathers in cortical social-understanding circuitry, and primary-caregiving fathers showed both, with amygdala activation scaling with the amount of direct care they performed.

The conclusion is that the parental brain is experience-dependent: committed caregiving itself, not sex or childbirth, recruits the full circuitry.

Biobehavioural synchrony is Feldman's name for the second great finding of this literature: parent and infant continuously align their behaviour and their physiology during interaction.

Gaze, vocal rhythms, touch, heart rhythms, oxytocin release, and even brain activity measured simultaneously in both partners - a method called hyperscanning - rise and fall together in well-attuned pairs.

Feldman's longitudinal work suggests that this micro-level coordination in infancy predicts children's later emotion regulation and empathy, making synchrony a plausible mechanism by which sensitive caregiving gets into the developing brain.

Effect sizes in synchrony research are modest and the field is young, but the central observation - that the attachment bond is a two-body physiological system, not two separate individuals signalling - is now supported across many laboratories.


38.3 The infant's side

This section completes the loop by asking what the caregiver does inside the infant's brain.

The answers come first from precise rodent experiments and then from human imaging, and they converge on a striking claim: for a young child, the caregiver is a piece of neural equipment, an external regulator of circuits the child cannot yet run alone.


38.3.1 Attachment learning and the amygdala switch under maternal presence

Regina Sullivan's laboratory has spent three decades studying how rat pups learn attachment, using odour learning as the window.

A rat pup must learn its mother's smell to nurse and survive, and nature stacks the deck: during roughly the first nine postnatal days, pups learn powerful odour preferences and are strikingly bad at learning odour aversions.

The signature experiment pairs an odour with a mild electric shock.

In an older animal this produces avoidance of the odour, but in a pup younger than about postnatal day 10 it paradoxically produces attraction - the pup approaches the odour that predicted pain.

The mechanism runs through the amygdala, the almond-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe that handles fear learning, and through corticosterone, the rat's main stress hormone, equivalent to human cortisol.

During the early sensitive period the pup's stress system is quiet and the amygdala does not engage during the odour-shock pairing, so the aversion circuit simply is not written to.

Giving corticosterone artificially switches the amygdala on and produces precocious fear learning, and blocking it extends the attachment-learning period.

The evolutionary logic is stark: a pup has no option but its caregiver, so the young brain is built to attach to whatever is present, even when care is painful - a mechanism with sobering relevance for understanding why abused children remain attached to abusive caregivers.

The switch is not just about age but about the mother herself.

Sullivan's group, in work with Gordon Barr published in 2009, showed that in pups aged about ten to fifteen days, the same odour-shock pairing produces fear if the pup is alone but preference if the mother is present, because her presence suppresses the pup's corticosterone release and thereby holds the amygdala offline.

The mother's body is thus literally a switch on the infant's fear circuitry, deciding which of two memory systems an experience is written into.


38.3.2 Maternal buffering of the stress response

Social buffering means the power of a trusted companion's presence to damp the stress response, and in development the caregiver is the buffer of first resort.

Megan Gunnar's laboratory at the University of Minnesota showed from the late 1980s that human infants receiving inoculations or facing strangers mount much smaller cortisol responses when a responsive caregiver is present, even when they cry just as much - the behaviour and the hormone dissociate, and the hormone is what the parent controls.

Gunnar and colleagues further showed that the buffering works best within secure attachment relationships, and a 2015 study by Camelia Hostinar and Gunnar found that for children around nine to ten years old a parent's mere availability by phone buffered stress, while for adolescents parental buffering of cortisol weakens, handing the job progressively to friends and to the adolescent's own maturing regulation.

The neural counterpart in humans comes from Nim Tottenham's laboratory.

A 2014 study by Dylan Gee, Tottenham, and colleagues found that in children roughly four to ten years old, viewing a photograph of their mother changed amygdala-prefrontal circuit function toward a more mature, regulated pattern and improved behavioural regulation, an effect absent in adolescents.

The same research programme showed that children with histories of institutional care - who lacked a stable buffering adult in infancy - show earlier-maturing but less flexible amygdala-prefrontal connectivity, a theme chapter 40 develops as the stress acceleration hypothesis.

The synthesis of this chapter is a single idea with rodent and human legs: early in life the stress and fear systems are designed to be co-regulated by a caregiver, the caregiver's presence is a biological signal that gates what the infant brain learns and how loudly its alarm rings, and the gradual handover of that regulation from parent to child is one of the central plot lines of emotional development.

Where the human evidence is correlational this book says so, and the causal anchors of the story remain the controlled animal experiments and the randomised human studies described in the next chapter.


CHAPTER 39. DEPRIVATION: THE NATURAL EXPERIMENTS (CORE)

This chapter concerns children who began life with almost none of what the previous chapter described.

In the late twentieth century, the policies of Nicolae Ceausescu's Romania filled state institutions with well over one hundred thousand infants and children, many of whom received food and shelter but almost no individual attention, conversation, or consistent caregiver.

Their tragedy became, through adoption and through one carefully designed trial, the most important body of evidence science possesses about what caregiving deprivation does to human development and about how much recovery is possible.

This chapter is written with the respect its subjects are owed: these are findings about harm done to real children, and the point of studying them is to prevent repetition and to guide care.


39.1 The Bucharest Early Intervention Project

This section describes the study that changed both science and policy: the first and only randomised controlled trial of foster care as an alternative to institutional care.

A randomised controlled trial assigns participants to conditions by chance, which is what allows a causal conclusion rather than a mere association.


39.1.1 The randomised design and the foster-care effect

The Bucharest Early Intervention Project (BEIP) was launched in 2000 by Charles Nelson, Nathan Fox, and Charles Zeanah, working with Romanian authorities.

The study enrolled 136 institutionalised children, averaging about 22 months of age, and randomly assigned half to remain in institutional care as usual and half to a high-quality foster care programme the project itself created, since Romania then had essentially no foster system.

A comparison group of children who had never been institutionalised was followed alongside.

The randomisation was ethically debated from the start, and the investigators' defence is carefully documented: foster care was not otherwise available, no child was ever moved from a family into an institution, and the researchers adopted a policy of never interfering with court decisions that moved children out of institutions.

The results, reported in the journal Science in 2007 by Nelson and colleagues and in many papers since, established the foster-care effect.

Children randomised to foster care showed higher intelligence quotient (IQ) scores - on the order of eight to ten points at 42 and 54 months - better language, better physical growth, more typical emotional expressiveness, and far higher rates of secure attachment than children who remained in institutional care.

Rates of anxiety and depression symptoms were roughly halved in the foster care group by 54 months, though the externalising problems of impulsivity and inattention proved more stubborn and showed little group difference.

Follow-up assessments at ages 8, 12, and 16 to 18 years found that the benefits of early foster placement were, in the investigators' word, remarkably stable across development.

The finding gave numbers to something long suspected: institutional rearing itself, independent of poverty or malnutrition, measurably harms cognitive and emotional development, and family placement causally improves it.


39.1.2 The sensitive-period finding: placement before roughly twenty-four months

The project's second headline is about timing.

Because children entered foster care at different ages, the investigators could ask whether earlier placement produced better outcomes, and for several core measures the answer was yes, with a threshold that recurred near the second birthday.

Children placed before roughly 24 months of age showed substantially greater gains in IQ than children placed later, and for attachment security and brain electrical activity the same boundary appeared.

By 42 months, children placed before about 24 months were far more likely to form secure attachments, approaching community rates, while later-placed children lagged.

This is the clearest human evidence for a sensitive period - a developmental window during which experience has outsized influence - in the domain of caregiving itself.

Two honest qualifications are required.

First, the 24-month figure is approximate and measure-specific: some outcomes showed thresholds nearer 15 or 20 months, others showed graded rather than sharp timing effects, and some, like growth, improved after placement at any age.

Second, a sensitive period is not a cliff edge, and later-placed children still benefited on many measures, so the finding argues for urgency in placement policy, never for hopelessness about older children.

With those cautions, the conclusion stands as one of developmental science's most consequential: the expected environment of the first two years includes a committed individual caregiver, and the brain builds differently without one.


39.1.3 The electroencephalographic normalisation and the long follow-ups

Electroencephalography (EEG) records the brain's electrical rhythms through sensors resting on the scalp, and it gave the project its most direct window on the developing brain.

At baseline, before randomisation, institutionalised infants showed a distinctive EEG signature: reduced high-frequency alpha and beta power and relatively increased slow theta activity, a pattern often read as cortical under-development, as if the brain's activity were dimmed.

The early follow-ups showed only limited EEG recovery in the foster care group, which was initially discouraging.

The long game told a different story.

At age eight, and decisively in the twelve-year follow-up published by Ross Vanderwert, Fox, Nelson, and colleagues in 2016, children who had been placed into foster care before approximately 24 months showed EEG alpha power indistinguishable from never-institutionalised community children, while children placed later and children who remained longest in institutional care continued to differ.

Brain electrical normalisation was therefore real but slow, taking years of family life to appear, and it obeyed the same sensitive-period boundary as behaviour.

Structural imaging in the project and in related samples found that institutional history was associated with reduced cortical grey and white matter volumes, with foster placement partially remediating white matter differences.

The follow-ups at sixteen to eighteen years, reported by Kathryn Humphreys, Zeanah, and colleagues, found the foster care group still showing lower psychopathology and better adjustment, with effect sizes largely stable, and the project has continued assessment into young adulthood.

The arc of the EEG story carries the chapter's central lesson in miniature: deprivation leaves a measurable mark, recovery is possible, recovery favours the early-placed, and recovery takes time on the scale of childhood itself.


39.2 The English and Romanian Adoptees study

This section describes the second great natural experiment, which followed Romanian children not into local foster care but into adoptive families in the United Kingdom, and followed them all the way into adult life.


39.2.1 Deprivation-specific patterns and quasi-autism

The English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) study, led by the psychiatrist Michael Rutter and later by Edmund Sonuga-Barke, followed 165 children adopted from Romanian institutions into English families in the early 1990s, compared with 52 children adopted within England before six months of age.

Because the Romanian children were adopted at different ages after institutional durations from a few weeks up to 43 months, duration of deprivation could be studied while the post-adoption environment - almost uniformly loving, well-resourced homes - was held favourable.

Catch-up was dramatic and fast in some domains: severely delayed, often malnourished infants showed rapid physical and cognitive gains after adoption, a testament to resilience.

But Rutter's team identified a cluster of problems that did not fit ordinary diagnostic categories and appeared specifically after institutional deprivation, which they called deprivation-specific patterns.

The cluster has four members: quasi-autism, disinhibited social engagement, inattention and overactivity, and cognitive impairment.

Quasi-autism, described by Rutter and colleagues in a 1999 paper, names autistic-like difficulties in social communication and circumscribed interests arising after deprivation, which differed from typical autism in showing more social approach and in improving, sometimes markedly, over childhood - hence quasi.

Disinhibited social engagement is an unusual friendliness toward strangers, wandering off with unfamiliar adults without checking back, and it proved the most persistent and the most specifically tied to institutional rearing.

The critical dose-response finding was a duration threshold: children who left the institutions before about six months of age were, as a group, largely indistinguishable from the within-England adoptees, while those institutionalised beyond six months carried substantially elevated rates of all four patterns.

The six-month boundary in ERA and the 24-month boundary in the Bucharest project differ partly because they index different things - onset of measurable lasting impairment after extreme global deprivation versus benefit of removal from ongoing but somewhat less severe deprivation - and this book resists collapsing them into one number.

Together they bracket the same truth: the timing of deprivation, not only its occurrence, writes the outcome.


39.2.2 The adult outcomes

The study's young-adult follow-up, published by Sonuga-Barke, Rutter, and colleagues in The Lancet in 2017, assessed the adoptees at ages 22 to 25.

The headline was persistence: adoptees who had endured more than six months of institutional deprivation showed elevated rates of autism-spectrum-type symptoms, disinhibited social engagement, and inattention and overactivity that had remained essentially stable from childhood into adult life, despite more than two decades in supportive families.

These difficulties were accompanied by higher rates of unemployment, lower educational attainment, and greater use of mental health services, and rates of emotional problems such as anxiety and depression rose in early adulthood in the high-deprivation group.

The under-six-months group, by contrast, continued to look much like the comparison adoptees, reinforcing the duration threshold.

One cognitive surprise softened the picture: the IQ deficit associated with long deprivation, clearly present in childhood, had substantially remitted by adulthood, showing that even a two-decade-old impairment can close.

The investigators' summary was measured and is worth preserving: early severe deprivation lasting longer than six months can have profound and lasting psychological consequences, and yet development remains open-ended enough that some deficits remit even in adulthood.

Interpretive cautions apply: the sample is one cohort from one historical catastrophe, deprivation there was unusually global - social, sensory, nutritional, and medical at once - and outcomes varied widely between individuals, with a substantial minority of long-deprived adoptees showing no measurable problems at all.

That heterogeneity, still incompletely explained, is one of the field's standing questions, touching genetics, prenatal history, and the details of each child's institutional experience.


39.3 The neural sequelae and the interventions

This section gathers what imaging has revealed about the brains of previously institutionalised children generally, and then turns to the practical question: what interventions help, and can help be measured in the brain?


39.3.1 Amygdala, prefrontal connectivity, and reward blunting after institutional care

Across studies of internationally adopted, previously institutionalised children - much of it from Nim Tottenham's, Seth Pollak's, and the Bucharest teams - a reasonably consistent neural profile has emerged.

Structurally, institutional history is associated with reduced total cortical volume, and several studies, including Tottenham's 2010 report, found relatively enlarged amygdala volume, particularly with later adoption, though amygdala findings vary across samples and ages and are stated here as a tendency rather than a law.

Functionally, previously institutionalised children show heightened amygdala reactivity to emotional faces, consistent with a vigilance system tuned up by an unpredictable early world.

The connectivity finding is the most theoretically pointed: Dylan Gee, Tottenham, and colleagues reported in 2013 that previously institutionalised children showed the mature, negatively coupled pattern of amygdala to medial prefrontal cortex connectivity years earlier than comparison children, as if deprivation had accelerated the circuit's timetable - evidence feeding the stress-acceleration hypothesis treated in chapter 40.

The reward system shows the opposite of vigilance: blunting.

Work by Michael Goff and Tottenham and related studies found reduced ventral striatum response to rewards in adolescents with early institutional care, the ventral striatum being the deep structure at the heart of the brain's reward circuitry, and this blunting statistically linked to depressive symptoms.

A parallel literature connects early deprivation to flattened cortisol rhythms, with Gunnar's work showing daytime cortisol profiles in post-institutionalised children that are lower and flatter than typical.

The composite picture is coherent: an alarm system tuned high, a reward system tuned low, a regulatory circuit matured early but with less headroom, and a stress axis recalibrated - a brain adapted to scarcity of care, carrying that adaptation into environments where it no longer fits.

Every element of this picture is group-average and probabilistic, with wide individual variation, and none of it licenses reading any individual child's scan as destiny.


39.3.2 The attachment-based interventions with neural endpoints

The intervention story begins with the Bucharest project itself, whose foster care programme is the proof of principle that a caregiving intervention changes brain-level outcomes, as the EEG normalisation of section 39.1.3 showed.

The best-developed targeted programme is Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC), created by Mary Dozier at the University of Delaware.

ABC is a ten-session, in-home coaching programme for caregivers of infants and toddlers at risk for neglect or in foster care, teaching three things: respond with nurturance when the child is distressed, follow the child's lead in play, and eliminate frightening behaviour.

Randomised trials of ABC - unusually for early interventions, run against an active control programme - found higher rates of secure and organised attachment, and its biological endpoints are the reason it appears in this chapter.

Children whose caregivers received ABC showed more normative diurnal cortisol rhythms, meaning the healthy morning-high evening-low pattern, an effect first shown after intervention and then found still present years later in middle childhood, with a 2020 report showing parental sensitivity mediated the effect.

EEG studies of ABC and related trials report shifts toward more mature cortical activity patterns, and effects have been reported on executive function, language, and even deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation, the chemical tagging of genes that can register experience, though the methylation findings are early and need replication.

A sibling programme, the Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up ideas translated for institutional settings, and video-feedback interventions in the Leiden tradition of Femmie Juffer and Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg, show related benefits.

The policy conclusion drawn by the Bucharest investigators has been consequential: no measurable amount of institutional care improves on family care, early placement matters, and several countries have cited this evidence in moving away from infant institutionalisation.

The scientific conclusion is equally plain: caregiving is a biological intervention, and its effects can be read in hormones and brain rhythms as well as in behaviour.


CHAPTER 40. STRESS, ADVERSITY, AND THE DEVELOPING BRAIN (CORE)

This chapter generalises from the extreme case of institutional deprivation to the broader science of how hardship shapes a growing brain.

It first introduces the body's stress machinery and how childhood calibrates it, then examines what is known about the neurobiology of child maltreatment, then presents the modern theoretical frameworks that organise this difficult evidence, and finally turns to poverty, the most common adversity of all, and to the experiment that tried to reduce it with cash.

The register of this chapter is deliberately careful: these findings describe group-level statistical tendencies in populations, never verdicts on individual children, and the repeated lesson of the literature is that outcomes are probabilistic, variable, and open to change.


40.1 The stress axis grows up

This section introduces the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the hormonal chain of command at the centre of the stress response, and explains the developmental discovery that this system does not arrive fixed but is calibrated by early experience.


40.1.1 The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal cascade and its childhood calibration

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a three-station relay.

When the brain judges a situation threatening, the hypothalamus - the deep regulatory hub already met in chapter 38 - releases corticotropin-releasing hormone.

That signal tells the pituitary gland, a pea-sized organ hanging beneath the brain, to release adrenocorticotropic hormone into the blood.

That in turn tells the adrenal glands, sitting atop the kidneys, to release cortisol, the body's main stress hormone, which mobilises energy, sharpens some functions, and suppresses others such as digestion and immunity.

Cortisol also feeds back on the brain, especially on the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, which are rich in its receptors and which act as brakes that shut the response down - and because those same regions are still developing across childhood, the developing brain is both the controller of the axis and one of its targets.

The axis also runs a daily rhythm, high within an hour of waking and low at night, and disturbances of this rhythm are among the most sensitive markers of early adversity.

The calibration story begins with rodents: work from Seymour Levine in the 1950s and, decisively, Michael Meaney's group in the 1990s showed that the amount of maternal licking and grooming a rat pup receives sets the sensitivity of its stress axis for life.

Meaney and Moshe Szyf's 2004 study traced the mechanism to epigenetics - chemical modifications that change how strongly genes are read without changing their sequence - showing that maternal care alters methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene in the pup's hippocampus, and cross-fostering experiments proved the effect was transmitted by behaviour, not inheritance.

A human echo was reported by Patrick McGowan and colleagues in 2009, who found increased methylation of the same receptor gene in the hippocampi of suicide victims who had suffered childhood abuse, a finding since extended though still resting on modest samples.

The concept that emerges is calibration: childhood experience does not simply stress or spare the axis, it sets its operating range, tuning how readily it fires and how quickly it recovers, in a way that once looked adaptive for the predicted environment and may misfit the actual one.


40.1.2 Social buffering and the hyporesponsive period

Development inserts a remarkable safety feature into this system.

In the rat, roughly postnatal days 4 through 14 constitute the stress hyporesponsive period, first characterised in the tradition of Sapolsky and Meaney's 1986 review, during which the pup's adrenal glands release very little corticosterone even to challenges that would provoke a strong response earlier or later.

The quieting is actively maintained by the mother: her presence, milk, and touch suppress the pup's axis, and prolonged separation reinstates reactivity, so the hyporesponsive period is less a property of the pup than of the intact mother-pup pair.

The presumed function is protection: the infant brain is undergoing rapid neuron birth, wiring, and synapse formation, and high cortisol interferes with these processes, so evolution damps the hormone precisely when the brain is most under construction.

Humans show a functional parallel rather than an identical mechanism.

Megan Gunnar's work, described in chapter 38, shows that across infancy and early childhood a responsive caregiver powerfully buffers the child's cortisol response, so that a well-attached young child in a stressful situation often shows behavioural distress without a hormonal storm.

Gunnar has argued that early childhood with adequate caregiving amounts to a socially buffered, relatively hyporesponsive period in humans, one that depends on the caregiver rather than the calendar.

The dark corollary organises much of this chapter: adversities that remove or corrupt the buffer - neglect, caregiver mental illness, foster care instability, maltreatment by the caregiver - expose the constructing brain to exactly the hormonal conditions the system evolved to prevent, and children in such circumstances show elevated or dysregulated cortisol where buffered children show none.

Puberty appears to close this era, as adolescent stress responses strengthen and parental buffering of cortisol weakens, handing regulation to a prefrontal system that chapter 39's populations approached with altered wiring.


40.1.3 Allostatic load

Allostasis, a term introduced by Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer in 1988, means stability through change: the body does not defend fixed set points but continuously adjusts its internal settings to meet anticipated demands.

Bruce McEwen and Eliot Stellar introduced allostatic load in 1993 to name the cost of doing this too much or too long: the cumulative wear and tear on body and brain when stress mediators such as cortisol, adrenaline, and inflammatory molecules are switched on repeatedly, fail to shut off, or fail to switch on normally at all.

McEwen distinguished several roads to load, including frequent hits, failed habituation to repeated stressors, prolonged responses that do not terminate, and a flattened, inadequate response that forces other systems to compensate - the last being exactly the profile seen in some severely neglected children.

Allostatic load is measured in research as a composite index across systems: blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, glycated blood proteins, cholesterol, cortisol, adrenaline, and inflammatory markers such as interleukin-6.

Applied to development, the concept explains how childhood adversity becomes adult disease.

The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) study of Vincent Felitti, Robert Anda, and colleagues, published in 1998 with over 17,000 adults, found dose-response relations between the number of categories of childhood adversity and adult heart disease, lung disease, depression, and early death.

Allostatic load supplies the mechanism sketch for such findings: a stress apparatus calibrated to a harsh childhood runs hot or runs flat for decades, and the accumulated physiological cost surfaces as illness far downstream.

The concept has limits that the field acknowledges - the composite indices vary between studies and the causal chain in humans is inferential - but it remains the standard bridge between the developmental findings of this chapter and lifelong health.


40.2 The maltreatment findings

This section reports what neuroimaging has found in people who suffered abuse or neglect in childhood, and then presents the interpretive reframing that has changed how the field speaks about those findings.

The subject is heavy, and the writing here stays factual: these are statistical differences observed in groups of survivors, they do not diagnose or define any person, and many maltreated individuals show no measurable brain differences at all.


40.2.1 The regional and pathway-specific effects and their sensitive exposure periods

The most systematic programme is that of Martin Teicher and colleagues at Harvard's McLean Hospital, synthesised in his 2016 reviews in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry and Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

Across studies, childhood maltreatment is associated on average with reduced volume in the hippocampus - especially in adults, less consistently in children - reduced area of the corpus callosum, the great fibre bridge connecting the two hemispheres, thinner anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex, heightened amygdala response to threatening faces, and reduced striatal response to anticipated reward.

Two refinements distinguish this literature from a simple catalogue of harm.

The first is pathway specificity: the alterations track the type of exposure with an almost anatomical logic.

Teicher's group reported thinning of the somatosensory cortex representing the genitals in women who suffered childhood sexual abuse, altered auditory-language pathways, particularly the arcuate fasciculus, in people exposed to parental verbal abuse, and altered visual pathways, including the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, in those who repeatedly witnessed domestic violence - as if the developing brain turned down the gain on the specific sensory channels through which the harm arrived.

The second refinement is timing: sensitive exposure periods, meaning ages at which a given region is maximally vulnerable to a given exposure.

Using machine-learning analyses of retrospective exposure histories, Teicher's group reported that hippocampal measures were most affected by maltreatment experienced at around ages 3 to 5 and again in early adolescence, the corpus callosum at around ages 9 to 10, and frontal cortex at around ages 14 to 16, matching each region's own growth spurt.

These timing estimates depend on adults' retrospective reports and on analytic choices, they have only partial independent replication, and this book therefore presents them as a promising, mechanistically sensible pattern rather than established constants.

What is firmly established is the general principle they illustrate: when adversity strikes matters as much as whether it strikes, because vulnerability follows the region-by-region construction schedule of the brain itself.


40.2.2 Adaptation against damage: the ecophenotype reading

The interpretive shift of the past decade has been from a damage vocabulary to an adaptation vocabulary.

On the damage reading, the differences catalogued above are injuries - toxic stress eroding tissue.

On the adaptation reading, championed by Teicher, by Bruce Ellis's evolutionary-developmental school, and by McLaughlin's group in a different register, many of the same differences are experience-driven recalibrations: an amygdala tuned high is a threat detector adjusted for a dangerous home, a blunted reward system spares disappointment where rewards are unreliable, and accelerated maturation trades later flexibility for earlier self-sufficiency.

These adjustments may have been protective in the environment that produced them and become costly when they persist into safer environments - a mismatch account of why survivors carry elevated psychiatric risk.

Teicher and Jacqueline Samson's 2013 ecophenotype proposal sharpens this into a clinical claim: individuals with a given diagnosis, such as depression, who were maltreated in childhood differ systematically from individuals with the same diagnosis who were not - in earlier onset, more severe course, poorer treatment response, and distinct neurobiology.

On this view, maltreatment-associated psychiatric conditions are ecophenotypes, meaning variants shaped by the ecology of a harsh childhood, and lumping them with non-maltreated cases blurs both research and treatment.

Supporting evidence includes consistently different treatment-response rates and distinct neuroimaging profiles in maltreated versus non-maltreated patients within the same diagnostic category, and the proposal has influenced arguments for recording maltreatment history in diagnosis.

The adaptation frame must not be allowed to soften the moral facts, and this book states them: maltreatment is harm, adaptation to it is costly, and nothing in this vocabulary implies that children are resilient enough for maltreatment to be tolerable.

What the frame changes is science and respect: survivors' brains are understood as having responded lawfully to the world they were given, not as broken, and interventions can aim at recalibration rather than repair of an imagined lesion.


40.3 The models of adversity

This section presents the two organising frameworks that modern developmental science uses in place of a single undifferentiated concept of stress: the dimensional model of threat and deprivation, and the stress-acceleration account of developmental timing.


40.3.1 Threat against deprivation as distinct dimensions

For decades, adversity research counted events: the cumulative-risk approach summed abuse, neglect, poverty, and loss into one score, as the Adverse Childhood Experiences index does.

In 2014, Katie McLaughlin and Margaret Sheridan proposed the dimensional model of adversity and psychopathology, arguing that adversities differ in kind, not just in amount, and that at least two dimensions have distinct neurodevelopmental consequences.

Threat means experiences of harm or threatened harm - physical or sexual abuse, witnessing violence, frightening environments.

Deprivation means the absence of expected inputs - neglect, institutional rearing, and impoverished cognitive and social stimulation.

The model predicts that threat acts primarily on the fear-learning circuitry of amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex, producing heightened threat detection and difficulty with fear extinction and emotion regulation, while deprivation acts primarily on association cortex through the use-it-or-lose-it economics of synaptic pruning, producing reduced cortical thickness and surface area in frontoparietal networks and lower performance on complex cognition.

Evidence has accumulated on both sides of the prediction: a 2019 systematic review of over one hundred imaging studies by McLaughlin and colleagues found threat-exposed children disproportionately showing amygdala and medial prefrontal alterations, and deprivation-exposed children disproportionately showing frontoparietal structural differences, with the Bucharest and adoption samples of chapter 39 providing the cleanest deprivation cases.

The model has critics and refinements, which belong in the record.

Real childhoods rarely sort cleanly, since abuse and neglect co-occur in a majority of maltreatment cases, and some empirical tests find the predicted dissociations only partially.

A rival dimensional scheme from evolutionary developmental psychology, associated with Ellis and colleagues, carves adversity into harshness and unpredictability, emphasising the timing structure of stressors, and integrative papers from 2021 onward, including a joint statement by McLaughlin, Sheridan, Ellis, and Belsky, treat the schemes as complementary lenses rather than rivals.

The consensus that survives the argument is the model's core negative claim: a single stress dial is the wrong picture, because different adversities enter the brain through different doors.


40.3.2 The stress-acceleration hypothesis and accelerated biological aging

The stress-acceleration hypothesis, articulated by Bridget Callaghan and Nim Tottenham in 2016, concerns tempo rather than target.

It proposes that early adversity speeds the maturation of emotional circuitry, particularly the connection between the amygdala and the medial prefrontal cortex, so that children who cannot rely on a caregiver's external regulation develop internal regulation early - an adaptive shortcut with a price, since circuits that mature early may close their windows of plasticity early and reach a less flexible endpoint.

The anchor findings include Gee and Tottenham's 2013 observation, described in chapter 39, that previously institutionalised children show the adult-like pattern of amygdala-prefrontal connectivity years ahead of typically raised peers, alongside rodent work by Callaghan and Rick Richardson showing that maternally separated rat pups exhibit adult-like fear extinction behaviour precociously.

The hypothesis gained a second, biochemical life in the accelerated-aging literature.

Puberty arrives measurably earlier on average in children exposed to threat-related adversity, an association documented in Belsky's psychosocial acceleration tradition and confirmed meta-analytically by Colich and McLaughlin in 2020, whose synthesis found early-life threat, but interestingly not deprivation, associated with earlier puberty and with accelerated epigenetic aging.

Epigenetic clocks - algorithms such as Steve Horvath's 2013 clock that estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns - run measurably fast in children with maltreatment histories in several cohorts, and telomere shortening, the fraying of chromosome ends with cellular aging, shows similar associations, with Idan Shalev's 2013 work among the early evidence.

The two literatures join into one idea: adversity shifts life-history strategy toward live fast, with faster reproductive maturation, faster neural closure, and faster cellular aging.

The cautions are substantial and stated plainly: most human evidence is correlational, epigenetic-clock effect sizes in children are small, some studies fail to find neural acceleration, and a 2020 review by McLaughlin's group notes the dissociation whereby acceleration tracks threat and early caregiving disruption better than it tracks poverty or deprivation broadly.

The hypothesis is therefore taught as a productive, partially supported framework - the best current explanation for why adversity-exposed children can look emotionally older and biologically older at once, and an open research front rather than a closed case.


40.4 Poverty and the brain

This section addresses the most widespread adversity in the world, and the newest science: the association between family income and brain development, the candidate pathways that might carry it, and the randomised experiment that tested whether money itself changes an infant's brain activity.

Nothing here stigmatises poor families; the entire thrust of the literature is that poverty is an environmental condition acting on children, not a property of them, and that it is modifiable.


40.4.1 The income and surface-area association

The landmark study is by Kimberly Noble, Elizabeth Sowell, and colleagues, published in Nature Neuroscience in 2015, analysing brain scans of 1,099 children and adolescents aged 3 to 20 in the Pediatric Imaging, Neurocognition, and Genetics sample.

Family income was associated with the surface area of the cerebral cortex - the total expanse of the brain's folded outer sheet - especially in regions supporting language, reading, executive function, and spatial skills.

The relation was logarithmic, meaning steepest at the bottom: among low-income families, an income difference of a few thousand dollars was associated with sizable surface-area differences, while the same difference among affluent families was associated with little.

Parental education was independently associated with surface area, and surface-area differences statistically accounted for part of the income gap in executive function scores.

Subsequent work has broadly confirmed the association at scale, including analyses of the roughly 12,000-child Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, which also show that the income association varies with state-level policy context, being weaker where anti-poverty benefits are more generous, per a 2023 report by David Weissman, McLaughlin, and colleagues.

The essential cautions: these are correlations, effect sizes are modest with enormous overlap between income groups, no child's brain can be read from family income, and the causal question - would money itself change the brain - is precisely what section 40.4.3's experiment was designed to ask.


40.4.2 The pathways: language exposure, stress, nutrition, toxins

Income is not an experience, so researchers ask what experiences carry the association.

Four pathway families dominate the evidence.

The first is language and cognitive stimulation: Betty Hart and Todd Risley's 1995 study made famous a large gap in words addressed to children across income groups, popularised as thirty million words by age three, a figure whose size has been contested by later work, including Douglas Sperry's 2019 replication showing much smaller and community-dependent differences, and this book reports the gap as real on average but smaller and more variable than the slogan.

Mechanistic support comes from Rachel Romeo and John Gabrieli's 2018 finding that the number of conversational turns a child experiences - dialogue, not raw word count - predicts Broca's area activation and language skill independent of income.

The second pathway is chronic stress, running through everything in sections 40.1 through 40.3: financial insecurity, crowding, and neighbourhood danger load caregivers and children, and Gary Evans's programme of work links childhood poverty to elevated allostatic load with parental responsiveness as a moderator.

The third is nutrition, from prenatal undernutrition - the Dutch Hunger Winter cohort of 1944 to 1945 remains the classic natural experiment linking gestational famine to later mental health risk - through iron and iodine deficiencies with documented neurodevelopmental costs, to food insecurity's effects on attention and behaviour.

The fourth is environmental toxins, where the evidence is unusually strong: childhood lead exposure, concentrated in poor housing, lowers IQ with no known safe threshold, as work by Bruce Lanphear and the Cincinnati and Flint literatures established, and air pollution exposure is increasingly linked to differences in white matter development.

These pathways compound and interact, they operate prenatally as well as postnatally, and their relative weights differ by place and family - which is why the field moved from cataloguing pathways to testing interventions.


40.4.3 The cash-transfer trial and its contested electroencephalographic finding

Baby's First Years, led by Kimberly Noble, Greg Duncan, Katherine Magnuson, and colleagues, is the first randomised trial of poverty reduction designed with infant brain outcomes as endpoints.

Starting in 2018, one thousand low-income mothers of newborns in four United States metropolitan areas were randomised to receive either 333 dollars per month or 20 dollars per month, unconditionally, on a debit card, for the early years of the child's life.

The first neural report, by Sonya Troller-Renfree, Noble, and colleagues in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in January 2022, measured EEG at age one and reported that infants in the high-cash group showed more mid-to-high-frequency brain activity - the pattern associated in correlational work with later cognitive skill - in several frequency bands.

The finding drew worldwide attention as the first experimental evidence that reducing poverty changes infant brain function, and it immediately drew methodological criticism.

Critics, in exchanges spanning academic commentary and public analysis during 2022, noted that the reported effects did not reach conventional statistical significance on the preregistered primary analyses, that a pandemic-related loss of part of the EEG sample complicated inference, and that the authors' interpretation leaned on a pattern across bands rather than on the planned tests.

The authors defended the work as appropriately reporting preregistered outcomes with effect sizes and uncertainty, and the honest description is that the age-one finding was suggestive rather than definitive from the day it appeared.

The follow-up sharpened the doubt.

The age-four EEG report, published by Troller-Renfree and colleagues in 2025, found no evidence of group differences on the preregistered primary outcome, the mid-to-high-frequency composite, nor on the secondary outcome of frontal gamma power, with only exploratory hints in alpha power that the authors themselves flagged as needing replication.

Parallel behavioural reports found no significant group differences on the trial's primary child developmental outcomes at age four, though the payments demonstrably changed family spending and mothers' reported time with children.

Interpretation is genuinely contested and is taught as such: one reading is that the age-one signal was a false positive now corrected by the preregistered follow-up, another is that 313 dollars per month is simply too small a dose against the scale of family poverty, and a third notes that the trial years coincided with a pandemic and with unprecedented temporary government transfers to all families, compressing the contrast between groups.

What the trial has already established is the standard: causal questions about poverty and the brain can be asked with randomisation and preregistration, and both its positive and its null results have entered policy debates about child allowances.

The chapter closes on the wider truth this trial illustrates: the science of adversity and the developing brain has moved from documenting harm to testing remedies, and its hardest, most valuable habit is saying plainly which of its findings are established, which are contested, and which are still to be earned.

CHAPTER 41. EMOTION, TEMPERAMENT, AND FEAR (CORE)

This chapter is about how feelings grow.

A newborn arrives able to be distressed, soothed, and delighted, but the machinery for reading other people's feelings, managing one's own, and learning what to fear is built slowly over the first two decades.

The chapter follows four threads: how babies express emotion and use the emotions of others, how the brain circuit that regulates emotion is wired up, why some children are born more wary than others, and how the rules of fear learning themselves change with age.

The last of these matters far beyond the laboratory, because anxiety disorders are the most common mental health problem of childhood and adolescence, and their treatment depends on how fear is learned and unlearned at each age.


41.1 Expression and recognition

Before an infant can speak a single word, emotion is already a two-way conversation.

This section looks at two famous demonstrations of that conversation: what happens when a parent suddenly stops responding, and what happens when a baby faces a situation it cannot interpret alone.

41.1.1 The still-face paradigm and mutual regulation

In 1978 Edward Tronick and his colleagues published a simple and unforgettable experiment now called the still-face paradigm.

A mother plays face to face with her baby as usual, then, on a signal, she holds her face completely still and unresponsive for about two minutes, and then she resumes normal play.

Babies as young as a few months old react strongly to the still face.

They first work hard to restart the interaction, smiling, reaching, vocalising, and pointing at the mother as if to say, in Tronick's words, that she is communicating hello and goodbye simultaneously.

When the efforts fail, the baby's mood collapses: gaze turns away, posture slumps, and distress and self-comforting behaviours such as thumb sucking appear.

A 2009 meta-analysis, which is a study that statistically combines the results of many previous studies, by Judi Mesman and colleagues confirmed this pattern across dozens of laboratories and cultures: less smiling and less looking at the parent during the still face, with distress that carries over into the reunion.

The experiment matters because it shows that infants are not passive receivers of care but active partners who expect contingent responses, meaning responses that are timed to and shaped by their own signals.

Tronick built this insight into his mutual regulation model, the idea that a baby's emotional state is regulated jointly by the pair, not by the baby alone.

On this view the ordinary mismatches of daily interaction are not failures, because the repeated cycle of mismatch and repair is precisely how the infant learns that distress can be fixed and that it has a hand in fixing it.

That learning is one of the earliest foundations of self-regulation, the later capacity to manage one's own feelings without help.

The still-face effect has proved robust in mothers and fathers, in different cultures, and even over video calls, though its strength varies with the usual style of interaction in a given culture.

41.1.2 Social referencing on the visual cliff

Around the end of the first year, babies begin to use another person's emotional expression as information about the world, a skill called social referencing.

The classic demonstration used the visual cliff, an apparatus with a sturdy glass surface extending over an apparent drop, so that a crawling baby sees a cliff edge but cannot actually fall.

In 1985 James Sorce, Robert Emde, Joseph Campos, and Mary Klinnert placed twelve-month-olds on the shallow side and their mothers at the far side, and asked the mothers to pose a single fixed facial expression.

The drop was made ambiguous, deep enough to give pause but not deep enough to be plainly dangerous, so that the baby genuinely needed more information.

When mothers posed joy or interest, most infants crossed the apparent drop.

When mothers posed fear or anger, almost none crossed.

When mothers posed sadness, an intermediate number crossed, suggesting that sadness signals something is wrong without specifying danger.

The experiment shows that by twelve months a baby can look to a trusted adult's face, extract its emotional meaning, and apply that meaning to a third thing in the world, which is a genuinely three-way, or triadic, act of communication.

Social referencing typically emerges between about nine and twelve months, alongside the other triadic skills described in the next chapter, and it becomes a major channel by which caregivers teach infants what is safe and what is not, long before language can do the job.

It is also one of the routes by which parental anxiety can be transmitted, since an infant who repeatedly references a fearful face may learn fear of things that were never dangerous.


41.2 The amygdala-prefrontal circuit's development

To understand how children come to manage fear, neuroscience focuses on a circuit linking two structures.

The amygdala is a small almond-shaped cluster of cells deep in each temporal lobe that acts as the brain's rapid threat and salience detector, flagging things that might matter for survival.

The prefrontal cortex is the large front portion of the outer brain surface that supports planning, control, and deliberate thought, and its middle wall, the medial prefrontal cortex, talks directly to the amygdala and can calm it.

This section describes how that conversation changes across childhood and how caregivers participate in it.

41.2.1 The connectivity switch from childhood to adolescence

In 2013 Dylan Gee, Nim Tottenham, and colleagues used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a scanning method that tracks brain activity through blood flow, to study people aged four to twenty-two while they viewed emotional faces.

They found a striking switch in how the amygdala and the medial prefrontal cortex worked together.

In children younger than about ten, activity in the two regions rose and fell together, a pattern called positive connectivity.

From about age ten onward, the pattern inverted: when prefrontal activity went up, amygdala activity went down, a negative or seesaw pattern that resembles the adult regulatory relationship in which the prefrontal cortex damps the amygdala.

Across the same ages, raw amygdala reactivity to fearful faces declined steadily.

The valence of the connection also tracked anxiety, since children showing the mature negative pattern tended to report less separation anxiety than children of the same age still showing the immature positive pattern.

The finding is best read as a marker of when the brain's top-down emotion regulation comes online: the wiring exists early, but the regulatory mode of using it is a developmental achievement of late childhood and adolescence.

Like all findings in developmental fMRI, the exact ages are estimates from cross-sectional samples, meaning different children of different ages scanned once each, and longitudinal work that follows the same children over years continues to refine the timing.

41.2.2 Caregiver buffering of the circuit and adversity's acceleration of it

If the child's own regulatory circuit is not yet mature, who regulates the amygdala in the meantime?

The answer, in a phrase used by Tottenham and colleagues, is that the parent acts as an external prefrontal cortex.

In a 2014 study, Gee and colleagues showed that for children, simply viewing a photograph of their own mother during scanning shifted amygdala-prefrontal connectivity toward the mature negative pattern and improved emotional task performance, whereas for adolescents the mother's image no longer had this buffering effect.

This parallels rodent work in which the mother's presence directly suppresses her pup's stress hormone response and quiets the amygdala, a mechanism described further in section 41.4.

Adversity bends this timetable.

Children who spent their infancy in institutional orphanage care before adoption, studied by the same group, showed the mature negative connectivity pattern years early, in childhood rather than adolescence.

One interpretation is that when caregiving is absent or unreliable, the circuit gives up waiting for external regulation and matures ahead of schedule, trading a longer period of plasticity for earlier self-sufficiency.

This has been called stress-accelerated development, and it fits a broader pattern, discussed in chapter 44, in which early adversity is associated with faster biological maturation on several clocks.

The acceleration is not free, because the early-maturing pattern in previously institutionalised children was associated with higher separation anxiety at the time, even though in some follow-up work the same mature-looking connectivity seemed to offer partial protection against later anxiety.

The honest summary is that caregiver presence is a real, measurable regulator of the child's emotion circuitry, and that losing it early changes the circuit's developmental schedule in ways whose long-term costs and benefits are still being worked out.


41.3 Temperament

Anyone who has spent time with more than one baby knows that babies differ from birth: some are easygoing, some are intense, some are shy of anything new.

Temperament is the scientific name for these early-appearing, biologically grounded differences in emotional reactivity and self-regulation.

This section covers the best-studied temperament type and the framework that organises the rest.

41.3.1 Behavioural inhibition from infancy to the adult amygdala

The Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan spent decades studying behavioural inhibition, the temperament of the child who is wary, quiet, and slow to approach anything unfamiliar.

Kagan showed that inhibition can be forecast from remarkably early in life: about fifteen to twenty percent of four-month-old infants are high reactive, meaning they thrash their limbs and cry vigorously at new sights and sounds, and these infants are disproportionately the toddlers who later hang back from strangers and novel toys.

Kagan proposed that the difference reflects a lower threshold of excitability in the amygdala.

In 2003 Carl Schwartz, Kagan, and colleagues delivered a striking confirmation in the journal Science: adults who had been classified as inhibited in their second year of life, roughly two decades earlier, showed greater amygdala responses to novel faces in fMRI than adults who had been uninhibited toddlers.

A 2012 follow-up by Schwartz extended the prediction all the way back to the four-month reactivity classification.

Behavioural inhibition matters clinically because it is one of the strongest known early temperamental risk factors for later anxiety, particularly social anxiety disorder, with stably inhibited children showing substantially elevated risk by adolescence.

Yet the risk is probabilistic, not fated: most inhibited children do not develop an anxiety disorder, outcomes depend on parenting, peer experience, and the child's developing attentional control, and inhibition also travels with traits many would count as strengths, such as caution and conscientiousness.

The lesson of this literature is double: early temperament leaves a real trace in the adult brain, and at the same time the path from a four-month-old's cry to an adult's clinic visit is long, branching, and open to influence at every step.

41.3.2 The reactivity and regulation dimensions and effortful control

Where Kagan sorted children into types, Mary Rothbart built the framework that now dominates the field, defining temperament as constitutionally based individual differences along two broad axes: reactivity and self-regulation.

Reactivity covers how quickly, how strongly, and how lastingly a child's emotions and arousal are triggered, and it includes both negative reactivity, such as fear and frustration, and positive reactivity, such as the eager approach the field calls surgency.

Self-regulation covers the processes that modulate that reactivity, and its centrepiece is effortful control, defined as the ability to suppress a dominant, automatic response in order to perform a subdominant, chosen one.

Effortful control is what a child uses to wait for a treat, to whisper when shouting is easier, or to look away from something frightening on purpose.

It emerges late in infancy, develops rapidly between roughly ages two and seven, and rests on the maturing anterior cingulate and prefrontal attention networks studied by Rothbart with Michael Posner.

The two axes interact: a highly fear-reactive child with strong effortful control can steer around their own wariness, while the same reactivity with weak control is a much stronger risk profile for anxiety.

Measured in childhood, effortful control predicts conscience development, school readiness, and social competence, and it is generally seen as the developmental ancestor of the adult trait of conscientiousness.

Temperament research is careful to say that none of these dimensions is good or bad in itself, because each profile carries costs and benefits that depend on the environment the child meets.


41.4 Fear learning across development

Fear learning is studied with a simple procedure called fear conditioning, in which a neutral cue, such as a tone, is paired with something unpleasant, such as a brief shock in animal studies, until the cue alone evokes fear.

Extinction is the reverse procedure, presenting the cue repeatedly without the unpleasant event until the fear response fades, and it is the laboratory model of exposure therapy for anxiety.

The startling discovery of the past two decades is that the rules of both processes change with age, in ways that make ecological sense.

41.4.1 The infant attachment suppression of fear learning

Regina Sullivan and colleagues discovered that newborn rat pups are, for a time, almost unable to learn fear.

For roughly the first nine days of life, a pup that experiences an odour paired with a mild shock does not learn to avoid the odour, but instead learns to prefer it, approaching it as it would its mother's scent.

The reason is a hormonal gate: fear learning through the amygdala requires the stress hormone corticosterone, and in the young pup corticosterone levels are held very low during a period called the stress hyporesponsive period, so the amygdala cannot be recruited and the attachment learning system wins by default.

Sullivan's 2006 work showed the switch directly, since injecting corticosterone into a young pup turned on precocious fear learning, and blocking it in an older pup restored infant-style preference learning.

Most remarkably, after the switch age the mother's physical presence still suppresses the pup's corticosterone surge, so that a pup shocked in its mother's presence again learns approach rather than fear.

The biological logic is stark: an infant mammal cannot survive without its caregiver, so evolution has built a system that attaches the infant to the caregiver almost no matter what, even when the caregiver is a source of pain.

This is thought to illuminate the tragic human observation that maltreated children usually remain intensely attached to the parents who hurt them.

Direct evidence in humans is necessarily indirect, but the caregiver buffering of stress physiology and of amygdala circuits described in section 41.2.2 is the human parallel most researchers point to.

41.4.2 Adolescent extinction resistance and its therapy implications

In 2012 Siobhan Pattwell, Francis Lee, B. J. Casey, and colleagues published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) that ran the same fear conditioning and extinction procedures in mice and in humans across development.

Adolescents in both species showed a specific deficit: they acquired fear normally, but extinction learning was markedly attenuated, so their fear faded much less with repeated safe exposures than that of children or adults.

In the human sample, adolescents aged twelve to seventeen extinguished less than children aged five to eleven and less than adults aged eighteen to twenty-eight.

In the adolescent mice, the infralimbic medial prefrontal cortex, the region whose job is to learn and signal that a cue has become safe, failed to show the synaptic plasticity that appears during extinction in younger and older animals.

Related work by Pattwell also found that fear expression itself fluctuates across development, with contextual fear temporarily suppressed around adolescence before returning, again pointing to a reorganising circuit rather than a simple linear improvement.

The clinical implication is direct and sobering: exposure therapy, the best-validated psychological treatment for anxiety, is built on extinction, and adolescence, when anxiety disorders surge, may be exactly the age when the extinction machinery works worst.

This has prompted research into adolescent-tailored approaches, such as timing exposures to exploit reconsolidation, enriching safety learning, or leaning on cognitive strategies that do not depend so heavily on infralimbic plasticity, though none of these has yet remade clinical practice.

The age specifics come mostly from rodents and modest human samples, so the field treats the exact boundaries as approximate while regarding the core phenomenon of adolescent extinction attenuation as well supported.

41.4.3 Early extinction as erasure: the developmental difference in mechanism

In adults, extinction does not erase a fear memory; it writes a second, competing safety memory on top of it.

The evidence is that adult fear returns after extinction in three classic ways: spontaneous recovery with the passage of time, renewal when the cue is met in a new context, and reinstatement after a fresh stressor.

Jee Hyun Kim and Rick Richardson showed that young animals play by different rules.

Rat pups extinguished at postnatal day seventeen, roughly infancy, showed no renewal and no reinstatement, as if the fear memory itself had been deleted, whereas pups extinguished at postnatal day twenty-four, past weaning, showed adult-style return of fear.

In 2009 Nadine Gogolla, Cyril Herry, and colleagues published in Science a molecular explanation for when the rules change.
