Perineuronal nets are lattice-like coats of extracellular matrix, the structural mesh between cells, that wrap around certain neurons as the brain matures and stabilise their connections.

These nets form around amygdala neurons at about the age the erasure-like extinction disappears, and when the researchers dissolved the nets in adult animals with the enzyme chondroitinase ABC, fear memories acquired afterwards became erasable by extinction again, just as in infancy.

The picture is that the infant brain holds fear memories in an unprotected, revisable form, and that the maturing brain deliberately armours them, presumably because a fear memory that survives is usually worth keeping.

The therapeutic dream of reopening the erasure state in adult humans belongs to the critical-period reopening literature, which, as this corpus records elsewhere, is robust in rodents and nearly untranslated in humans, so it should be understood as a mechanism discovered, not a treatment achieved.

For developmental psychology the message is that even so basic a process as unlearning fear is not one process but several, swapped in and out on a developmental schedule.


CHAPTER 42. THE SOCIAL BRAIN AND THEORY OF MIND (CORE)

Human beings are the most relentlessly social of animals, and the brain reflects it.

This chapter follows the construction of the social brain from the newborn's pull toward faces, through the infant's discovery that attention can be shared, to the preschooler's discovery that minds can hold false beliefs, and finally to the brain network that carries mature social reasoning.

It also teaches two live scientific disputes as disputes: the replication crisis around infant theory of mind, and the long argument over mirror neurons.

Both are worth learning precisely because they show how the field corrects itself.


42.1 The infant social brain

Long before an infant can think about minds, its perceptual systems are tuned to the signals minds give off: faces, eyes, voices, and biological motion.

This section covers that early tuning and the communicative revolution it makes possible at around nine months.

42.1.1 Faces, gaze, and the superior temporal specialisation

Newborns, within hours of birth, orient more to face-like arrangements of blobs than to the same blobs scrambled, a bias demonstrated by Mark Johnson and John Morton in 1991 and interpreted as a crude subcortical mechanism they called Conspec.

Johnson's two-process theory holds that this early bias serves to feed faces to the developing cortex, which then slowly specialises through experience.

Recent imaging supports early cortical involvement too: work from Rebecca Saxe's laboratory using fMRI in awake infants found face-selective responses in the fusiform and superior temporal regions in babies of only around two to five months, though these responses are weaker and less selective than in adults.

The superior temporal sulcus, a long groove on the side of the temporal lobe, deserves special mention because in adults it is the hub for the moving, changeable aspects of faces: gaze direction, expression, and mouth movements, as well as voices and biological motion.

Gaze is a particularly rich signal, and infants are sensitive to it almost immediately, preferring direct gaze from birth and, by around three to four months, using another person's gaze shift to move their own attention.

Gaze following proper, meaning reliably looking where another person looks even at targets outside the visual field, consolidates over the second half of the first year.

The general developmental story is one of specialisation: face and social processing begin broadly tuned, then narrow with experience, as shown by the perceptual narrowing literature in which young infants discriminate monkey faces and other-race faces better than older infants do.

So the social brain is neither hard-wired at birth nor a blank slate; it is a set of biases that guarantee the right experience, plus cortical machinery that specialises on that experience across the first years and beyond.

42.1.2 Joint attention as the nine-month revolution

Somewhere around nine months of age, human infants begin to do something no other species does so readily: they share attention.

Michael Tomasello named this transition the nine-month revolution.

Before it, infant interaction is dyadic, meaning two-way, either baby-and-person or baby-and-object.

After it, interaction becomes triadic: baby, partner, and object are bound into a single shared frame, with the baby checking back and forth between the partner's eyes and the thing in question.

The new abilities arrive as a package across roughly nine to fifteen months: following points and gaze to distant targets, imitating actions on objects, and, most tellingly, producing declarative points, which are points made not to obtain something but simply to share interest in it.

Tomasello's interpretation is that the infant has begun to understand other people as intentional agents, beings with goals and attention of their own that can be aligned with the infant's.

Joint attention is the cradle of language, since a word can only be learned when child and adult are attending to the same thing, and individual differences in early joint attention predict later vocabulary.

It is also clinically important, because reduced initiation of joint attention is among the earliest reliable behavioural signs of autism, visible before the second birthday and a target of early intervention.

Whether the nine-month change is a single conceptual revolution or the gradual assembly of separate skills is still debated, with researchers such as Chris Moore and colleagues favouring leaner, more piecemeal accounts, but the behavioural facts of the transition are not in dispute.


42.2 Theory of mind

Theory of mind is the everyday capacity to attribute mental states, such as beliefs, desires, and intentions, to oneself and others, and to use those attributions to predict behaviour.

Its development is anchored by one famous test, complicated by one famous set of infant findings, and possibly reconciled by a two-systems theory.

This section takes the three in turn.

42.2.1 The explicit false-belief transition near age four

The false-belief task, introduced by Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner in 1983, asks whether a child understands that someone can believe something the child knows to be untrue.

In the classic Sally-Anne version, Sally hides her marble in a basket and leaves, Anne moves the marble to a box, and the child is asked where Sally will look for her marble when she returns.

The correct answer, the basket, requires representing Sally's outdated belief as distinct from reality.

The developmental result is among the most replicated in psychology: three-year-olds systematically answer with reality, the box, while children from around four to four and a half years answer with Sally's belief.

In 2001 Henry Wellman, David Cross, and Julanne Watson published a meta-analysis of one hundred seventy-eight studies confirming the transition and showing that no task manipulation, however helpful, pushed genuinely competent performance into the early threes.

The transition is not an isolated trick but part of a sequence, since Wellman and David Liu showed that children pass diverse-desires tasks before diverse-beliefs tasks, and those before false belief, in a reliable scale.

Passing false belief correlates with language development, with executive function, and with having siblings, and deaf children of hearing parents, whose early conversational input is reduced, pass it years late, which shows that conversation about minds is part of what builds the understanding.

Cross-cultural work finds the same transition at broadly similar ages with some variation in the sequence of easier steps.

Whatever infants may or may not know implicitly, the explicit, articulable understanding that minds can misrepresent the world is an achievement of the fifth year of life.

42.2.2 The implicit infant findings and their replication crisis

In 2005 Kristine Onishi and Renee Baillargeon published a study in Science suggesting that fifteen-month-old infants already expect an actor to search according to her false belief.

Their method was violation of expectation, which measures how long infants look at events, on the logic that infants look longer at what surprises them, and the infants looked longer when the actor searched where the object really was rather than where she should have believed it to be.

A wave of related findings followed, using looking time, anticipatory gaze, and even helpful interventions by toddlers, and for a decade the textbooks said that theory of mind was present in infancy and the age-four transition was merely a performance limit.

Then the replications began to fail.

This must be taught as a genuine, unresolved dispute, not as a settled story in either direction.

From about 2016 onward, laboratories led by researchers including Diane Poulin-Dubois, Hannes Rakoczy, Ulf Liszkowski, and Louisa Kulke attempted direct and conceptual replications of the anticipatory-looking and violation-of-expectation findings, and many failed outright or replicated only partially.

A large multi-laboratory effort found that a widely cited anticipatory-looking result did not replicate, and a 2018 review by Kulke and Rakoczy concluded that the implicit task battery was, across paradigms, not reliably replicable.

Powell, Hobbs, Bardis, Carey, and Saxe likewise failed in 2018 to reproduce key violation-of-expectation results, and Dorrenberg, Rakoczy, and Liszkowski found that different implicit measures did not even correlate with each other in the same infants, undermining their claim to tap one underlying competence.

The original researchers responded: Baillargeon, Buttelmann, and Southgate argued in a 2018 commentary that many failed replications altered small procedural details that matter, and that the positive evidence base remains large.

Critics answered that a competence so fragile that invisible procedural details destroy it cannot bear the theoretical weight placed on it.

As of the mid-2020s the honest summary is that the field does not know whether infants represent false beliefs, that some looking-time phenomena are probably real but open to leaner explanations such as attention to salient events or three-way associations among agent, object, and location, and that this episode has become a canonical example of psychology's broader replication crisis.

42.2.3 The two-systems account as the candidate reconciliation

The leading attempt to reconcile the infant findings with the age-four transition is the two-systems account of Ian Apperly and Stephen Butterfill, published in Psychological Review in 2009.

Their proposal is that humans possess two distinct capacities for tracking other minds.

System one is early developing, fast, automatic, and cognitively cheap, but inflexible: it tracks belief-like states, registrations of where an agent last encountered an object, without representing beliefs as beliefs, and it fails when contents get complicated, for example with beliefs about identity or number.

System two is late developing, slow, effortful, and dependent on language and executive function, but fully flexible: it represents beliefs as such, and it is what the explicit false-belief task measures at age four.

The account predicts signature limits, specific situations where the fast system should fail even in adults, and some supporting evidence exists, including adult studies where automatic belief tracking breaks down for identity-based contents.

The theory's attraction is that it explains why infants might pass looking-time tasks while three-year-olds fail direct questions, and why adults still show fast, unbidden belief tracking alongside deliberate reasoning.

Its difficulty is that it presupposes the infant findings it was built to explain, so the replication crisis of the previous sub-section eats at its foundations: if the infant effects are unreliable, there may be nothing for system one to account for.

Rival views remain on the table, including Rakoczy's suggestion that infants have rich but non-representational social expectancies, purely deflationary associative accounts, and the original rich account on which infants really do represent beliefs and later development is all performance.

The dispute is live, the data are contested, and the two-systems account is best taught as the leading candidate reconciliation rather than the answer.


42.3 The network

In the adult brain, thinking about other minds reliably activates a specific set of regions: the temporoparietal junction on each side, the medial prefrontal cortex, the precuneus, and parts of the superior temporal sulcus.

This section asks when that network assembles in childhood and how specialised it becomes.

42.3.1 Temporoparietal junction selectivity and its childhood specialisation

The temporoparietal junction is the patch of cortex where the temporal and parietal lobes meet, just above and behind the ear.

Rebecca Saxe and Nancy Kanwisher showed in 2003 that the right temporoparietal junction responds selectively when adults reason about beliefs, more than for other facts about people.

Hyowon Gweon, Saxe, and colleagues then traced the childhood story in a 2012 study of children aged five to eleven.

The network's broad architecture was already adult-like at five: the same regions activated for stories about minds.

What changed with age was selectivity: in younger children the right temporoparietal junction responded to stories about people generally, including their appearance and social relationships, and it became increasingly selective for mental states specifically across middle childhood.

Crucially, the degree of that selectivity, independent of age, predicted the child's performance on behavioural theory-of-mind tasks.

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy, a method that measures the same blood-flow signal with light through the scalp, has even suggested temporoparietal responses to belief-relevant events in infants under a year, though such findings inherit all the caution owed to infant paradigms.

The pattern, early architecture plus slow specialisation, mirrors the face-processing story of section 42.1.1 and appears to be a general law of the developing social brain.

42.3.2 The theory-of-mind network distinct from the pain network by age three

For younger children, a 2018 study by Hilary Richardson, Saxe, and colleagues in Nature Communications changed the method and the picture.

Instead of asking children to lie still through stories and questions, they showed children aged three and up a short animated film, the Pixar short Partly Cloudy, which contains both mind-reading moments and bodily pain moments, while scanning them.

Even in three-year-olds, the theory-of-mind network and the so-called pain matrix, the separate set of regions that responds to others' bodily states and suffering, responded to different moments of the film, were internally correlated within each network, and were anticorrelated with each other.

In plain words, by age three the brain already keeps thinking about minds and reacting to bodies in two distinct systems.

The distinction sharpened with age, and children who had passed explicit false-belief tasks showed somewhat more mature network responses than those who had not, but the basic division was present years before the age-four behavioural transition.

This finding sits awkwardly and interestingly with the replication crisis: it shows that some neural machinery for social processing is organised very early, while leaving open exactly what computations that machinery is performing in a three-year-old.

Richardson's later work extended the movie-watching approach downward and found adult-like response timecourses emerging gradually, with no sharp neural discontinuity at age four.

The measured conclusion is that the network is built early and refined slowly, and that the dramatic behavioural change at four reflects gradual neural change plus the maturation of language and executive resources needed to answer questions.


42.4 The mirror-system dispute

Few findings in modern neuroscience became famous faster than mirror neurons, and few have been fought over harder.

This section presents the claims and the critiques together, because the dispute itself is the lesson.

42.4.1 The claims, the critiques, and the associative-learning alternative

In the early 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti's group in Parma, with Vittorio Gallese and Leonardo Fogassi, reported neurons in area F5 of the macaque monkey's premotor cortex, part of the movement-planning cortex, that fired both when the monkey performed a grasping action and when it merely watched the experimenter perform the same action.

They named them mirror neurons, and the interpretive claim followed quickly: that we understand others' actions by internally simulating them in our own motor system.

Over the following decade the claims inflated dramatically, with mirror neurons proposed as the basis of imitation, empathy, language evolution, and, in the broken mirror hypothesis of autism, as the deficient mechanism behind autistic social difficulties, while the philosopher Vilayanur Ramachandran predicted they would do for psychology what deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) had done for biology.

The critiques then arrived on several fronts, and they must be taught alongside the claims.

Gregory Hickok, in a 2009 paper and a 2014 book titled The Myth of Mirror Neurons, argued that the action-understanding interpretation was never well supported even in monkeys, and pointed to dissociations in humans: patients with severe motor production deficits, such as apraxia or anarthria, can still recognise and understand the actions and speech they cannot produce, which should be impossible if understanding required motor simulation.

Direct single-neuron evidence in humans is nearly absent, resting mainly on one 2010 study by Roy Mukamel and Itzhak Fried recording in patients during surgery, and human evidence otherwise depends on indirect signals such as fMRI adaptation, which have been contested.

The broken mirror hypothesis of autism fared badly, with reviews by Antonia Hamilton and others finding no consistent evidence of mirror-system dysfunction in autistic people.

Cecilia Heyes advanced the most influential alternative: mirror neurons are real but are a product, not a cause, of social development, created by ordinary associative learning whenever seeing and doing are correlated, as when an infant watches its own hands, is imitated by adults, or acts in synchrony with others.

Her laboratory showed the tuning is malleable in exactly the way this predicts, since brief counter-mirror training, seeing one action while performing another, reverses mirror responses in adult humans.

On Heyes's account the developmental question flips: instead of mirror neurons explaining imitation and empathy, social experience explains mirror neurons.

Defenders including Rizzolatti, Gallese, and Marco Iacoboni maintain that a core contribution to action recognition survives the critiques, and genetic-evolutionary counterarguments to a purely associative origin have been published.

The related claim of neonatal imitation, that newborns imitate tongue protrusion and other gestures, once offered as evidence of innate mirroring from birth, failed a large longitudinal replication by Janine Oostenbroek and colleagues in 2016 and is now doubted, a correction this corpus records explicitly.

The balanced teaching position is this: mirror neurons exist in monkeys and very likely in humans, their tuning is shaped by sensorimotor experience, their role in understanding others is contested and was certainly oversold, and the grand claims about empathy, language, and autism should be regarded as historical enthusiasm rather than established science.


CHAPTER 43. EMPATHY, MORALITY, AND THE SELF (CORE)

This chapter is about the growth of the moral and self-aware person.

It traces how raw emotional contagion becomes genuine concern for others, how toddlers become helpers and sharers, what a developmental disorder of empathy looks like, how moral judgment shifts from outcomes to intentions, and how a child comes to recognise, evaluate, and finally narrate a self.

The brain story runs through the circuits of the previous two chapters, since empathy borrows the emotion circuitry of chapter 41 and moral judgment borrows the mentalizing network of chapter 42.


43.1 Empathy and prosociality

Empathy is feeling with another person; prosociality is acting for another person.

Development supplies first the feeling, then the acting, and this section follows both, ending with the contrast case in which the feeling is diminished.

43.1.1 From contagion to concern

The developmental starting point is emotional contagion, the automatic catching of another's emotional state.

Newborns show it within days: they cry more at the sound of another newborn's cry than at equally loud non-social sounds or even recordings of their own cry, a finding from Martin Hoffman's collaborators Marvin Simner in 1971 and Abraham Sagi and Hoffman in 1976.

Contagion is empathy without boundaries, since the newborn does not distinguish whose distress it is feeling.

Hoffman's influential stage account describes development as the gradual addition of a self-other boundary to this shared feeling.

Across the second year, as self-recognition emerges, contagion matures into empathic concern, meaning other-directed sympathy: the toddler no longer merely becomes distressed but orients to the sufferer, with concerned facial expressions, comforting touches, and attempts to help.

Carolyn Zahn-Waxler's longitudinal studies documented this transition, showing comforting behaviour toward distressed others emerging and consolidating between roughly fourteen and twenty-four months, and later work by Zahn-Waxler and colleagues found precursors of concern even earlier than the classical account expected.

Neuroscience distinguishes the components: experience sharing rides on the same interoceptive and emotional circuits engaged by one's own states, including the anterior insula, a fold of cortex tucked deep between the frontal and temporal lobes that maps bodily feeling, and the anterior cingulate cortex, while understanding another's situation recruits the mentalizing network of chapter 42, and Richardson's movie data showed these systems already separated by age three.

Jean Decety's developmental imaging work found that when children view others in pain, younger children's responses are dominated by the affective circuits, with mentalizing and regulatory prefrontal regions increasingly recruited across childhood and adolescence, consistent with empathy shifting from being caught by feeling to being guided by understanding.

Mature empathy, on this account, is a managed alliance between an old contagion system and a newer understanding system, with regulation deciding whether shared feeling becomes concern for the other or overwhelmed personal distress in oneself.

43.1.2 Infant helping and the development of sharing and fairness

In 2006 Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello published a study in Science showing that eighteen-month-old toddlers spontaneously help an unfamiliar adult: when the experimenter dropped a clothespin and reached for it vainly, or bumped into a cabinet with full hands, most toddlers toddled over and helped within seconds, without being asked and without reward.

Control conditions showed the behaviour was genuinely goal-directed, since toddlers did not retrieve objects thrown down on purpose.

Follow-up work found helping at fourteen months for simple cases, found that young chimpanzees help in some easier tasks, and found, strikingly, that external rewards can undermine toddlers' subsequent helping, suggesting the motivation is intrinsic rather than trained.

Sharing follows a slower and more instructive timetable.

Children understand fairness long before they practise it: by around age three they endorse equal division in words, but in action they keep the larger share for themselves until about age seven or eight, when behaviour finally catches up with the stated norm.

Experiments with collaboration show an important wrinkle, since even three-year-olds share spoils equally when the resources were produced by working together, which suggests that collaboration is a cradle of fairness.

Inequity aversion also has two faces that mature at different times: dislike of receiving less than a peer appears early, by around age four in behavioural economics games such as those of Katherine McAuliffe and Peter Blake, whereas dislike of receiving more than a peer, the costly rejection of an advantage, appears only around age eight and varies across cultures.

A large seven-society study by Blake, McAuliffe, Warneken, and colleagues, published in Nature in 2015, confirmed that disadvantageous inequity aversion emerged in every society tested while advantageous inequity aversion emerged late and only in some societies, pointing to a universal core with a culturally tuned upper storey.

The overall picture is that prosocial motivation starts early and cheaply, while genuinely costly fairness is a middle-childhood construction built from norms, self-control, and reputation.

43.1.3 The callous-unemotional contrast case

Development sometimes teaches by contrast, and the contrast case for empathy is the small group of children with conduct problems accompanied by callous-unemotional traits.

Callous-unemotional traits mean persistently low empathy and guilt, shallow emotional expression, and indifference to others' distress, and they mark out a distinct subgroup within childhood conduct problems, now recognised in diagnostic manuals under the specifier limited prosocial emotions.

The empirical signature, established by researchers including Essi Viding, Alice Jones, James Blair, and Abigail Marsh, is specific: these children are poor at recognising fearful faces, look less at the eyes, and show reduced amygdala responses to fearful expressions.

Marsh and colleagues in 2008 and Jones, Viding, and colleagues in 2009 both reported amygdala hypoactivity to fearful faces in this group, the opposite direction from the amygdala overreactivity seen in anxious and in reactively aggressive children.

Blair's interpretation is a deficit in the violence inhibition mechanism: normally, another creature's distress is an unconditioned brake on aggression and a teaching signal for conscience, and if distress cues do not register in the amygdala, that whole channel of moral learning through empathy is weakened.

Twin studies by Viding found that conduct problems with high callous-unemotional traits are substantially more heritable than conduct problems without them, though heritable never means unchangeable.

The developmental evidence gives reasons for hope: warm and responsive parenting predicts decreases in callous-unemotional traits over time, some prevention trials targeting parental warmth and emotion coaching have reduced them, and a longitudinal finding by Rachael Bedford and colleagues that reduced attention to faces in the first year predicts later callous-unemotional traits suggests very early windows for support.

The scientific value of the contrast case is that it dissociates knowing from feeling, since these children can typically pass theory-of-mind tests and state the rules they break, which shows that moral development is not one stream but at least two: an understanding stream that is intact, and an empathic-learning stream that, in this group, is running dry.

Care with framing matters here, because these are children, not diagnoses walking, and the traits are dimensional, changeable, and strongly shaped by the caregiving environment.


43.2 Moral development

How does a child come to judge right and wrong?

Psychology's answer has changed shape twice, first from stages to intuitions in theory, and second from outcomes to intentions in the description of childhood itself, with a specific brain region tracking the second change.

43.2.1 From stages to intuitions in the theory

Jean Piaget began the modern study of moral judgment in 1932 by interviewing children about marbles and mishaps, and he described a shift from heteronomous morality, where rules are sacred and damage is what counts, to autonomous morality, where rules are agreements and intentions matter.

Lawrence Kohlberg extended this in the 1950s and onward into six stages across three levels, preconventional, conventional, and postconventional, using moral dilemmas such as the famous case of Heinz, who must decide whether to steal an unaffordable drug to save his dying wife.

Kohlberg's stages captured something real about the development of moral justification, but they drew lasting criticisms: Carol Gilligan argued in 1982 that the scheme undervalued an ethic of care, cross-cultural work found the highest stages rare outside Western educated samples, and, most damagingly, reasoning stage predicted actual moral behaviour only weakly.

Elliot Turiel's social domain theory showed that even young children distinguish moral violations, which involve harm and are wrong everywhere regardless of rules, from conventional violations, which are wrong only where the rule holds, a competence visible by around age three and inconvenient for any theory that has young children treating all rules alike.

The second theoretical turn came in 2001, when Jonathan Haidt published The Emotional Dog and Its Rational Tail, arguing from phenomena such as moral dumbfounding, where people maintain a judgment while unable to justify it, that moral judgment is usually a fast intuition, with reasoning arriving afterwards as a press secretary.

Joshua Greene's fMRI work on trolley-style dilemmas added a dual-process brain story in which emotional responses drive judgments against personal harm while controlled processing supports cost-benefit judgments.

Developmentally, the intuitionist turn was reinforced by infant studies, since Kiley Hamlin, Karen Wynn, and Paul Bloom reported in 2007 that six-month-olds and even three-month-olds prefer puppet characters who help a struggling climber over characters who hinder it.

Honesty requires noting that these infant helper-hinderer findings have had a mixed replication record, with some large replications succeeding under exact conditions and others failing, so the strength of infant moral evaluation remains debated.

The current synthesis holds that early-emerging affective intuitions, built on the empathy systems of section 43.1, provide the seeds of morality, while the slow Kohlbergian growth of justification, perspective-taking, and principled reasoning determines how those seeds are pruned, weighted, and defended across development.

43.2.2 Intent overtaking outcome, with the temporoparietal junction

Ask a four-year-old who is naughtier, a boy who broke fifteen cups by accident or a boy who broke one cup while stealing jam, and, in Piaget's classic finding, the young child says fifteen cups is worse.

Modern studies with cleaner designs confirm the underlying trajectory: young children weight outcomes heavily, and across roughly ages four to eight the weight shifts to intentions, so that an attempted harm that fails comes to be judged worse than an accidental harm that succeeds.

Part of the shift depends on theory of mind, since a child cannot weight an agent's belief before being able to represent it, and false-belief understanding from chapter 42 predicts intent-based moral judgment.

The brain evidence centres on the right temporoparietal junction, the same region that specialises for mental states in section 42.3.1.

In adults, Liane Young and Rebecca Saxe showed that this region's response tracks the use of belief information in moral judgment, being especially engaged when an agent's innocent intention must excuse a bad outcome.

In 2010 Young, Saxe, and colleagues showed causation, since disrupting the right temporoparietal junction with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique that briefly and safely interferes with a small patch of cortex using magnetic pulses, made adults judge more by outcomes and less by intentions, nudging them toward the young child's pattern.

Developmentally, imaging work with children, including studies in Decety's and Saxe's laboratories, finds that with age, responses in the temporoparietal junction and connected mentalizing regions increasingly differentiate intentional from accidental harm, and that the region's functional selectivity tracks the behavioural shift toward intent across roughly ages six to eleven.

Interestingly, even adults never fully outgrow outcomes, since accidental harms still attract more punishment than harmless accidents, and Fiery Cushman's work shows that punishment judgments stay outcome-sensitive even when wrongness judgments have gone over to intent.

The developmental summary is that outcome-based judgment is the default of the young mind, that the mentalizing network's maturation progressively installs intent at the centre of moral evaluation, and that the old outcome machinery is overwritten only partially, remaining visible in adult punishment, in law's treatment of negligence, and in everyone's flash of anger at the person who steps on their foot by accident.


43.3 The self

The self is not installed at birth; it is constructed in stages.

This section covers its three great installments: recognising the self in the second year, evaluating the self through others' eyes in adolescence, and narrating the self as a life story.

43.3.1 Mirror self-recognition at eighteen to twenty-four months

The classic test of bodily self-recognition is the rouge test, introduced for infants by Beulah Amsterdam in 1972 and for chimpanzees by Gordon Gallup in 1970.

A spot of rouge is surreptitiously dabbed on the child's nose, and the child is placed before a mirror.

A child who reaches for the mirror treats the reflection as another child; a child who touches their own nose understands that the image is me.

Amsterdam found, and many replications confirm, that mark-directed self-touching emerges at around eighteen months and is shown by a clear majority of children by twenty to twenty-four months.

Before that age, infants often smile at, reach toward, or look behind the mirror for the other baby.

The timing is developmentally meaningful because a cluster of self-related abilities arrives together in the same window: personal pronouns such as me and mine, the self-conscious emotions of embarrassment, pride, and shame described by Michael Lewis, and, as section 43.1.1 noted, the maturation of empathic concern, which requires knowing whose distress is whose.

Cross-cultural work complicates any simple maturational reading, since studies by Joscha Kartner, Heidi Keller, and colleagues found much later and rarer mirror self-recognition in some rural non-Western communities where child-rearing emphasises relatedness over autonomy, suggesting the test partly measures a culturally fostered focus on the individual self.

Mirror self-recognition also appears in chimpanzees, orangutans, dolphins, elephants, and magpies, in some but not all tested individuals, which places the human two-year-old's achievement on a comparative continuum rather than an island.

The cautious conclusion is that the second birthday marks the reliable arrival of an objective self-concept in the environments most studied, while the test itself is a window on the self, not the self entire.

43.3.2 The medial prefrontal self and its adolescent intensity

Thinking about oneself has a cortical address: the medial prefrontal cortex, the middle wall of the frontal lobes, activates when people judge whether adjectives describe them, retrieve autobiographical memories, or imagine how they look to others.

Jennifer Pfeifer's developmental imaging work shows that this region is not merely present in youth but hyperengaged: in her 2007 and 2013 studies, children and especially adolescents showed stronger medial prefrontal activation than adults during self-evaluation, with activity in early adolescence exceeding both childhood and adulthood for direct self-appraisals.

Adolescents also blur self and audience, since Pfeifer found that appraising yourself and appraising what others think of you recruit overlapping medial prefrontal and mentalizing territory more in adolescents than in adults, a neural echo of the imaginary audience of adolescent psychology, the pervasive sense of being watched and judged.

Leah Somerville showed in 2013 that simply believing a peer is watching produces, in adolescents more than in children or adults, elevated medial prefrontal activity, embarrassment, and physiological arousal, and that medial prefrontal coupling with the striatum, a reward-processing hub, tracks this peer sensitivity.

Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's group, including work with Catherine Sebastian, similarly found that the medial prefrontal node of the social brain is used more heavily by adolescents than adults during mentalizing and self-processing, with activity declining toward adult levels as the region thins structurally through the second decade.

The functional interpretation is that adolescence is a period in which the self is under construction precisely through social evaluation, so the circuitry that computes what do they think of me runs hot.

This intensity has costs, since sensitivity to social evaluation is a plausible ingredient in the adolescent surge of social anxiety and in the power of peer influence, and benefits, since the same sensitivity drives the identity work that section 43.3.3 describes.

The honest note on mechanisms is that lower adult activity is usually interpreted as greater processing efficiency, but the imaging data by themselves show a difference in engagement, not a certified explanation of it.

43.3.3 Narrative identity emerging in adolescence

The final installment of the self is a story.

Narrative identity, in Dan McAdams's definition, is the internalised and evolving story of one's life that integrates the reconstructed past and the imagined future to give life unity and purpose.

Tilmann Habermas and Susan Bluck showed in a landmark 2000 review that the capacity to tell such a story is a specifically adolescent achievement, because it requires four kinds of coherence that develop across roughly ages twelve to twenty: temporal coherence, ordering events in time; causal coherence, explaining how one event and one's own character led to another; thematic coherence, finding recurring meanings across episodes; and command of the cultural concept of biography, the local template of what a life story should contain.

Children can narrate single events well before this, thanks to the parent-scaffolded reminiscing described in the memory chapters, but they cannot yet bind episodes into an explanatory whole, and studies by Habermas and colleagues confirm that global causal and thematic coherence rise steeply across adolescence.

The timing is no accident, since narrative identity draws on precisely the late-maturing capacities catalogued in this part of the book: hypothetical reasoning, perspective-taking through the mentalizing network, autobiographical memory consolidation, and the future-oriented prefrontal machinery of planning.

Erik Erikson had marked adolescence as the stage of identity versus role confusion in 1968, and narrative identity research is the empirical descendant of that claim, replacing a crisis with a measurable construction project.

The way adolescents narrate matters for their wellbeing, since McAdams and Kate McLean's work shows that stories featuring redemption sequences, where bad events lead to good outcomes or growth, and a sense of agency are associated with better mental health, while rumination without resolution is associated with worse.

Narrative identity is also where culture enters the self most explicitly, because the biographical template is cultural property, and Qi Wang's comparative work shows systematic differences, for example between typically more individual-focused American and more relationally focused Chinese self-narratives.

The self of this section is therefore three achievements deep by the end of adolescence: a body recognised at two, an evaluated social self felt acutely in the teens, and a story that, from late adolescence onward, a person continues to revise for the rest of their life.



================================================================================

PART ELEVEN. ADOLESCENCE: THE SECOND RECONSTRUCTION

================================================================================

CHAPTER 44. PUBERTY AND THE REORGANISED BRAIN (CORE)

Adolescence begins with a chemical event: after a decade of quiet, the hormonal systems of childhood wake up and remodel the body and the brain.

This chapter covers that reawakening, the second great wave of structural brain change it accompanies, and the disputed science of sex differences in the developing brain.

The disputes are taught as disputes, because on this topic the field itself is honestly divided, and because few areas of neuroscience are more often misreported.


44.1 The hormonal reawakening

Puberty is not one switch but at least two, thrown years apart.

This section separates them, asks whether hormones or birthdays better explain adolescent brain change, and examines why puberty's timing has been drifting earlier and why adversity accelerates it.

44.1.1 Adrenarche and gonadarche and their separable effects

The first switch is adrenarche, the awakening of the adrenal glands, the small hormone factories that sit atop the kidneys.

Between roughly ages six and eight the adrenal glands begin ramping up production of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and its sulphate, weak androgens, meaning hormones of the testosterone family, and this quiet chemical event eventually contributes to body odour, skin oiliness, and early pubic hair.

The second switch is gonadarche, the true reproductive awakening, in which the hypothalamus, the brain's hormonal control centre, resumes pulsed release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which drives the pituitary gland to signal the gonads, the ovaries or testes, to produce oestradiol or testosterone.

Gonadarche typically begins around ages eight to thirteen in girls and nine to fourteen in boys, and it produces the visible transformation: breast development and menarche, meaning first menstruation, in girls, and testicular growth, voice change, and the growth spurt pattern of boys.

The two switches are biologically separable, controlled by different signalling systems, and each can occur without the other, since children with adrenal failure still undergo gonadarche and fertility.

The separation matters for neuroscience because the two hormone waves may sculpt the brain differently: adrenarcheal DHEA levels have been associated in imaging studies, including work by Anne-Lise Goddings and by the Melbourne imaging group of Sarah Whittle, with structural and functional variation in cortical and limbic regions years before gonadal hormones arrive, and early or exaggerated adrenarche is a risk marker for emotional and behavioural problems.

Some researchers therefore argue that the neurodevelopmental story of puberty starts around age seven, not at the first visible signs.

Against this enthusiasm stands the fact that adrenarche is evolutionarily odd, being robust only in humans and some great apes, and that its function, if any, remains genuinely unknown, so its brain effects are an active research frontier rather than settled science.

44.1.2 Hormones against age in the imaging trajectories

Adolescent brain change could in principle be driven by chronological age, meaning time and experience, or by puberty, meaning hormonal exposure, and because the two are tightly correlated, separating them is one of the field's hardest measurement problems.

The available strategies are to compare same-age children at different pubertal stages, to model hormone levels alongside age in longitudinal samples, and to exploit natural experiments such as precocious puberty or its medical suppression.

The findings so far suggest that puberty carries explanatory weight of its own, especially below the cortex.

In longitudinal analyses by Megan Herting, Elizabeth Sowell, and colleagues, and in the work of Goddings with the Blakemore group published in 2014, development of subcortical structures including the amygdala, hippocampus, and striatum tracked pubertal stage and hormone change, in several cases better than age, with testosterone change predicting volume trajectories in structures such as the amygdala in boys.

Herting's 2017 review concluded that puberty-linked effects are most consistent for subcortical volumes and for cortical thinning in frontal and temporal regions, while also cataloguing how often studies disagree.

Those disagreements deserve emphasis: samples are modest, hormone assays are noisy because levels swing by time of day and cycle, self-reported pubertal stage is imprecise, and a 2021 replication-minded review by Nandita Vijayakumar and colleagues found that many specific hormone-brain associations do not reproduce across cohorts.

The fairest current summary is that puberty is a genuine driver of adolescent brain reorganisation, distinguishable in principle and sometimes in data from age, that subcortical limbic structures show the clearest hormonal signatures, and that any specific claim linking one hormone to one region should be held loosely until it has replicated.

This measured uncertainty is itself a finding, and textbooks that state simple hormone-region facts with confidence are ahead of the evidence.

44.1.3 The secular trend and adversity-accelerated timing

Puberty's timing is not fixed in the species; it responds to conditions, on two timescales.

The long timescale is the secular trend, meaning a change across generations: average age at menarche in Western Europe fell from around sixteen to seventeen years in the mid-nineteenth century to around thirteen by the mid-twentieth, driven by improved nutrition, growth, and health.

The decline slowed after that but has continued at a gentler pace worldwide, with meta-analytic estimates around two to three months earlier per decade for the age of breast development onset, and boys showing a smaller parallel trend.

Rising childhood body fat is a leading suspect for the continuing drift, since the hormone leptin, secreted by fat tissue, is a permissive signal telling the hypothalamus that energy reserves suffice for reproduction, while endocrine-disrupting chemicals are a debated additional suspect with suggestive but unresolved evidence.

The short timescale is the individual life, where a robust and initially surprising finding holds: children exposed to early adversity, including father absence, family conflict, harsh environments, and childhood maltreatment, tend to reach puberty earlier, not later, provided nutrition is adequate.

The association between father absence and earlier menarche has survived meta-analysis, and a 2020 meta-analysis by Jay Belsky's collaborators and others found that threat-type adversity such as abuse predicts earlier pubertal timing while deprivation-type adversity such as neglect or food scarcity does not show the same acceleration.

The going explanation comes from life history theory, an evolutionary framework proposing that organisms adjust the pace of development to expected conditions: where the environment signals danger and unreliability, a faster schedule that reaches reproductive capability sooner is the better bet, and Belsky, Steinberg, and Draper made exactly this prediction for humans in 1991, before most of the data existed.

Severe energy shortage still delays puberty, which is why the acceleration appears in psychosocial adversity with adequate calories rather than in famine.

Early pubertal timing matters for mental health, particularly for girls, since early maturation predicts elevated depression, anxiety, and risk behaviour, through a plausible mismatch between an adult-looking body with adult-level hormones and a still-developing brain and social world.

This links back to section 41.2.2, since accelerated puberty and accelerated amygdala-prefrontal maturation may be two hands of the same clock, both turned forward by early stress.


44.2 The structural second act

The first act of brain construction, the exuberant growth and pruning of infancy and childhood, was covered earlier in this book.

Adolescence is the second act: a decade-long remodelling in which grey matter recedes, white matter advances, and the prefrontal cortex is rebuilt synapse by synapse into its adult form.

44.2.1 The grey-matter thinning and white-matter growth of the second decade

Grey matter is the tissue of cell bodies, synapses, and local connections that forms the brain's outer sheet, and white matter is the tissue of myelinated long-range cables beneath it, white because myelin, the fatty insulation that speeds electrical signals, is pale.

Longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), pioneered at scale by Jay Giedd and colleagues at the National Institute of Mental Health from the 1990s, first suggested that cortical grey matter volume rises through childhood, peaks around early adolescence, and then declines.

Later and larger longitudinal analyses, notably by Kathryn Mills, Christian Tamnes, Blakemore, and colleagues in 2016 across four independent cohorts, revised the timing: cortical grey matter volume is at its maximum in late childhood, before age ten in most samples, and declines steadily across the whole second decade, so the old picture of a mid-adolescent peak was partly an artefact of sparse early data.

The decline is not damage but refinement, and its causes are still being sorted out: synaptic pruning, the elimination of little-used connections, is the classic explanation, but part of the apparent thinning is now believed to reflect ongoing myelination creeping into the lower cortical layers, which makes tissue look more like white matter to the scanner without any loss of neurons.

White matter volume, meanwhile, increases through adolescence into the twenties, and diffusion imaging shows fractional anisotropy, an index of organised myelinated cabling, rising along the major tracts, with association tracts connecting distant cortical regions, such as those linking prefrontal cortex with parietal and temporal cortex, among the last to mature.

The developmental gradient is consistent across studies: sensory and motor cortices finish thinning earliest, while the prefrontal and lateral temporal association cortices, the regions carrying the highest human cognition, continue changing into the mid twenties.

This corpus records, and this chapter repeats, that no evidence supports a specific maturational finish line at age twenty-five, since brain change is measurable into the third decade and beyond, the age twenty-five figure is largely an artefact of studies whose samples stopped there, and different measures mature at different times.

The functional meaning of the structural second act is best summarised as a shift from local to distributed processing: as cables mature and excess synapses go, brain networks become faster, sparser, and more integrated, which parallels the gains in executive function and self-regulation of the same years.

44.2.2 The prefrontal spine elimination into the third decade

The scanner's view of grey matter loss has a microscopic counterpart that can only be seen in post-mortem tissue: the elimination of dendritic spines.

A dendritic spine is a tiny protrusion, a fraction of a thousandth of a millimetre across, on the receiving branches of a neuron, and each spine houses one excitatory synapse, so counting spines is counting connections.

In 2011 Zdravko Petanjek, Ivica Kostovic, and colleagues in Zagreb published in PNAS the definitive human count, analysing Golgi-stained prefrontal tissue, meaning tissue treated with a classic silver stain that renders whole neurons visible, from donors ranging from newborns to the tenth decade of life.

They found that spine density on prefrontal pyramidal neurons in childhood exceeds adult values by two to three times, and that the elimination of this excess begins around puberty but then continues far past adolescence, throughout the third decade of life, stabilising at adult levels only around age thirty.

They called the pattern extraordinary neoteny, borrowing the term for the retention of juvenile traits, because no other primate is known to keep its prefrontal synapses provisional for so long.

The functional reading is that an overproduced synapse population is a reservoir of plasticity, letting experience select the connections worth keeping, and that the human prefrontal cortex extends this selection window across the entire apprenticeship of adult life: education, work, and early adulthood's social choices are, on this view, literally sculpting which connections survive.

The timing also carries clinical weight, since late adolescence and the early twenties are the peak onset years for schizophrenia, and Irwin Feinberg's 1982 hypothesis that schizophrenia involves aberrant adolescent synaptic pruning has been strengthened by the 2016 genetic finding of Aswin Sekar and Steven McCarroll that risk variants in the complement component 4 gene, part of an immune tagging system that marks synapses for removal by microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, are associated with the disorder.

A necessary caution is that the human spine data rest on precious but small numbers of post-mortem brains, so the exact curves carry uncertainty even though the childhood surplus and the prolonged decline are seen consistently, including in comparable primate work.

Together with the previous sub-section, the message is that the prefrontal cortex is the last-finished structure of human development, and that its finishing is not growth but choice among overgrown possibilities, a choice still being made well into the third decade.


44.3 Sex differences and their disputes

Puberty makes male and female bodies diverge visibly, and it is natural to ask what happens in the brain.

This section reports what is actually measured, then teaches the central dispute about what the measurements mean, and ends with the idea that puberty is itself a second window in which hormones organise the brain.

Throughout, sex refers to the biological categories defined by reproductive anatomy and chromosomes, while gender refers to identity and social role, and the studies described here classify participants by sex.

44.3.1 The measured differences and their small size after volume correction

The largest and most reliable sex difference in the human brain is total size: male brains are on average about ten to eleven percent larger in volume, a gap present from childhood and persisting after accounting for body size differences.

Developmental imaging, including Giedd's longitudinal cohorts, also reports that boys' cortical grey matter peaks on average one to two years later than girls', roughly in step with their later puberty.

Beyond global size, the picture becomes contested, and the contest must be taught rather than smoothed over.

Large-sample studies, such as Stuart Ritchie and colleagues' 2018 analysis of about five thousand United Kingdom Biobank adults, find many statistically significant regional differences, with amygdala and hypothalamus proportionally larger in males and some cortical thickness measures greater in females, but the effect sizes are mostly small, with wide overlap between the sexes, and much of the regional difference shrinks when total brain volume is statistically controlled.

Lise Eliot and colleagues pressed this point in a sweeping 2021 review titled Dump the Dimorphism, concluding that beyond size, human brains are not meaningfully dimorphic, meaning not divided into two distinct forms, because once individual differences in overall brain size are accounted for, regional differences are small, inconsistent across studies, and dwarfed by within-sex variation.

Critics replied in commentaries and analyses, including work by Sophie Andrews and colleagues arguing that the differences are not trivial, and analyses showing that brain size differences are not simply explained by body size and that some regional differences survive rigorous volume correction in both directions.

Complicating everything is the correction problem itself, since larger brains differ systematically in composition regardless of sex, so the choice of statistical adjustment method changes which differences survive, and this methodological choice, rarely visible in headlines, drives much of the disagreement between papers.

Two further agreed points frame the dispute: average differences say nothing about any individual, because the distributions overlap massively, and no measured structural difference has been convincingly mapped onto the cognitive or behavioural differences the public most often asks about.

The state of the field, stated plainly, is that global size differs clearly, that small average regional differences probably exist, that their functional meaning is unknown, and that experts genuinely disagree about whether the regional differences are biologically important or largely artefacts of scaling.

44.3.2 The mosaic-brain argument and its counters

In 2015 Daphna Joel and colleagues published in PNAS an analysis of more than fourteen hundred brains that reframed the whole question.

Rather than asking whether averages differ, Joel asked whether individual brains are internally consistent, meaning whether a brain that is male-typical in one feature is male-typical in the rest.

Her answer was no: taking the most sex-differentiated features and defining male-typical and female-typical zones for each, she found that brains showing substantial variability, mixing male-typical and female-typical features, were common, at around twenty-three to fifty-three percent depending on the sample, while internally consistent all-male or all-female brains were rare, at zero to eight percent.

Her conclusion was that human brains do not belong to two distinct classes and are better described as unique mosaics of features, and the paper became a touchstone for arguments against binary brain typologies.

The counters came quickly and must be taught with equal care.

Marco Del Giudice and colleagues showed by simulation that Joel's consistency criterion is so strict that it returns mosaic verdicts even for artificial data built to contain large, consistent sex differences, and that it fails the same way when applied to the faces of men and women, which plainly do differ.

Adam Chekroud, Amy Kuceyeski, and colleagues applied multivariate classification, meaning statistical models that use all brain features at once, to the same kind of data and correctly predicted a person's sex from brain structure about sixty-nine to ninety-three percent of the time depending on dataset and method, far above chance.

Joel's response distinguished the questions: high classification accuracy shows that sex-related information is distributed across the brain, which she does not deny, while her claim concerns internal consistency, whether individual brains line up as uniformly male-typical or female-typical, and on that question her mosaic description stands.

Later work has also shown that classification accuracy drops substantially when brain size is properly controlled, tying this dispute back to the correction problem of the previous sub-section.

The two sides are, in part, answering different questions with different definitions of what a sexed brain would mean, which is why the argument continues, and the honest classroom summary is that sex explains real but distributed variance in brain structure, that few individual brains are uniformly typical of either sex, and that whether one calls this a mosaic or a predictable multivariate difference is partly a choice of emphasis with scientific and social stakes on both sides.

44.3.3 Puberty as a second organisational window

Endocrinology distinguishes two kinds of hormone effect on the brain.

Organisational effects are permanent structural changes made during a sensitive developmental window, while activational effects are reversible changes in function that last only while the hormone is present.

The classical formulation by Charles Phoenix, Robert Goy, and colleagues in 1959 located the organisational window in prenatal and early postnatal life, when testosterone exposure durably shapes the developing rodent brain.

The modern revision, argued most influentially by Cheryl Sisk and Julia Zehr in a 2005 review, is that puberty is a second organisational window: in rodents, gonadal hormones at puberty do not merely activate circuits built earlier but further and lastingly remodel them.

The decisive experiments manipulate hormone timing, and in Sisk's and Kalynn Schulz's studies, male hamsters deprived of testosterone during puberty and given it back in adulthood never fully develop normal adult social and sexual behaviour, showing that the pubertal hormone exposure itself does organising work that later exposure cannot replace.

Rodent work also shows pubertal hormones regulating adolescent synaptic pruning, cell addition, and the maturation of inhibitory signalling in prefrontal and limbic circuits, and Linda Spear's and later reviews frame adolescence as a broad sensitive period for these systems.

In humans the direct evidence is necessarily observational, but several lines fit the second-window idea: the hormone-linked subcortical trajectories of section 44.1.2, the association of pubertal timing with lasting mental health risk in section 44.1.3, and natural experiments such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a condition of elevated prenatal androgen exposure, and clinical puberty suppression, each of which is studied for what it reveals about timing-dependent effects, so far with limited and debated neural findings.

The second-window framing carries a double meaning that this part of the book will keep returning to: a window is a time of opportunity as well as vulnerability, so the same pubertal plasticity that makes adolescence a period of risk for psychopathology also makes it a period when environments, relationships, and interventions may have outsized and lasting effect.

Stated with appropriate caution, the organisational role of puberty is established in rodents, plausible and actively investigated in humans, and not yet demonstrated in humans with the directness the rodent experiments allow.

CHAPTER 45. THE DUAL-SYSTEMS DEBATE (CORE)

Every era has a story it tells about teenagers, and for the past two decades neuroscience has supplied the dominant one.

The story says that the adolescent brain is like a car with a powerful accelerator and unfinished brakes.

This chapter lays out that story in its strongest form, then gives the critics their full say, because the critics have landed real blows.

By the end you will see why most researchers now hold the model loosely, as a useful sketch rather than a settled fact.

45.1 The models

Three closely related theories were proposed within a few years of each other, and together they form what is loosely called the dual-systems family.

This section introduces each one and explains what they share and where they differ.

45.1.1 The dual-systems, imbalance, and driven accounts

In 2008, two laboratories independently proposed strikingly similar theories of why adolescents take more risks than children or adults.

Laurence Steinberg at Temple University called his version the dual-systems model.

BJ Casey, then at the Sackler Institute at Weill Cornell, called her version the maturational imbalance model.

Both start from the same anatomical observation, which earlier chapters of this book have traced in detail.

A set of deep brain structures that respond to reward, often called the socioemotional or incentive system and centred on the striatum, changes rapidly around puberty.

The striatum is a cluster of structures near the middle of the brain that helps signal how rewarding or motivating something is, and its lower portion, the ventral striatum, is especially tied to the anticipation of pleasure.

Meanwhile the prefrontal cortex, the region behind the forehead that supports planning, self-restraint, and weighing the future, matures on a slower schedule that continues into the twenties.

The dual-systems claim is that these two systems develop on different timetables, so that in the middle teen years the reward system is running near its lifetime peak while the control system is still consolidating.

The result is a temporary imbalance, and the models predict that risk taking should peak in adolescence for that reason.

Steinberg's version emphasises trajectories, with sensation seeking rising steeply at puberty and then declining, while impulse control improves gradually and linearly from childhood into the mid twenties.

Casey's imbalance version emphasises the changing balance of connections, arguing that subcortical reward circuitry is functionally mature earlier than the prefrontal circuitry that regulates it, so behaviour is governed by whichever system is stronger at that moment of development.

A third account arrived later, proposed by Beatriz Luna and colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh and set out fully in a 2016 paper by Luna and Wright, and it is called the driven dual-systems model.

The driven account differs in an important way, because Luna's own careful work on tasks that measure voluntary control of eye movements showed that basic cognitive control is largely adult-like by around age 15.

So instead of blaming weak brakes, the driven model says that adolescent cognitive control is essentially available but plateaus in mid adolescence, while a peak in signalling by dopamine, the brain chemical that marks rewards and motivates action, drives the whole system toward immediate rewards.

On this view the adolescent is not failing to control impulses, but is being actively pulled by an especially loud reward signal, sometimes even using good planning abilities in the service of getting the reward.

A useful review by Elizabeth Shulman, Steinberg, and colleagues in 2016, published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience under the title The dual systems model: review, reappraisal, and reaffirmation, treats these three accounts as variations on one theme rather than as rivals.

All three predict an inverted U for reward drive, meaning it rises in early adolescence, peaks in the middle teens, and falls in the twenties.

They differ mainly on the shape of the control curve, whether it climbs steadily into the twenties or levels off by mid adolescence.

45.1.2 What each predicts about risk, reward, and control

A theory earns its keep by making predictions, so it is worth being precise about what each version predicts.

All the models predict that self-reported sensation seeking, which is the appetite for novel and intense experiences, should follow an inverted U across age, peaking somewhere in the mid teens.

Large questionnaire studies, including a study by Steinberg and colleagues across 11 countries published in 2018, broadly find that pattern, with sensation seeking peaking around age 19 in that dataset and impulse control still improving into the twenties.

All the models predict that brain responses to reward, measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which is a scanning method that tracks blood flow changes linked to brain activity, should be larger in adolescents than in children or adults in reward regions such as the ventral striatum.

The models also predict that risky behaviour should track the gap between the two systems, so that a person with high reward drive and low control is at the greatest risk.

They differ in where they place the leverage for change.

Steinberg's version implies that risk taking should decline as impulse control catches up in the twenties.

Casey's version implies that risk taking should be most visible in emotionally charged situations, when the subcortical systems are most engaged, and her group indeed showed that adolescents fail at restraint mainly when the task involves emotional or appetitive cues.

Luna's driven version implies that adolescents can perform at adult levels when properly motivated, and that the developmental story is about the incentive landscape rather than about missing machinery.

Notice one thing the models do not predict, although popular coverage often implies it.

None of them says that adolescents cannot reason about risk, and laboratory studies show that by mid adolescence young people estimate the dangers of driving, drugs, and unprotected sex about as accurately as adults do.

The models locate the difference in what the risks feel like in the heat of the moment, not in what the person knows.

45.2 The critiques

No model in developmental neuroscience has been attacked as vigorously as this one, and the attacks deserve to be presented at full strength rather than as footnotes.

This section gives the critics the floor.

45.2.1 The weak links to real-world risk taking

The first and sharpest critique is that the model was built to explain real-world adolescent recklessness, yet its measured variables connect to real-world recklessness only weakly.

James Bjork and Dustin Pardini put this case forcefully in a 2015 paper in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience titled Who are those risk-taking adolescents, and the question mark in their title was pointed.

They observed that in brain imaging studies, age typically explains only a small fraction of the differences between people in ventral striatum responses, because the variation among adolescents of the same age is enormous.

They also marshalled epidemiological evidence that serious real-world risk taking, such as repeated dangerous driving, early substance dependence, and delinquency, is concentrated in a minority of adolescents, many of whom showed impulsive and disinhibited tendencies from early childhood.

If the reckless minority were already different as children, then their teenage behaviour may reflect a lifelong trait rather than a stage that every adolescent passes through, and a model that attributes recklessness to normal adolescent brain development is aiming at the wrong target.

A related methodological critique landed in 2018 and 2019 under the memorable title Mind the gap, from Kathryn Modecki and colleagues.

They pointed out that the imbalance idea is a claim about the difference between two systems within a person, yet almost no studies had actually computed and tested that difference statistically.

Most studies had measured reward response or control separately and then told an imbalance story afterwards, which is not a rigorous test of an imbalance hypothesis.

There is also the problem of measurement itself.

Laboratory risk tasks, such as simulated driving games and gambling tasks, correlate with each other and with real-world behaviour only modestly, so a finding in the scanner cannot simply be assumed to describe behaviour on an actual Saturday night.

And a plain demographic fact sits awkwardly with the simplest version of the story, which is that some risky behaviours, such as binge drinking in many countries, actually peak in the early twenties, after the supposed peak of the imbalance, when the prefrontal brakes should already be improving.

45.2.2 The lifespan-wisdom and exploration reframings

The second family of critiques accepts much of the data but rejects the framing of adolescence as a period of deficit.

Jennifer Pfeifer and Nicholas Allen published influential critiques in 2012 and 2016 arguing that the dual-systems picture is too tidy.

They noted that studies of adolescent reward response were split, with some finding heightened striatal activity and some finding reduced activity, and that cognitive control does not improve in a single smooth line across all tasks.

They warned that arranging a complicated literature into a simple two-system cartoon risks making the model unfalsifiable, because almost any finding can be absorbed into it after the fact.

Daniel Romer, Valerie Reyna, and Theodore Satterthwaite offered a constructive alternative in 2017 known as the lifespan wisdom model.

Their claim is that the adolescent peak in sensation seeking is not a design flaw but an adaptive feature, an exploration drive that pushes young people out into the world to gather the experience that adult judgment is made of.

On this account, most adolescent risk taking is exploratory and self-limiting, and the seriously harmful outcomes belong mainly to the subset of young people with longstanding weak self-regulation, which echoes the Bjork and Pardini point from a different direction.

Evolutionary and comparative work supports the exploration framing, since adolescent rodents and adolescent primates also show peaks in novelty seeking and in leaving the natal group, which suggests the pattern is ancient and functional rather than a defect of slow frontal wiring.

A further reframing points out that heightened reward sensitivity can serve learning and prosocial ends, and studies have linked adolescent ventral striatum responsiveness to better learning from feedback and, in some work, to positive outcomes such as declining depressive symptoms when the reward responses occur in family and prosocial contexts.

The moral of these reframings is not that the developmental changes are unreal, but that calling them an imbalance imports a value judgment that the data do not force.

45.3 The present verdict

Where does the debate stand now, after nearly two decades of argument?

This closing section states the current consensus as fairly as it can, and names what evidence would actually settle the matter.

45.3.1 Reaffirmation with nuance, and what would settle it

The 2016 reappraisal by Shulman, Steinberg, and colleagues conceded openly that presentations of the model had sometimes oversimplified the evidence and overlooked inconsistencies, while arguing that the framework survives as a useful heuristic, meaning a simplifying tool for generating testable ideas.

That concession and defence together capture the present verdict rather well.

The behavioural backbone of the model has held up, since the inverted U in sensation seeking and the gradual climb of self-control have been replicated across many countries and cultures.

The strongest neural claims have softened, since meta-analyses, which are studies that pool the results of many studies, find adolescent striatal reward responses that are elevated on average but heterogeneous across tasks and reward phases.

The claim that normal adolescent brain development explains serious real-world recklessness has fared worst, and most careful writers now restrict the model to explaining population-level tendencies in specific hot contexts, especially peer-charged and emotionally arousing ones, rather than explaining which individual will crash a car.

What would settle it is reasonably clear.

First, studies must measure both systems in the same people over time and statistically test whether the within-person gap between them predicts later behaviour, which is exactly what the Mind the gap authors demanded, and large longitudinal projects such as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, which is following more than eleven thousand United States children from around age 9 into adulthood, finally make that possible.

Second, the field needs measures of risk taking with real-world validity, such as smartphone-based reports of daily behaviour, rather than relying on gambling games in a scanner.

Third, the exploration account and the imbalance account make different predictions about the character of adolescent risk taking, since exploration should look like structured novelty seeking that declines with experience, while imbalance should look like failures of restraint under arousal, and studies designed to tell those apart are still few.

Until that work is done, the honest summary is this.

Adolescence really does bring a rise in reward drive that outpaces the slower consolidation of self-control, and that asymmetry really does shape behaviour in emotionally charged moments.

But the asymmetry is a population tendency with wide individual variation, it is plausibly adaptive rather than defective, and it explains far less of real-world adolescent risk than the car-with-no-brakes story suggested.


CHAPTER 46. REWARD, PEERS, AND THE SOCIAL REORIENTATION (CORE)

If one theme unifies adolescent neuroscience, it is that the teenage brain turns toward other teenagers.

This chapter follows that turn through three linked stories, the striatum's changing response to reward, the startling power of a merely watching peer, and the slow construction of the brain network we use to think about other minds.

Together they describe what researchers call the social reorientation of adolescence.

46.1 The striatal adolescence

The striatum, introduced in the previous chapter as the brain's reward hub, has its own adolescence.

This section examines the famous claim that the adolescent striatum is hyperreactive to reward, the contrary findings that complicated the claim, and the reconciliations that followed.

46.1.1 Reward hyperreactivity, its contrary findings, and the reconciliations

The hyperreactivity story began with a 2006 study by Adriana Galvan, then working with BJ Casey, which scanned children, adolescents, and adults while they received rewards of different sizes.

Adolescents showed larger responses than either children or adults in the nucleus accumbens, which is the core of the ventral striatum, and this became the emblematic finding of the field.

But almost simultaneously, James Bjork and colleagues reported the opposite, finding that adolescents showed weaker ventral striatal activity than adults while anticipating rewards in a task called the monetary incentive delay task, in studies published in 2004 and repeated with a larger sample in 2010.

For several years the field lived with a straightforward contradiction, with some laboratories finding adolescent hyperreactivity and others finding hypoactivation, meaning a weaker than adult response.

The reconciliations came from looking closely at what, exactly, each task measured.

One resolution concerns the phase of reward processing, because a reward event unfolds in stages, first a cue that a reward is possible, then a period of anticipation, then the outcome itself.

Studies that separated these stages found that adolescents could show a weaker response than adults to the initial cue and a stronger response during anticipation or at the moment of receiving the reward, so two studies probing different moments of the same task could honestly reach opposite conclusions.
