A second resolution concerns effort and agency, since Bjork's task required a fast button press to win the reward, and adolescents may engage anticipatory circuitry less when the reward hangs on an effortful response, while tasks like Galvan's deliver the reward as an outcome of a simple choice.

A third resolution concerns what the reward is, because adolescent striatal responses are most reliably elevated for rewards that are immediate, uncertain, or social, and flatter for abstract or delayed ones.

Meta-analyses pooling dozens of studies now support a moderate version of the original claim, finding that on average adolescents do show elevated ventral striatal responses to receiving rewards compared with adults, with the strongest elevation in mid adolescence, while anticipation findings remain mixed.

There is also a temperamental layer, since work such as a 2021 study linking novelty seeking to striatal and prefrontal responses shows that individual personality differences within adolescence are often larger than the average difference between age groups.

And an important reinterpretation, argued by Eva Telzer in a 2016 review, notes that the same heightened striatal responsiveness predicts good outcomes when it is engaged by learning, family, and prosocial contexts, which cautions against reading hyperreactivity as a synonym for vulnerability.

The fair summary is that the adolescent striatum is not simply louder, but differently tuned, most responsive to immediate, uncertain, and social rewards, with wide individual variation around the average.

46.2 The peer effect

Adults often say that a teenager alone is a different person from a teenager in a group, and this is one of the few pieces of folk wisdom that laboratory neuroscience has confirmed almost exactly.

This section covers the famous driving simulator experiments and the related finding that adolescents are acutely sensitive to being left out.

46.2.1 Peer presence doubling risk taking in the simulator

In 2005, Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg published a deceptively simple experiment.

Adolescents, college-aged young adults, and adults played a video driving game called Chicken, either alone or with two friends watching, and the measure was how much risk they took.

Among the adolescents, around ages 13 to 16, the mere presence of peers roughly doubled risk taking, the effect was smaller in the college-aged group, and it was essentially absent in adults.

Nobody was daring anybody, and the friends often said nothing at all, so the effect could not be explained by explicit peer pressure.

In 2011, Jason Chein, Steinberg, and colleagues took the paradigm into the scanner using a driving task called the Stoplight game, in which the player approaches a series of intersections and must decide at each yellow light whether to brake safely or run the light and risk a crash, with faster finishes earning more money.

Each participant played twice, once alone and once while two same-age, same-sex friends watched from an adjacent room, in a design where every person served as their own comparison.

Adolescents, but not adults, took significantly more risks when their friends were watching.

Crucially, the brain data showed why, because during peer observation the adolescents showed heightened activity in the ventral striatum and the orbitofrontal cortex, which is the reward-linked region on the underside of the front of the brain, and the size of that reward activation predicted how much risk they subsequently took.

Prefrontal control activity did not differ much between conditions, which suggested that peers were not disabling the brakes but were turning up the perceived reward of the risky choice, making running the light feel more worth it.

The finding has been extended in telling ways.

Work by Ashley Smith, Steinberg, and colleagues showed the peer effect even when the observing peers were anonymous and unseen, and a 2018 study by Joao Guassi Moreira and Eva Telzer found that having a parent present, rather than a peer, eliminated the adolescent rise in risky choices and dampened the associated striatal response.

Animal work found something similar in its own key, since a 2014 study by Zoe Logue, Steinberg, and colleagues reported that adolescent mice, but not adult mice, drank more alcohol when housed with other adolescents.

Real-world statistics complete the picture, because crash data show that a teenage driver's risk of a fatal accident rises steeply with each additional teenage passenger in the car, while adult drivers show no such passenger effect, and this evidence contributed to graduated driver licensing laws that restrict passengers for new drivers.

Replications of the laboratory effect have not been uniformly successful, and some studies find the peer effect only in males or only under some conditions, so the honest reading is that peer presence reliably shifts adolescent decision-making on average, with the size of the shift varying across samples and tasks.

46.2.2 Social exclusion sensitivity

The other side of the peer coin is the pain of being left out, and researchers study it with a disarmingly simple game called Cyberball.

In Cyberball, invented by Kipling Williams in 2000, the participant plays a virtual ball-tossing game with two other players who are supposedly real people online but are actually controlled by the computer, and after a friendly start the other two players begin throwing only to each other.

Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman, and Williams showed in a landmark 2003 study of adults that this mild exclusion activates regions including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and the anterior insula, areas that also respond to the distress of physical pain, which is why the finding was reported under the phrase social pain.

Developmental studies then asked whether adolescents feel this more keenly, and the broad answer is yes.

Catherine Sebastian, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, and colleagues showed in studies published in 2010 and 2011 that adolescent girls reported larger drops in mood after exclusion than adult women did, and that the neural response to exclusion was still developing, with adolescents engaging ventrolateral prefrontal regions, which help regulate distress, less effectively than adults.

A developmental study by Sandy Overgaauw, Berna Guroglu, Eveline Crone, and colleagues comparing participants aged 10 to 12, 14 to 16, and 19 to 21 found that exclusion distressed every age group, but the youngest group showed heightened activity in the subgenual anterior cingulate, a region tied to negative mood and later implicated in depression.

Adolescents are also more likely than adults to change their stated preferences to match peers after exclusion, which links the pain of exclusion directly to conformity.

A note of scientific caution belongs here, because a 2021 meta-analysis of Cyberball imaging studies by researchers pooling many samples found that exclusion most reliably engages the default network, the set of midline regions active during self-reflection and thinking about others, and found weaker consistency for the classic pain-region story than early papers suggested.

So the mature summary is that exclusion reliably engages brain systems for social meaning and self-relevant emotion, that adolescents feel exclusion unusually strongly, and that the once-popular claim that social pain literally shares the brain's physical pain circuitry is now contested.

Evolutionary thinking makes the heightened sensitivity intelligible, since for an adolescent leaving the protection of the family, acceptance by the peer group has been, for most of human history, a matter of survival and future mating, and a brain that treats exclusion as an emergency is a brain tuned to those stakes.

46.3 The social reorientation

The phrase social reorientation was given currency by a 2005 paper by Eric Nelson, Ellen Leibenluft, Erin McClure, and Daniel Pine, which proposed that puberty triggers a shift in the brain's social information processing, redirecting motivation from parents toward peers, status, and potential partners.

This section follows the brain networks that carry out that shift.

46.3.1 The mentalising network's continued construction

Mentalising is the everyday miracle of thinking about what someone else thinks, feels, or intends, and it runs on a well-mapped brain network.

The core regions are the medial prefrontal cortex, on the middle surface of the frontal lobe, the temporoparietal junction, where the temporal and parietal lobes meet above the ear, the superior temporal sulcus, a groove along the side of the brain that tracks biological motion and gaze, and the temporal poles at the tips of the temporal lobes.

Children pass the classic false-belief tests of mentalising around age 4, so it is tempting to assume the system is finished in the preschool years, but the adolescent data say otherwise.

Structural imaging, summarised in the work of Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Kathryn Mills, and colleagues including a 2014 structural study by Mills, shows that grey matter volume in medial prefrontal and temporoparietal regions continues to change across the second decade, with cortical thinning and synaptic remodelling continuing into the early twenties.

Functional imaging shows a consistent and initially puzzling pattern, in which adolescents activate the medial prefrontal cortex more than adults do during mentalising tasks, with activity in this region declining from adolescence into adulthood across many studies.

The favoured interpretations are that adolescents rely more on effortful self-referential simulation when reading others, while adults shift toward more automatic, experience-based strategies supported by temporal regions, though the field acknowledges this is not fully settled.

Behaviour matures late as well, and a 2010 study by Iroise Dumontheil, Ian Apperly, and Blakemore using a communication game called the director task, where the participant must move objects while accounting for what a director on the other side of a shelf can and cannot see, found that performance was still improving between late adolescence and adulthood.

So the machinery for understanding other minds, first assembled in the preschool years, is being rebuilt and refined exactly when the adolescent's social world is becoming most complicated, which is either a happy coincidence or, as the next section argues, a design.

46.3.2 Adolescence as a proposed sensitive period for sociocultural processing

A sensitive period is a stretch of development during which a particular kind of experience shapes the brain more powerfully than the same experience would earlier or later, and earlier chapters described such periods for vision and for language in early life.

In a 2014 Annual Review of Psychology article titled Is adolescence a sensitive period for sociocultural processing, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore and Kathryn Mills proposed that adolescence may be a second such period, this time for learning the social and cultural world, and they posed it deliberately as a question rather than a conclusion.

The circumstantial case is strong.

The social brain regions are undergoing deep structural remodelling in adolescence, and periods of remodelling are, on general plasticity principles, periods of heightened susceptibility to experience.

Adolescents show heightened sensitivity to precisely social inputs, to peer evaluation, exclusion, status, and social reward, as the earlier sections of this chapter documented.

And the skills being acquired, such as navigating alliances, norms, reputation, and romantic life, are exactly the sociocultural skills a second sensitive period would be for.

Supportive evidence has accumulated, and a striking example is a series of studies by Lisa Knoll, Blakemore, and colleagues in 2015 and 2016 showing that adolescents adjust their risk judgments more in response to other teenagers' opinions than adults adjust to anyone's, and that training-related gains in certain cognitive skills were larger in late adolescence than earlier, hinting at windows of elevated learning.

The hard evidence, however, is still thin, and the authors themselves and later commentators have said so plainly.

Demonstrating a sensitive period strictly requires showing that matched experience has larger or qualitatively different effects at one age than at others, which in humans demands rare natural experiments or long training studies, and few exist for adolescence.

A 2024 reappraisal in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews revisiting the hypothesis a decade on concluded that the idea remains plausible and generative but not yet demonstrated in the strict sense.

The stakes of the question are considerable, because if adolescence is a sensitive period for sociocultural learning, then the social environments societies build for teenagers, their schools, their neighbourhoods, and their online platforms, are not merely contexts but formative inputs, with effects that may echo for decades.

The next chapter takes up the darker half of that thought, since a window that lets the world in cannot choose what the world sends.


CHAPTER 47. SLEEP, PSYCHOPATHOLOGY ONSET, AND THE ADOLESCENT WINDOW (CORE)

This chapter braids together three facts that at first seem unrelated.

Teenagers cannot fall asleep early, most mental illness begins in youth, and the adolescent brain is unusually open to being changed.

Seen together, they describe adolescence as a window, one that lets in both harm and help.

47.1 The circadian shift

Everyone who has lived with a teenager knows the nightly standoff over bedtime and the morning battle with the alarm clock.

This section explains why biology, not laziness, is the main author of that script.

47.1.1 The pubertal phase delay and the school-start-time evidence

The body's daily timing is governed by the circadian system, an internal clock of roughly twenty-four hours seated in a small cluster of brain cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which sits just above the crossing of the optic nerves and is reset each day by light.

One of the clock's outputs is melatonin, a hormone released by the pineal gland in the evening that signals to the body that the biological night has begun.

The central discovery, established across the 1990s and 2000s by Mary Carskadon at Brown University, is that puberty shifts this whole system later, a change called a phase delay.

As adolescents move through the pubertal stages, evening melatonin release moves later by roughly one to three hours, so a teenager's brain may not issue its darkness signal until 11 at night, at a clock time when the same child a few years earlier was already sleepy.

The pressure to sleep also builds more slowly across the day in adolescents, which makes late evening wakefulness easier, and modern evening light, especially from screens, pushes the delayed clock later still.

Yet sleep need does not shrink, and the evidence indicates adolescents still need roughly 8 to 10 hours a night.

The collision comes at the other end of the night, because school starts on adult time.

A teenager whose biology favours sleep from midnight to 9 in the morning, forced to wake at 6:30 for a 7:30 bell, is being asked to start the day near the lowest point of their circadian cycle, and Carskadon memorably compared it to permanent jet lag.

Her field studies made the cost measurable, and in one key study of a school district whose start time moved earlier between ninth and tenth grade, students showed daytime sleepiness in the laboratory at levels typical of patients with clinical sleep disorders, with some falling directly into dream sleep during morning nap tests.

The school-start-time literature turned this science into one of the clearest policy experiments in developmental neuroscience.

When the Edina and Minneapolis districts in Minnesota moved high school start times later in the late 1990s, Kyla Wahlstrom's evaluations found students slept more, attended more, and reported better mood.

Later studies, including work by Judith Owens, found that even modest delays of 25 to 30 minutes increased sleep duration and reduced daytime sleepiness, and district-level analyses associated later starts with fewer motor vehicle crashes among teenage drivers.

The evidence base is largely observational rather than randomised, and effect sizes vary across studies, but the direction of the findings has been consistent enough that in 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics formally recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 in the morning, and California enacted a statewide law to that effect that took full force in 2022.

Chronic adolescent sleep restriction matters for this book because short and mistimed sleep in adolescence is associated with worse emotion regulation, more risk taking, and elevated depressive symptoms, which connects the nightly standoff directly to the chapter's next topic.

47.2 The epidemiology of onset

Epidemiology is the science of counting who gets ill and when, and for mental health its findings about age are among the most important numbers in this entire book.

This section presents them plainly.

47.2.1 Most mental disorders beginning before the mid-twenties, peaking near fourteen

For decades, psychiatry was organised around adults, yet the counting shows that mental illness is overwhelmingly a condition of the young.

The modern anchor was set by Ronald Kessler and colleagues in 2005, using the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, a diagnostic interview study of more than nine thousand adults in the United States.

They found that half of all lifetime mental disorders had begun by age 14, and three quarters by age 24.

In 2021, Marco Solmi, Joaquim Radua, Paolo Fusar-Poli, and colleagues published in Molecular Psychiatry a meta-analysis of 192 epidemiological studies covering more than seven hundred thousand people, the largest synthesis of age-of-onset data ever assembled.

Across all mental disorders combined, the peak age at onset was 14.5 years, with about a third of individuals experiencing onset before age 14, nearly half before 18, and about 62 percent before 25.

The timing differs by condition in an orderly way.

Neurodevelopmental conditions such as attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder declare themselves earliest, followed by anxiety and fear-related disorders, whose median onsets fall in childhood and early adolescence, then eating disorders and substance use disorders in adolescence and the late teens, then psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia around age 20, and mood disorders somewhat later still.

Two cautions keep these numbers honest.

Retrospective surveys, which ask adults to remember when problems began, tend to place onsets later than prospective studies that follow children forward, so if anything the true onsets are earlier than the classic figures.

And onset of a diagnosable disorder is usually preceded by years of milder difficulty, so the peak at 14.5 marks the visible surfacing of processes that often began earlier.

The implication, drawn explicitly by the authors of these studies, is that mental health systems built around adult services are structurally aimed at the wrong ages, arriving after the developmental moment when most disorders take root.

47.2.2 The sex divergence at puberty

Before puberty, the overall landscape of mental health problems does not favour girls, and several conditions, including attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism as currently diagnosed, are identified more often in boys.

At puberty the landscape reorganises, and the clearest case is depression.

In childhood, depression rates in boys and girls are similar.

A 2017 meta-analysis by Rachel Salk, Janet Hyde, and Lyn Abramson, pooling representative samples covering millions of people across many nations, found that a female excess in depression diagnoses is detectable by around age 12, widens sharply through the teen years, with girls aged 13 to 15 roughly two to three times as likely as boys to be diagnosed, and then narrows to the stable adult ratio of roughly two to one.

The divergence tracks pubertal stage better than it tracks chronological age, and girls who go through puberty earlier than their peers show elevated risk of depression, which points at pubertal processes rather than the calendar.

Anxiety disorders and eating disorders show a similar female preponderance emerging across adolescence, while boys remain more likely to show conduct problems and early substance issues, a split often summarised as internalising problems rising in girls and externalising problems in boys, where internalising means distress turned inward as sadness and worry and externalising means distress turned outward as rule-breaking and aggression.

Why the divergence happens is genuinely unsettled, and honest writing must say so.

Candidate contributors include the direct effects of ovarian hormones such as estradiol on stress and mood circuitry, sex differences in the reactivity of the stress hormone system, the earlier average timing of female puberty colliding with the social pressures of early adolescence, higher rates of certain exposures for girls including sexual harassment and appearance-focused evaluation, and cognitive styles such as rumination, meaning repetitive dwelling on distress, which is more common in adolescent girls.

Most researchers now favour models in which pubertal biology creates a susceptibility that social context then acts upon, rather than any single-cause account.

The sex divergence matters scientifically because it is one of the largest and most reliable facts about adolescent mental health, and any complete theory of the adolescent window has to explain it.

47.3 The window framing

Having seen that the adolescent brain is remodelling and that mental illness clusters its beginnings in exactly these years, we can now name the framing that organises this part of the book.

Adolescence is a window, and the same openness that permits harm permits growth.

47.3.1 Risk and opportunity in the same plasticity

Plasticity is the brain's capacity to be changed by experience, and this book has repeatedly shown that plasticity is not spread evenly across life but concentrated in periods of remodelling.

Adolescence is such a period, with cortical grey matter thinning as circuits are pruned and refined, connections between distant regions strengthening, and neurochemical systems, including dopamine and the maturing balance of excitation and inhibition, shifting their set points.

The window framing, articulated in a widely cited 2015 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences by Delia Fuhrmann, Lisa Knoll, and Sarah-Jayne Blakemore titled Adolescence as a sensitive period of brain development, holds that this plasticity makes adolescence simultaneously a period of vulnerability and a window of opportunity.

The vulnerability side is written in the epidemiology just reviewed, since a brain being remodelled is a brain that stress, social adversity, and toxic exposures can push onto lasting tracks, and rodent studies show that stress in the adolescent period can have effects on later anxiety-like and depression-like behaviour that the same stress does not produce in adults.

The opportunity side is the same coin, since heightened plasticity means interventions, education, and improved environments should also bite deeper in adolescence.

Evidence for the opportunity side includes the training studies by Knoll and colleagues suggesting late adolescence can be an especially effective time for certain kinds of cognitive learning, the school-start-time results showing that a structural change in the environment yields measurable benefits, and prevention research finding that programs targeting adolescent depression and substance use can shift trajectories when delivered before disorders consolidate.

Honesty requires bounds on the claim.

The strict demonstration that adolescent plasticity exceeds adult plasticity for any particular human function is available in only a few domains, the rodent evidence is far ahead of the human evidence, and the window language can be oversold into a new deadline panic, as if a person unhelped by 25 is beyond help, which the recovery and treatment literature flatly contradicts.

The defensible claim is comparative and probabilistic, that inputs during adolescence tend to matter more than the same inputs later, which is reason to concentrate care and good environments on the young without ever writing off the old.

47.3.2 Substance use and the developing brain

The window framing predicts that psychoactive substances, which are chemicals that alter brain function, should matter more when the brain is still under construction, and adolescence is when most substance use begins.

Epidemiologically the prediction holds, since starting alcohol or cannabis use in early adolescence is associated with substantially higher rates of later dependence than starting the same use in adulthood, though how much of that reflects the age itself versus the pre-existing traits of early starters is contested, as we shall see.

Alcohol is the best-studied case.

Adolescent rodents are less sensitive than adults to alcohol's sedating effects, which permits longer and heavier drinking bouts, and adolescent alcohol exposure in rodents produces lasting changes in the hippocampus, the seahorse-shaped memory structure deep in the temporal lobe, and in prefrontal circuitry.

In humans, longitudinal imaging studies, including work by Susan Tapert and colleagues in the National Consortium on Alcohol and Neurodevelopment in Adolescence, find that adolescents who begin heavy episodic drinking show altered trajectories of grey and white matter development compared with non-drinking peers, though disentangling cause from pre-existing difference remains the central difficulty.

Cannabis is where the science is most contested, and this book records the dispute rather than smoothing it over.

The famous finding is from Madeline Meier, Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi, and colleagues in 2012, using the Dunedin cohort of about one thousand New Zealanders followed from birth, which reported that persistent cannabis dependence beginning in adolescence was associated with a decline of roughly six to eight intelligence quotient (IQ) points from childhood to age 38, with no comparable decline in adult-onset users.

The finding was promptly challenged, most prominently in a 2013 analysis by Ole Rogeberg showing that time-varying effects of socioeconomic status could in principle reproduce the association without any causal effect of cannabis, and twin studies later found that cannabis-using twins did not decline relative to their non-using co-twins, which points toward shared family and predispositional factors explaining much of the association.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies found that frequent or dependent adolescent cannabis use was associated with an IQ decline of about two points, far smaller than the headline Dunedin figure, and imaging claims of cannabis-related structural brain change have also been mixed, with a well-known 2015 study by Barbara Weiland and colleagues finding no morphometric differences once alcohol use was controlled.

The newest evidence comes from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, and a 2026 analysis of more than eleven thousand youths followed for six to seven years reported that adolescents who initiated cannabis use showed slower gains in memory, attention, and processing speed than non-using peers even after controlling for family and socioeconomic factors, which strengthens the case for a real but modest effect while still falling short of experimental proof.

The balanced summary is that heavy and early adolescent substance use is reliably associated with worse cognitive and mental health outcomes, that some portion of the association reflects pre-existing differences in the young people who start early, that the causal residue appears most likely for heavy and persistent use beginning young, and that on the window framing even a modest causal effect lands on a brain at its most formative, which is why every major health body counsels delaying use as long as possible.

Nicotine deserves a closing word, since adolescent rodent studies show lasting changes to attention and to the acetylcholine signalling system from adolescent nicotine exposure, and the rise of high-concentration nicotine vaping has re-exposed a generation to a substance the developing brain handles badly.

PART TWELVE. WHEN DEVELOPMENT GOES DIFFERENTLY

================================================================================

CHAPTER 48. THE DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOPATHOLOGY FRAMEWORK (APPARATUS)

Before this book can examine autism, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and the other conditions of the coming chapters, it needs a set of thinking tools.

Those tools come from a discipline called developmental psychopathology, founded in the 1980s by figures including Dante Cicchetti, Alan Sroufe, and Michael Rutter, which insists that disorder can only be understood as development gone along a different path, and that studying atypical development illuminates typical development in return.

This chapter lays out the framework's founding concepts and then its more recent dimensional turn.

48.1 The founding concepts

The founding concepts are a small vocabulary of ideas about how lives unfold, and once learned they change how every later chapter reads.

This section introduces them one by one with concrete examples.

48.1.1 Equifinality and multifinality

The two strangest-looking words in this book are also among the most useful, and they were imported into developmental psychopathology from general systems theory, the study of complex self-organising systems associated with Ludwig von Bertalanffy, in a short and hugely influential 1996 paper by Dante Cicchetti and Fred Rogosch in the journal Development and Psychopathology.

Equifinality means that the same end state can be reached from many different starting points along many different routes.

Two adults may both meet criteria for depression, yet one arrived there through childhood maltreatment and an overactive stress system, another through a strong genetic loading and a series of losses, and their identical-looking diagnosis conceals entirely different developmental histories.

Multifinality is the mirror image, meaning that the same starting point can lead to many different end states.

Two children may both experience early maltreatment, yet one later develops depression, another develops conduct problems, and a third develops no disorder at all, because the effect of any single influence depends on the whole system of other influences it lands among, including genes, relationships, temperament, and chance.

Together these two principles demolish the simple ideas of one cause per disorder and one outcome per cause, and they explain at a stroke why the search for the single gene for depression or the single early sign of any disorder kept failing.

They also carry a practical message for research design, which is that studies must follow many children along their actual pathways over time, rather than comparing snapshots of diagnosed and undiagnosed groups, and the longitudinal studies that fill the coming chapters are the fruit of taking that message seriously.

48.1.2 Developmental cascades and heterotypic continuity

A developmental cascade is the process by which an effect in one domain of life spills into other domains and grows over time, the way a small stream high on a mountain becomes a river in the valley.

The concept was formalised most influentially by Ann Masten and Dante Cicchetti in a 2010 special issue of Development and Psychopathology.

A classic documented cascade runs from early behaviour problems to academic failure to deeper problems, since a child whose aggression and inattention in the early grades interfere with learning falls behind academically, the failure and peer rejection then feed frustration and low mood, and by adolescence the original modest behaviour problem has cascaded into academic disengagement and internalising distress, a chain traced empirically in longitudinal work by Masten and colleagues in 2005.

Cascades matter for intervention because they identify leverage points, since interrupting the chain early, for instance by supporting reading or peer relationships, can prevent downstream problems that no amount of later treatment addresses as cheaply.

Heterotypic continuity is the companion idea, and it means that an underlying difficulty can persist over time while completely changing its outward costume.

The word heterotypic simply means of a different form.

The irritable, tantrum-prone preschooler, the worried school-age child, the withdrawn adolescent, and the depressed young adult may in some lives be the same underlying vulnerability wearing four different age-appropriate costumes, and longitudinal studies find exactly such chains, for example childhood anxiety predicting adolescent and adult depression more strongly than it predicts adult anxiety in some cohorts.

Its opposite, homotypic continuity, where the same disorder persists in the same form, also occurs, and disentangling the two patterns is a central task of developmental epidemiology.

Heterotypic continuity carries a warning for both parents and diagnostic systems, which is that counting how many children keep the same diagnosis over time will understate how much genuine continuity of difficulty there is, because the difficulty keeps changing its name.

48.1.3 Resilience as ordinary magic

Resilience is the observation that many children exposed to serious adversity nonetheless develop well, and its scientific study began with researchers including Norman Garmezy, Michael Rutter, and Emmy Werner, whose Kauai Longitudinal Study followed every child born on that Hawaiian island in 1955 and found that about a third of those born into high-risk circumstances grew into competent, caring adults.

The early literature sometimes described such children as invulnerable or extraordinary, and the field's most important correction of that idea came in a 2001 paper in American Psychologist by Ann Masten titled Ordinary Magic: Resilience Processes in Development.

Masten's argument, distilled from decades of longitudinal evidence, was that resilience is not rare and does not come from rare qualities.

It is common, and it arises from the ordinary operations of basic human adaptive systems, including at least one committed caregiving relationship, adequately functioning brain systems for learning and self-regulation, connections to competent adults and prosocial peers, effective schools, a sense of self-efficacy, and cultural sources of meaning such as faith and tradition.

The magic, in other words, is ordinary, and the phrase was chosen to retire the image of the invulnerable superkid.

The flip side of the claim is sobering, because if resilience flows from ordinary protective systems, then the greatest threats to development are precisely those adversities that damage the protective systems themselves, which is why maltreatment by a caregiver, chronic poverty that exhausts parents, and institutional deprivation, all of which strike the caregiving system directly, appear throughout this book as the heaviest risks.

Modern resilience science has moved from listing protective factors to studying processes and systems, and Masten's later work frames resilience as the capacity of a whole system, child, family, school, and community together, to adapt to disturbance, which relocates responsibility from the lone heroic child to the web around the child.

Neuroscience has joined in, examining how protective relationships buffer the stress hormone system and how individual differences in brain reactivity make some children more sensitive to both bad and good environments, a theme the differential susceptibility literature discussed earlier in this book develops.

For the chapters ahead, resilience is the constant counterweight, the reminder that every risk statistic describes probabilities across groups, never destinies for individuals.

48.2 The dimensional turn

The framework's newest chapter is a shift from asking which category of disorder a person has to asking where a person falls along continuous dimensions of functioning.

This section explains the two most influential expressions of that shift and the criticisms each has drawn.

48.2.1 The research domain criteria and their underdeveloped developmental axis

In 2010, the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the primary funder of mental health research in the United States, launched the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) initiative, led by Bruce Cuthbert and then-director Thomas Insel.

RDoC begins from a frustration this book has already met, which is that diagnostic categories such as those in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) do not map cleanly onto genes, brain circuits, or treatment response, since people with the same diagnosis differ profoundly and people with different diagnoses share underlying features.

The RDoC proposal is to reorganise research, not around diagnostic categories, but around basic functional domains that cut across diagnoses, such as negative valence systems for threat and loss responses, positive valence systems for reward, cognitive systems, systems for social processes, arousal and regulatory systems, and sensorimotor systems.

Each domain is to be studied across multiple units of analysis at once, from genes and molecules through circuits and physiology to behaviour and self-report, with the hope that natural clusters found this way will carve mental illness closer to its joints than committee-defined categories do.

The framework nominally includes two orthogonal axes running through everything, one for development and one for environment, and here the developmental psychopathology community lodged its central complaint.

Critics, in a literature that includes commentaries by developmental researchers such as Theodore Beauchaine, Dante Cicchetti, and colleagues across the 2010s and a 2021 review calling for a neurodevelopmental framework to translate RDoC into real-world impact, argued that the developmental axis was left as a promissory note.

A dimension such as reward sensitivity is not one thing across life, since the same striatal measure means different things at 8, 14, and 30, as chapter 45 and 46 showed in detail, and a static snapshot of a circuit says little about the pathway by which it came to its present state.

Equifinality and multifinality apply to circuits as much as to diagnoses, so the same neural profile can arise from different histories and lead to different futures, which means that circuits without trajectories cannot deliver the predictive power RDoC promised.

NIMH has acknowledged the gap, and later RDoC statements emphasise neurodevelopmental trajectories and environmental interaction more strongly, while large longitudinal projects such as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study are, in effect, the attempt to give RDoC the developmental spine it lacked.

The fair summary is that RDoC's dimensional ambition is broadly shared, its concrete achievements in changing clinical practice remain modest after fifteen years, and its developmental axis is still the least built part of the structure.

48.2.2 The p-factor and the continuum view of neurodevelopmental conditions

The second expression of the dimensional turn is a statistical discovery with large implications.

When researchers measure many different symptoms in the same large population, every kind of problem correlates positively with every other kind, so a person with more anxiety symptoms also tends, on average, to have somewhat more conduct problems, more attention problems, and so on.

In 2014, Avshalom Caspi, Terrie Moffitt, and colleagues, analysing the Dunedin cohort, showed that this web of correlations can be summarised by a single general factor of psychopathology, which they called the p-factor, by deliberate analogy with the general intelligence factor g that summarises the positive correlations among cognitive tests.

A person's standing on p indexes their overall liability to develop any and many forms of mental disorder, with higher p associated with more severity, more comorbidity, meaning the co-occurrence of multiple diagnoses, worse developmental history, and greater impairment.

The finding has been replicated in many cohorts and in children as well as adults, and it gives statistical flesh to the developmental psychopathology claims of this chapter, since a general liability flowing into different specific outcomes is multifinality written as an equation.

The p-factor is also seriously contested, and the criticisms deserve full statement.

Statisticians have shown that a general factor can emerge from correlated data for many different underlying reasons, so good model fit does not establish that p is a real causal entity rather than a summary score, a point pressed in critiques by Eiko Fried, Ashley Watts, and colleagues, and even Caspi and Moffitt's own 2024 reappraisal concedes that competing statistical models fit about equally well and that p should be interpreted cautiously.

What p actually is remains open, with proposed interpretations including a general disposition toward negative emotionality, impairments in thought and reality processing, poor executive regulation, or simply the sum of many small transdiagnostic causes, and no interpretation has won.

The same dimensional logic has been applied to the neurodevelopmental conditions that occupy the next chapters, and here it is transforming how the conditions are understood.

Twin and population studies show that the traits defining autism and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder are continuously distributed through the whole population, with diagnosed individuals occupying one end of a continuum rather than forming a separate natural kind, and the genetic influences on diagnosed cases are largely the same common variants that shape trait levels in everyone.

Researchers such as Anita Thapar and Michael Rutter have argued that the neurodevelopmental conditions are best seen as overlapping dimensional outcomes of early brain development, sharing genetic liability with each other, which fits the clinical reality that co-occurrence among autism, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, language disorder, and motor coordination difficulties is the rule rather than the exception.

The continuum view has consequences beyond the laboratory, since it underpins the neurodiversity perspective's claim that these conditions are variations within the human distribution rather than diseases apart from it, while also raising hard questions about where and why to draw diagnostic lines that give access to support.

An organised alternative to the DSM built on these ideas now exists, the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), launched by a consortium in 2017, which arranges psychopathology as a hierarchy of dimensions with p or a general spectrum at the top.

The dimensional turn is not complete and may never fully replace categories, which remain practical necessities for clinics, insurers, and schools.

But the reader now has the full apparatus this part of the book requires, pathways rather than fates, cascades rather than single causes, continuity in changing costumes, ordinary protective magic, and dimensions beneath the categories, and with these tools in hand we can turn to the conditions themselves.

CHAPTER 49. AUTISM SPECTRUM (CORE)

This chapter is about autism, a lifelong difference in how the brain develops that shapes how a person communicates, relates to other people, and experiences the sensory world.

It matters because autism is common, because it touches families everywhere, and because the science of autism has had to correct itself in public more than once.

We will meet the history of the idea, the brain findings and their honest revisions, the competing cognitive theories, the genetics, and the evidence about what help actually helps.

Throughout, the register is the one the autistic self-advocacy community has taught the field: autism is a way of being, not a broken version of a standard person, and the science is at its best when it describes rather than condemns.

One framing rule governs everything in this chapter: every brain finding reported here is a difference between group averages, and no finding described here can diagnose or characterise any individual autistic person.


49.1 The construct and its history

This section tells the story of how the word autism came to name a spectrum, and how one famous fraud tried to hijack that story.


49.1.1 From Kanner and Asperger to the spectrum, and the vaccine fraud refuted

In 1943 the Austrian-American psychiatrist Leo Kanner published a paper describing eleven children who showed, in his words, an extreme aloneness and an obsessive insistence on sameness.

In 1944, working separately in Vienna, the paediatrician Hans Asperger described a group of boys with marked social difficulties alongside fluent, often precocious language.

For decades these were treated as two conditions, autistic disorder and Asperger syndrome.

Careful field studies then showed that experienced clinicians could not reliably tell the two apart when assessing the same children.

So in 2013 the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), the manual American clinicians use to define psychiatric diagnoses, folded them into a single category called autism spectrum disorder.

The word spectrum is doing real work: autistic people range from those who need round-the-clock support to those living fully independent lives, and the diagnosis describes a pattern, not a level of ability.

Early psychoanalytic writing blamed cold parenting, the cruel refrigerator mother idea, and that claim was simply wrong; the evidence reviewed later in this chapter shows autism is among the most heritable of all developmental conditions.

The darkest episode in the modern history of the construct was a fraud.

In 1998 the British physician Andrew Wakefield published a paper in The Lancet suggesting, from just twelve children, a link between the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and autism.

The investigative journalist Brian Deer showed, beginning in 2004, that Wakefield had undisclosed payments from lawyers suing vaccine manufacturers and that the data in the paper had been altered.

The Lancet fully retracted the paper in 2010, Wakefield was struck off the United Kingdom medical register, and in 2011 the editors of the British Medical Journal (BMJ) described the study plainly as an elaborate fraud.

Large studies following millions of children, including a Danish cohort of over 650,000 children published by Hviid and colleagues in 2019, find no association whatsoever between the MMR vaccine and autism.

This corpus states it without hedging: vaccines do not cause autism, the claim that they do began as fraud, and the outbreaks of measles that followed the scare killed children.


49.2 The brain findings and their revisions

This section covers what brain imaging has found in autism, and, just as importantly, which famous findings had to be revised when the methods were checked.


49.2.1 Early overgrowth: the finding, the confounds, and the surviving subgroup version

One of the most cited claims in autism neuroscience was that autistic children's brains grow too fast in the first years of life, a claim advanced most prominently by Eric Courchesne and colleagues in the early 2000s.

The early evidence came largely from head circumference, the simple tape-measure distance around a child's head, compared against published population growth norms.

Later work found a serious problem: the older norms, including widely used ones from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), underestimated how big typical children's heads actually are, so autistic children looked unusually large partly because the yardstick was miscalibrated.

Studies that used their own locally measured comparison children, including a large Israeli cohort reported in 2017, found no early head enlargement at all in children later diagnosed with autism.

A related prediction of the original theory, that early overgrowth is followed by a normalising slowdown, has also failed in longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) work, the technology that photographs the living brain with magnetic fields; a 2020 study in Molecular Autism found evidence against that normalisation.

What survives is a subgroup version: roughly 15 to 20 percent of autistic children, mostly boys, do show genuinely enlarged brains, a pattern called megalencephaly, meaning a brain that is large for the child's body, and this subgroup tends to have higher support needs.

The lesson is a general one for this whole book: a group-average difference can be created by a minority subgroup, and population norms are only as good as the population they were measured in.


49.2.2 The infant-sibling surface-area expansion and the prediction studies

Because autism runs in families, the younger siblings of autistic children have a raised likelihood of being autistic themselves, roughly one in five, and researchers can therefore scan these infants before any diagnosis is possible.

In 2017 Heather Hazlett, Joseph Piven, and the Infant Brain Imaging Study network published a landmark paper in Nature using exactly this design.

They found that in the infants who went on to an autism diagnosis at age two, the surface area of the cortex, the brain's folded outer sheet, expanded unusually fast between 6 and 12 months of age, before any brain volume overgrowth and before autistic behaviours appeared.

A computer algorithm trained on the 6-month and 12-month scans predicted which high-likelihood infants would meet autism criteria at 24 months with about 80 percent accuracy, with a positive predictive value of 81 percent and a sensitivity of 88 percent.

The suggested sequence is a cascade: surface-area expansion in sensory regions in the first year, volume overgrowth in the second year, and the emergence of autistic behaviours by age two.

Two cautions belong beside the excitement.

The number of infants who actually converted to a diagnosis in that study was small, only fifteen in the key analysis, so the finding needs replication at scale before it could ever guide practice.

And prediction in a high-likelihood sibling sample does not transfer directly to the general population, where autism is rarer and the same algorithm would produce many more false alarms.


49.2.3 The connectivity accounts after motion correction

For years the leading imaging story was underconnectivity: the idea, prominent from work by Marcel Just and colleagues from 2004 onward, that in autism the long-distance conversations between far-apart brain regions are weaker while local chatter is stronger.

Much of this evidence came from functional MRI measured at rest, which infers connectivity from whether distant regions' activity rises and falls together.

Then came a humbling methodological discovery, driven by work from Jonathan Power and colleagues in 2012: tiny head movements in the scanner, even fractions of a millimetre, systematically fake exactly that pattern, weakening apparent long-distance connectivity and strengthening apparent short-distance connectivity.

Children move more than adults in scanners, and autistic children on average move more than non-autistic children, so the celebrated underconnectivity pattern was partly an artefact of wriggling.

After strict motion correction, some findings dissolve, some shrink, and some survive; differences in specific white-matter tracts such as the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, a cable running along the bottom of the temporal lobe, have withstood the stricter methods.

The honest current summary is that connectivity differences in autism are real but smaller, less uniform, and less tidy than the original slogan, with mixtures of over- and underconnectivity that vary by region, age, and analysis choice.

There is also a selection problem: throwing out the high-motion scans throws out disproportionately the children with the highest support needs, so the cleanest studies describe the least representative samples.


49.2.4 The excitation-inhibition hypothesis and its trial disappointments

In 2003 John Rubenstein and Michael Merzenich proposed that autism involves an increased ratio of excitation to inhibition in cortical circuits, meaning too much neural gas pedal relative to neural brake.

The brake system runs on gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the brain's main inhibitory chemical messenger, and the hypothesis drew on findings of reduced GABA signalling in autism.

The idea is attractive because it connects genetics, the high rate of epilepsy in autism, and sensory sensitivities under one mechanism.

But its translation into medicines has so far disappointed.

Arbaclofen, a drug that boosts a GABA receptor, showed promise in open trials but failed to beat placebo significantly in its randomised controlled trial, the study design where neither families nor doctors know who receives the real drug.

Bumetanide, a diuretic proposed to restore GABA's inhibitory action by lowering chloride inside neurons, produced encouraging small trials, and then two large phase 3 trials in over 400 children reported around 2021 found no difference from placebo, and development was stopped.

The hypothesis is not dead; it may be true for subgroups, and measuring an individual child's excitation-inhibition balance non-invasively remains hard.

But the pattern, small positive trials followed by large null trials, recurs throughout this chapter and deserves to be taught as a pattern.


49.3 The cognitive accounts against the neural data

This section lines up the main psychological theories of autism and asks how each fares against behavioural replication and brain evidence.


49.3.1 Theory of mind, central coherence, enhanced perception, predictive coding, social motivation

Theory of mind is the everyday ability to attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to other people.

In 1985 Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie, and Uta Frith reported that most autistic children failed a false-belief task, a puzzle about where a character will look for a hidden object, and proposed that autism centrally involves a theory-of-mind difficulty.

The account has weakened over time: many autistic people pass such tasks, performance depends heavily on language ability, and autistic scholars have pressed the double empathy problem, Damian Milton's 2012 argument that misunderstanding runs in both directions between autistic and non-autistic people rather than being a one-sided deficit.

Weak central coherence, proposed by Uta Frith in 1989, holds that autistic cognition favours detail over gist, seeing the trees vividly and assembling the forest less automatically.

Evidence of superior detail-focused performance, for example on embedded-figures puzzles, is real, but the claim of a deficit in global processing has replicated inconsistently.

Enhanced perceptual functioning, developed by Laurent Mottron and colleagues in the 2000s, reframes the same data positively: autistic perception is genuinely superior in some domains, such as pitch discrimination and visual search, and perception plays a larger role in autistic cognition.

Predictive coding accounts, articulated from about 2012 by Elizabeth Pellicano and David Burr and by Karl Friston's colleagues, treat the brain as a prediction machine and propose that in autism the brain weights raw sensory input heavily relative to its own predictions.

This single move elegantly explains sensory overwhelm, the comfort of sameness and routine, and difficulty with fast-moving social signals, and it is currently the most unifying candidate, though direct neural tests are young and mixed.

The social motivation account, associated with Coralie Chevallier and Robert Schultz in 2012, proposes reduced spontaneous reward from social engagement early in life, which then deprives the developing brain of social learning experience.

It has intuitive appeal and some eye-tracking support, but autistic adults' own testimony, frequently describing strong desire for connection alongside exhausting effort to obtain it, cuts against a simple lack of social interest.

No single account wins against the neural data, and the field increasingly accepts that a condition defined behaviourally and arising from hundreds of genetic routes may simply not have one cognitive essence.


49.4 The genetics

This section explains why autism is called highly heritable, what kinds of genetic variation are involved, and where in the cell the many genes converge.


49.4.1 High heritability, the de novo variants, and the chromatin-synapse convergence

Twin studies, which compare identical twins sharing all their deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) with fraternal twins sharing half, consistently estimate autism's heritability at roughly 70 to 90 percent, making it one of the most heritable conditions in psychiatry.

Heritability is a population statistic, the share of variation across people attributable to genetic variation, and it says nothing about any single person and nothing against the value of support.

Most of that heritability comes from common variants, ordinary genetic spelling differences each of tiny effect, spread across thousands of places in the genome.

Layered on top are de novo variants, meaning brand-new mutations present in the child but in neither parent, which arise spontaneously in the egg, the sperm, or the earliest embryo.

Exome sequencing, technology that reads the protein-coding portion of the genome, showed from about 2012 onward, in work by Evan Eichler, Matthew State, Stephan Sanders, and others, that damaging de novo variants are markedly enriched in autistic individuals, especially in those with intellectual disability.

By 2020 the Satterstrom and colleagues analysis of over 35,000 sequenced people had implicated more than one hundred genes with high confidence.

The remarkable finding is convergence: these many genes cluster into a small number of cellular jobs.

One cluster is chromatin regulation, the machinery that packs and unpacks DNA to decide which genes are switched on during brain development; its flagship is CHD8, short for chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 8, a master regulator whose targets include many other autism genes.

The other main cluster is synaptic function, the working of the synapse, the junction where one neuron signals to the next; its flagship is SCN2A, the gene for the sodium channel protein NaV1.2 that lets neurons fire.

A third recurring theme is signalling pathways of early development such as Wnt signalling, a chemical conversation that guides cell division and fate in the embryo.

So autism genetics tells a developmental story twice over: many routes disturb either how the genome is read while the brain is being built, or how the built brain's junctions transmit and adjust.


49.5 The intervention evidence

This section reviews what controlled trials show about early supports for autistic children, including an honest account of modest effects, one striking preventive-style trial, a famous drug failure, and the reframing of what interventions should even aim at.


49.5.1 The naturalistic developmental behavioural interventions and their moderate effects

The naturalistic developmental behavioural interventions (NDBIs) are the current mainstream of early autism support; they blend behavioural teaching principles with developmental science and are delivered inside play and daily routines rather than at a therapy table.

Examples include the Early Start Denver Model and pivotal response treatment.

The most rigorous summary is Project AIM, the autism intervention meta-analysis led by Micheal Sandbank and Kristen Bottema-Beutel, published in 2020 with an NDBI-focused analysis by Crank and colleagues in 2021.

A meta-analysis is a study of studies, pooling many trials into one overall effect estimate.

Across 27 studies of children aged up to eight, NDBIs showed small to moderate benefits: effect sizes of about 0.32 for expressive language, 0.23 for play, 0.48 for cognitive development, and 0.65 for social engagement, where an effect size is the group difference expressed in standard deviations and 0.2 is conventionally small.

Effects were larger for skills directly practised and measured in contexts resembling the therapy, and smaller for generalised, independently assessed outcomes.

Project AIM also flagged that many trials had detection bias, that adverse effects were almost never measured, and that when only the strongest designs were counted the evidence thinned considerably.

The fair summary for a beginner: the best-studied early supports help modestly and most clearly on what they directly practise, and the field has historically oversold them.


49.5.2 The parent-mediated prodromal trial

A parent-mediated intervention is one where therapists coach parents, and the parents, not the therapists, deliver the interaction changes at home.

The landmark school of work here is British: the Preschool Autism Communication Trial (PACT), led by Jonathan Green, showed in 2010 that coaching parents to notice and respond to their child's communication improved parent-child interaction, and the 2016 follow-up in The Lancet found reduced autism symptom severity fully six years after the therapy ended, an effect size of about 0.55.

The prodromal step came next, prodromal meaning the period when early signs exist but no diagnosis is yet possible.

Green's team adapted a video-feedback programme called iBASIS-VIPP, the intervention in the British Autism Study of Infant Siblings version of Video Interaction to Promote Positive Parenting, for infants under one year old.

In Australia, Andrew Whitehouse and colleagues then ran the AICES trial, delivering iBASIS-VIPP to clinically referred infants around 12 months old who showed early behavioural signs, and reported in 2021 that by age three the supported group had lower symptom severity and only about a third the odds of meeting full diagnostic criteria compared with usual care.

This result must be handled with the care the authors themselves urged.

The trial was single-site by design logic, the diagnostic difference rests on modest numbers, and the intervention did not remove autistic traits; it plausibly shifted how severely early differences came to interfere with communication.

Crucially, the ethos of this intervention is not training the baby to seem typical; it teaches adults to read and respond to the infant's own communication style, which is why many neurodiversity-oriented commentators view it more warmly than older compliance-based approaches.


49.5.3 The oxytocin failure and the neurodiversity reframing of goals

Oxytocin is a small hormone made in the hypothalamus, a deep brain structure that manages basic drives, and it earned the nickname of the social bonding molecule from animal research.

Small trials of oxytocin nasal spray in autism generated enormous hope through the 2010s.

Then Linmarie Sikich and colleagues published the decisive test in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021: 290 autistic children and adolescents, 24 weeks, randomised and placebo-controlled, and the result was flatly null, with the oxytocin and placebo groups improving by almost identical amounts.

The improvement in both groups is itself instructive: parents in the placebo arm reported marked gains, a reminder of why uncontrolled observations mislead.

The oxytocin failure landed in the middle of a larger rethink driven by the neurodiversity movement, the position, articulated by autistic self-advocates and by scholars such as the sociologist Judy Singer who coined the term in the late 1990s, that neurological variation is a natural form of human diversity.

On this view the goal of intervention is not to make an autistic child indistinguishable from peers, the explicit aim of some older behavioural programmes, but to support communication, learning, wellbeing, and self-determination while changing environments as well as children.

Intervention science has begun responding: researchers including Sue Fletcher-Watson and Kristen Bottema-Beutel argue for outcomes that autistic people themselves prioritise, for measuring harms, and for partnership with autistic communities in trial design.

The scientific and the ethical points converge: the largest drug trial failed on a goal of normalising social behaviour, while the best-supported interventions work by improving the fit between the child and the responsive people around them.


CHAPTER 50. ATTENTION-DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (CORE)

This chapter is about attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), a common neurodevelopmental condition involving persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity strong enough to interfere with daily life.

It matters for this book for two reasons: ADHD is one of the most frequent reasons a child meets a developmental clinician, and its most famous brain finding has just been publicly contested, making it the book's clearest live lesson in how developmental neuroscience corrects itself.

As with autism, every finding here is a group average, and none of it describes any individual child.


50.1 The construct

This section defines the condition, how common and how persistent it is, and the leading psychological model of why it is not one thing.


50.1.1 Prevalence, persistence, and the dual-pathway model

ADHD is diagnosed from behaviour: developmentally excessive inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in childhood and impairing function in more than one setting.

Careful meta-analyses, notably by Guilherme Polanczyk and colleagues in 2007 and 2014, put worldwide childhood prevalence at roughly 5 percent, with the wide country-to-country differences explained mostly by diagnostic method rather than by geography.

Boys are diagnosed more often than girls, at roughly twice the rate in community samples, and girls, whose presentation tilts toward inattention without disruptive behaviour, have historically been under-recognised; that fact returns with force later in this chapter.

ADHD often persists: symptoms continue into adulthood in a large fraction of cases, with something like two thirds of children carrying impairing symptoms forward, while adult prevalence is estimated around 2.5 to 5 percent.

Recent longitudinal work from the multimodal treatment study described below adds nuance: for many people ADHD fluctuates across life, with periods of remission and recurrence, rather than simply persisting or vanishing.

The leading account of the condition's psychology is the dual-pathway model, proposed by Edmund Sonuga-Barke in 2002 and 2003.

It holds that ADHD arises by two partly separate routes: a cognitive route involving weak executive control, the brain's management functions of holding goals in mind and inhibiting impulses, linked to circuits between the prefrontal cortex, the front region behind the forehead that plans and inhibits, and the striatum, a deep hub for action and habit; and a motivational route involving delay aversion, an unusually steep discounting of delayed rewards, linked to reward circuits between the striatum and its dopamine inputs.

Some children show mainly one route, some the other, some both, which is why no single cognitive test diagnoses ADHD.

Later work by Sonuga-Barke and colleagues in 2010 added a third dissociable pathway involving timing, the ability to estimate and reproduce durations.

The model matters pedagogically because it predicted, correctly, that ADHD would prove neurobiologically heterogeneous, a warning that should have been remembered when a single brain-maturation story became famous.


50.2 The maturation-delay account, now contested

This section teaches the most cited brain finding in ADHD, the 2026 reanalysis that contests it, and the general lesson about norms.

The two are taught together, as this corpus requires for contested findings.


50.2.1 The 2007 delayed-cortical-peak finding

In 2007 Philip Shaw and colleagues at the United States National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) published, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), a longitudinal study of cortical thickness, the depth of the brain's outer grey matter sheet, measured repeatedly by MRI.

They analysed 824 scans from 223 children with ADHD and 223 typically developing children, tracking more than 40,000 points across the cortex.

Cortical thickness in childhood typically rises to a peak and then thins through adolescence, and the age of peak thickness was used as a milestone of maturation.

Shaw's team reported that the ADHD group reached peak thickness markedly later, at a median age of about 10.5 years versus about 7.5 years in the comparison group, with the delay most pronounced in prefrontal regions important for attention and self-control.

The interpretation was memorable and humane: ADHD reflects a delay in cortical maturation, not a deviant brain, and the delayed brain follows the normal architectural sequence a few years behind.

The finding entered textbooks, clinical explanations, and public understanding, often compressed into the phrase that the ADHD brain matures about three years late.


50.2.2 The 2026 reanalysis: the delay largely dissolving once sex differences are modelled

In 2026, again in PNAS, a reanalysis using more than 26,000 scans from large modern cohorts asked a question the original design could not settle: what happens to the apparent ADHD maturation delay when the normal difference between boys' and girls' cortical development is fully modelled.

Boys' and girls' cortices mature on reliably different timetables, with girls reaching several maturational milestones earlier on average.

ADHD samples contain far more boys than girls, and comparison samples are closer to balanced, so a sex-composition difference between groups can masquerade as a disorder effect.

The 2026 analysis reported that once sex differences in cortical maturation were properly accounted for, the association between ADHD or attention problems and delayed cortical maturation largely dissolved.

On this reading, two decades of the delayed-maturation story rested substantially on comparing mostly-male patient groups against more mixed comparison groups using developmental curves that ignored sex.

This corpus teaches the pair exactly as it stands: the 2007 finding was real in its data and honestly analysed by the standards of its time, the 2026 reanalysis is larger and methodologically stronger on this specific confound, and the field has not yet finished adjudicating between them.

A single reanalysis, however large, is itself one study; the responsible statement is that the delayed-cortical-maturation account of ADHD is now contested and may be substantially an artefact of unmodelled sex differences.


50.2.3 The lesson about norms and about teaching contested findings as contested

The deepest lesson here is not about ADHD; it is about yardsticks.

A developmental claim always compares a group against some norm, and the norm silently encodes decisions: which population, which ages, which sexes, which scanner, which era.

The autism head-circumference story of Chapter 49 fell partly to miscalibrated growth norms; the ADHD maturation-delay story is now contested because of sex-blind maturation norms; and this book's repeated statement that the brain does not switch to mature at age 25 falls the same way, since that figure was an artefact of studies whose oldest participants were in their twenties.

Three habits follow.

First, always ask what the comparison group was and what the growth curves assumed.

Second, treat memorable summaries with extra suspicion precisely because they spread faster than their caveats.

Third, when a finding is contested, teach the dispute itself, with both dates and both designs, rather than quietly picking a winner; a student who learns the 2007 and 2026 papers together has learned more neuroscience than one who learns either alone.

None of this revision unsettles the reality of ADHD, which is established by behaviour, impairment, heritability, and treatment response, not by any single imaging result.


50.3 The dopamine account and the medications

This section covers the chemical-signalling story of ADHD and what the largest treatment trial actually showed over time.


50.3.1 The reward-pathway findings

Dopamine is a chemical messenger that, among other jobs, signals the value and expectation of reward and energises action toward it.

The main reward pathway runs from dopamine-making neurons in the ventral tegmental area, a small cluster deep in the midbrain, to the nucleus accumbens, a striatal region often called the brain's reward hub.

The most direct human evidence comes from positron emission tomography (PET), an imaging method that tags molecules with mild radioactivity to count receptors and transporters in the living brain.

In 2009 Nora Volkow and colleagues, in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), reported that adults with ADHD had reduced markers of dopamine signalling, specifically dopamine receptors and dopamine transporters, in the nucleus accumbens and midbrain, and a 2011 follow-up tied these reductions to the severity of inattention and to motivation deficits.

This fits the delay-aversion pathway of the dual-pathway model: a reward system that signals future rewards weakly makes waiting genuinely costlier.

It also fits the medications: methylphenidate and the amphetamines, the stimulant drugs used in ADHD since Charles Bradley's serendipitous 1937 observation that benzedrine calmed and focused children, act by blocking or reversing the dopamine transporter, thereby raising dopamine and noradrenaline signalling.

The caveats are the usual ones: PET samples are small, medication history complicates interpretation, and genome-wide genetics, discussed below, has notably failed to place classic dopamine genes at the top of the risk list, so dopamine is part of the story rather than the story.


50.3.2 The multimodal treatment study and the attenuation of its early advantage

The Multimodal Treatment of ADHD study, universally called the MTA, was launched by the NIMH in the 1990s as the largest treatment trial in child psychiatry: 579 children aged 7 to 9 randomised across six sites to fourteen months of carefully managed medication, intensive behavioural therapy, their combination, or routine community care.

At the 14-month endpoint, published in 1999, carefully managed medication, with or without behavioural therapy, clearly beat behavioural therapy alone and community care for core ADHD symptoms.

That result reshaped practice worldwide toward stimulant medication.

The sobering part came later.

By the 36-month follow-up, published by Peter Jensen and colleagues in 2007, the treatment groups no longer differed significantly on any measure; the early advantage of managed medication had attenuated as random assignment dissolved into real-world choices, with many children starting, stopping, or changing treatments.

Longer follow-ups into adolescence and adulthood confirmed the pattern: whatever a child had been assigned at ages 7 to 9 no longer predicted outcomes years later, and the cohort as a whole continued to show impairments relative to peers alongside a modest suppression of adult height growth in those with sustained stimulant use.

The 2022 to 2024 MTA analyses by Margaret Sibley and colleagues also revealed the fluctuating course described earlier, with about 30 percent of the cohort showing full remission at some point and most of those experiencing later recurrence.

The fair reading, and the one this corpus records, is that stimulants reliably reduce symptoms while actively taken and well managed, that fourteen months of any particular starting strategy does not set a life trajectory, and that long-term outcomes depend on continuing, adjusted support rather than on which door a family entered first.


50.4 The genetics and the environmental correlates

ADHD is strongly heritable: twin studies put heritability around 70 to 80 percent, comparable to height.

For decades candidate-gene studies chased individual dopamine genes with results that largely failed to replicate, another instance of this book's recurring replication lesson.

The turning point was the genome-wide association study (GWAS), the design that scans the whole genome in huge samples without favourites.

In 2019 Ditte Demontis, Anders Borglum, Benjamin Neale, and colleagues published the first well-powered ADHD GWAS in Nature Genetics, finding 12 significant genetic regions in about 20,000 affected individuals and 35,000 comparison individuals; their 2023 expansion found 27 regions.

The implicated variants are common, individually tiny in effect, concentrated near genes active in brain development, and shared substantially with the genetics of educational attainment, smoking, and other psychiatric conditions, showing that ADHD sits on continuous dimensions of variation rather than behind a wall.

Notably, the classic dopamine receptor and transporter genes did not dominate the results.

Environmental correlates include prematurity and low birth weight, prenatal tobacco and alcohol exposure, early severe deprivation of the kind documented in the Romanian orphan studies discussed elsewhere in this book, and exposure to lead, a toxic metal that damages developing neurons.

Correlate is the operative word: for several of these, including prenatal smoking, genetically informed designs show that shared familial genetics explains much of the association, so the arrow from exposure to ADHD is established only for some factors, with lead and extreme deprivation among the most convincing.

Popular explanations blaming sugar, television, or ordinary parenting practices have not survived controlled testing.


CHAPTER 51. THE LEARNING AND LANGUAGE DISORDERS (CORE)

This chapter gathers the conditions in which a specific academic or language skill develops along an atypical path in a child whose broader development may be otherwise ordinary, together with intellectual disability, where development is globally affected.

It matters because these conditions are among the most common of all developmental differences, because they are routinely mistaken for laziness or poor teaching, and because two of them carry famous scientific corrections this corpus is obliged to record.

As throughout this part of the book, all brain findings are group averages and describe populations, never a particular child.


51.1 Dyslexia, cross-referenced to Chapter 32

This section summarises the neuroscience of dyslexia, whose full treatment alongside the neuroscience of reading lives in Chapter 32; here we keep only the disorder-focused essentials.


51.1.1 The signature, the prediction, and the remediation neurobiology
