PART THIRTEEN. THE CLASSIC THEORIES AGAINST THE NEURAL EVIDENCE

================================================================================

CHAPTER 54. PIAGET RE-EXAMINED (CORE)

This chapter takes the most famous theory in all of developmental psychology, that of the Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget, and holds it up against the modern behavioural and neural evidence.

Piaget, working from the 1920s to his death in 1980, proposed that children's thinking passes through qualitatively different stages, and his clever tasks with hidden toys and poured water remain the shared vocabulary of the field.

The modern verdict is neither that he was right nor that he was wrong, but something more interesting: babies often know more than his tasks could reveal, and what limits them is frequently the immaturity of the brain's control systems rather than the absence of the concept.

Understanding that verdict teaches a general lesson about how to read any developmental experiment, which is why this chapter matters beyond Piaget himself.


54.1 The system

Before re-examining Piaget we must state his system fairly, because it is a genuine intellectual monument and not a straw man.

He offered both a mechanism of learning and a timetable of stages, and the two parts have fared very differently against the evidence.


54.1.1 Schemas, assimilation, accommodation, and the four stages

Piaget's central idea was that children are not passive recipients of knowledge but active little builders who construct their understanding through interaction with the world.

The unit of construction he called a schema, meaning an organised pattern of knowledge or action, such as a baby's grasping routine or an older child's concept of what an animal is.

Assimilation is fitting a new experience into an existing schema, as when a toddler who knows dogs calls a sheep a dog.

Accommodation is the opposite movement, changing the schema to fit the world, as when the toddler learns that woolly field animals need a category of their own.

Development, for Piaget, was the endless alternation of these two processes, driven by the discomfort of encountering things that do not fit, a state he called disequilibrium.

On top of this mechanism he laid a timetable of four universal stages.

The sensorimotor stage, from birth to about age 2, is when the infant knows the world only through senses and actions, and its crowning achievement is object permanence, the understanding that things continue to exist when out of sight.

The preoperational stage, from about 2 to 7, brings language and pretend play but, in Piaget's account, thinking that is egocentric, meaning centred on the child's own viewpoint, and easily fooled by appearances.

The concrete operational stage, from about 7 to 11, brings logical operations applied to tangible things, including conservation, the understanding that quantity survives changes of shape.

The formal operational stage, from about 11 or 12 onward, brings abstract, hypothetical, systematic reasoning, the ability to think about thinking and to test possibilities in the head.

Piaget held that the stages arrive in a fixed order, that each rebuilds thought wholesale, and that a child in one stage reasons in that stage's way across the board.

It is the stage claims, far more than the construction mechanism, that the last fifty years of research have taken apart.


54.2 The re-examinations

Each of the following four re-examinations follows the same pattern: take a classic Piagetian failure, ask whether the task demanded abilities beyond the concept supposedly being tested, and then locate the true bottleneck, often in the slow-maturing frontal control systems of the brain.


54.2.1 Object permanence earlier than the reach: the looking evidence

Piaget dated object permanence to around 8 months, because that is when infants first reach for a toy they have watched being hidden under a cloth.

But reaching is a high bar: it requires the infant to represent the hidden object, plan a two-step action, and execute it, all at once.

Renée Baillargeon and her colleagues asked whether looking, a far easier response, would reveal the knowledge earlier.

The method, called violation of expectation, rests on a simple fact: infants look longer at events that surprise them.

In the famous drawbridge experiment of Baillargeon, Spelke, and Wasserman in 1985, 5-month-old infants watched a screen rotate like a drawbridge, then saw a box placed in its path.

The infants looked longer when the screen rotated a full 180 degrees, apparently passing through the space the hidden box should occupy, than when it stopped where the box would be, suggesting they represented the box's continued existence behind the screen.

Baillargeon later reported similar results in infants as young as three and a half months.

Honesty requires reporting that this literature has its own dispute.

Critics including Bogartz, Shinskey, and Schilling, and Rivera, Wakeley, and Langer in 1999, failed to reproduce some effects and argued that infants may simply prefer watching more motion, since the impossible event contains a bigger rotation, a leaner perceptual explanation that does not require any concept of the hidden box.

Baillargeon and colleagues answered with control conditions, and a large body of violation-of-expectation work across many tasks, summarised in a 2024 overview by Margoni, Surian, and Baillargeon, supports the view that young infants hold expectations about hidden objects, though the debate over how rich those expectations are, full concepts or thinner perceptual predictions, has never fully closed.

The measured conclusion most of the field accepts is this: some representation of hidden objects is present months before Piaget's reaching milestone, and the reach at 8 months marks not the birth of the concept but the point where action systems become able to use it.


54.2.2 A-not-B as prefrontal immaturity rather than missing concept

Piaget's strangest observation is called the A-not-B error.

Hide a toy repeatedly at location A, and let a 9-month-old retrieve it each time; then, in full view of the infant, hide it at location B, and the infant will often reach confidently back to A.

Piaget read this as an immature object concept, the object being bound up with the infant's own past action upon it.

Adele Diamond's work in the 1980s reread it as a failure of control, not of concept.

Diamond showed that the error is exquisitely sensitive to the delay between hiding and reaching: at around 7 and a half months infants err after even a second or two of delay, and the delay they can tolerate grows steadily to roughly 10 seconds by 12 months.

Infants also sometimes look at the correct location B even while their hand travels to A, which is hard to square with a missing concept and easy to square with a habit the infant cannot yet override.

The decisive evidence came from comparative neuroscience: Diamond and Goldman-Rakic showed in 1989 that adult rhesus monkeys with lesions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the upper side portion of the frontal lobes that supports working memory, meaning the holding of information in mind, and response inhibition, meaning the stopping of a prepotent action, fail the A-not-B task in exactly the way human 9-month-olds do.

Passing A-not-B thus requires holding the new location in mind across the delay while suppressing the practised reach, two functions of a prefrontal cortex that is among the last brain regions to mature.

Later work by Thelen, Smith, and colleagues in 2001 added a dynamic-systems reading in which the reach to A is a motor habit attractor, and showed the error could be manipulated by posture and practice, a theme Chapter 56 returns to.

On either modern reading, the infant's problem is performance, not knowledge, and A-not-B became the founding case study of developmental cognitive neuroscience.


54.2.3 Conservation errors as inhibition failures

In Piaget's conservation-of-number task, a child sees two equal rows of counters, watches one row being spread out longer, and is asked which row has more.

Children below about 6 or 7 say the longer row has more, and Piaget took this as the absence of the logical concept that number survives spatial rearrangement.

The modern rereading, led by Olivier Houdé and colleagues in Paris, holds that the young child's problem is a misleading shortcut that has not yet been brought under control.

Length usually does track number in a child's everyday experience, so the brain builds a fast heuristic, meaning a quick rule of thumb, that longer means more, and the conservation task is precisely engineered to make that heuristic give the wrong answer.

Succeeding therefore requires inhibiting the heuristic, and inhibition is once again the business of the slow-maturing prefrontal cortex.

Neuroimaging supports this reading: a 2012 functional magnetic resonance imaging study by Houdé's group found that children who succeed at the number-conservation task activate a fronto-parietal control network, including the right inferior frontal region associated with stopping responses, while children who fail do not, and a 2013 high-density electrical-recording study found brain signatures of conflict detection and inhibition in successful conservers.

Supporting behavioural evidence goes back further: even educated adults show measurable slowing when they must judge number against misleading length, indicating that the heuristic is never deleted but only held down, and training studies show that teaching children to resist the trap improves conservation performance.

So the conservation error joins A-not-B in the same verdict pattern: the number knowledge is substantially present earlier than Piaget thought, and what arrives at age 6 or 7 is the executive machinery to defend that knowledge against a tempting perceptual lie.


54.2.4 Formal operations against the long prefrontal build

Piaget's final stage, formal operations, was supposed to arrive around 11 or 12 and to equip essentially all adolescents with systematic, abstract, hypothesis-testing thought.

Both halves of that claim have failed.

First, formal operational reasoning is not universal: studies from the 1970s onward, including work by Neimark and reviews by Keating, found that large fractions of adolescents and adults, in every society tested, fail classic formal-operations tasks such as the pendulum problem, in which one must vary one factor at a time to discover what determines a pendulum's swing.

Performance depends heavily on schooling, familiarity with the content, and the situation, which contradicts the notion of a general stage that transforms all reasoning at once.

Second, the neural timetable is wrong for a stage that completes at 12.

Structural imaging, including the longitudinal studies of Giedd, Gogtay, and colleagues at the National Institute of Mental Health in the 2000s, showed that the prefrontal cortex is still thinning its grey matter and strengthening its long-range white-matter connections throughout the teenage years and into the twenties, with the exact endpoint varying by person and by measure and with no single finish-line age, a caution this corpus records against the popular myth of a magic age 25.

Abstract reasoning capacity accordingly keeps improving well past 12, while its reliable use remains hostage to the still-maturing control systems, which is why the same adolescent can reason like a scientist in a calm classroom and quite differently among peers at night.

The fair summary is that Piaget correctly saw that a new quality of hypothetical thought becomes possible in early adolescence, but wrongly modelled it as a universal, completed, all-purpose stage, when it is better described as a gradually strengthening skill, unevenly applied, riding on one of the longest construction projects in the brain.


54.3 The verdict pattern

Looking across the re-examinations, the corrections to Piaget are not a scatter of unrelated fixes but two repeated patterns, and stating them explicitly is the real payoff of this chapter.


54.3.1 Competence early, performance limited by control systems

The first pattern is a distinction the field now states as competence versus performance.

Competence is the underlying knowledge or representational capacity; performance is what a child can actually demonstrate under the demands of a particular task.

Again and again, when researchers lowered the task demands, by measuring looking instead of reaching, shortening delays, or removing misleading cues, the knowledge showed up months or years earlier than Piaget's timetable.

And again and again, the bottleneck that had hidden the knowledge turned out to be an immature control function, working memory, response inhibition, or attention, with the slow-maturing prefrontal cortex as the common anatomical thread from A-not-B through conservation to formal reasoning.

This yields a general methodological moral: a failed task never shows the absence of a concept, it shows only that this task, with these demands, exceeded this child, and every claim that children lack some understanding must be read with the question, what else did the task require?

The moral cuts both ways, and the field's self-corrections, the drawbridge replication dispute of section 54.2.1 and the infant false-belief replication crisis recorded elsewhere in this corpus, show that easy tasks can also mislead by detecting less than was claimed.

Competence-early is therefore a well-supported generalisation with honestly contested edges, not a licence to attribute rich knowledge to infants whenever they look at something for an extra second.


54.3.2 Stages replaced by overlapping waves

The second pattern replaces Piaget's staircase with a different picture of change.

Robert Siegler, studying children's arithmetic and problem solving from the 1980s onward, found that an individual child does not use one stage-typical strategy but several competing strategies at once, sometimes counting on fingers, sometimes retrieving from memory, sometimes decomposing the problem, even within a single session.

Development, in Siegler's overlapping waves model, published fully in his 1996 book Emerging Minds, is the gradual shift in the mixture, with each strategy rising and falling like a wave over years, rather than a step from one uniform way of thinking to the next.

This picture fits the data that stages could not: the decades of findings, dating back to Piaget's own observation of decalage, meaning the staggered arrival of the same logical ability across different contents, that children conserve number years before they conserve weight, and reason well in familiar domains while failing in unfamiliar ones.

It also fits the brain, in which many circuits mature on their own overlapping timetables rather than in synchronised society-wide leaps, and it fits Houdé's account in which older strategies are not erased but inhibited, still detectable in the reaction times of adults.

What survives of Piaget is substantial and should be said plainly: the child as active constructor of knowledge, the power of his tasks, the reality of qualitative change in what thinking can do, and the broad ordering of achievements.

What has been replaced is the machinery: universal, wholesale, one-at-a-time stages have given way to overlapping waves of strategies, domain-by-domain timetables, and control systems whose slow maturation, not the absence of concepts, sets much of the pace.


CHAPTER 55. VYGOTSKY AND THE SOCIAL ROUTE (CORE)

This chapter turns to Piaget's great historical counterpart, the Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, who died of tuberculosis in 1934 at the age of 37 and whose short career produced the field's most influential account of how minds are built socially.

Where Piaget's child is a solitary little scientist experimenting on the world, Vygotsky's child is an apprentice, growing a mind inside relationships, language, and culture.

We will state his claims, then ask how kindly modern developmental neuroscience looks upon them, and finally be honest about the gap between the richness of the theory and the coarseness of the mechanisms so far in hand.

The chapter matters because education systems worldwide lean on Vygotsky's ideas, and it is worth knowing which parts the biology actually supports.


55.1 The claims

Vygotsky's system was left unfinished at his death and reached the West in translation decades later, so this section states its three load-bearing claims in their standard modern form.


55.1.1 The zone of proximal development, tools, and internalised speech

Vygotsky's most famous idea is the zone of proximal development, defined in his 1934 book Thought and Language, published in English in 1962, as the distance between what a child can do alone and what the same child can do with guidance from a more capable partner.

The zone is where teaching belongs: tasks fully within the child's solo reach teach nothing new, tasks far beyond the zone teach only frustration, and tasks inside it are where a parent's or teacher's support converts shared achievement into independent ability.

The related everyday term scaffolding, meaning the adjustable support the partner provides and gradually removes, was coined not by Vygotsky but by Wood, Bruner, and Ross in 1976, and it has become the standard image for teaching within the zone.

Vygotsky's second claim concerns tools: humans master their own minds the way they master the world, through tools, and the crucial tools are symbolic, above all language, but also counting systems, writing, and diagrams, each of which restructures the thinking of the person who acquires it.

The third claim is internalisation: the higher mental functions appear twice, first between people, as actual social exchange, and then within the child, as the social dialogue is taken inside.

The showcase case is private speech, the audible self-talk of preschoolers narrating and directing their own actions.

Piaget had dismissed it as egocentric noise that fades; Vygotsky predicted instead that it is self-guidance in training, that it should increase when tasks get harder, and that it does not disappear but goes underground as silent inner speech, the voice in the head with which adults plan and self-regulate.

Subsequent research, reviewed by Berk and by Winsler, has sided with Vygotsky on the empirical points: private speech peaks in the preschool years, rises with task difficulty, predicts better performance when task-relevant, and dwindles into muttering and then silence on the developmental path to inner speech.


55.2 The neural friendliness

A theory written in the 1930s could cite no brain evidence at all, so it is striking that several modern research programmes read almost as if designed to test Vygotsky.

This section presents three of them, each showing biology that is friendly to the social route, while the next section will weigh how far friendliness falls short of proof.


55.2.1 Natural pedagogy and ostensive cues

If minds are built through teaching, one might expect evolution to have prepared infants to receive teaching, and that is precisely the claim of natural pedagogy, a theory proposed by Gergely Csibra and György Gergely in Budapest, stated most fully in a 2009 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

Their proposal is that humans possess a dedicated communication system for transmitting generalisable knowledge, and that infants are born sensitive to ostensive cues, meaning the signals that say this message is for you: direct eye contact, being addressed by name, and infant-directed speech, the melodic, exaggerated register adults spontaneously adopt with babies.

The supporting evidence begins at birth: newborns prefer faces with direct gaze over averted gaze, shown by Farroni and colleagues in 2002, and electrical recordings of the newborn brain respond differently to direct gaze within days of birth.

Behavioural experiments by the Budapest group show that ostensive cues change what infants learn: after eye contact and infant-directed speech, infants treat what follows as general information about kinds of things rather than a passing episode, and Gergely, Egyed, and Kiraly showed that infants generalise an adult's demonstrated object preference to other people only when it was communicated ostensively.

A related and famous finding is rational imitation, reported by Gergely, Bekkering, and Kiraly in 2002, in which 14-month-olds copied an adult's odd head-touch action selectively, though the interpretation of that particular result has been debated and a large multi-laboratory replication effort has complicated it, so it is best held lightly.

The theory itself has critics, notably Cecilia Heyes, who argues that sensitivity to these cues may be built by rapid early learning rather than installed by genes, but on either reading the developmental fact stands: within weeks of birth, human infants are differentially open to communicative address, which is exactly the receiving apparatus Vygotsky's theory needs.


55.2.2 The social gating of language learning

The cleanest experimental demonstration that social interaction changes what young brains learn comes from Patricia Kuhl's laboratory at the University of Washington.

By around 9 to 10 months, infants ordinarily narrow their hearing toward native speech sounds, losing the easy discrimination of foreign contrasts, a process treated earlier in this book.

In a 2003 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Kuhl, Tsao, and Liu exposed 9-month-old American infants to Mandarin Chinese across about twelve play sessions.

Infants who experienced a live Mandarin-speaking adult, playing and reading with them, preserved the ability to discriminate a Mandarin consonant contrast, performing like infants raised hearing Mandarin.

Infants who received the same amount of Mandarin from the same speakers by television or audio recording learned essentially nothing, performing like infants never exposed at all.

Kuhl named the resulting hypothesis social gating, proposed formally in a 2007 paper: the computational machinery of language learning is present, but social interaction acts as the gate that opens it, plausibly by driving attention, arousal, and contingency, meaning the live back-and-forth responsiveness that a recording cannot supply.

Supporting details include the finding that infants' gaze-following of the live tutor predicted their learning, and later work linking the quality of one-to-one parental speech, rather than sheer word count, to language growth.

The gate is not absolute, and later childhood learning from screens is far better than infant learning from screens, but for the opening years the result is one of the strongest experimental planks under the Vygotskian claim that the road into language runs through other people.


55.2.3 Parent-child neural synchrony and learning

The newest line of Vygotsky-friendly evidence watches two brains at once.

Hyperscanning is the method of recording brain activity from two or more people simultaneously, using electroencephalography (EEG), which reads the brain's electrical rhythms from the scalp, or functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which tracks blood-oxygen changes through the scalp with gentle light and tolerates the wriggling of small children.

The robust core finding is that when a parent and child interact, play, solve puzzles, sing, converse, their brain activity becomes measurably coupled, rising and falling together beyond chance, a phenomenon called interpersonal neural synchrony.

Representative studies include Reindl and colleagues in 2018, who found mother-child prefrontal synchrony during cooperation but not competition, and Nguyen and colleagues in 2021, who extended the finding to fathers and children and showed synchrony tracking problem-solving together.

Synchrony is not mere simultaneity of stimulation: it is stronger in live, contingent, turn-taking interaction than in passive or independent conditions, it relates to gaze, touch, and conversational reciprocity, and in several studies higher synchrony during teaching-like interaction predicts better subsequent learning and cooperation by the child.

Leong and colleagues showed in 2017 that direct gaze from an adult increases infant-adult neural coupling during song, tying this literature back to the ostensive cues of section 55.2.1.

Caution is owed here in proportion to the field's youth: samples are small, analysis choices vary widely, synchrony is a correlate whose causal role in learning is not established, and reviewers within the field, including a 2026 integrative framework by Zhou and colleagues, warn against treating synchrony as a magic ingredient rather than a measurable signature of well-timed interaction.

Read with that caution, the literature still delivers something Vygotsky could only assert: a physiological picture of the zone of proximal development occupied, two nervous systems transiently organised into one teaching-and-learning system.


55.3 The honest gap

Friendly evidence is not a mechanism, and this closing section states plainly how much of Vygotsky's theory still floats above the biology.


55.3.1 Mechanisms still coarse where the theory is rich

Vygotsky's theory is rich exactly where our neuroscience is still coarse.

The theory's central event is internalisation, a social dialogue becoming an inner mental function, and there exists today no circuit-level account of how that happens: no one can trace how overheard regulation becomes self-regulation in identified neural populations, and inner speech itself is studied in adults, by Fernyhough and others, with imaging methods too blunt to watch its childhood construction.

The zone of proximal development has never been given a neural definition; synchrony studies decorate it with correlates but do not explain why guidance inside the zone teaches while guidance outside it does not.

The demonstrations of section 55.2 are also narrow relative to the theory's scope: social gating is firmly shown for phonetic learning in infancy, but the theory claims social construction for attention, memory, planning, and the whole of higher cognition, claims for which the evidence is thin, indirect, or untested.

Much of the strongest evidence is correlational, and the field's small samples and flexible analyses, noted for synchrony research above, apply here with full force.

None of this is a refutation, and the contrast with Piaget's fate is instructive: Piaget made sharp timetable claims that the evidence could and did overturn, while Vygotsky's claims are directional and mechanistic in a way the tools are only beginning to reach.

The honest summary is that the biology so far points the way Vygotsky pointed, infants tuned to communicative address, learning gated by live interaction, teaching visible as two-brain coordination, while the theory's core machinery remains a promissory note that developmental neuroscience has yet to cash.


CHAPTER 56. NATIVISM, NEUROCONSTRUCTIVISM, AND THE LEARNING ACCOUNTS (CORE)

This chapter stages the field's deepest argument: how much of the mind is there at the start, and how much is built?

Nativism is the position that infants begin with substantial built-in knowledge; empiricism, its historical opposite, holds that knowledge comes from experience; and the modern contenders reviewed here, core knowledge theory, neuroconstructivism, and a family of learning accounts, are all sophisticated descendants of that old quarrel.

No side has won, and the chapter's aim is to show what each explains best, what each struggles with, and how the modern synthesis borrows from all of them.

The question matters practically, because how one thinks children start determines how one thinks education, intervention, and disability work.


56.1 Core knowledge and its neural claims

The strongest modern nativism is not the claim that everything is innate, but the precise claim that a few evolutionarily ancient systems of knowledge are present from the start, and this section presents that theory and the infant and brain evidence offered for it.


56.1.1 The infant findings and the early cortical organisation evidence

Core knowledge theory, developed above all by Elizabeth Spelke at Harvard, with Susan Carey and colleagues, and summarised in Spelke and Kinzler's 2007 paper Core Knowledge, proposes that human infants are equipped with a small number of ancient, dedicated systems of expectation.

The usually listed systems cover objects, expected to be solid, continuous in motion, and persistent; agents, expected to act toward goals; number, an approximate sense of quantity; geometry, the layout of space; and, in later statements, the social distinction of likely allies.

The infant evidence uses the looking methods of Chapter 54 and includes the object findings of Baillargeon and Spelke from the 1980s and 1990s, Woodward's 1998 demonstration that 6-month-olds encode a reaching hand as goal-directed, and the number findings of Xu and Spelke in 2000, in which 6-month-olds discriminated 8 from 16 dots but not 8 from 12, the ratio signature of an approximate number system shared with rats and monkeys.

Newborn studies push some sensitivities to the first days, including Izard and colleagues' 2009 report that newborns match the number of sounds to the number of objects in view.

The neural side of the claim is that the infant cortex is organised for these domains far earlier than learning accounts would expect.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging of awake infants, pioneered for this question by Deen, Saxe, and colleagues in 2017, found that the visual cortex of 4-to-6-month-olds already shows regions responding preferentially to faces versus scenes, in roughly the adult locations, though with less adult-like selectivity than first hoped, and infant brains show organised connectivity between future face areas and scene areas before behaviour could have trained them, as argued from resting connectivity work by Kamps and colleagues in 2020.

The standing counter-evidence must be stated with equal strength.

The looking-time foundation itself is contested, as the drawbridge dispute of Chapter 54 and the collapse of neonatal imitation under large replication show, and this corpus separately records the replication crisis around infant implicit false-belief.

Early cortical biases are also not proof of innate knowledge: side-preferring visual biases exist at birth, but the case of literacy shows the same cortex developing a specialised word-form area purely from cultural experience, so early organisation may reflect innate connectivity scaffolds that make certain learning easy rather than knowledge already present, a reading advanced by the experience-expectant tradition and pressed hard by the school treated next.

The fair current statement is that infants demonstrably arrive with structured expectations and biased cortical wiring in a few domains, while the words knowledge and innate both claim more than the data have settled.


56.2 The neuroconstructivist answer

Between nativism and blank-slate learning stands a distinctively developmental position, built largely by one researcher out of the study of genetic syndromes, and this section gives its argument.


56.2.1 Development itself as the key, and the syndrome evidence

Neuroconstructivism, associated above all with Annette Karmiloff-Smith, who worked with Piaget in Geneva before founding her own school in London and who died in 2016, holds that the question is not what is innate versus learned but how structure emerges, because development itself is the key.

Its central claim, stated in Karmiloff-Smith's 1992 book Beyond Modularity and her 1998 paper Development itself is the key to understanding developmental disorders, is that the adult brain's specialised modules are the outcome of development, not its starting point: genes specify not knowledge but small initial biases in timing, connectivity, and processing style, and domain-specific structure emerges gradually as these biases interact with experience, a process her collaborators formalised in the 2007 book Neuroconstructivism by Mareschal, Johnson, Sirois, Spratling, Thomas, and Westermann, and in Mark Johnson's related interactive specialisation account, in which cortical regions compete and specialise through activity rather than switching on prebuilt.

The distinctive evidence is the study of genetic developmental syndromes, above all Williams syndrome, a rare condition caused by the deletion of about 26 genes on chromosome 7, producing a striking profile of relatively fluent language and sociability alongside severe spatial difficulty.

Nativists had cited Williams syndrome as proof of separable innate modules, language spared, space impaired.

Karmiloff-Smith's work dismantled that reading by looking at development rather than the adult end state: infants and toddlers with Williams syndrome are not simply spared in language, they are delayed and take an atypical route, with early vocabulary abnormally dissociated from pointing and other precursors, and detailed studies showed their seemingly normal adult abilities, including face processing, are achieved by measurably different underlying processes, featural where typical processing is configural.

Her general argument, made in the 1998 paper and sharpened against what she called the residual normality assumption in work with Michael Thomas, is that a genetic difference present from the start perturbs the whole developing system in cascading ways, so no syndrome can cleanly delete one innate module and leave the rest untouched, and inferring the typical start state from adult impairment profiles is a logical error.

The position's own vulnerabilities should be named: it is more framework than predictive theory, its explanations are often after the fact, and the strong claim that no domain-specific knowledge is present at the start sits uneasily with the newborn findings of section 56.1.1.

But its core methodological lesson, that the developmental trajectory and not the end state is the unit of explanation, is now accepted far beyond its own school and has reshaped how disorders across this corpus are described.


56.3 The learning accounts

The third family of positions holds that powerful general-purpose learning, rather than built-in knowledge, carries most of the explanatory weight, and this section reviews its five main modern forms, which are complementary rather than rival.


56.3.1 Statistical learning as the general engine

Statistical learning means the automatic, unconscious extraction of patterns and probabilities from experience.

The founding demonstration is Saffran, Aslin, and Newport's 1996 study in Science: 8-month-old infants heard two minutes of a continuous made-up speech stream, syllables with no pauses, in which the only clue to word boundaries was transitional probability, the likelihood of one syllable following another, high inside the invented words and low between them.

After two minutes, infants distinguished the words from syllable sequences spanning word boundaries, showing they had computed the statistics from raw exposure, a result that stunned the field because it required no built-in linguistic knowledge at all.

The mechanism proved general in every direction tested: it works on musical tones, shown by Saffran and colleagues in 1999, on visual shape sequences, shown by Kirkham, Slemmer, and Johnson in 2002, and on spatial patterns, by Fiser and Aslin; it is present in newborns, indexed by brain responses in near-infrared spectroscopy studies; and versions of it appear in monkeys, rats, and songbirds, so it is ancient machinery, not a human speciality.

Individual differences in infant statistical learning correlate with later language, and computational analyses by Swingley and others confirmed that real infant-directed speech contains statistics rich enough to be worth mining.

The honest limits: extracting statistics is segmentation, not yet meaning or grammar, and debate continues, for example between Saffran's tradition and researchers such as Yang, over how far pure statistics reach before structured biases must be invoked; and as section 55.2.2 showed, in live infancy the engine appears to run best when social interaction opens the gate.

Statistical learning is therefore the learning accounts' foundation stone: a demonstrated, general, early mechanism that shrinks, without eliminating, the work that innate knowledge is needed to do.


56.3.2 The connectionist ancestor and the modern deep-learning analogies

Connectionism is the modelling tradition that builds simulated networks of simple neuron-like units whose connection strengths change with experience, so that knowledge lives in the weights rather than in stored rules.

Its founding developmental provocation was Rumelhart and McClelland's 1986 model of the English past tense, which learned regular and irregular verbs, and reproduced children's famous overregularisation errors such as goed, in one network with no rules at all, drawing a fierce rebuttal from Steven Pinker and colleagues in a debate that ran for two decades and ended without a clean winner.

The tradition's developmental manifesto was the 1996 book Rethinking Innateness by Elman, Bates, Johnson, Karmiloff-Smith, Parisi, and Plunkett, which argued that networks can develop stage-like shifts, critical-period-like effects, and emergent structure from small initial biases plus experience, giving neuroconstructivism its computational engine, and models such as Plunkett and Marchman's vocabulary networks and McClelland's simulations of Piagetian balance-scale stages made those claims concrete.

The modern descendants of these small networks are deep learning systems, artificial neural networks with many layers, whose successes have revived every side of the old argument.

On one hand, deep networks trained on visual input develop internal representations that partially match the primate visual hierarchy, and language models learn impressive syntax from raw text, which learning theorists read as proof that statistics can build far more structure than nativists believed.

On the other hand, such systems consume vastly more data than any child receives, a gap made vivid by the BabyLM effort from 2023 onward, which challenges modellers to learn language from roughly one hundred million words, about a childhood's worth, and by work training models on head-camera recordings from single infants, including Vong and colleagues' 2024 study in Science showing word-object learning from one child's first-person view of daily life.

The measured conclusion is that connectionism permanently changed the field's imagination, by proving that structured-looking development can emerge without built-in rules, while the data-hunger and the failures of today's systems keep the nativist question alive rather than settling it.


56.3.3 Dynamic systems and the embodied route

Dynamic systems theory imports from mathematics the study of systems whose many parts interact over time, and its developmental claim is that new behaviour emerges from the real-time interplay of brain, body, and environment, with no plan, program, or stage directing it.

Its founder in this field was Esther Thelen, working with Linda Smith at Indiana University, and her signature demonstration concerned the stepping reflex: newborns step when held upright, the stepping vanishes around 2 months, and textbooks attributed the disappearance to brain maturation.

Thelen showed in the early 1980s that the movements had not vanished at all: the same pattern persisted in kicking, returned when the fattening legs were buoyed in warm water, and disappeared in younger infants when weights were added, so the reflex's disappearance was chubby thighs outgrowing muscle strength, a body fact, not a brain switch.

The theory's flagship formal success is the dynamic field model of the A-not-B error by Thelen, Schoner, Scheier, and Smith in 2001, met in Chapter 54, which treats the infant's reach as the settling of a field of activation shaped by looking, memory, posture, and habit, and which correctly predicted oddities such as the error appearing or vanishing when the infant's posture is changed between trials.

The embodied route generalises the lesson: development proceeds through the body's changing capacities, and each motor achievement re-engineers the infant's learning environment, as Karen Adolph's work on the tens of thousands of steps and dozens of falls in a toddler's day makes concrete, and as studies of sitting and reaching show for object exploration.

Dynamic systems theory is the learning family's most radical member, dissolving even the distinction between knowing and doing, and its acknowledged weakness is the mirror of its strength: superb at explaining motor and near-motor development in real time, it has been harder to extend to abstract cognition, where the Bayesian account of the next section currently does more work.


56.3.4 Bayesian rational constructivism and the child as scientist

Bayesian inference, named for the 18th-century clergyman Thomas Bayes, is the mathematics of updating belief: combine what you believed before, the prior, with how well each hypothesis predicts the new evidence, and you obtain what you should believe now.

Rational constructivism proposes that children learn in essentially this way, holding graded hypotheses about how the world works and updating them rationally as evidence arrives, a view developed by Alison Gopnik at Berkeley, Joshua Tenenbaum at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Fei Xu, and Laura Schulz, and popularised in Gopnik's phrase the scientist in the crib, the title of her 1999 book with Meltzoff and Kuhl.

The signature experiments have a common shape: give children ambiguous evidence and ask whether their conclusions track the statistics the way a rational learner's would.

They do, strikingly early: Gopnik and Sobel's blicket detector studies from 2000 onward showed preschoolers inferring which objects have hidden causal powers from patterns of covariation; Xu and Garcia showed in 2008 that 8-month-olds use the composition of a sample of balls drawn from a box to form expectations about the box; Kushnir, Xu, and Wellman showed toddlers inferring a person's preferences from the improbability of their choices; and Schulz and Bonawitz showed that preschoolers play longer with a toy exactly when the evidence about its workings has been left confounded, exploration aimed where information is.

The framework also explains learning-to-learn: hierarchical Bayesian models, developed by Tenenbaum, Griffiths, and Kemp, show how a learner can acquire not just facts but overhypotheses, higher-level expectations such as the shape bias in word learning, from surprisingly little data, addressing the nativist challenge of fast generalisation without building the knowledge in.

The standard criticisms deserve their space: Bayesian accounts are often computational-level descriptions, saying what an ideal learner would conclude without specifying the mental or neural process, the modeller's freedom in choosing priors and hypothesis spaces gives the framework great flexibility and correspondingly weak falsifiability, and exact Bayesian updating is computationally intractable, so current work explores approximate sampling schemes that might be child-realistic.

Even its critics concede the central empirical yield: across dozens of paradigms, infants and children treat evidence quantitatively, not just qualitatively, and that fact is now a fixed constraint on every theory of learning.


56.3.5 The explore-exploit reading of childhood itself

The final account zooms out and asks not how children learn but why childhood exists at all, and answers with a concept from decision theory: the explore-exploit trade-off, the dilemma faced by any learner who must divide effort between exploiting what already works and exploring what might work better.

Alison Gopnik's proposal, developed through the 2010s and stated fully in a 2020 paper in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, is that human childhood, the longest and most helplessly dependent in the animal kingdom, is evolution's dedicated exploration phase: because adults provision and protect them, children are freed from the need to be efficient, and can afford wide, variable, low-stakes search of the world's possibilities before adult life demands exploitation.

On this reading the traits adults are tempted to call deficits, distractibility, variability, impulsivity, endless why-questions, and pretend play, are the design working: an exploring system should have broad attention rather than focus, should try odd actions rather than the known best one, and should simulate possibilities beyond the actual.

The proposal has empirical teeth: studies by Gopnik with Lucas and colleagues in 2014 and after found that preschoolers actually outperform adults at learning unusual causal rules, because adults exploit their strong priors while children search the hypothesis space more broadly, and work by Sumner, Blanco, Sloutsky, and others finds that children's choices are systematically more exploratory than adults' even when exploration costs them reward.

The account also connects to the brain's timetable: the long, slow prefrontal maturation documented throughout this book, so often described as immaturity, becomes on this view a scheduled feature, late-arriving cognitive control that keeps the exploration window open, with the settling into efficient, focused, exploiting cognition timed to arrive with independence, and Gopnik links this to the broader life-history evidence that across species, longer childhoods accompany bigger brains and more flexible intelligence.

The caveats are real: much of this is interpretive synthesis rather than tested prediction, the developmental switch from exploration to exploitation is gradual, individual, and not mapped to any dated neural event, and the evolutionary claims are, as always, hard to test directly.

But as a closing image for this part's long argument it earns its place: where nativism sees childhood as knowledge unfolding, and learning theory sees it as data accumulating, the explore-exploit reading sees childhood as a strategy, a protected season of search that the slow-building brain does not merely permit but implements, and on that view the growing that this whole book chronicles is not a delay before the mind arrives, it is the mind arriving.


================================================================================

PART FOURTEEN. THE LIFESPAN VIEW

================================================================================

CHAPTER 57. FROM EMERGING ADULTHOOD TO AGING AS DEVELOPMENT (CORE)

Most books about development stop at the end of the teenage years, as if the story were finished once the person can vote.

This chapter refuses that ending and follows development across the whole of adult life, from the unsettled twenties to the last decades.

It matters because the same rules that build a child's brain - growth, pruning, plasticity, and the trading of one strength for another - keep operating in a fifty year old and an eighty year old.

Reading the adult years as development, rather than as a long plateau followed by decay, changes how we think about justice for young offenders, about dementia, and about what any given age is actually good at.

57.1 The lifespan framework

Before we walk through the adult decades, we need the general idea that organizes them.

That idea, called lifespan developmental psychology, was worked out most fully by the German psychologist Paul Baltes and his colleagues from the 1980s onward.

57.1.1 Development as gain and loss at every age

The core claim of the lifespan framework is simple to state and surprisingly radical: at every age, development is a mixture of gains and losses, never pure growth and never pure decline.

A toddler who learns the sounds of her own language is simultaneously losing the ability to hear certain foreign sound contrasts, so even infancy involves loss.

An older adult who is slower at raw mental arithmetic may at the same time be gaining vocabulary, judgment, and skill at reading other people, so even old age involves gain.

Paul Baltes formalized this in his 1987 statement of lifespan theory, arguing that development is lifelong, multidirectional, plastic, and shaped by history and culture.

Baltes and his colleagues also proposed a model called selection, optimization, and compensation, usually shortened to SOC, which describes how people at every age cope with the shifting balance of gains and losses.

Selection means narrowing your goals to the ones that matter most, optimization means practicing and investing in those goals, and compensation means finding workarounds when an ability fades.

The famous illustration comes from the pianist Arthur Rubinstein, who explained in old age that he played fewer pieces, practiced them more, and slowed down before fast passages so that the fast parts still sounded fast by contrast.

Psychologists also distinguish two broad families of mental ability that age differently, a distinction introduced by Raymond Cattell and John Horn in the 1960s.

Fluid intelligence is the raw ability to solve brand new problems quickly, and it tends to peak early in adulthood and then slowly decline.

Crystallized intelligence is the accumulated store of knowledge, vocabulary, and skill, and it keeps rising into the sixties and beyond in most healthy people.

The gain-and-loss picture is therefore not a comforting slogan but a measurable pattern, and the rest of this chapter traces it decade by decade.

57.2 Emerging adulthood

Between the end of high school and the settling of career and family there is a stretch of life that is neither adolescence nor full adulthood.

This section introduces the name that psychology has given that stretch, and then follows the evidence about it into the courtroom.

57.2.1 The construct, and the twenty-five myth refused again

In the year 2000 the psychologist Jeffrey Arnett published a paper in the journal American Psychologist proposing a new named stage of life, emerging adulthood, covering roughly ages 18 to 25 and sometimes stretched to 29.

Arnett argued that in wealthy societies where marriage, parenthood, and stable careers now arrive later than they once did, the years after adolescence have become a distinct period of identity exploration, instability, self focus, feeling in between, and wide open possibility.

The construct is genuinely useful and genuinely contested: critics such as James Côté have argued that emerging adulthood describes an economic situation, not a universal developmental stage, since young people who must work full time at 18 do not get to have one.

Both readings can be true at once, because a life stage can be real in the societies that afford it without being a fixed biological program.

The brain science of these years is where a famous popular claim needs to be refused, and this corpus refuses it deliberately: the brain does not finish maturing at age 25.

The number 25 became folklore largely because many early brain imaging studies simply stopped recruiting participants in their mid twenties, so the growth curves appeared to flatten exactly where the data ran out, which is an artefact of study design rather than a fact about brains.

Long running work such as Jay Giedd's and Elizabeth Sowell's structural imaging studies did show that the prefrontal cortex - the front part of the brain most involved in planning and self control - is among the last regions to mature, but the maturing is gradual, varies enormously between individuals, and by some measures continues into the thirties.

The white matter of the brain, meaning the insulated cabling that connects brain regions, keeps increasing in volume until roughly the late thirties in large aggregated datasets, which sits awkwardly beside any claim of a finish line at 25.

Honest science therefore says that brain development is a slow fade into adulthood with no cliff edge, no birthday on which maturity arrives, and no measurement that could certify a finished brain.

What is well supported is a softer claim: on average, the psychological capacities that depend on prefrontal circuitry, such as resisting impulses under emotional pressure, are still improving through the early and mid twenties.

57.2.2 The juvenile-justice use of the maturity-gap evidence

The developmental science of the late teens and early twenties has had real consequences in courtrooms, and this sub-section explains how.

The key scientific idea is the maturity gap, articulated in the dual systems model of Laurence Steinberg and colleagues from around 2008.

The dual systems model holds that the brain systems that generate reward seeking and sensation seeking surge early, around puberty, while the brain systems that supply self control mature slowly across the teens and twenties, leaving a gap of years in which the accelerator is stronger than the brakes.

A large cross national study led by Grace Icenogle, published in 2019 with data from more than 5,000 people in eleven countries, gave the gap concrete numbers: basic cognitive capacity reached adult levels by around age 16, but psychosocial maturity, meaning self control in emotionally charged situations, did not reach adult levels until the early twenties.

That finding supports what the researchers called a maturity gap of roughly 16 to the early twenties, during which a young person can reason like an adult on a calm test yet still act like an adolescent in a hot moment.

The United States Supreme Court drew on this body of science in a sequence of landmark cases.

In Roper v. Simmons in 2005 the Court abolished the death penalty for crimes committed under age 18, citing adolescents' immaturity, susceptibility to peer pressure, and unformed character.

In Graham v. Florida in 2010 the Court barred life imprisonment without parole for juveniles convicted of crimes other than homicide.

In Miller v. Alabama in 2012 the Court barred mandatory life without parole for any crime committed under 18, and in Montgomery v. Louisiana in 2016 it made that rule retroactive.

The American Psychological Association filed friend of the court briefs in these cases summarizing the developmental evidence, and the majority opinions cited the science of adolescent brain development explicitly.

The honest caveats matter as much as the victories.

Group averages about brain maturation cannot diagnose the maturity of any individual defendant, and leading researchers including Steinberg have said so plainly.

The same logic that protects adolescents also raises an unsettled question about 18 to 20 year olds, who fall on the immature side of the maturity gap but on the adult side of the legal line, and some jurisdictions, including Germany's youth courts and recent reforms in a few American states, have begun treating that age band with intermediate rules.

The science supports a boundary that is fuzzy and gradual, while the law demands a boundary that is sharp, and the courts have essentially chosen 18 as a workable compromise rather than a biological truth.

57.3 The aging half of the arc

If childhood is the building of the brain, later life is often described as its slow unbuilding, but that description is too simple.

This section introduces the three ideas that organize modern research on brain aging - reserve, maintenance, and compensation - then the striking observation that aging sometimes retraces development in reverse, and finally the evidence that dementia risk is built across the whole life course.

57.3.1 Reserve, maintenance, and compensation, with their consensus definitions

For decades researchers noticed a puzzle: at autopsy, some people's brains carried heavy Alzheimer's disease pathology, meaning the plaques and tangles of misfolded protein that define the disease, yet those people had shown little or no dementia in life.

The classic demonstration came from the Nun Study led by David Snowdon in the 1990s, in which some elderly nuns with substantial pathology had remained cognitively sharp, and in which the linguistic richness of essays the nuns had written in their twenties predicted their dementia risk sixty years later.

The idea invoked to explain such puzzles is reserve, but for years different laboratories used the word in different ways, so in 2018 and again in 2020 an international group led by Yaakov Stern published consensus definitions in the journal Alzheimer's and Dementia, and this sub-section uses those.

Cognitive reserve is the adaptability of the brain's functional processes - the flexibility of how the brain does its work - that helps explain why some people cope better than others with aging or damage, and it is shaped by education, occupation, and mentally engaging life experience.

Brain reserve is a simpler, more hardware like idea: the sheer amount of neural resource a person has, such as the number of neurons or overall brain size, so that the same absolute loss removes a smaller fraction of a larger brain.

Brain maintenance, a term pushed forward by Lars Nyberg and colleagues in 2012, is different again: it names the relative absence of damage over time, meaning some people simply accumulate less pathology and less wear, often for genetic and lifestyle reasons.

Compensation names the observable strategy of an aging brain doing the same task with different circuitry, and functional imaging studies have repeatedly found that older adults often activate both hemispheres for tasks that young adults handle with one, a pattern Roberto Cabeza named HAROLD, short for hemispheric asymmetry reduction in older adults, in 2002.

Whether such extra activation is truly helpful compensation or just inefficient spillover is still argued, and the field's honest position is that it is probably compensation when it correlates with better performance and dedifferentiation when it does not.

Together the three ideas explain why chronological age is such a weak predictor of cognitive health: two eighty year olds can differ more from each other than either differs from an average fifty year old, because they differ in reserve, in maintenance, and in how well they compensate.

57.3.2 Last in, first out: the retrogenesis pattern

One of the most elegant hypotheses about brain aging is that it partially retraces development in reverse order, so that the abilities and brain regions that matured last are the first to decline.

This is called the last in, first out hypothesis, and in the context of dementia it has an older name, retrogenesis, coined by the psychiatrist Barry Reisberg in 1999.

Reisberg observed that the functional losses of Alzheimer's disease unwind the milestones of childhood in roughly reverse sequence: the capacity to manage finances goes before the capacity to dress, dressing before bathing, bathing before continence, and continence before walking, mirroring in reverse the order in which a child gains those abilities.

Reisberg built this observation into staging tools, the Global Deterioration Scale and the Functional Assessment Staging Test, which clinicians still use, and he argued that a person at a given stage of Alzheimer's disease needs care analogous to a child at the corresponding developmental age, an analogy that must be used for planning care and never for stripping dignity.

At the level of brain tissue, the hypothesis has real anatomical support.

The regions that myelinate last during development - myelin being the fatty insulation that speeds electrical signals along nerve fibers - are association areas in the prefrontal and temporal cortex, and studies by Naftali Raz, by George Bartzokis, and later by large imaging consortia found that these late maturing regions show the steepest age related decline, while early maturing sensory and motor regions hold up best.

Bartzokis proposed a specific mechanistic version: the oligodendrocytes, the cells that manufacture myelin, that wire up the cortex last produce thinner and more vulnerable myelin, so the newest cabling fails first.

A 2014 study by Gwenaëlle Douaud and colleagues, using data from hundreds of brains, identified a specific network of higher order regions that develops late, declines early, and is disproportionately vulnerable both to Alzheimer's disease and to schizophrenia, tying the developmental and degenerative stories together.

The pattern is a tendency, not a law: vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia each carve their own paths, and even in Alzheimer's disease the reverse ordering is approximate.

But as an organizing principle, last in, first out gives aging research a genuinely developmental shape, which is exactly why it belongs in this book.

57.3.3 The life-course origins of dementia risk

Dementia is an umbrella word for the loss of memory and thinking severe enough to disrupt daily life, with Alzheimer's disease as its most common cause, and one of the most important discoveries of recent decades is that the risk of dementia in the eighties is assembled across the entire life that came before.

The clearest summary of this evidence is the standing Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care, whose 2024 report, led by Gill Livingston, identified fourteen modifiable risk factors distributed across the life course and estimated that around 45 percent of dementia cases worldwide are in principle attributable to them.

In early life the listed factor is low education, because schooling in childhood builds the cognitive reserve described above.

In midlife the listed factors are hearing loss, high LDL cholesterol - LDL standing for low density lipoprotein, the cholesterol carrying particle associated with artery damage - hypertension, meaning chronically high blood pressure, obesity, excessive alcohol, traumatic brain injury, and physical inactivity.

In later life the listed factors are smoking, depression, social isolation, diabetes, air pollution, and untreated vision loss, the last two being the newer additions of the 2020 and 2024 reports.

The word attributable needs honest handling: the 45 percent figure describes the share of cases statistically associated with these factors in populations, not a promise that any individual can cut personal risk by that amount, and some of the associations may be partly reverse causation, as when early undiagnosed dementia causes social withdrawal rather than the other way around.

Even so, several strands of evidence support genuine causality, including the finding that age specific dementia rates have actually fallen in some high income countries as education and cardiovascular health improved, a trend documented in the Framingham Heart Study by Claudia Satizabal and colleagues in 2016.

The developmental point is profound: a policy that keeps a seven year old in school, a rule that gets a fifty year old's blood pressure treated, and a hearing aid fitted at sixty five are all, in a real sense, dementia prevention, which means the aging brain is a lifelong construction project and never only an old age story.

57.4 The whole-arc trajectories

Having looked at the two ends of adulthood, this final section steps back and looks at the entire arc at once.

Two bodies of work make that possible: massive behavioral studies charting when each mental ability peaks, and massive imaging studies charting the growth and shrinkage of the brain itself from before birth to age one hundred.

57.4.1 Different abilities peaking at different ages

If someone asks at what age the mind is at its best, the scientifically correct answer is a question back: best at what?

The landmark study here is by Joshua Hartshorne and Laura Germine, published in Psychological Science in 2015, which combined data from standardized tests with results from tens of thousands of online participants - the headline analysis drew on 48,537 people - across ages from the teens to the seventies.

Their finding was that different cognitive abilities peak at strikingly different ages, a pattern they called the asynchronous rise and fall of abilities.

Raw processing speed, the sheer quickness of simple mental operations, peaked around ages 18 to 20 and declined steadily afterward.

Working memory, the mental workspace that holds and manipulates information, peaked around the late twenties to mid thirties.

The ability to read emotions from other people's eyes, a measure of social cognition, peaked in the forties and stayed high through the fifties.

Vocabulary kept climbing latest of all, peaking in the mid sixties to around seventy in their web samples, later than the age of about 50 found in older standardization data, probably because today's older adults are more educated and read more than earlier generations.

Hartshorne and Germine put the conclusion memorably: at almost any given age, most people are getting better at some things, worse at others, and holding steady at still others, and there may be no age at which humans are at peak performance on everything, and perhaps not even an age at which they peak on most things.

This behavioral mosaic matches the gain and loss framework of Baltes with which the chapter opened, and it dissolves the folk picture of a single summit at 22 followed by a long slide.

It also carries a practical message for workplaces and societies: mixed age teams hold complementary peaks, with the fastest processors and the deepest vocabularies rarely being the same people.

57.4.2 The lifespan brain charts as the reference frame

Pediatricians have long plotted a child's height and weight on growth charts to see whether growth is on track, but until recently nothing comparable existed for the brain.

That changed in April 2022, when Richard Bethlehem, Jakob Seidlitz, and a consortium of more than two hundred researchers published Brain charts for the human lifespan in the journal Nature.

The team aggregated more than 120,000 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans - MRI being the technique that uses strong magnets to picture soft tissue - from over 100 studies, spanning ages from about 115 days after conception to 100 years, and used them to fit standardized growth curves for the brain's major tissue classes.

The resulting charts put real numbers on milestones that had previously been guesses.

Cortical gray matter, the sheet of cell bodies on the brain's surface where most computation happens, increases rapidly from mid gestation and reaches its peak volume just before age 6, earlier than older, smaller studies had suggested.

White matter, the insulated wiring beneath the surface, peaks much later, at close to age 29 in these charts, then declines with an accelerating slide after about age 50.

Subcortical gray matter, the deep structures involved in movement, motivation, and memory, peaks in adolescence at around fourteen and a half years.

Ventricular volume, the fluid filled spaces inside the brain, rises sharply in later life, which is why enlarged ventricles are a common radiological sign of age related shrinkage.

The purpose of the charts is not trivia but reference: just as a pediatric growth chart turns a single weight measurement into a percentile, brain charts let a researcher or eventually a clinician express an individual scan as a centile score for age, flagging brains that deviate markedly from the typical trajectory.

The authors themselves flagged the limitations honestly, above all that the underlying scans came disproportionately from wealthy, mostly European ancestry populations, so the charts do not yet represent humanity fairly and must be broadened before clinical use anywhere else.

The charts also settle this chapter's opening argument in pictures: the curves rise and fall on different schedules for different tissues, with no common milestone at 18, none at 25, and no age at which the brain is simply finished.

For this outline, the lifespan brain charts serve as the reference frame onto which every earlier chapter's events - the prenatal surge, the childhood gray matter peak, the adolescent reorganization, the long adult plateau, and the late decline - can be placed as one continuous, lawful arc.

PART FIFTEEN. TRANSLATION: FROM THE LABORATORY TO THE CHILD

================================================================================

CHAPTER 58. SCREENING AND EARLY INTERVENTION (CONTEXT)

Everything in this book so far has been about understanding how children develop, and this chapter turns to the question of what that understanding is for.

It covers the tests that societies run on newborns and toddlers to catch problems early, and the programs that try to change a disadvantaged child's trajectory.

It matters because this is where developmental neuroscience touches actual children, actual budgets, and actual political promises, and because the honest record contains both spectacular successes and sobering disappointments.

The rule of this chapter is to report the real effect sizes, meaning the actual measured size of each program's benefit, rather than the sizes implied by enthusiasm.

58.1 The screening successes and debates

Screening means testing everyone in a population, not because each individual seems ill, but because a treatable condition is worth catching before symptoms show.

This section covers the newborn screening programs that are among medicine's quiet triumphs, and then the newer, more contested effort to screen toddlers for autism with digital tools.

58.1.1 The newborn panels and early hearing detection

The story of newborn screening begins with a single disease and a piece of filter paper.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a rare inherited condition in which the body cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in ordinary food, and in which the buildup poisons the developing brain, causing severe intellectual disability.

The tragedy of untreated PKU is that the damage is entirely preventable: a child kept on a low phenylalanine diet from the first weeks of life develops a essentially healthy brain.

In the early 1960s the microbiologist Robert Guthrie developed a cheap test that could detect high phenylalanine in a drop of blood taken from a newborn's heel and dried on filter paper, and the heel prick card is still called the Guthrie card in his honor.

Massachusetts began universal screening in 1963, other jurisdictions followed, and PKU became the proof that a whole population screen at birth could convert an untreatable brain disease into a manageable diet.

Modern newborn panels have grown far beyond PKU, using a laboratory technique called tandem mass spectrometry, which weighs molecules with great precision, to check a single dried blood spot for dozens of metabolic and hormonal disorders, including congenital hypothyroidism, a thyroid hormone deficiency that once caused widespread preventable disability and is now caught and treated within days.

In the United States a Recommended Uniform Screening Panel guides the states, and most now screen for more than thirty core conditions.

Hearing is the other great newborn screening success, and it is directly a developmental neuroscience story.

Roughly 1 to 2 babies per 1,000 are born with significant permanent hearing loss, and because language circuits are built by early auditory experience, an undetected deaf infant loses irreplaceable input during the very months when the auditory brain is most plastic.

Before universal screening, congenital deafness was commonly identified around age 2 to 3, after the child failed to speak, which is developmentally late.

Two technologies made newborn testing possible: otoacoustic emissions, in which a tiny microphone detects the faint sounds a healthy inner ear itself produces, and the automated auditory brainstem response, in which electrodes on the scalp confirm that sound is reaching the brainstem.

Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) programs adopted the 1-3-6 benchmark, endorsed by the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing: screen by 1 month, confirm the diagnosis by 3 months, and begin intervention - hearing aids, cochlear implants where chosen, or sign language exposure - by 6 months.

Research by Christine Yoshinaga-Itano and colleagues, beginning with a landmark 1998 study, showed that children whose hearing loss was identified and treated before 6 months developed substantially better language than those identified later, which supplied the evidence behind the benchmark.

The debates in newborn screening today are mostly about expansion, and above all about whether to sequence every newborn's genome.

Projects such as the Generation Study in England, which set out in the 2020s to sequence 100,000 newborns for a set of treatable childhood onset conditions, and the BabySeq research project in the United States, test the idea, while critics raise unresolved questions about uncertain results, findings the family cannot act on, and a child's right not to know things about her own adult future, a theme this outline returns to in chapter 60.

58.1.2 Autism screening and the digital phenotyping devices

Autism, described with care earlier in this outline, is a developmental condition affecting social communication and behavioral flexibility, present in roughly 1 in 31 eight year olds in the most recent United States surveillance by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Because behavioral signs are often detectable in the second year while the average age of formal diagnosis remains around 4 to 5 years, and because early support helps, there is a strong argument for screening toddlers.

The standard tool is a parent questionnaire, the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised, with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F), developed by Diana Robins and colleagues, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends administering it universally at the 18 month and 24 month checkups.

Its real world performance is the debate: in a large 2019 study of about 26,000 children screened in pediatric practices, Whitney Guthrie and colleagues found that the checklist missed a substantial share of children later diagnosed with autism and that most children who screened positive did not turn out to have autism, with accuracy lowest for girls and for children from minority and lower income families.

In 2016 and again in 2025 reviews, the United States Preventive Services Task Force declined to endorse or reject universal screening, concluding the evidence was insufficient, while the American Academy of Pediatrics continued to recommend it, and both positions are defensible readings of the same imperfect data.

Into this gap have come the digital phenotyping devices, which try to measure autism related behavior directly with cameras and eye tracking instead of asking parents to report it.

Digital phenotyping means using sensors and computation to quantify behavior - where a toddler looks, how she smiles, how she turns her head - precisely and objectively.

The scientific root is Ami Klin and Warren Jones's eye tracking research, which showed that toddlers later diagnosed with autism look less at people's eyes and faces and that this divergence emerges within the first six months of life.

That work became EarliPoint, an eye tracking device from the company EarliTec Diagnostics, which received United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance in 2022 to aid diagnosis of autism in children as young as 16 months, with supporting trials published by Jones and Klin in 2023 in the Journal of the American Medical Association family of journals.

A second cleared product, Canvas Dx from the company Cognoa, authorized by the FDA in 2021, combines parent questionnaires, a home video reviewed by specialists, and a clinician input through a machine learning algorithm to help primary care doctors diagnose or rule out autism between 18 months and 6 years.

A third line is the SenseToKnow tablet application from Geraldine Dawson, Guillermo Sapiro, and colleagues at Duke University, which shows a toddler short movies while the tablet's own camera measures gaze, facial expression, head movement, blink rate, and response to the child's name.

In a 2023 study in Nature Medicine with 475 toddlers aged 17 to 36 months, the application detected autism with about 88 percent sensitivity and about 92 percent specificity, and combining it with the parent checklist raised the positive predictive value - the chance that a positive screen is correct - to about 63 percent, well above the checklist alone.

The honest summary is that these devices are promising and cleared, but not yet proven to improve children's lives at population scale, because a screening tool earns its keep only if earlier detection leads to earlier support and better outcomes in ordinary clinics, and those downstream trials are still being run.

There is also a values question, raised by autistic self advocates, about what screening is for, and chapter 60 takes it up directly.

58.2 The intervention evidence with its real effect sizes

Screening only matters if something can be done, and this section examines the flagship claim of applied developmental science: that intensive early programs for disadvantaged children pay lifelong dividends.

The evidence is real, the effect sizes are genuine but smaller than the rhetoric, and one famous recent trial went the wrong way entirely, so this section walks through the record with the honesty the topic deserves.

58.2.1 The preschool trials and their economics

Three small, old, randomized experiments anchor the whole field, and their names recur in every policy debate.

The Perry Preschool Project, run in Ypsilanti, Michigan from 1962 to 1967, randomly assigned 123 low income African American children to a high quality half day preschool with weekly home visits, or to no program.

The children's IQ - intelligence quotient, a standardized test score of reasoning ability - rose sharply at first, but the IQ gain faded within a few years, which at the time looked like failure.

The astonishment came decades later: by age 40, the preschool group had higher earnings, higher rates of high school completion, and markedly fewer arrests than the control group.

The economist James Heckman, who won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics in 2000, reanalyzed the trial and estimated its society wide annual rate of return at roughly 7 to 10 percent per year, counting reduced crime, higher earnings, and lower welfare costs, and later work by Heckman and colleagues in 2019 found benefits reaching into the participants' children.

The Abecedarian Project, run in North Carolina from 1972, was more intensive still: full day, year round, educational child care from infancy to age 5 for 111 randomly assigned children, and its adult follow ups found lasting IQ effects, more college attendance, and in a 2014 study led by Frances Campbell and Heckman, significantly better cardiovascular and metabolic health in the participants' thirties.

The Chicago Child-Parent Centers, a large public program studied by Arthur Reynolds, was not randomized but showed similar long run patterns at much larger scale, with an estimated return near 7 dollars per dollar spent.
