Gopnik's computational metaphor is simulated annealing, a technique from optimisation in which a search starts hot, jumping widely between possibilities, and cools slowly into a settled solution; childhood is the hot phase, the long human childhood is a long, slow cooling, and the protected dependence of the child is what makes the hot phase affordable, since an agent that explored while also having to feed itself would be eaten by its first mistake.

The theory also gives adolescence a place, as a second, socially targeted exploration phase, and it predicts the timetable this book has documented, in which plasticity is front-loaded and consolidation, myelination, and pruning progressively cool the system into adult efficiency.

Its limits should be stated in the same breath: it is a functional interpretation, not a tested mechanism, its evolutionary claims are hard to falsify, and long childhoods also serve rival, compatible explanations, including brain-energy budgeting, skill learning for a complex foraging niche, and the social brain.

But as a single sentence for what childhood is for, the field currently has nothing better: childhood is when a mind can afford to search, because someone else is paying.

68.3.2 What the species differences suggest a long childhood buys, and what a build like konnectome should take from that

Set the species side by side and the purchase becomes visible.

The precocial animal buys immediate competence and pays with rigidity: what it can do at birth is close to all it will ever do.

The mouse buys speed, the macaque buys a richer cortex and a year of infancy, the songbird buys one open window for one learned skill, and the human buys the longest, most expensive immaturity in the living world.

What the human purchase gets, the preceding sixty-seven chapters have itemised.

It buys a brain built by experience rather than merely unpacked by genes, because construction continues for decades in the presence of the world it must model.

It buys the stacked sensitive periods of Part Four, each system holding itself open until its inputs arrive, vision before phonemes, phonemes before words, words before the social mind.

It buys the installable inventions of Chapter 67, literacy and numeracy colonising cortex that evolution never earmarked for them, which is to say it buys culture itself, the capacity of each generation to inherit the discoveries of the last without waiting for genes.

It buys the deep exploration of the previous sub-section, a decades-long hot search phase that no shorter-lived architecture can afford.

And it buys all this at the price Chapter 66 stated, near half the child's energy for years, and at the price of vulnerability, since every open window admits harm as readily as instruction, which is why the chapters on deprivation, adversity, and disorder sit in this book beside the chapters on learning.

For a build like konnectome, which is an attempt to assemble a mind deliberately, layer by layer, the comparative view reads as a set of design lessons rather than a metaphor.

The first lesson is that competence should be grown, not installed: the human result argues that a system intended for open-ended intelligence should begin overcomplete, noisy, and wrong, and earn its final wiring from data, because circuits carved by experience fit the world in ways no specification written in advance can.

The second is that the schedule is the teacher: development succeeds because plasticity is staged, with early layers stabilising before later ones, sensory foundations freezing before abstractions are built on them, and the whole system cooling slowly rather than converging fast, which for an artificial build argues for curricula, for layerwise consolidation, and against training everything everywhere at once.

The third is that exploration must be subsidised: the child searches boldly because caregivers absorb the cost of error, and a built system will only explore as widely as its designers make failure safe, so the equivalent of the protected childhood is an explicit budget of tolerated error, sandboxed play, and deferred demands for usefulness.

The fourth is that openness is bought with vulnerability: every mechanism that let experience improve the child, from sensitive periods to slow prefrontal closure, is also a mechanism by which deprivation and distortion entered, and a build that copies childhood's plasticity inherits childhood's need for a good environment, which makes the curation of what the system meets during its formative phase not an implementation detail but the central safety problem.

The last lesson is the one this book has taught in every chapter without saying so: the human mind is not the output of a program but the residue of a process, eighteen years and more of lawful, staged, energy-hungry, socially subsidised construction, and anyone who would build a mind must budget not just for the architecture but for the childhood.

That is what a long childhood buys: a mind fitted to a world too complicated to specify in advance.

It is the most expensive purchase our species makes, it is paid for by others before the buyer can consent, and it is, on the evidence assembled across these sixty-eight chapters, the best bargain in the natural history of intelligence.
